Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: When will Poundland close? Five questions about its future
events.summary: Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas. The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the the company. This is the question that is most difficult to answer. In short, we don't know yet. Poundland stores will continue trading for now and remain open as usual, at least in the short term. Poundland collapsing has acted as a reset button on the process of selling the company. Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, the more likely outcome. Before the collapse, Poundstretcher owner Fortress was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand. But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. A source close to one of the bidders for the whole of Poundland when it was a going concern, Martin Property Group, has already said it is "unlikely" to make a fresh bid now due to "irreparable harm" having been done to the brand by the administration process. Poundland's managing director Barry Williams believed Poundland was turning a corner and seeing a "strong recovery". Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, in the year to September it recorded a profit of £18.1m, swinging back from a £68m loss in the previous 12 months. Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter sales were up 3.3% . The picture Poundland's management paint is of a retailer undergoing a turnaround until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock. The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, said the owners forced Poundland into administration. And Steve Smith, who co-founded Poundland in 1990, said "this shouldn't be happening really", adding that staff and suppliers have "worked so hard" to turn the business around. Labour MP Antonia Bance said she had been "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going. However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was not turning a profit, and had missed budget forecasts. A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even" on paper. "Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround." Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added. Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said. And Julie Palmer, managing partner at the insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" and pointed the finger at challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff. "There's plenty of other retailers that are feeling this cost squeeze at the moment, and this is the big name. But I think there will be another huge number of other retail failures as well," she told the BBC. Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable. The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators. This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers. But here's the catch. The administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations. But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business proves viable. If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on. Will shoppers still be able to buy from Poundland? From 26 November refunds for goods which people just change their minds about will not be given (but if the item is faulty you will still get a refund). The immediate reason Poundland collapsed was that Gordon Brothers locked up funds for the day-to-day running of the business, including to pay suppliers. This meant that stock was running dry at Poundland. But those funds have now been unlocked, meaning suppliers can be paid, and supply chains can be re-established, at least in the short term. If an item is on the shelves, then shoppers can buy it. How will Poundland's collapse change the High Street?

The Australian uranium producer said on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project. Peninsula Energy said it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected. "The company's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it said in an update to the Australian Securities Exchange. The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing. Peninsula has not given a restart date and says it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said. The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site. The November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's update clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time. Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance. Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈. Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors. The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb. Peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. events.title: Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
events.summary: More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show. About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals. That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July. In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments. For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage. Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years. On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts. Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals. However, the Bank's report points out that the average £100 increase in monthly repayments was half the rise experienced by those refinancing during 2023 and 2024. Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living. She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother-of-two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month. How much could my mortgage payments change? At this rate, your payments could change by… The information you provided on your monthly payments would not be sufficient to pay off your mortgage within the number of years given. This calculator does not constitute financial advice. It is based on a standard mortgage repayment formula dependent on the mortgage size and length and a fixed interest rate. It should be used as a guide only and does not represent the suitability, eligibility or availability of mortgage offers for users. For exact figures, users will need to approach an official mortgage lender. Interest rates fluctuate based on the Bank of England's base rate and market conditions She is far from alone, with one million homeowners facing a similar increase often because they are coming off deals that were agreed before interest rates began rising in 2022. The Bank's report said that households facing higher payments "may need to reduce discretionary spending or draw down savings as higher energy and other essential costs feed through". Most had savings buffers but lower-income households, including renters, had less wriggle room owing to spending a greater proportion of their income on essentials. Early in November, the Bank raised the benchmark interest rate , which influences borrowing costs for individuals and businesses, for the first time in more than three years, from 3.75% to 4%. The numbers could change were mortgage rates to fall, primarily if international economic volatility eased. Even so, the Bank said around 350,000 were already projected to see monthly mortgage repayments fall when they fixed their next deal within three years. The report also suggested there were no signs of an increase in borrowers defaulting on their loans, while UK households remained resilient. "We have not seen the scale of mortgage arrears that we saw if you go back to earlier periods, the early 90s, the early 80s, actually even the financial crisis. And we are not seeing the scale of house repossessions, and that has to be a good thing," said the Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey. However, separately, the Bank warned that cyber attacks had become a more prominent threat to the UK's financial stability. Financial firms needed to "keep pace with the growing scale and sophistication of cyber threats", the report said. Are your mortgage payments rising? Share your experience. events.title: Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute wants to bring $60tn purse to G20 investment summit
events.summary: The chairman of the Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute is seeking to bring “the largest investment pool” possible to Miami next month, as it targets $5 trillion in long-term institutional investment in the US. The SWFI will convene the inaugural Investment 20 (I20) Summit alongside the G20 Leaders Summit. The independent forum aims to create an environment to enable cross-border investment from sovereign wealth funds and participating nations after the US-hosted leadership summit concludes on December 15. “Our objective is to bring in the largest investor pool,” Lakshmi Ramanujam, chairman of the Dallas-based SWFI, said. The world's sovereign wealth funds surpassed $15 trillion in assets this year. Mr Ramanujam said pension endowments and foundations were holding an additional $45 trillion, bringing $60 trillion of liquidity into the market. “All these global sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, endowment funds, in the last 30 years have invested more than $50 trillion in the US,” he explained. The US chairmanship of the G20 comes as President Donald Trump touts foreign investment in the country. Mr Trump has claimed he has secured nearly $20 trillion in foreign investment during his second term in office. Gulf states have committed roughly $4 trillion, including $1.4 trillion from the UAE , $1.2 trillion from Qatar, $1 trillion from Saudi Arabia and $17 billion from Bahrain. Saudi Arabia is the only Gulf state that is a member of the G20, with the UAE and Qatar named invitees. “The whole conference has been planned with the vision of mobilising $5 trillion for the G20 countries and its allied countries for the global good around the policies that have been framed in the G20 leadership summit,” Mr Ramanujam said. Of the $15 trillion of global sovereign wealth fund assets, roughly $4 trillion to $6 trillion are from Gulf sovereign wealth funds. Four of the 10 largest sovereign funds in the world by total assets are based in the Gulf. The Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Kuwait Investment Authority each hold more than $1 trillion in assets, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund had $900 billion, with the Qatar Investment Authority at $600 billion. These sovereign wealth funds are seen as key drivers for Gulf countries' diversification efforts, with investment in artificial intelligence coming more into focus. Led by Abu Dhabi AI firm G42 alongside OpenAI, Nvidia, Oracle and Cisco, the UAE is aiming to build a 5-gigawatt AI data centre in the emirate. The PIF, Adia, Mubadala and QIA are also investing heavily in AI. Mr Ramanujam cited Anthropic as an example underscoring not only UAE investment in AI, but also how the US remained the largest market for sovereign wealth funds. “At the end of the day, any sovereign wealth funds want to hold liquidity. That's the bottom line,” he said. Anthropic ’s public debut brought a windfall to Gulf funds after it closed at $117.50 per share on its first day of trading last week. Mubadala-backed MGX touted $20 billion in unrealised gains, while the Abu Dhabi Investment Council and Qatar Investment Authority were also early investors. Damac founder Hussain Sajwani said his $50 million stake was now worth $3 billion. Shares in Anthropic were trading at roughly $82 on Wednesday, slightly below its offering price. “There's no market in the world that they can pull a trillion dollars in the same day,” Mr Ramanujam said. The Nasdaq is one of world's two leading stock exchanges based in the US, along with the New York Stock Exchange. The US is the world's largest equity market with a total market capitalisation of roughly $78 trillion, according to Siblis data to September 30, in addition to the $32 trillion US Treasury market. “That's why everybody wants the US as a geographical destination,” Mr Ramanujam said.

events.title: What to watch for as volatility in markets spikes
events.summary: Volatility is spiking. Stocks are swinging more wildly in both directions on headlines that would have elicited shrugs a year ago. The VIX index, which measures twitchiness in S&P 500 stocks, hit a post-“Liberation Day” high this week, and its tech-stocks cousin is even higher. The amount of money Goldman Sachs could potentially lose on a single day in the markets, known as value-at-risk, rose 84% from last December to Sept. 30 — and that was before nerves fried in tech markets over Nvidia, the AI trade, and export controls. Here are a few things I’m keeping an eye on: Taps on shoulders across Wall Street. Volatility also goes into models that manage risk on trading floors. Even winners will find their leash tightened, and some heavy hitters will leave. Hedge funds are already reducing their market exposure , which can feed volatility in a loop. Convertible bonds. This should be boom time for convertible bonds — debt-like instruments that pay little, sometimes zero, interest but are swappable for shares of stock in the future. Volatility is a key input into their pricing because stocks that swing around are more likely to end up in-the-money. Issuance is already at a record this year, with $163 billion through September, according to SIFMA, though higher credit spreads have dampened the mood lately. One rule of corporate finance is to sell whatever investors are buying: If stock prices are high, issue stock and if debt is cheap, issue bonds. The market is buying volatility right now, so companies should be selling it. IPO freeze. Bankers have a rough rule that deals get shelved once the VIX sits in the high 20s, because nobody can price a new stock when old ones are swinging around. Anthropic’s post-IPO fizzle has already sent listing-curious companies back to their bunkers, and they’re unlikely to venture out anytime soon. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Nvidia's credit rating, the AI trade's collateral, is at risk
events.summary: Not only is Nvidia’s share price tumbling as the halo of CEO Jensen Huang’s return fades, but now its credit rating — on which hinge tens of billions of dollars in financing spread throughout the AI ecosystem — is in danger. Moody’s changed the company’s outlook from positive to stable, and S&P Global cited worries over the departure and subsequent return of its CEO. We’re not there yet, but an official downgrade would be a dramatic blow, not just to Nvidia, but to big customers, startups, and construction projects that rely on its role as the central banker of the AI trade . It would also be expensive: Nvidia often essentially rents out its AA rating to less creditworthy companies by backstopping their debt, leases, and hardware purchases. Such “credit enhancement” techniques have also been used by Alphabet and Broadcom to help their customers afford chips , but it means that AI risk is concentrated at a handful of tech giants just as interest rates are rising. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Number of Neets in UK falls below a million as Burnham pushes to tackle crisis
events.summary: Latest figure of young people not in education, employment or training remains close to highest level in a decade The number of young people across the UK not in education, employment or training (Neet) has decreased but remains close to a million as Andy Burnham’s government pushes to tackle Britain’s youth jobs crisis. As ministers prepare to make sweeping changes in response to Alan Milburn’s landmark report into young people and work, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the number of Neets fell by 22,000 in the three months to September, to 959,000. On an annual basis, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds not earning or learning was 17,000 higher than a year ago. Although down from a peak of just over a million in March, the latest figure remains close to the highest level in a decade. The prime minister last week promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people after Milburn said Britain risked “losing a generation of young people” without a radical change in course. Milburn also called for a radical shake-up of employment support to guarantee young people would get help, alongside changes to education policy and healthcare. A parallel review into disability benefits by Labour minister Stephen Timms this week called for significant changes to a welfare system that was “no longer fit for purpose”. Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said young people deserved better. “That’s why we’re fundamentally reforming how we support young people to grow up in this country,” he said. “As part of our response to the Milburn review, we’re building a new settlement that invests in young people’s success instead of paying for failure.” It is understood the government is preparing a full response to Milburn’s recommendations spelling out the changes that will be made. Ministers will then publish a white paper next year on welfare reform. Overhauling welfare will, however, stand as one of the biggest challenges for Burnham’s government as he pushes to curb a rising welfare bill without triggering a repeat of the backbench rebellion faced by Keir Starmer. Business leaders last week seized on elements of Milburn’s report calling for tax cuts and for the government to take a more cautious approach on its plan to boost workers’ rights, which he said could hit youth hiring. events.title: Ministers have ‘failed to make the case’ for Heathrow third runway, MPs says
events.summary: Transport committee says policy papers show expanding airport would fall short of pledges on economy and climate Ministers have “failed to make the case” for a third runway at Heathrow , according to a damning report by MPs. The Commons transport committee said on Thursday that the detailed policy papers laid out by the government showed expansion of the London airport would fall short of pledges on the economy and climate. The chair of the committee, Ruth Cadbury, said plans for the third runway “should be grounded” and the government needed to “go back to the drawing board”. Heathrow’s owner is seeking to build a third runway and expand its terminals at a cost of about £33bn. It says its plan would almost double passengers numbers and add up to 276,000 flights a year. The committee was tasked with examining the government’s Heathrow expansion national policy statement (HENPS) – but Cadbury said there was a “complete disjoint” between the plans and a lack of wider aviation strategy. The report found the case was not made across the four tests ministers had set for expansion: that it generated growth across the country, without harmful impacts on climate, noise and air quality. The report said that while the government was designating the runway as a critical national project, the economic growth projections in modelling commissioned by the Department for Transport were a fraction of previous estimates – a 0.05% boost to GDP rather than 0.5% – and did not justify the designation. It said the expansion was “not currently compatible with the UK’s legally binding climate targets”, adding: “It seems impossible for the additional carbon dioxide emissions it will generate to be offset elsewhere in the economy.” The case for “potential compatibility rests too heavily on delivery of technologies” such as greener fuel and carbon capture, which was “nowhere near the necessary trajectories”, MPs said. The committee said it did not agree that reversing hard-won improvements in local air quality was an acceptable consequence and the HENPS did not take into account World Health Organization guidelines or emerging pollutants. It added that the government still needed to set out how commitments relating to noise mitigation were “secured and delivered”. “It is highly concerning that there are no clear, committed, funded plans in place to improve surface public transport to an expanded Heathrow,” the report said. “Expansion should not go ahead at any price, or at any cost to society or the environment.” Cadbury said: “Our report should be a wake-up call for ministers. We found that the government should have set out its overall strategy for aviation before publishing the draft HENPS. It did not do so and now it has failed to make the case for Heathrow expansion. “Plans for a third runway should be grounded for now and the government should go back to the drawing board before proceeding any further.” The government under Keir Starmer had strongly backed a third runway, particularly the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves. However, Andy Burnham has historically opposed the third runway and while he had stated it was “a matter for Londoners”, continued support for the scheme appears in doubt. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Responding to the committee’s report, Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, said the third runway still had strong support. “The overwhelming weight of evidence and support remains strongly behind Heathrow expansion. Trade unions, business groups, airlines, regional airports, senior cabinet ministers and the majority of MPs back expansion because they recognise it is vital to creating quality jobs and supporting long-term economic growth across the UK,” Woldbye said. He added: “The case for expanding Heathrow has been examined more thoroughly than almost any infrastructure project in modern Britain … The focus now should be on delivering this privately financed project which will unlock opportunity across the country while meeting clear tests on affordability, financeability and sustainability.” Heathrow on Wednesday released polling that suggested three-quarters of Labour MPs backed the expansion plan. It hopes to secure planning permission for a third runway by 2029, building it over the course of the following decade. Despite Burnham’s ambivalence, the chancellor, John Healey, and the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, have said it remains government policy , with the Conservatives and Reform UK recently speaking out strongly in favour of the third runway. However, campaigners said the transport committee report showed that an expansion of Heathrow should not go ahead. Friends of the Earth said continued government support for the plan “would be flying in the face of the evidence”.

events.title: Banks look to dump AI debt
events.summary: Banks are increasingly shopping around their AI portfolios as they look to offload some of their exposure to AI-related debt. Banks including Citi and JPMorgan are marketing portfolios of loans, people familiar with the deals tell me, to manage risk or, in some cases, ready themselves to take on even more. In some instances, banks are pitching structures that would keep the loans on their balance sheets while shifting the risk of losses to investors. That financial engineering tool, known as synthetic risk transfer, has been a popular way for banks to move risk off their books while maintaining close relationships with the corporate borrowers. Some of this naturally occurs in December when banks are eager to close out the year with a clean bill of health, but it’s notable that banks lending into the buildout are joining hyperscalers in trying to push AI obligations off their books. There’s been so much AI-related debt issuance, it’s crowded out Treasurys and some investors are starting to feel tapped out. Others say they are offloading risk so they can lend more, not to pull back. But either way, the risk isn’t so much disappearing as moving somewhere harder to see.

events.title: Simon Jack: Is Poundland's US owner to blame for its collapse?
events.summary: Watch: Why has Poundland collapsed into administration? The blame game for the demise of Poundland is in full swing. The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for £1 and have taken nearly £20m out of the business already. Gordon Brothers stand to get paid back a further £22.5m, as their share of an existing £30m loan is set to be one of the first debts that the administrators will have to pay out of the proceeds of any sale of the business in whole or in part. The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period. They point to improving sales over October as proof the business had a future. MPs also laid into the US firm with members of the Business Committee accusing it of "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping". Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk Published 5 hours ago What's gone wrong at Poundland? Published 3 hours ago No-one appears to dispute the fact that Gordon Brothers' insistence that they get paid most of their £22.5m debt was a major stumbling block to a sale. Potential buyers balked at paying out millions on a loan that Gordon Brothers inherited for nothing. Martin Property Group offered £5m up front with the balance to be deferred, while Xyra Holdings offered £12.5m up front but, according to sources close to the deal, were thought unable to actually pay. Unsurprisingly perhaps, Gordon Brothers dispute a lot of how they have been characterised. First, they insist that they lent the business £85m to try to keep it alive for the 17 months since they bought it. Without them, this collapse would have happened in June last year. The £20m taken out of the business since then has mostly been interest on that loan. Despite brief periods of sales growth compared with a year earlier, Poundland was not generating enough cash to sustain itself. Sales were forecast to be £115m lower than predicted when Gordon Brothers bought the business - more than offsetting a £100m cost-cutting programme. Like other retailers Poundland was hit by rising labour costs, employment taxes and business rates. In the end, argue Gordon Brothers, none of the potential buyers could meet their terms and prove they had the money and expertise to make a go of it. Such is the discrepancy between the two versions that the chair of the Business Committee wants Gordon Brothers and the management back in front of them to get to the truth. It is still possible that a bidder may emerge in the coming hours and days to save the business as a whole but most industry observers think that looks unlikely. Julie Palmer of insolvency specialists Begbies Traynor told the BBC: "This sort of direction of travel seemed somehow inevitable. Obviously, if one of those interested parties steps up and buys the whole business and assets, that's the best, quickest and cleanest outcome. I think realistically, though, there is a chance now that there will be a breakup." Like previous busts such as Woolworths, BHS and Wilko, many of these stores will find new owners and they will need local, experienced staff. But none of that will be much comfort to those workers facing grave uncertainty a month before Christmas, when they should be at their busiest and most needed. Gordon Brothers specialise in situations of commercial distress. When they take on a distressed company, they try to make sure that the worst possible outcome is still one that makes money for them. In this situation, the worst outcome would mean they get paid back £22.5m, earn interest on the loan they provided the company (secured against the company assets) and a few other miscellaneous fees. Little wonder then that many people say they had little incentive to strain every sinew to secure a buyer. They argue they kept a business that would have collapsed last June going for another 17 months, which extended employment for thousands of workers. But if, as some retail veterans have told the BBC, Gordon Brothers never really intended to turn this business around, why would the previous owners PepCo give them a no-lose gamble? Why didn't they do what Gordon Brothers are doing - profiting with no risk? The answer is simple: Pepco have other businesses, which could have got tangled up in the administration of Poundland. events.title: The US Navy wants drones to work alongside warships. Sometimes they're better off on their own, defense analysts say.
events.summary: A new report analyzes the US Navy's plans for the future fleet and offers several key takeaways. US Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Andrew Langholf Pairing drones with warships isn't always the best approach, defense analysts say. Drones operating separately from crewed ships could be more flexible and effective. The approach could shape how the US uses drones to counter a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. The US Navy wants naval drones to help its crewed warships do more, but a new report argues that making them work together might not always be the best approach. Sometimes, drones might prove more useful on their own, defense analysts wrote. The US military has experimented with crewed-uncrewed teaming for years, focusing on how uncrewed systems can complement crewed naval elements by extending reach, sensing, and firepower. But forced manned-unmanned teaming can limit their biggest advantages, specifically their flexibility and the ability to take risks that humans can't. In a new report from the Hudson Institute think tank, authors Bryan Clark, David Byrd, and Dan Patt analyze the Navy's plan to grow the fleet, proposing a more affordable design and structure that adapts to new threats and embraces emerging technologies. Discussing a new theory of victory for the Navy, the authors argue that pairing crewed and uncrewed platforms "tend to suboptimize both the manned and unmanned components of the team and fail to exploit the advantages of each." For example, uncrewed ships could carry additional munitions for crewed vessels, but limitations in speed, range, and protection could demand more frequent refueling and the use of defensive escorts, potentially defeating the purpose of using a naval drone in the first place. Furthermore, drones that aren't equally low-observable could compromise nearby stealthier platforms, while fixing that could get expensive, sacrificing their affordability. Meanwhile, deploying drones alongside crewed warships could undermine the ability to quickly modify and adapt the uncrewed systems. "Manned platforms cannot change sensors, EW [electronic warfare] systems, C2 [command and control] software, or weapons quickly because engineers need to assess the impact on safety and other systems," the report says. Autonomous systems can be modified much faster but could be subject to the same limitations if operating nearby. Clark, Byrd, and Patt provided several real-world examples that demonstrate how uncrewed technologies can operate as independent units. Over the past year, for instance, Ukrainian troops have expanded their use of uncrewed ground vehicles (UGVs) for logistics and medical evacuations, as well as engineering and fire support. Ukraine has increased its employment of ground robots throughout this year, especially for logistics operations and medical evacuations. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images "These operations deliberately use unmanned systems for operations or in places where the Ukrainian commanders do not want to risk human troops, increasingly producing a human-free front line," the authors write. In less-contested environments, soldiers and ground robots can work together, but communications problems, difficult terrain, and the need to refuel and repair robots can complicate operations, potentially putting accompanying troops at risk. The authors argue that the more hands-off approach to uncrewed systems could help the US military counter a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. According to the Hudson report, recent Navy Integrated Battle Problems examining a potential Chinese invasion have experimented with using autonomous systems in ways that draw on lessons from Ukrainian, Iranian, and Houthi operations. "By attacking troop transports and their escorts with drone boats, undersea vehicles, and loitering munitions, a force of mostly RAS [robotics and autonomous systems] could slow or disrupt the invasion. This would give US and allied forces targeting information and time to destroy PLA [People's Liberation Army] ships with long-range missiles and torpedo fires," the authors write. US military officials have also explored using large numbers of drones to disrupt Chinese invasion forces in the Taiwan Strait. Adm. Samuel Paparo, the head of US Pacific Command, has referred to it as an "unmanned hellscape" that would effectively act as a first line of defense and buy US, allied, and partner forces time to respond. Clark, Byrd, and Patt's observations come as the US military figures out the roles of uncrewed systems and autonomy and when it's better to use them together with crewed assets or independently. The Navy has looked at drone boats for port security and also used them for rescue and attack missions in the Middle East. The Hudson report's argument isn't that drones should never work alongside crewed ships, but the Navy could get more out of them by giving them missions that take advantage of what they can do on their own. events.title: What is ‘texture-maxxing’? The food trend putting crunch on the menu
events.summary: Texture-maxxing is the latest social media trend as consumers look for a more sensory food experience. Waitrose's latest food and drinks report highlighted the top food and beverage trends of the year. "This year, the sound of food went mainstream," the U.K. grocer's senior development chef said. Texture-maxxing is the latest food trend taking social media by storm as consumers, driven by aesthetics and taste, look for a sensory experience. British supermarket Waitrose's latest food and drink report highlighted "texture-maxxing" as one of the trends of the year. It describes the phenomenon as a multi-sensory indulgence that is "fuelled by texture-maxxing crunch and intense flavour hits," pushing shoppers to fill their trolleys with crunchy peanut butter, dumplings, and trifles. "This year, the sound of food went mainstream," Waitrose's Senior Development Chef Will Torrent said in the Wednesday report. "Driven by social media's obsession with audible, multi-sensory cooking, we're creating high-contrast meals that combine shatter-crisp crunch with pillowy chew." "The emphasis in social media content has flipped from narrative voiceovers to ASMR-inspired audio, where the evocative sounds of food are just as important as the visuals," he added. Food trends on social media have ranged from the obvious to the absurd. Fibermaxxing and proteinmaxxing have taken off in the past few years. Meanwhile, food and beverages like Dubai chocolate , protein coffee , and ube were some of the big social media hits. Nestlé's USA 2026 trends found that 75% of Gen Z and 80% of millennials sought out texture in snack cravings with the hashtag "crunchtok," amassing 1.5 billion views. Waitrose noted that shoppers looking to maximize on texture bought its viral No.1 Alphonso Mango Dessert, which involves "cracking through the crisp shell" to access a "smooth mango mousse and passion fruit curd on a crunchy white chocolate base." Waitrose's TikTok and Instagram videos of eating the dessert were watched by more than two million people, with a whopping 6,173 hours and 36 minutes of play time on TikTok. Its videos featuring crunchy toast also went viral. The U.K. grocer's sales of jarred chili crunches, which include crispy rayu oils such as itsu Crispy Chilli Oil, saw a 13-fold jump. Meanwhile, crunchy peanut butter outsold smooth. Dumplings also had a moment, with sales of chicken gyoza dumplings up 116% this year and searches on waitrose.com for gochujang and peanut butter udon noodles jumped 60%. "We've seen an explosion in demand as shoppers treat dumplings not just as a quick weeknight bite, but as a total sensory experience," Waitrose's Executive Chef Stephen Parkins-Knight said. "Driven by the rise of texture-maxxing, people want that ultimate contrast: delicate skins, juicy fillings and crispy skirts, topped with very chilli crunch. With innovation ranging from fusion fillings to rich dipping broths, dumplings have taken a delicious centre stage in 2026," he added. Texture-maxxing also extended to desserts, as shoppers bought twice as many chocolate trifles compared to 2025, and sales of strawberry trifles increased 160%. Tiramisu was also popular, with searches for waitrose.com's tiramisu recipe page increasing 155% year-on-year.

events.title: Haftar meets Erdogan: Can Turkiye reunify Libya as it courts rival sides?
events.summary: Analysts say a unified Libya best protects Turkiye’s economic and maritime interests, but instability and divisions remain major hurdles. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted eastern Libyan military commander Khalifa Haftar in Ankara on Wednesday, days after the Tripoli-based prime minister from the rival administration held talks with the Turkish foreign minister in Istanbul. Haftar’s first trip to Ankara comes nearly seven years after Turkiye helped the internationally recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) repel a military offensive led by his self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA). list 1 of 3 Could Russia-Ukraine war threaten Libya’s fragile reunification process? list 2 of 3 Libya’s Haftar visits Turkiye days after Ukraine hits Russian warship list 3 of 3 Two Libyan soldiers die after Ukraine attack on Russian vessel But following the 2020 United Nations-brokered ceasefire, Turkiye has pivoted towards a pragmatic approach, working to bring the rival administrations towards a unified government and military as it seeks to safeguard its maritime interests in the Mediterranean Sea. The meetings come ahead of an expected visit by Erdogan to Libya, his first in 15 years, as Ankara seeks to reconcile the country’s rival administrations. So what are Ankara’s interests in forging closer ties with Haftar, and what are the challenges ahead as Ankara seeks to reunify Libya? Why did Turkiye invite both leaders? Turkiye’s 2019-20 military intervention in support of the Tripoli-based government turned the tide of the Libyan civil war, forcing Khalifa Haftar’s forces to retreat from western Libya. But after the ceasefire later that year, Ankara began establishing contacts with the eastern authorities. This rapprochement accelerated in 2025, after the United States launched efforts to reconcile Libya’s rival governments. A concurrent UN track produced the 4+4 agreement this past August, a political roadmap for a unified government and nationwide presidential and parliamentary elections within two years. Turkiye was among the states to welcome and encourage the reconciliation process, while deepening its diplomatic and military ties with the east. In July, Ankara reached agreements with Haftar’s LNA on military infrastructure and training. Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst, told Al Jazeera that Turkiye’s military strength and staying power have granted it prestige across Libya. “Today, no Libyan leader of consequence can afford to spurn Ankara,” he said. Of particular importance to Ankara’s relations with Libya is a maritime boundary agreement that it signed with the Tripoli-based government in 2019, but which was only adopted by the east last month. The deal is a political flashpoint for several countries in the Eastern Mediterranean, opposed by Greece and Israel, and has been criticised by Egypt, which argued that it violated its own maritime rights. But Ankara has defended the agreement as lawful. What steps has Turkiye taken to unify Libya? Turkiye has sought to bring Libya’s rival military leaderships together. In May, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler met Abdulsalam al-Zoubi, the deputy defence minister in Tripoli, and Saddam Haftar, Khalifa Haftar’s son and a senior LNA commander. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin later met Saddam Haftar in the eastern city of Benghazi. In October, Ankara hosted further talks on military reunification, including discussions on establishing a joint military command in the central city of Sirte. However, disagreements over who would exercise political authority over a unified military remain unresolved. On the economic front, Turkiye was among 10 countries that welcomed Libya’s adoption of its first unified national budget in more than a decade. Ankara has also coordinated its diplomatic efforts with other countries involved in the reconciliation process. In June, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan held talks in Cairo with his Egyptian and Saudi counterparts and with Massad Boulos, a senior adviser to US President Donald Trump. In August, Fidan travelled to Tripoli and Benghazi for separate meetings with Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah and Khalifa Haftar respectively. Ankara has, however, not publicly endorsed a specific power-sharing arrangement. US mediators have backed a contentious proposal to make Saddam Haftar chairman of the Presidency Council, the three-member body that serves as Libya’s head of state. It is unclear whether Erdogan’s December visit will bring Dbeibah and Khalifa Haftar together for direct negotiations. No such meeting has been confirmed. Why does Turkiye want a united Libya? For Turkiye, much is at stake in Libyan reconciliation. Ankara has military and economic interests in both parts of the country, as well as the maritime boundary agreement that underpins its claims to potentially gas-rich waters in the Eastern Mediterranean.

events.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
events.summary: Published 26 November 2026, 11:38 GMT The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation. The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy. The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo. Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket. One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening. The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic. PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night. In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet. Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund. Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card." Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added. Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier. It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic. But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran. Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices. This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began. In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m. In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations. After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution". However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy". Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July. Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May . The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases. If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes. events.title: DoorDash global food access head: Hunger doesn’t take a holiday. Putting food on the table will take all of us
events.summary: Hunger gets harder to bear at the holidays, when everyone else seems to be gathering around a full table. With nearly 48 million Americans experiencing food insecurity in recent years, including 14 million children, millions of Americans will be facing a Thanksgiving table that has less on it.  No single organization can close this gap. It will take food banks, businesses, neighbors and public leaders all showing up. At a time when everything seems to cost more, putting food on the table has become harder than ever. Hunger exists in every county, and increasingly often among those who never expected to need food assistance before. More than eight in ten people surveyed by Feeding America identified rising costs as the primary driver of food insecurity.  The pressure is building for those in need. Recent changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the nation’s largest federal nutrition assistance program, have contributed to a significant decline in participation. According to the Food Research Action Center, approximately 5.5 million people have lost access to SNAP benefits since last year. Food banks and pantries have always been the country’s backstop. But now, like everyone else in this economy, they are being asked to do more with less. Organizations are bracing demand rivalling or surpassing experienced during last fall’s government shutdown that created unprecedented disruption to SNAP. Some food banks are experiencing demand levels exceeding the COVID-19 pandemic. Getting food to people can be just as challenging as securing it. Many of those served by food banks — including seniors, people with disabilities, or those without reliable transportation — cannot easily get to a distribution site on their own.  Tackling this challenge requires everyone contributing what they do best. For DoorDash , that’s logistics, and closing the gap between food and the people who need it. Through Project DASH, DoorDash transports goods from food banks and pantries to doorsteps. Since 2018, 9 million deliveries of an estimated 150 million meals across the U.S. and Canada have arrived via DoorDash.  This holiday season, we’re waiving fees for more than 300 Project DASH partners between Thanksgiving and Christmas, supporting delivery of an estimated 2 million meals. By removing that expense, food bank partners can plan larger holiday distributions with confidence and reach more people. Many of our grocery partners are also doing everything they can to make the holidays more affordable for Americans who are struggling to get by, such as offering discounts for SNAP users to stretch their budgets further. The data is clear: Making it easier to use SNAP benefits can also have a significant impact in the fight against hunger. Since introducing SNAP payments on our platform in 2023, more than 4.5 million consumers have added their SNAP cards to DoorDash, and nearly a third of those we surveyed said it has helped make them less likely to run out of food. This is only one incremental step in a larger national conversation about hunger. No single company, program, or nonprofit can solve it alone. Food banks understand their neighbors and the needs of their communities, and businesses can bring their resources, technology, and expertise to bear.  Hunger is a neighbor-helping-neighbor issue. Americans of every background can agree that no one should go without a meal, especially at the holidays.  There is enough food for everyone in America. What’s missing is a way to get it to every table. With everyone at the table, we can build toward that together. events.title: Ukraine's fight showed the British Army it needs to be digging trenches in different shapes and places
events.summary: Watching Ukraine, the British Army has changed how it trains its future leaders for trench warfare. John Moore/Getty Images The British Army is changing how it trains future leaders for trench warfare based on lessons from Ukraine. Cadets are digging L-shaped trenches to better protect themselves from grenades and gunfire. Instead of digging in open fields, cadets now seek tree cover to avoid detection by drones. The war in Ukraine showed the British Army that it was training its future leaders to dig trenches in the wrong shape and in the wrong locations. Defensive trench training for future British Army officers at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst had remained largely unchanged for decades, but the war in Ukraine is changing how cadets are taught to build and defend their positions. Trenches that were once straight now have bends to offer better protection from grenades and gunfire. And instead of digging in open fields, cadets are seeking cover from the drones that have made exposed positions increasingly dangerous. Business Insider recently observed elements of a six-day defensive exercise for officer cadets on England's Salisbury Plain. Lessons from Ukraine's battlefields are being incorporated into the training. A Ukrainian officer is also on site to share his experiences and answer questions on modern warfare. The goal of the training is to be "as realistic as possible" about the realities of modern warfare, Brigadier Nick Wight-Boycott, the commander of the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, told Business Insider. Achieving that has meant reconsidering long-standing practices based on lessons from Ukraine. Wight-Boycott said it's about preparing for the kind of "operations the British Army might be asked to do." A different trench shape The resurgence of trench warfare in Ukraine has driven partner militaries to give it more attention in training. At Sandhurst, that means making trenches L-shaped, Wight-Boycott said. Previously, "they were just straight," he said. "If you dropped a grenade in, all the shrapnel just went one way, and everybody who was in the trench would probably get a bit of the fragmentation." British officer cadets are digging small, L-shaped trenches that would be connected if they had more time. Sinéad Baker With L-shaped trenches, "if someone does throw a grenade in, you can hide around the other side, and you're not going to get any of the frag," he said. "Or if someone gets in and they start shooting, you could hide behind it." Capt. Will Kriehn, a British platoon commander, told Business Insider that previously trenches in the exercise were "essentially a deep hole." Now, they're focusing on the new shape because it's what they're seeing in Ukraine. Business Insider observed small groups of officer cadets digging independent L-shaped trenches close together. In a real conflict, the goal would be to dig further to link the trenches. "If we had more time, we would connect them," Kriehn said. Zero, an advising Ukrainian officer who has served as a platoon commander on Ukraine's front lines, told Business Insider that the change is a positive development. Ukrainian troops and unit representatives have said trenches with turns better protect troops from the kind of threats becoming more pervasive in battle. Ideally, they've said in local media interviews, trenches should not have long, straight sections. Elements of the US Army have made similar observations on survivability from the war in Ukraine. Citing observations of conflict, a 2024 US Army Center for Army Lessons Learned report said that "fighting positions should be made as deep as possible with a blocked 'L-shaped' entrance." L-shaped and zigzag trenches are nothing new, having been used in World War I, but Ukraine's war has renewed attention to how these defenses are built and adapted to modern threats. Ukraine's experience has pushed allies to focus more on drone warfare again in their own training. TETIANA DZHAFAROVA/AFP via Getty Images Working with Ukrainians has challenged some British Army assumptions about what trenches actually look like in a modern war. Instead of being clean and surgical, they are likely to be messy, uneven, and full of traps . It's also triggered changes in how the army defends its fighting positions. Wight-Boycott said his officer cadets are using nets and chicken wire to protect fighting positions from grenades and drones, drawing those lessons from Ukraine. Digging away from the open The hills of the Salisbury Plain were scarred by old trenches dug in open fields. Kriehn said that when he did the exercise in 2022, cadets were "deployed into an open field" where they dug for days and "there was no cover." Now, cadets are digging under trees, reflecting lessons from Ukraine about how easily reconnaissance drones can spot exposed positions. Officer cadets used to dig in open fields, but now work under tree cover. Sinéad Baker "In the past," Wight-Boycott said, "they've basically gone into an empty field in the middle of Salisbury Plain and dug trenches where you can see the whole of the field." But, he continued, "everything that we've seen in warfare, not just in Ukraine, is that nobody ever digs in an open field." The training also wants officer cadets to be faster at digging and moving between defensive positions. For instance, instead of spending much of an exercise digging and defending a single position, cadets might now practice quickly digging in, defending, and falling back to do it all over again. The intent is to slow an enemy advance and buy time for other forces to counterattack. The new approach at Sandhurst doesn't mean a change for everything the British Army does. Officers leaving Sandhurst may be deployed away from Europe, or face a conflict that needs different defenses. But the army is preparing for a potential land war with Russia in Europe, and wants its future leaders to be ready to adapt to different threats and battlefield conditions. Sandhurst wants "to make them agile leaders, thinking leaders so that when they leave, no matter what job they go into, they can apply those skill sets to them," Kriehn said. For Sandhurst, new knowledge comes in part from its instructors training Ukrainian soldiers , who have "seen how the Ukrainians have changed their tactics," Wight-Boycott said, and brought that knowledge back. "We've adapted really quickly to that changing character of conflict." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: House votes to refer draft amendments to the 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law to its Legal Committee for review. Jordan’s Parliament is reviewing proposed amendments to its “antiterrorism” law that would double minimum prison sentences for “terrorism”-related offences after an attack at a church in Karak last month that killed nine people. The legislation will return to the chamber for debate and a vote before proceeding to the Senate and, if approved, royal ratification. On October 23, gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority. Authorities said 34 people were wounded. Last week, Jordan’s State Security Court sentenced three men to death for the attack. On Wednesday, the court sentenced another man to death for killing the police officer in Amman. The officer was stabbed while on guard duty near the Sri Lankan embassy on November 5. The government-backed amendments would raise minimum prison terms to 10 years and up to 15 years in certain cases while retaining the death penalty for the most serious offences, the state-run Jordan News Agency reported. The proposed amendments drew criticism from First Deputy Speaker Ayatollah Freihat, who said legislation should not be based on knee-jerk reactions to events, FactJo, a Jordanian news agency, reported. He raised concerns that the amendments could also harm freedom of expression in Jordan. Freihat called on the government to withdraw the draft amendments and form a committee of legal experts to review the state’s criminal policy, criticising the use of “vague” formulations in defining “terrorism”, including “disrupting public order” and “harming the public interest”. Earlier, King Abdullah II had said the kingdom would not be shaken by the attack on the church. Opening the new session of parliament this month, Abdullah said “the treacherous hand of terrorism” had reached out “to test the resilience of our state and the resolve of our people”.

But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated. Our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft , a company that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too. The manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that showed the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning. However, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account. So the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them. “Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li said. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.” Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his company to make sure that this couldn’t happen again. Li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. events.title: China and other U.S. trading partners hit back at Trump's new tariff plans
events.summary: China, Japan, and other U.S. trading partners have protested planned tariff hikes by President Donald Trump's administration HONG KONG -- China, Japan and other U.S. trading partners protested planned tariff hikes by the Trump administration and hit back Thursday at allegations they have excess manufacturing capacity. The new tariffs, which are likely to take effect early next year, were announced Wednesday . They are intended to help reinstate tariffs for most of the economies after the Supreme Court ruling in February struck down most of U.S. President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs implemented last year. The new import duties followed a monthslong Section 301 probe. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he determined that practices of the 14 economies relating to excess capacity and production in manufacturing are “unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce.” China , one of the biggest trading partners of the U.S., is facing a 20% tariff. It slammed the notion of “overcapacity” as a “false premise.” The tariffs could double to 40% if the U.S. finds China not engaging adequately. “China opposes its use as a pretext for political maneuvering,” Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said at a regular press briefing. “Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests.” Beijing will take “necessary measures to defend its legitimate rights and interests,” he added. The U.S. and China have extended by two months a trade truce that’s set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. The two countries also have agreed on tariff cuts on reciprocal lists of non-sensitive products worth about $60 billion in total. Japan faces new U.S. tariffs of up to 15%. The Japanese government said it protested to Washington. “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a regular news conference Thursday. “It is regrettable that the United States announced the proposed measures targeting Japan, and we have conveyed our position to the U.S. side.” Singapore, due to be hit by an up to 20% tariff rate, said it was “very disappointed” with the U.S. proposal. Malaysia said it “does not have excess capacity in its manufacturing sectors that distorts or disrupts global markets,” adding that it will continue to engage and consult with the United States. Vietnam, facing tariffs of up to 35%, said it's working with the U.S. on a trade deal. Analysts say the 14 economies targeted by the Trump administration together account for roughly half of the global economy. The latest U.S. tariffs are not as alarming as they look, said Stephen Brown, a chief economist with Capital Economics, as they are essentially broadly replacing, rather than adding to, earlier announced U.S. tariffs related to forced labor allegations announced in July. Still, the new tariffs will likely help push prices higher and may “keep core goods inflation firm into next year,” he said in a commentary. The 27-nation European Union, which could be hit by a potential 15% tariff rate by the U.S., rejected “the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity” and pointed to the lack of joint action by the EU and the U.S. Associated Press journalists Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Mari Yamaguchi and Mayuko Ono in Tokyo, Aniruddha Ghosal in Hanoi, Vietnam, Jintamas Saksornchai in Bangkok and Lorne Cook and Sam McNeil in Brussels contributed to this report. events.title: Necessities join gifts in Black Friday shopping carts as AI and higher costs steer spending
events.summary: Black Friday comes with a few twists this year NEW YORK -- Stocking up on discounted shampoo while grabbing a flat-screen TV and several Lego sets for under the tree. Making a holiday list, comparing style options and delivery dates, and finding the best price with help from artificial intelligence. Black Friday, the retail industry's version of the Super Bowl, comes with a few twists this year. Brands and stores have promoted steep discounts online and in stores all month, making the day once considered the holiday shopping season's unofficial kickoff seem more like the fourth quarter of a football game. AI-powered shopping tools and cost concerns fueled by the U.S. war with Iran also are influencing how, where, when and on what consumers are spending, according to industry analysts. When Black Friday deals are available, basics like T-shirts, toiletries and pet supplies are going into shopping carts along with gift items, analysts said. “Usually, when you think of holiday shopping, it’s premium handbags and jewelry and those types of items, but we’re fast seeing shoppers also use this season to stock up on the essentials,” said Vivek Pandya, director of digital insights at technology company Adobe. Black Friday still has enough die-hard traditionalists to make it the biggest day of the year for retail foot traffic, according to Sensormatic Solutions, which tracks activity at physical stores. Retailers large and small view the occasion as an opportunity to improve their year-end footing and to attract new customers. “Black Friday is still the day for in-store shopping,” Grant Gustafson, Sensormatic's head of retail consulting and analytics, said. This year's holiday shopping takes place in a U.S. economic environment marked by lackluster consumer confidence, high inflation and shoppers who have kept spending regardless. Foot traffic data show Americans are visiting stores less often this season, and their purchases appear more intentional than impulse-driven, Gustafson said. Here are some of the emerging trends for Black Friday and holiday shopping overall in 2026: Analysts and economists closely scrutinize retail spending on the five days that begin with Thanksgiving Day and end on Cyber Monday for clues about consumers’ financial staying power and retailers’ prospects during the crucial holiday period and into the new year. The good news for retailers is that consumer confidence jumped this month as U.S. gasoline prices continued a steady decline. Online sales have beaten expectations so far this holiday season, according to Adobe Digital Insights, a research and market intelligence program that Pandya leads. U.S. consumers spent $82.5 billion online from Nov. 1 to Nov. 22, 9.1% more than during the same three weeks last year. Adobe predicted that U.S. online sales for the holiday shopping season that runs through Dec. 31 would grow by 6.7% and total $275.1 billion. The National Retail Federation estimated that higher prices would account for about half of the 4.1% sales growth it expected in stores and online in November and December. The group forecast U.S. shoppers collectively spending $1.01 trillion. U.S. retailers have broadly held the line on prices instead of making big increases across the board, and offered solid discounts that persuaded customers to shop earlier, industry analysts said. Technology company Salesforce, which tracks digital spending at a range of retailers, including grocery stores, said November discounts are 8% bigger than last year. The seasonal promotions pushed average selling prices of physical merchandise 1% below last November's prices, Salesforce said. For example, discounts on TVs are expected to average 23% on Friday compared with 11% during the first 22 days of the month. Self-gifting is an established holiday shopping trend. Black Friday's expansion to a multiweek event also has some consumers filling their cupboards with toiletries and clothes they would typically buy at another time, according to analysts. Online sales of personal hygiene products were 40% higher from Nov. 1 through Nov. 22 compared to the October average, according to Adobe's data.

events.title: Semiconductor chips are the new oil. Here's why
events.summary: For decades, oil has been the linchpin of global trade in essential commodities. But semiconductors have surpassed oil and gas in global export value in 2026. One Wall Street analyst says the shift could change how trade surpluses flow through the global economy. The milestone comes as investors exhibit caution about the AI boom driving chip demand, especially after last Friday’s sharp market selloff. The artificial intelligence boom has pushed semiconductors past oil and gas in global export value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data . Yet the milestone arrives at an awkward moment, just as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and drive down the price of semiconductor stocks. Last week, before Monday's breathtaking reversal, semiconductor stocks suffered their worst weekly loss in a quarter century, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone, capping a more than 17% weekly decline. Nvidia soared more than 31% Monday after the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips had fallen for a seventh straight week, plunging 46% during that stretch. Then it fell again, dropping almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 20% in two days last Thursday and Friday. Micron Technology sank 27% over the seven days ended last Friday. "For decades we've talked about the petrodollar. Perhaps increasingly we need to think about the chip dollar," Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank wrote in a report this month. Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time during the January-March quarter of 2026, reaching about $1.61 trillion, compared with $1.53 trillion for oil and gas, the report said, using four-quarter rolling totals. The gap widened in the second quarter, when semiconductor exports totaled about $1.60 trillion and oil and gas exports reached about $1.47 trillion. Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz after the Iran war helped widen the gap. Daily oil flows through the Strait collapsed nearly 77%, to 4.9 million barrels in the second quarter of 2026 from 21.6 million barrels in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration . Yet the demand for semiconductor has proven insatiable in the face of soaring data center construction, boosting global trade in the increasingly scarce AI component. Hundreds of billions of dollars of orders for graphics processing units and data centers aim at providing AI computing power, Rothschild & Co. Redburn wrote in a report last Thursday. "Compute will be the new commodity fueling this transformation on a global scale," Rothschild analyst Cara Thomson said. The shift toward chips has macroeconomic implications just as the explosion in oil trade did in the 1970s. Oil-exporting countries historically recycled much of their surpluses into the purchase of U.S. Treasuries and other bonds, helping finance U.S. deficits and underpin demand for other government debt. Reid at Deutsche Bank said that since semiconductor-surplus countries in Asia are more closely tied to U.S. tech companies, some chip-export earnings could flow back into U.S. technology stocks, startups and data centers, further helping to finance the AI investment cycle. The changing dynamics in global trade could also tilt the mix of global financial flows, Reid said. "So welcome to the chip-dollar era: potentially more growth, more excitement, more volatility, and structurally higher yields" in corporate and government debt.

events.title: OpenAI's pricing mix-up means most users of its new AI models will hit limits faster
events.summary: OpenAI said it resolved a billing error that allowed some users to do more than intended within their usage limits. VCG/VCG via Getty Images OpenAI accidentally gave users a discount on its new models. Users of 6.2 Astra and Sol will now start hitting their usage limits 40% and 25% faster, an OpenAI exec said. Users and AI companies are both grappling with compute costs, especially as agents become more popular. Black Friday savings briefly and unintentionally came to OpenAI. The company made a billing mistake that "incorrectly discounted" GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol earlier this month, Thibault Sottiaux, the engineering lead for Codex, OpenAI's coding agent, said on X. Now that it's been fixed, most users can expect to hit their usage limits 40% and 25% faster on Astra and Sol, respectively, for doing the same tasks, Sottiaux said in his early-morning post on Thursday. Astra is OpenAI's newest frontier model for the most difficult tasks, whereas Sol is cheaper and for everyday tasks, according to OpenAI's website. Sottiaux said OpenAI wouldn't retroactively charge users for the difference in past usage with the new models, which both launched on November 17. "As a small token to apologize for the mistake, we'll be adding one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business," Sottiaux wrote, meaning everyone on the listed paid plans gets one opportunity to reset their usage limit early. Usage limits are measured in tokens , the basic unit of data inputted or outputted by an AI model. More intensive tasks require more compute, and therefore rack up a higher token bill. Different ChatGPT subscriptions have different limits, and pricing plans across models have become a moving target for AI companies. This isn't Sottiaux's first X post about problems with usage limits . In June, some Codex users reported reaching their usage limits more quickly than usual, even when performing the same tasks. OpenAI set up a "warroom" to look into the issue, Sottiaux said at the time, and eventually determined that Codex was doing more behind-the-scenes work than intended, causing it to use more compute. The company also reset everyone's limits in that scenario. Coding tasks can get expensive quickly for users, since they typically use more compute compared to basic tasks like asking a chatbot a question. Companies, too, are grappling with ballooning AI bills , as employees burn through tokens and cash. JPMorgan, for example, instituted $2,000 monthly caps for some of its engineers using Claude Code earlier this year. Yet agents for both coding and mundane tasks are also pricey for AI companies, and questions remain about how they will make money. Earlier this month, Elon Musk said the cost of maintaining SpaceX's GrokBot , an AI agent, was "unsustainably high relative to revenue." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg told investors in October that Muse, the wildly popular AI agent, isn't making money yet and is "very compute-intensive." Read the original article on Business Insider
