events.title: I couldn't afford culinary school, so I got a $10-an-hour bakery job. It taught me skills I still value today.
events.summary: The author worked at a bakery to learn. Courtesy of the author I dropped out of college because I wanted to pursue my passion for baking instead of a 9-to-5 job. I couldn't afford culinary school, so I created a portfolio and approached local bakeries for work. I landed a $10-an-hour job that led to new opportunities and taught me how to pursue my dreams. When I was in college for a traditional four-year degree, I became disillusioned about getting a job post-graduation. When I really thought about the 9-to-5 positions I would be pursuing after school, my stomach would drop. I started thinking about what I did for fun and what would bring me joy, and baking came to mind immediately. I had been baking my whole life , but by college, I was inviting friends over to share my weekly baked goods . For my sweet 16, I asked for a subscription to Bon Appétit magazine and had a pancake party with my best girlfriends, where I made all the pancakes and experimented with different flavors. My dad was well aware of my passion for baking, but I still knew that he would not be supportive of a switch to culinary school. The author started working at a bakery in a small town. Courtesy of the author So I made an extreme decision to chase my baking dreams and moved out of Miami — where the rent was skyrocketing — to a smaller town . I couldn't afford culinary school Since I couldn't afford culinary school without my dad's financial help, I decided to pursue work experience. I put together a photo album of my best desserts as a portfolio to show prospective employers and went to bakeries all over town. Many explained they were family-run, while one suggested I obtain my Florida Certified Food Manager certification to increase my odds. I agreed and found a local restaurant supply company that offered the state's required course, followed by the certification exam. It was a small investment for me at the time, and I do feel like it gave me an edge. After I received my official certificate from the state, I went into a nearby bakery that, quite frankly, intimidated me. But I had already done the same thing half a dozen times all over town, and gotten my feet wet with rejection. The owner of this particular bakery was impressed by my portfolio and asked if I could begin the next day. She even offered me $10 an hour to start, rather than as an unpaid intern, which I was willing to do at the time just to gain some professional experience. I started working at a bakery I eventually worked my way up to being in charge of the vegan and gluten-free baked goods. It was around 2010, so I felt really proud to be given something new in the baking world to learn about and perfect. I bought a used textbook from the Culinary Institute of America on gluten-free baking and discovered the cookbooks of Isa Chandra Moskowitz, my favorite vegan chef to this day. Without the money for school, I thought the work experience was just as valuable. It was; I eventually used my experience at the bakery to get a job in a restaurant and start a small catering company on my own. After closely observing the business of running a bakery, I decided I wanted to work toward opening my own. With a restaurant position, I was able to start saving money and investing it right back into my own dessert catering business. I proudly tried to get that catering business off the ground, going to local farmers' markets and filling personal orders. I did that for about two years until life happened and my career path changed several times. The experience taught me not to let obstacles get in the way After I had my son, I went through the same process of thinking about what I love to do. Having done that once before made the thought process less intimidating; I was starting over in my career for a second time. Since that one big decision to drop out of a four-year university and get a job at a small-town bakery, there hasn't been one career leap that's phased me. If there's an obstacle, such as the cost of schooling, I have always found a way. For instance, I applied for a scholarship for my 200-hour yoga training, so that I could teach my own classes while I went back and finished my four-year degree. As a yoga instructor and owner of a small cleaning business, I worked my way through those last two years of college and eventually became an English teacher. Without having made that one terrifying decision nearly two decades ago to pursue my dream — despite the financial challenges — I know I wouldn't have eventually gained all the work experience I did. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed UK Home Office waved through border system without a working fix for bad data 4 hours ago UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models 8 days ago Up to 99% of UK civil servants rely on Microsoft for comms, minister admits 9 days ago MPs ask what the break clause was for as Palantir wins two more years in the NHS 9 days ago Palantir's NHS cancer app gets plenty of praise, precious few users 13 days ago UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found. The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies. LEPs brought together councils and businesses to promote economic growth in England under a coalition government initiative launched in 2010. Central government funding ended in April 2024, with their core functions transferred to local and combined authorities. Among other things, Digital Royalty builds and looks after websites, which means chasing down old links. In August, it found that a link on Surrey County Council's website led to a former LEP address now displaying casino content. It went looking for more. Digital Royalty founder Alex De Sousa said: "Slow is usually a sign of caution and diligence, but 31 months after the LEPs wound up, it's crossed into inefficient and dangerous." The consultancy offered The Register four examples of websites run by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), Hull City Council, Parliament, and the Local Government Association. One example is a government page about the Digital Skills Partnership, originally published under an earlier incarnation of DCMS. The page includes a link that appears to be for the Humber Digital Skills Partnership within the Humber LEP website, but in fact takes users to a site advertising "Independent Non GamStop Casinos UK – New Casino Sites Outside GamStop." GamStop is the self-exclusion scheme designed to help people restrict their online gambling, which makes the links more concerning than ordinary website clutter. The same link appears on the Hull City Council website under a list of Joint Committees, Partnerships and Trusts where it appears as Local Economic Partnership (Humber LEP). An old page for the Parliament website detailing the Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy committee's Industrial Strategy report includes a footnote (135) that appears to be for the Business Central funding finder service, but takes the user to the "Highest RTP Non GamStop Casinos for UK Players." The Local Government Association's (LGA) sustainability and waste route map included a link to the former York and North Yorkshire LEP website. The destination initially appeared legitimate but contained links promoting crypto casinos. The LGA now appears to have removed the link. All the organizations mentioned have been contacted by The Register to offer them the opportunity to comment. Digital Royalty checked former web addresses associated with about 70 LEPs and growth hubs, then used a backlink index to identify roughly 3,000 incoming links from public sector sites. Most were simply outdated rather than leading to gambling content. The findings are not exhaustive: the index may miss pages, and the research did not cover other types of defunct public body whose domains may have been repurposed.

events.title: Mandelson tried to set up meeting between Trump adviser and lobbying firm he held shares in
events.summary: Then ambassador to US wanted to discuss alternatives to World Trade Organisation in ‘under the radar’ meeting, documents reveal Peter Mandelson sought to organise an “under the radar” meeting between an economic adviser to Donald Trump and a member of his former lobbying firm, Global Counsel, while he still held shares in the company, newly released documents reveal. In April 2025, while ambassador to Washington, Mandelson wanted to hold a lunch to discuss “alternative options” to the World Trade Organization and on how “like-minded partners come to terms with China and its practices”. He told the economic adviser he wanted to bring “a former trade colleague of mine” with “interesting views” who could “lead off”. He added: “It would be best to keep this under the radar”. Mandelson then forwarded the emails to a Global Counsel employee to ask for their availability. Mandelson had already refused to dispose of his shares in the company after he was appointed ambassador because, according to an official’s letter, the firm had “not made an offer that Lord Mandelson considers commensurate with the fair value”. One July 2025 email reveals his frustration in response to media queries about his ongoing shareholding: “They [Global Counsel] should pull their fingers out and buy my shares.” By the time Mandelson was trying to arrange the lunch with the presidential adviser and the Global Counsel employee, the top civil servant in the Foreign Office, Olly Robbins, had told him he needed to “avoid any perception that he is consciously or even unconsciously furthering [Global Counsel’s] commercial interests”. Mandelson, however, continued to consult his former colleagues on his work as ambassador while holding shares, sharing a draft of a speech to the Ditchley Foundation with a Global Counsel director for comments. After receiving feedback, Mandelson said he would “soften the lecture on China”. Several crucial documents about Mandelson’s appointment to Washington continue to be withheld from the public. They include his conflict of interest declaration form and a summary document produced by vetting officials about his security clearance. The Guardian revealed in April that Mandelson had failed the developed vetting process after Keir Starmer announced in December 2024 that he would the next British ambassador to Washington. The Foreign Office overruled vetting officials’ recommendation Mandelson be denied clearance, clearing him to take up the post. Among the vetting agency’s concerns, according to sources, were his associations with senior figures in China, Russia, and Israel , as well as a £1m loan. Those concerns were separate to Mandelson’s relationship with the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, the issue that led to Mandelson’s sacking in September 2025. Starmer also sacked Robbins, who told MPs investigating the issue that he believed vetting officials considered Mandelson to be “borderline” and so could be cleared with “mitigations”, but no documents have been disclosed to back up his claims. He told them his office had been under “constant pressure” from Downing Street to get Mandelson in post as soon as possible. Robbins went on to receive a six-figure payout from the government for his dismissal. In February, parliament passed a motion known as a humble address requiring the government to publicly release “all papers” relevant to his appointment. But some documents were held back from disclosures in March and June at the request of the Metropolitan police, in case they could “potentially prejudice” its investigation into Mandelson. Ministers previously revealed that these documents included “vetting information and conflicts of interest process material”. The newly released documents include an email from Ian Collard, the Foreign Office security chief, to his line managers noting Mandelson had been given clearance. Collard said Mandelson’s “private sector engagements” were being handled through the conflict of interest process and that Mandelson had been sent a letter about his responsibilities regarding personal conduct as an employee. Collard said questions about Mandelson’s “overseas contacts” would be reviewed by other authorities responsible for higher levels of security clearance. In July, the foreign affairs select committee concluded that Mandelson’s appointment was “nothing short of disastrous”, “highly damaging” for the British government and “painful and offensive to the victims of Jeffrey Epstein”. Mandelson has been approached for comment.

events.title: 2 companies linked to lash, hair and nails chain Milly’s wound up after outlets closed
events.summary: Milly’s first opened at Far East Plaza in 2008 and was a go-to for eyelash and hair extensions in Singapore. Two Milly’s companies, Milly’s Group and Milly’s Co. Singapore, were wound up by High Court orders on Nov 13 after Maybank Singapore filed claims. Liquidators said outlets had already closed, and they are checking assets, debts, unused prepaid packages and any unpaid wages for customers and former staff. Milly’s, once a popular lash and hair extension chain since 2008, now has closed outlets and rebranded social media, while ST has contacted the firm and the Ministry of Manpower. SINGAPORE – Two companies associated with Milly’s, a well-known Singapore salon chain offering beauty services such as lash and hair extensions, have been wound up. Milly’s Group and its wholly owned subsidiary, Milly’s Co. Singapore, were wound up by High Court orders on Nov 13 , according to notices published in the Government Gazette on Nov 20, which said creditors should submit their proofs of debt to liquidators. Maybank Singapore was the claimant in both cases. It filed the winding-up application on Oct 21. Gary Loh and Dev Kumar Harish Nandwani of BDO Advisory were appointed liquidators of both companies. In response to The Straits Times’ queries, the liquidators said the company’s outlets had ceased operations before the winding-up order. They are taking control of assets and records, and will assess creditors’ claims, they said. The liquidators also said they were reviewing the company’s records to determine customers’ unused prepaid packages. Customers with packages that have not been fully used may submit a proof of debt with supporting documents, they added. Checks were also being conducted to see if sums remained owing to former employees. Those with outstanding salary or other entitlements may submit claims to the liquidators, they said. Milly’s website continued to list a phone nu mber and an email address for customers to contact for package enquiries, verification and appointment arrangements on Nov 25, but the site is now offline. Go-to for eyelash and hair extensions Milly’s first opened at Far East Plaza in 2008. It became a go-to spot for eyelash and hair extensions at a time when such services were less widely available here, and expanded to other mall outlets over the years. Milly’s Group was incorporated in 2011, and the subsidiary Milly’s Co. Singapore, formerly known as Milly’s (Orchard), in 2015. Emily Xu was listed as a director of both companies. Online listings now show Milly’s outlets at Plaza Singapura, JEM, Tanjong Pagar, Tampines 1 and Suntec City marked as permanently closed. It is not known when the original Milly’s outlet at Far East Plaza exited the mall. ST checks found that Milly’s Facebook account has been deactivated, while its Instagram account has been rebranded as Mii Wellness. Incorporated in June, Mii has a different shareholder and director. Mii Wellness’ social media profile lists locations at Tanjong Pagar Plaza and JEM, which were previously Milly’s outlets, and Tampines Downtown Line station. ST has contacted Milly’s and the Ministry of Manpower for further information.

events.title: Is UBI the solution to mass unemployment in an AI economy?
events.summary: AI’s rapid advance has fueled calls for universal payments to prevent poverty and wealth inequality. As rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) raise fears of mass job losses, calls for the rollout of universal basic income (UBI) are gaining traction. UBI is a regular cash payment made to every citizen regardless of employment status, income or wealth. list 1 of 3 ‘Stand with Jensen’: Why US tech titans are backing Nvidia ex-CEO Huang list 2 of 3 California files lawsuit against OpenAI alleging lack of proper safeguards list 3 of 3 China’s Xi pitches free trade at APEC amid Trump’s global trade disruptions Proponents of UBI in the United States argue that governments should look to UBI to offset AI’s expected impact on the labour market and prevent extreme poverty and wealth inequality. The idea of universal payments is not new. In 1797, Thomas Paine, one of the key thinkers of the American Revolution, proposed an early version of UBI in a pamphlet titled Agrarian Justice. He argued that land was originally common property, shared by all of humanity. Those with no land, he said, were owed compensation as a basic human right. Under Paine’s proposal, each person would have received a lump sum of 15 pounds when they turned 21, followed by an annual payment of 10 pounds from age 50, paid for by a tax on inherited property. The idea resurfaced in the 1960s from opposing ends of the ideological spectrum. US economist Milton Friedman proposed a “negative income tax”, under which the government would top up the earnings of anyone falling below a set threshold. Friedman, a champion of free-market policies, argued that his proposal would be cheaper than existing welfare programmes. US civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, in his 1967 book Where Do We Go from Here, called for a guaranteed income as a way to end poverty. King Jr’s vision came close to being enshrined in law in 1969, when President Richard Nixon proposed the Family Assistance Plan, a minimum income for families with children. Nixon’s proposal passed the House of Representatives but stalled in the Senate, and the plan was eventually abandoned. After falling out of fashion in subsequent decades, proposals for universal payments have re-entered the mainstream in recent years amid the rise of automation and AI. Some of the loudest proponents of UBI are the people developing AI. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been pushing the idea for years. In a 2024 interview with the All-In Podcast, Altman proposed a twist on UBI that would give everyone a stake in the productive gains of AI. “I wonder if the future looks something like more like universal basic compute than universal basic income and everybody gets like a slice of GPT 7’s compute and they can use it, they can resell it, they can donate it to somebody to use for cancer research,” Altman said, suggesting that citizens could “own part of the productivity” generated by AI instead of receiving cash. In April, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said in an X post that a government-distributed “Universal High Income” would be the best way to deal with large-scale unemployment caused by AI. Musk said AI and robotics would produce an abundance of goods and services far in excess of the increase in the money supply in future, so there would not be inflation. Some observers have questioned the motivations of such proposals from billionaire tech executives. Jonathan Portes, a professor of economics and public policy at King’s College, London, said tech leaders promoting UBI are acting out of “perceived self-interest”. In his view, a basic income could make job losses easier to accept as people are more likely to tolerate AI replacing their work if they are being paid. “Partly it’s just another cool sounding idea,” Portes told Al Jazeera. “We should not take these people seriously on public policy issues at all.” Who would pay for UBI, and how is it different from social welfare? Most UBI proposals envision a system paid for by taxes, much in the same way as existing welfare programmes, though some pilot schemes have been funded by private donations. Unlike traditional social welfare, which typically requires applicants to demonstrate financial hardship, UBI is paid to every member of a population without conditions. Portes said UBI high enough to support acceptable living standards is not likely to be economically or politically viable in the near future. While “a realistic UBI could help provide a better level of protection, increase individual autonomy and increase labour market flexibility, getting there would be complex”, he added. “Many of the claims for it and fears are grossly exaggerated,” Portes said. While everyone would get some financial benefit, some economists and technologists argue that the biggest beneficiary could be the economy. In a scenario where AI leads to mass layoffs, people will have less money to spend.

events.title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel with thousands of flights delayed or canceled
events.summary: A storm is headed toward the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day. Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel with flight delays and cancellations across the US. Over 6,500 flights were delayed on Wednesday, and over 300 were canceled early on Thursday morning. Bad weather has even led to the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Parade. Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel, with more severe weather expected to hit the East Coast on Thursday. More than 6,500 flights within, into, or out of the US were delayed on Wednesday, and about 160 were canceled, according to FlightAware. As of about 7:30 a.m. ET Thursday, roughly 400 flights had been delayed and 360 canceled. The National Weather Service wrote in a Wednesday report that the East Coast can expect "major coastal flooding, beach erosion, strong wind gusts, and heavy rainfall" during Thanksgiving. Scattered power outages and tree damage are also likely, it added. A map from the weather service showed winter, gale, coastal flood, and wind warnings along the country's eastern coast. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Wednesday X post that New Yorkers should expect severe weather on Thursday, including winds up to 60 miles per hour. On Thursday morning, LaGuardia Airport recorded wind gusts of up to 39 knots, or 45 miles per hour. While such strong winds can disrupt flying, most flights at New York's airports were operating normally as of Thursday morning. Mamdani said that, to protect New Yorkers, the city, along with Macy's and the local police department, had decided to postpone the 100th Annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday. This is the first time in history that the iconic parade has been rescheduled. "The worst of the storm is expected to hit on Thanksgiving Day in the afternoon through the late evening," he added in his X post. He provided a list of steps New Yorkers should take to protect themselves ahead of the storm, such as staying indoors, moving cars away from coastal areas to higher ground, and budgeting extra time for travel. The Transportation Security Administration said in a Saturday X post that it expects to screen nearly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between November 24 and November 30, including more than 3 million on Sunday, November 29. It recommended that travelers arrive early for their flights. The Federal Aviation Administration wrote in a Wednesday X post that gusty winds may slow flights at LaGuardia Airport, Newark Liberty Airport, JFK, and San Francisco International Airport that day. It added that thunderstorms may cause delays at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. Disruption was worsened in Miami when a FedEx plane overshot the runway on Wednesday evening. No injuries were reported, but the incident caused inbound flights to be grounded for about 90 minutes. events.title: The US Army tested whether it could still deploy forces to war if attacks knocked out comms at American ports
events.summary: Army vehicles are loaded onto the USNS Charlton at Joint Base Charleston, South Carolina, March 25, 2024. Tech. Sgt. Alex Fox Echols III/US Air Force The Army simulated attacks that knocked regular communications offline at US deployment hubs. Troops used backup networks to reconnect units and restore access to cargo-tracking systems. More than 85% of US combat power is based in the continental US, a top general previously told lawmakers. The US Army tested whether it could keep communicating with units at American ports after simulated attacks knocked their normal networks offline, rehearsing how it would deploy forces overseas if critical infrastructure at home came under attack. During a recent homeland defense exercise at Fort Eustis, Virginia, the Army's 597th Transportation Brigade used backup communications to connect with units in South Carolina and Texas. The drill simulated physical and cyberattacks that knocked military and commercial networks offline, creating a "catastrophic communications blackout" at key deployment hubs, according to an Army news release. Troops had to restore access to a key system that tracks military cargo moving by air and sea. Losing those connections could make it tougher to track equipment, ensure it reaches the right ports and ships, and move forces overseas on schedule. The service said in the release that the exercise proved successful, though it did not provide deeper details on the amount of stress put on the system, or any persistent challenges More than 85% of US combat power resides in the continental United States, Gen. Randall Reed, the head of US Transportation Command, told lawmakers in March, making the military's ability to swiftly move troops and equipment vital for a major conflict or national emergency. "A disconnected mobility force threatens the Joint Force's ability to win," Reed wrote in his testimony, calling for communications that can resist jamming and cyberattacks. The threat isn't limited solely to military networks. Potential adversaries could also target civilian infrastructure that US forces depend on. Some US military experts have characterized the current threat situation as "the end of strategic sanctuary ." In February 2024, US cybersecurity and intelligence agencies warned that China-backed Volt Typhoon hackers had compromised critical infrastructure , including transportation and communications networks, positioning themselves to cause disruption during a major crisis or conflict. More recently, refrigeration systems in military commissaries have seen power outages linked to suspected malicious attacks. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UK government ‘has not made case’ for third runway at Heathrow Airport
events.summary: Heathrow’s expansion plans have been dealt a blow by MPs, who said they had not been persuaded there was a case for a third runway at the UK’s busiest airport . The parliamentary transport committee said the government’s policy statement on expansion required “improvement and clarification” before it could give its support and be able to see off any legal challenge. The case for expansion had weakened since previous analyses and should not go ahead in its current form, the MPs said. The airport’s owner, Heathrow Airport Limited, wants to build a third runway, arguing that the site in west London has reached capacity and is being overtaken by other hub airports such as Istanbul. It says its £33 billion plan would almost double passenger numbers from 85 million to 150 million and add up to 276,000 flights a year. The plan involves a runway built above a diverted M25 motorway, new terminals and an overhaul of its current infrastructure. A rival plan has been put forward by the Arora Group . The MPs from all parties were tasked with examining the government’s Heathrow expansion national policy statement (HENPS), which set out four tests: delivering growth across the country without harmful effects on climate, noise and air quality. They said the economic argument had not been made well enough, with the government’s own analysis showing the benefit to the wider economy of expanding Heathrow would be outweighed by societal and environmental costs to the tune of £53 billion. They said that treating Heathrow expansion as “uniquely critical” to national growth was not justified as it was forecast to increase annual GDP by 0.05 per cent by 2056, a fraction of the 0.5 per cent predicted a decade ago. It was initially claimed that 60 per cent of additional growth would occur outside London and the south-east; this was downgraded to a range of 14 per cent – 40 per cent. The MPs suggested the government should find better evidence if it wished to continue with the growth infrastructure designation. They also raised concerns about the impact that changes to landing charges would have if demand from airlines fell. They were heavily critical of the government’s approach, saying before it published its draft plans it should have set out its overall strategy for aviation, “examining how Heathrow along with other UK airports support international trade and connectivity, and their climate impacts”. The legislators called for a parliamentary vote on a new policy statement once an overall aviation strategy had been published to “underpin the conclusion that a third runway is necessary or the best way to deliver he benefits the government wants from aviation”. They said it was “highly concerning” that there were no committed, funded plans for improving public transport to the airport and said improvements to road and rail access would be needed. Finally, the government was “failing the climate test”, they said, as Heathrow expansion was not compatible with the UK’s legally binding climate targets and it “seems impossible for the additional carbon dioxide emissions it will generate to be offset elsewhere in the economy”. They also raised concerns over noise. Wake-up call “Our report should be a wake-up call for ministers," said Ruth Cadbury, chairwoman of the committee and Labour MP for Brentford and Isleworth, which is on the airport’s flight path. “We found that the government should have set out its overall strategy for aviation before publishing the draft HENPS. It did not do so and now it has failed to make the case for Heathrow expansion. “Plans for a third runway should be grounded for now and the government should go back to the drawing board.” Paul McGuinness, chairman of the lobby group No Third Runway Coalition, said the expansion would "leave the country worse off, once the negative costs are taken into account". Decades of flight at Heathrow - in pictures Support for Heathrow expansion has been mixed within the Labour government. It was backed by Keir Starmer, prime minister at the time, and his chancellor Rachel Reeves , who promised 'spades in the ground' by 2029. But new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been less effusive, having opposed it when he was mayor of Manchester, which has put the scheme in doubt. He has said the committee’s decision would influence his views. A Department for Transport spokesperson, said: "The Government has been clear that Heathrow expansion can only proceed if it meets our four tests on economic growth, climate, noise and air quality. “We note the findings from the Committee’s report and will consider these as we continue to review responses to our consultation on the policy framework underpinning expansion.” Heathrow chief executive Thomas Woldbye said earlier this week that Mr Burnham needed to deliver a decision on the third runway by early in the new year or the project risked collapse. Watering down the scheme by opting for a shorter runway would force the need for an entirely new blueprint, he said. Reacting to the MPs' report, Mr Woldbye said on Thursday that "the overwhelming weight of evidence and support remains strongly behind Heathrow expansion". "Trade unions, business groups, airlines, regional airports, senior cabinet ministers and the majority of MPs back expansion because they recognise it is vital to creating quality jobs and supporting long-term economic growth across the UK," he said. “The case for expanding Heathrow has been examined more thoroughly than almost any infrastructure project in modern Britain. “Successive governments, independent commissions and industry experts have repeatedly concluded that you either expand Heathrow so the UK can compete and grow, or you accept a steady erosion of the UK’s connectivity and global competitiveness.” Members of the Heathrow Reimagined campaign, which includes the Heathrow Airline Operators Committee, American Airlines, AMEX GBT, the Arora Group, International Airlines Group (IAG) and Virgin Atlantic, said the report reinforces its position that an “affordable Heathrow is critical to unlocking the benefits of expansion”. A spokesperson said: “From the outset, we have expressed our support for expansion, but not at any cost. “Today's publication cites that the current approach to economic regulation at Heathrow 'could work harder' and demonstrates that regulatory reform is not simply confined to expansion.” It called on the Civil Aviation Authority to “move at pace on the fundamental regulatory reform needed to ensure Heathrow delivers for passengers, businesses and communities across the UK, both now and for generations to come”.

events.title: Cost of living roadshow highlights support on offer
events.summary: Nichola Hermitage from Positively Connected Kent A cost of living roadshow held in a Kent town is the "starting point" and "first step on the ladder" to resolve financial problems, a local councillor has said. Organisations, including those which help people with health and wellbeing, managing bills and getting back into work, have been in Sheerness for the Swale Borough Council event on Thursday morning. This event, funded by the Crisis and Resilience Fund which helps households facing financial crisis, Councillor Angela Harrison, deputy mayor of Swale, wants residents to know that "there is help support and guidance for you". Among those in attendance was Nichola Hermitage from Positively Connected Kent, which helps people manage energy costs and fuel debt. Reacting to the recent announcement that energy prices are due to go up by 26% in January, Hermitage said there were small measures people can take to mitigate the impact. She said: "It's about 45p to have a ten minute electric shower; cut that down by in half and you know you can save." Hermitage stressed that people should not "suffer alone" if they have built up energy debt, with help from the providers themselves and charities. Charriss Thorne and Alex Emery from Connect To Work Connect To Work, a 12-month voluntary scheme designed to help people get back into work, offers "individual support" including with travel, clothing and job searching. Alex Emery said the roadshow was "about being present in the community to meet people face-to-face for them to understand what we do". The event comes as Save the Children has released new research into the rising cost of Christmas for families, centred around a survey of 2,000 people including 233 from the South East. About two thirds of South East respondents expressed concern about being able to afford Christmas. Harrison said: "It's about time we stopped trying to keep up with the Jones'. "Christmas is actually about family. It's not about how much you can spend on your kids and the rest of your family." events.title: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals
events.summary: The U.S. proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, with China, Vietnam and India among those facing some of the steepest potential rates. The proposals could give some countries an incentive to accelerate trade talks, with lower tariff rates available if agreements are reached. South Korea and Taiwan stand to benefit from exemptions in technology and electronic goods. The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington. The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam. The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington. The overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February. Still, the proposal could give some countries an incentive to speed up trade talks in order to lock in lower tariff rates, analysts said. On Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the new policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying the duties could take effect as early as January. China faces a capped rate of 20%, on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. The rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, the USTR said. Beijing has rejected Washington's claim of excess capacity while vowing to take measures necessary to protect its rights. On Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue." He was responding to Washington's plan to raise tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, while the ministry also urged the U.S. to implement $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed by the two sides in late September. The renewed tensions come despite several conciliatory meetings between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this year, as well as what Williams described as Trump's "apparent lack of concern" about allegations that Chinese technology firms have circumvented U.S. chip export controls. The two leaders are expected to meet for a fourth time this year at the Group of 20 leaders summit in Miami in December. "While not happy, Beijing seems prepared to live with the new rates provided that they don't exceed 20%," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute. By retaining the option to raise levies if bilateral talks deteriorate, Washington is using the tariffs as leverage to "secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of U.S. agricultural goods," Cutler said. Washington has warned that tariffs on Chinese goods could double to 40% if the USTR finds that Beijing is not engaging. "If the trade war did start up again, today's measures provide the U.S. with some ammunition," Williams said. Even the sweeping actions against the other 13 trading partners appear aimed squarely at China, said Williams, who tallied that the word "China" appears 253 times in the USTR's report on Vietnam, and 315 times in the document on the European Union. "Foremost among the 'unreasonable acts, policies, and practices' that these countries are criticised for is being slow to restrict imports and FDI from China," Williams said. While the proposed tariffs generally lift average rates only modestly, India and Vietnam stand out because of the wider gaps between the rates they would face with and without a deal, analysts said. India and Vietnam face proposed tariffs of 25% and 35%, respectively, but those rates could fall sharply to 17% and 20% if ongoing talks with the U.S. produce reciprocal trade agreements. The two countries have "a strong incentive" to conclude deals with Washington to secure the lower rates, Cutler said. Vietnam's trade ministry said Thursday that it was working with the U.S. to complete a trade deal as soon as possible, according to Reuters . India could also gain an edge over some Asian rivals through comparatively lower levies if New Delhi concludes its long-pending trade deal with Washington. Singapore faces a similar challenge. The proposal sets a maximum potential rate of 20% on its exports, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, which could fall to 10% if it reaches an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S.

events.title: 430,000 UK homeowners face £500-plus jump in monthly mortgage payments
events.summary: Bank of England warns of increases for millions coming off fixed deals over next three years as interest rates rise More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a £500-a-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next three years, as rising interest rates heap extra pressure on households, the Bank of England has said. The Bank’s financial policy committee said on Thursday that out of the 7 million borrowers coming off fixed-rate deals before December 2029, about 6.5 million would have to cough up extra funds to cover their home loan payments. For about 3.4 million borrowers the monthly increase would be less than £100, while for a further 2.7 million it would be £100-£500. The increase would be even greater for those borrowers coming off much lower interest rates, with about 430,000 likely to see their monthly mortgage payments surge by more than £500. Warnings about the increases came after policymakers at the Bank of England hiked interest rates from 3.75% to 4% this month. The Bank also hinted at another increase in interest rates to combat inflationary pressure caused by the Iran war. The financial markets have predicted three quarter-point rate rises by summer 2027. Over the next year, about 1 million households will see their payments rise by almost £200 a month. The news will put further pressure on Andy Burnham’s efforts to offset cost of living pressures, with the chancellor, John Healey, having used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers . The figures came a day after the energy regulator for Great Britain raised the cap on household energy bills by 26% . The Bank of England on Thursday also raised further concerns about cybersecurity and AI threats, recent outages at Google and Microsoft that had laid bare businesses’ growing dependence on outside technology, and how “disruption at a single provider” could “affect many firms at once”. The financial policy committee also flagged concerns about emerging quantum computing technologies potentially undermining the crypto technology that protected essential financial transactions. It said the evolving risks reinforced the need for “significant and sustained investment by the financial sector in building resilience”, adding that banks needed to have credible arrangements to ensure they could bounce back quickly from any disruption and maintain “vital financial services”. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The committee acknowledged this would place competing demands on lenders’ tech experts and management teams, but added that a failure to take action would “compromise firms’ operational resilience with potential system-wide implications”. The Bank on Thursday also announced plans to further reduce capital requirements for UK banks, as part of a wider package that it said could unleash an extra £175bn in lending capacity. However, extra funding could end up being used to payout shareholders and investors.

events.title: It's not Thanksgiving déjà vu: NBC is replacing the postponed Macy's parade with a rerun of last year's
events.summary: A Labubu on Pop Mart's float for last year's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Michael Simon/Getty Images for POP MART Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade is taking a rain check. NBC is going to re-air last year's edition on Thursday instead. Organizers will deflate the balloons, take them back to New Jersey, then re-inflate them for Saturday. As Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade takes a rain check for its landmark 100th edition, NBC is airing a replay instead. The network will show last year's parade on Thursday at 8:30 a.m. ET/CT/MT and 7:30 a.m. PT, after severe weather forced organizers to move the event to Saturday. That means another outing for Cynthia Erivo's opening performance of "Feeling Good," and the singers from "KPop Demon Hunters" performing "Golden." Busta Rhymes, Ciara, Shaggy, and Teyana Taylor also appeared in the 99th edition, hosted by Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker. But some of the floats might already feel a bit dated looking back, like one for "Stranger Things" — which aired its final season last year — plus some Labubus . New York City officials warned of heavy rain, coastal flooding, and gusts reaching 60 to 65 mph on Thursday, with the strongest winds expected in the afternoon and evening. "There is no destination worth risking your safety," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. The rescheduled parade is due to start Saturday at 8:30 a.m. ET, airing on NBC and streaming on Peacock. "While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," Will Coss , the parade's executive producer, said during a Wednesday news conference with city officials. Moving a show this big takes some juggling. Coss said the balloons would be deflated, returned to a facility in New Jersey, then inflated again for Saturday's parade. The parade first took place in 1924 and was canceled from 1942 to 1944 during World War II. In 1971, bad weather grounded the balloons, but the parade went ahead. events.title: A Mark Cuban-backed AI startup is helping families turn Thanksgiving conversations with their elderly relatives into lasting memories
events.summary: As 81.5 million Americans travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving, conversations around the dinner table could present a rare opportunity for people to learn more about their aging loved ones. A new class of AI startups wants to help them preserve those conversations forever. Charlie Greene, the cofounder and CEO of Remento, first learned about the importance of recording memories when his father, Don Greene, died during the hijacking of United Airlines Flight 93 on 9/11. A 10-year-old boy at the time of the terrorist attack, which resulted in his father’s plane crashing in Shanksville, Penn., the now 34-year-old Greene mostly has a collection of old home videos to remember him by.  So when his mother Claudette, 74, was diagnosed with stage-three lung cancer, he quickly acted to record her memories. With the intention of conducting an oral history interview, Greene searched “questions to ask a parent,” which Google morbidly autocompleted with “before they die.” When he started asking her the questions like “How did you get to elementary school as a kid,” she lit up, surprised he was interested at all. “The thing that blew me away about that experience was how unmorbid it felt,” he said. Claudette is in remission, but her battle with cancer still left Greene “unhealthily fixated” on the idea of how to best preserve loved ones’ memories. In October 2023, he launched Remento, which sends older “storytellers” a weekly text or email reminder prompting them to respond to photos or questions chosen in advance by their family members, such as, “What was the hardest thing you had to overcome as a child?” After gathering a maximum of a year’s worth of responses, the AI converts the raw transcript into a naturally flowing narrative that goes into a physical book complete with images and QR codes linking the text to the original recordings.  Greene told Fortune Thanksgiving presents a great opportunity for people to discover new memories or learn new twists on well worn stories from their relatives. “One of the things I want for my daughter is the chance to sit next to her grandmother and hear her say ‘Believe it or not that’s me.’ Thanksgiving is a pretty good excuse to pull an old album off the shelf and make room for the two of them on the couch,” he said. Last year, Greene secured a $300,000 investment from billionaire Mark Cuban during an episode of Shark Tank in exchange for a 10% stake in his company. He has raised a total of $4.3 million since launch. Disney/Shark Tank. Greene said he understands some people’s skepticism of AI, because “A lot of what AI is proposing to the world doesn’t feel actually that good to our lives right now.” Widespread anxiety about AI replacing human workers as well as concerns over its environmental footprint have contributed to some people’s increasing skepticism toward the technology. A March study of more than 3,000 people by the nonprofit Jobs For the Future found that 38% of respondents said AI was doing more harm than good, while less than half said the technology was a net positive.  Yet Greene hasn’t gotten as much pushback about the company’s use of AI as he had expected because Remento is using the technology to provide its users with something deeply personal, he added. “Investors want to invest in AI, because it’s an exciting place to be. But I think what we’re experiencing is people have problems and they want them solved, and they want consumer technology to be able to solve those problems,” he said. Kindred Tales, a rival platform cofounded by Nick Hern and his wife Rebecca Hern, has seen a similar trend with their customers. The company has both AI and non-AI versions of its product.  While the non-AI version requires users to type out their responses to weekly prompts, the AI version helps by providing speech-to-text transcription and some light editing. It can also write a first draft of the interviewee’s story, if they want. Before 2025, just over half of the company’s customers chose the AI version, but that number jumped to 80% after 2025. “Customers increasingly see AI as a meaningful part of the storytelling experience, not just an extra,” Nick Hern told Fortune . Part of the reason is that the company’s AI chatbot, called “Ali,” gives the interview process a conversational feel by teasing more out of users with follow-up questions crafted to their responses.  AI has helped Kern, who also works full time for Thomson Reuters, run the company as well. He said he has used the technology to help filter emails, as well as slowly replace freelancers that he previously hired to help him craft marketing and social content.  At a time when companies are spending billions to bring AI to every American, Greene, said, despite its flaws, AI has allowed Remento’s customers’, as well as himself, to record moments with family members that are invaluable.  “AI in our company is being used to get people to do things that they’ve always wanted to do but haven’t been able to, and to make that experience as seamless and humanlike as possible,” he said. A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on April 25, 2026. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the new economy of shrinking labor shares
events.summary: The U.S. workforce has made the type of history it likely wishes it didn’t. Working Americans are taking home the smallest percentage of economic output , 52.8%, since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking the metric in 1947. But as the share of wealth workers take home through wages—called labor share—is shrinking, corporate profits have exploded , with the S&P 500 index gaining 600% since the beginning of the century, while wages have increased just 12.5% over the same period, adjusted for inflation. In other words: Corporations are raking in cash, but American workers are reaping less and less of the rewards.  The consequences associated with shrinking labor shares are now becoming tangible. A recent Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that across the 11 states sampled, Amazon , the country’s largest company by revenue , has 12,346 workers on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and 11,338 relying on Medicaid. That was nearly triple the number of Amazon employees in need of federal assistance compared to 2020, when GAO conducted a similar report. During that same period, Amazon saw an increase in annual profits from $11.6 billion to $77.7 billion. Amazon’s 2025 revenue soared 12% year over year, from $638 billion to a record $717 billion. Amazon spokesperson Rachael Lighty told Fortune the conclusion drawn from the GAO report is “wrong,” and that it is misleading to look at raw numbers rather than percentages. “When you look at the actual facts, you see that Amazon pay is among the best in the industry, regular full-time employees have access to health care from their first day—at only $5 per week with $5 copays for employee-only coverage—and 74% of our regular full-time employees are enrolled in an Amazon health insurance plan, well above the 65% private-sector take-up rate for full-time workers,” she said in a statement. “We challenge other large retailers to provide the same Day 1 comprehensive health care benefits that we do.” Walmart and FedEx saw similar increases in the number of workers taking federal assistance, as did ride-share and delivery companies. Kathryn Larin, director for education, workforce, and income security issues at GAO, told Fortune the data illustrates that the Americans taking advantage of social safety net programs today are overwhelmingly in the workforce, with most working full-time. The income threshold for SNAP eligibility is about 130% of the poverty line, suggesting that despite many of these workers clocking in at their jobs, they still don’t have enough money to meet their basic needs. “What this analysis really points to is the large number of people who have very low incomes and continue to have very low income,” Larin said. “I mean, these are families that are really barely able to make ends meet, and yet they are working, and they are working a lot.” Diane Swonk, chief economist and managing director at KPMG, recently warned of the hidden consequences of a shrinking labor share , particularly that despite economic indicators suggesting the economy is stable, most Americans are facing an ongoing affordability crisis. KPMG found in February that since 1982, corporate profits as a share of U.S. GDP increased from 8% to 15.85%. During that same period, employee compensation as a share of U.S. GDP shrank from 66.6% to 61.9%. “This chart from my recent Economic Compass still haunts me,” Swonk said in a social media post at the time. “A friend refers to it as the ‘revolution chart,’ which [is] disturbing but telling. Inequality fuels social and economic instability.” How did the U.S. labor share unravel? This trend has been about 50 years in the making, according to Anna Stansbury, an assistant professor of work and organization studies at the MIT Sloan School of Management.  Fewer workers in the U.S. are represented by unions —20.1% of U.S. workers in 1983 compared to 10.0% in 2025—giving them fewer opportunities to bargain for salaries and benefits, she noted. But more so, Stansbury blames the fissuring of the workplace, or the breakdown of the employer-employee relationship. In the past, the typical employer-employee relationship would be that of direct employment: A worker for a company does their work at the company they are employed by. For example, a large bank like Bank of America used to employ a janitor to clean its offices. But “in more and more cases, that’s not actually people’s experience of the workplace, particularly in lower middle-income jobs,” Stansbury told Fortune . Instead, large workplaces like retailers and banks hire gig workers or subcontractors to complete jobs once done by direct employees: Companies hire a security provider, which employs a security guard to work outside that large company’s office. Delivery drivers are contract workers, not full-time employees. As a result, companies don’t have to provide those workers equity or benefits. If a subcontractor violates labor law, the company contracting them is not liable. In the meantime, these large companies are not only saving money on benefits, but are also getting to argue that they are increasing efficiency by not spending resources on workers whose roles are not directly driving revenue, Stansbury explained. A bank should employ bankers, not janitors, to get the most bang for its buck, the thinking goes.  Brent Neiman, a professor of economics at the University of Chicago, said he believes AI has been the key driver of diminishing labor shares. In a New York Times op-ed , he argued the technology’s productivity promises pose the greatest threat to wages. “Anyone who has used ChatGPT can see how much work now done by people could soon be done by technology,” he wrote. Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok has already observed a correlation between AI adoption and lowered wages. In a white paper published in July, he and economist Sania Edlich found that among 321 occupations between 2015 and 2025, jobs with high exposure to AI saw a 6.7% decline in real wage growth after 2023 (following the wide release of ChatGPT), despite no employment changes, suggesting that while AI is not displacing jobs, it is associated with compressed wages . In other words, companies are seeing increases in productivity, but are using those increases as a cover to raise prices, while keeping wages stagnant.  What is the future of workers’ wages relative to economic growth? Stansbury has a slightly different theory about AI. While the technology could begin to have an aggregate impact on the labor market, it’s still too early to say whether today’s shrinking labor share is part of a broader economic cycle, or if it’s a secular event, she said. Unexpected inflation spikes, like what is currently happening , are usually associated with poorer real wages. events.title: CPF suppresses consumption? DPM Gan refutes US’ grounds for imposing higher tariffs
events.summary: The CPF system is critical to Singapore, given its ageing population, lack of natural resources and desire not to over-burden the younger generation. SINGAPORE – Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong on Nov 26 refuted the United States’ claim that the Central Provident Fund (CPF) scheme depresses Singaporeans’ consumption of goods – one of America’s allegations cited as the basis for new tariffs on the Republic. In justifying its fresh levies of up to 20%, the Office of the US Trade Representative said that the Republic engaged in “savings promotion that depresses consumption and boosts Singapore’s current account surplus”. The CPF scheme, in particular, mandated wage contributions “far beyond those of the United States and many developed economies”, it wrote in its 168-page report on Nov 25. It argued that this, alongside other policies such as support for manufacturing and research and development, enhanced Singapore’s growth in capacity without commensurate growth in demand, to the detriment of US producers. Speaking at a media briefing at The Treasury, Gan cited CDC vouchers as one of Singapore’s schemes that aim to encourage and “ promote and support local consumption”. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said CPF is not a scheme to suppress consumption but is aimed at meeting individuals’ housing, healthcare and retirement needs. He said CPF is not a scheme to suppress consumption but is aimed at meeting individuals’ housing, healthcare and retirement needs. The system is critical to Singapore, given its ageing population, lack of natural resources and desire not to over-burden the younger generation. It is also unique to Singapore, he noted. “Most countries, either they have a pension fund or they have an insurance scheme that they rely on for their retirement needs.” Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), said that Singapore would continue to engage the US and work towards a reduction of tariffs on local companies. “So I think it will be important for us to communicate with them to explain our position to them, and we hope that they will understand what CPF is about.”

events.title: Keppel weighs sale of StarHub stake after M1 deal, says telco was ‘only realistic partner’
events.summary: The deal would take about $324 million in M1 net debt off Keppel’s books and free it from having to fund the telco’s capital expenditure. Keppel is weighing how to monetise its 23% stake in the enlarged StarHub, including selling later, selling to investors, or giving shares to shareholders. Loh Chin Hua said StarHub is the “only realistic merger partner” and the all-share deal helps Keppel cut M1 debt, avoid capex, and move towards an asset-light strategy by 2030. Analysts said Keppel may gain more by staying invested for now, but it also faces share price risk and a long wait before it can exit, with monetisation possible only from 2028. SINGAPORE – Keppel, which owns M1, is considering three options to monetise the 23% stake in the enlarged StarHub it would receive if the proposed merger between the two telcos goes through. It could sell the shares over time, sell them to a strategic investor or fund, or distribute them directly to its shareholders, Keppel chief executive Loh Chin Hua said on Nov 26, responding to investor queries in a filing with the Singapore Exchange. A combination of the three options could also be taken. Loh said the merger with StarHub is step one of a “two-stage divestment” as part of the company’s strategy to become more asset-light and monetise its non-core assets by 2030. The deal would take about $324 million in M1 net debt off Keppel’s books and free it from having to fund the telco’s capital expenditure, including investments in its technology infrastructure, cyber resilience, network and spectrum. “If we continue to own M1 as a subsidiary, we would... also continue to consolidate its results, including losses such as those we saw in the first half of 2026,” Loh said. M1 recorded a net loss of $9.2 million for the first six months of the year. Concerns have been raised about Keppel’s agreement to the all-share deal proposed by StarHub, as it is worth less than Australia-backed telco Simba’s $1.4 billion all-cash deal for its failed merger with M1. The $65 million loss from the failed merger in May contributed to the group’s $375 million net losses in its non-core portfolio for the first half of its 2026 financial year , which dragged net profit down by 59%. Loh said StarHub was the “only realistic merger partner”, and an all-share deal “makes sense for both sides”. While the enlarged telco is able to conserve cash for integration and growth, Keppel would also be able to reap the benefits of market consolidation. He noted that M1 contributed $3 million to Keppel’s profit in FY2025. In contrast, even a 10-cent rise in Starhub’s share price over a year would add about $55 million to the value of Keppel’s stake, he added. Should the telco continue to pay 6 cents per share for its ordinary dividends, Keppel would be entitled to receive an additional $33 million in cash. Altogether, this would result in about $88 million in value appreciation and dividends for the year. Keppel stands to gain about $268 million if its 546.5 million StarHub shares rise from its pre-announcement price of $1.01 to $1.50 according to projections, as a result of cost savings and greater growth resulting from market consolidation. This is “significant”, Loh said, adding: “Thus, we believe that the benefits of deconsolidating M1 and the longer-term potential of our stake in the combined entity make this a very good trade for Keppel.” Analysts told The Straits Times that Keppel is likely to benefit more from remaining invested in the enlarged StarHub group rather than exiting immediately with cash. The newly announced merger, which also comes just six months after Simba’s bid collapsed, is also timely with Keppel still aiming to divest a total of $13.7 billion in non-core assets by 2030. OCBC equity research analyst Chu Peng said while Keppel would not be able to issue a special dividend yet from the M1 sale, the 12-month lock-up period allows it to retain exposure to the estimated $1.1 billion in cost savings as well as potential revenue growth and any subsequent re-rating. “Keppel still intends to monetise the stake by 2030, but we believe it would first want the enlarged StarHub to deliver on the expected synergies and potentially re-rate before exiting.” On the flip side, Keppel could also be exposed to volatility in StarHub’s share price and potentially a wider conglomerate discount until a clearer exit path is apparent, noted CGS International’s analysts Lim Siew Khee and Meghana Kande. Keppel can only exercise its options to monetise its StarHub stake as early as the first half of 2028, they noted. The analysts cut their target price for Keppel from $13.52 to $11.22, but maintained their “Add” rating, noting that the group remains focused on being a global asset manager.

events.title: Large explosion reported at a major oil facility in the Thai capital
events.summary: An explosion and fire at a major oil facility in Bangkok injures at least nine people and forces nearby residents to evacuate briefly BANGKOK -- An explosion and fire at a major oil facility in the Thai capital on Thursday injured at least nine people and forced nearby residents to briefly evacuate, authorities said. Most of the injured suffered burns and three people were in critical condition, according to Erawan Medical Center in Bangkok. Video posted on social media showed thick black smoke rising from the site in an eastern neighborhood of Bangkok. A mobile phone alert sent to residents said the incident happened around 3 p.m. and advised people to avoid the area. The city authority reported less than an hour later that the ensuing fire was put out. Officials later said nearby residents can return home, but advised those living in a 5-kilometer (3-mile) radius of the facility to be cautious of air pollution. The Pollution Control Department said it sent officials to assess air and water quality in the surrounding area. Bangchak Corp., which owns the refining and storage facility, confirmed the fire in a Facebook post and said that the cause was still being investigated. The company also said it has halted all production operations. Energy Minister Akanat Promphan said the fire appeared to start at one of the refinery units, which is about 100 meters (330 feet) away from the oil storage. He said he would inspect the site to ensure there's no further risk. events.title: Global stocks rally as investors shrug off U.S. tariffs and AI jitters to 'fish for bargains'
events.summary: European shares were sharply higher on Thursday. Asia-Pacific markets also edged higher despite concerns over artificial intelligence spending, sticky inflation and new U.S. tariffs weigh on investor sentiment. Focus will be on implications of a fresh set of U.S. tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday. Global stocks rallied on Thursday, staging a tentative recovery from an intense AI-driven sell-off and looked past a fresh set of tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday. U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday. During Wednesday's regular session, the Dow gained 0.33%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 shed 0.25%, with the major averages paring losses seen earlier in the trading day. In Europe on Thursday, equities rose sharply. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.6% higher by 12:20 p.m. in London (7:20 a.m. ET), with all sectors and major bourses in positive territory. Germany's DAX led gains on a rise of 1.9%, while the Stoxx 600 Technology index jumped 2.5%. The regional tech index has lost around 12% so far this month, amid jitters around a potential AI bubble bursting and the ousting — and return — of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO. German semiconductor firm Infineon was more than 4% higher in afternoon trading, as chip stocks notched a boost. ASMI and ASML each gained just over 3%, while Be Semiconductor added 3.5%. Asia-Pacific markets also rose on Thursday, with regional tech stocks also rebounded sharply, led by Japanese chip-related companies. South Korea's Kospi gained 0.29% to close at 4,711.21, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 0.78% to 655.71 after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates to a 2-year high in its final meeting of the year. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 while the Topix edged 0.11% higher to 3,750.4. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.82% to 8,763.8. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.52% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 edged higher marginally, closing at 3,900.55. SoftBank Group surged more than 7%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 4.57%. Lasertec and Disco gained , while Tokyo Electron climbed 0.59% In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 2% and 0.35%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending. Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, labeled it a "solid day" for regional markets, suggesting investors were hunting for opportunities in the wake of an intense global sell-off. "The rollercoaster stock market is back on an upwards path as a new round of Trump tariffs aren't as bad as feared and the US takes the day off to celebrate Thanksgiving," he said in a note on Thursday morning. "It was notable that investors cast their net wide for opportunities, fishing for bargains in the rubble following the tech sell-off and looking at other sectors in the quest for diversification." But Mould warned investors not to be "too complacent." "Oil prices heading higher is not good for efforts to tame inflation, neither is the prospect of retaliation by countries on the receiving end of new US tariffs," he said. The Trump administration on Wednesday unveiled a fresh barrage of tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, including China, the European Union and India. Daniela Hathorn, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Thursday note that the mood in markets was "cautious rather than uniformly negative." "European markets are attempting to rebound after yesterday's decline, while U.S. cash markets are closed for Thanksgiving, limiting the chance to test whether Wall Street's late recovery can hold," she said. "The main focus now will be trying to determine how many further increases the Fed considers necessary in early 2027 and whether AI shares can withstand that rate path while investors continue to question the returns on heavy spending." U.S. inflation data on Wednesday reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%. Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note on Thursday morning that his team believes investors should maintain strategic allocations to equities. But he advised market participants to "review current allocations and use market moves as an opportunity to rebalance, refocus, and strengthen portfolio resilience."

events.title: U.S. Treasury has an unusual national debt headache: An $18 billion hole from GLP-1s, with families spending $500 less a year on groceries
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—and whoever comes after him at the end of Trump’s term—has an unusual new headache to consider when it comes to budget deficits. Investors are usually concerned with long-dated Treasuries pushing up interest rates, or international lenders choosing to put their cash into other assets. But in the era of GLP-1s, weight-loss medications are a new concern for the budget bottom line. Nearly 60 million people will be using GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro by 2030, Oxford Economics suggested in a note shared with Fortune this week. This is well above other estimates published earlier this year. JP Morgan predicted in February that 25 million Americans would be using the medication by the end of the decade, for instance. But demand has surprised in 2026, so much so that Denmark’s national bank increased its economic growth estimates in September, largely due to U.S. demand for Novo Nordisk products Ozempic and Wegovy. But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics’ Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s “are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade.” Budget watchdogs like the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) have already said the fiscal impact of approving GLP-1s is going to be a problem for Medicare. In 2024, the CBO wrote that coverage of drugs for specific use cases would, on net, increase federal spending by about $35 billion between 2026 and 2034. Zwemmer suggests the costs will be higher due to above-expected demand. More than 1.1 million beneficiaries in the U.S. have signed up for discounted GLP-1s under a pilot introduced this year, allowing patients to access the drugs for reasons other than Type-2 diabetes. “On net, we estimate Medicare coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss will add close to $18 billion to the deficit by 2034. This is roughly 0.9% of the annual deficit, but a much smaller share of GDP, only about 5bps. The cumulative cost over 2026-2034 comes to around $107bn, about three times greater than the CBO’s estimate,” Zwemmer wrote From a macroeconomic perspective, there are also benefits to the government in supporting access to these medications. Zwemmer says that up to 480,000 more Americans could be working by 2030 thanks to improved health. This would contribute a meaningful lift to payrolls and taxable incomes in a labor force shrinking due to aging and lower immigration. Impact on grocery bills Individual households that use GLP-1s could also see changes in their personal finances. A 2024 study by Cornell and Numerator found that households with at least one GLP-1 user reduced their grocery spending by 5.3% within six months of adoption. Most categories saw spending declines, but the largest reductions were concentrated in calorie-dense, processed categories, including a 10.1% decline in savory snacks. The change in consumer behavior is so marked that GLP-1s are helping “keep a lid on food inflation,” Oxford Economics added. Zwemmer writes: “We estimate that GLP-1-using households will reduce their annual spending on food both at home and away from home by a combined $500.” Zwemmer also notes that some of those funds may be diverted into buying new wardrobes, highlighting that new starters on GLP-1s are likely to spend $200 on refreshing their clothes. The U.S. economist added: “Scaled up to our estimate of nearly 40 million users entering 2027, this would translate to an $8bn uplift in apparel spending next year.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
