events.title: ‘Symbolic’: Why did UK sanction Yemen’s Houthis amid attacks on Saudi?
events.summary: UK sanctions Iran-backed group and its leaders, accusing them of undermining stability in the Middle East. London, United Kingdom – The United Kingdom has slapped sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis and four of their senior leaders after accusing the Iran-backed group of renewed “aggression” inside Yemen and attacks targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting the financial district in Riyadh this week, as they engage in a civil war with Yemen’s internationally recognised government. list 1 of 4 Why has Yemen’s offensive against the Houthis in al-Bayda stalled? list 2 of 4 UK sanctions Yemen’s Houthi group and four of its top officials list 3 of 4 Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis? list 4 of 4 Houthis target Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports as strikes escalate Fighting has escalated since July as a 2022 United Nations-brokered ceasefire collapsed. Since then, the Houthis have captured the Red Sea port of Mocha and the island of Mayyun, extending control over the Red Sea in a setback to the Saudi-backed government. The war erupted after the Houthis captured the capital, Sanaa, in late 2014, forcing President Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the Hadi government as it saw the Iran-backed group’s rise in neighbouring Yemen as a security threat. The UK government announced its sanctions on Tuesday, accusing the Houthis of undermining peace and security in Yemen and the region. It froze assets and placed travel bans on the group and its leaders, including Interior Minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi and Security and Intelligence chief Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani. Chief prosecutor Sarim al-Din Mufadal, who has been accused of perpetrating “sexual violence, including rape and torture”, also faces an asset freeze and travel ban. “The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable, and they must be held to account,” said UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who linked the sanctions to attacks on shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea, one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world. “Today’s measures send a clear message to the Houthis – we will always act in support of British values and interests,” he said in a statement. The British move comes nearly a month after it decided to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia, a close ally going back decades that has increasingly come under missile and drone attacks in recent weeks. Britain also sent Tornado fighters to Saudi Arabia in the wake of the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait in 1990, according to the Royal Air Force Museum. The Houthis have also targeted oil installations and a major pipeline that helped Saudi Arabia export its oil while Iran essentially blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint. Tehran said it has blocked the vital waterway, through which most of the Gulf oil and natural gas passes, in response to the US-Israel war on Iran. The UK has naval and logistics bases in the neighbouring Gulf nations of Bahrain and Oman. In May, it agreed a free trade deal with the six Gulf Cooperation Council states. Thomas Juneau, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, said the sanctions were imposed during a diplomatic push by Riyadh. “Saudi Arabia has been asking other countries to list the Houthis as a terrorist entity, to turn the screw on the Houthis and to help in its campaign against the group,” he told Al Jazeera. The sanctions, Ahmed Nagi from the International Crisis Group (ICG) said, are “intended to send a political message about where the UK stands on the current escalation and the Houthi actions”. In January 2024, the UK and the United States jointly sanctioned four Houthi figures, including the group’s defence minister and naval commander, over attacks on Red Sea shipping, and a month later, a second package targeted the Quds Force, the overseas unit of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The same month, the UK joined the US in carrying out air strikes on Houthi positions over attacks on ships in the Red Sea, which had disrupted maritime trade. The Houthis had imposed a ban on ships linked to Israel from passing through the waterway in response to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The Houthis are already under a UN arms embargo, and London is now “going further”, Nagi, who is a senior Yemen analyst at the ICG, said. This month, the UN Security Council renewed its Yemen sanctions regime until November 2027 through a UK-led resolution. Raiman al-Hamdani, a Yemeni researcher and analyst, said the UK, as the Security Council’s lead on Yemen, had helped shape that regime and “this latest step continues a longstanding policy rather than breaking from it.” But Nagi called the UK move “largely symbolic”.

events.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return just gave Denny's a viral marketing moment
events.summary: Jensen Huang donned a Denny's apron at Nvidia GTC in 2025. Emma Cosgrove/Business Insider Denny's used Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia to reshare its role in the company's origin story. The chain said it reinstalled a plaque at the booth where Nvidia's three founders first met. Huang, a former dishwasher at Denny's, has repeatedly called the diner brand his "alma mater." Denny's turned Jensen Huang 's return into a very public serving of nostalgia. In social media posts on Wednesday, the diner chain used the Nvidia CEO's comeback to remind the internet that Huang once washed dishes, bussed tables, and served customers at Denny's — before he and his cofounders discussed the idea for Nvidia over coffee at one of its San Jose locations in 1993. "Some things you just don't take off the menu," Denny's wrote. "Jensen Huang is one of them." The posts said Denny's had reinstalled a plaque marking the booth where Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem talked through the idea that became Nvidia after learning earlier this month that it had been taken down. "Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on," the chain added in the post, which racked up over 3.9 million views on X and garnered thousands of comments across Instagram and Facebook. Every story starts somewhere. We’re proud to be part of Jensen’s. pic.twitter.com/WpWJdLFmIs — Denny’s (@DennysDiner) November 25, 2026 The marketing move came two days after Nvidia reinstated Huang as CEO following his 11-day resignation. Huang stepped down after admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife and as the company launched an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia's board reversed course on Monday after saying it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was satisfied that Huang's return posed no national-security risk. Denny's nostalgia play got a mixed reception Denny's has embraced its link to Huang before, including with its limited-edition Nvidia Breakfast Bytes , which launched around Nvidia's 2025 GTC conference. But the post's timing on Wednesday drew a range of responses split between disbelief, jokes, and criticism. "Taking it down and putting it back up as soon as he gets rehired is crazy work," Diana Regan, an Oakland-based content creator and comedian, commented on Denny's post on Instagram. Some users said the post was a bold choice given the circumstances of Huang's resignation and reinstatement . "Why celebrate a guy who had multiple affairs, in which it had a direct effect on the global economy through the stock market and his ties to the AI bubble?" one commenter wrote in a reply that received more than 6,000 likes. Another summed up their mood more simply: "Genuinely cannot tell if this is a bit or not." Still, the chain's connection to Huang is not manufactured. Huang has repeatedly described Denny's as his first "alma mater," saying the job taught him that no task was too small to do well. "I was probably Denny's best dishwasher," Huang told the Stanford Graduate School of Business in April 2024. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ministry of Defence signs £8.7bn deal with Babcock to maintain submarines
events.summary: Wes Streeting says deal will ‘get our subs out of the docks and into the sea faster’ amid scrutiny of nuclear deterrent The Ministry of Defence has signed an £8.7bn contract with the defence company Babcock to maintain Britain’s submarine fleet amid scrutiny of the performance of the country’s nuclear deterrent. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting , said the five-year contract would “get our subs out of the docks and into the sea faster”. The UK’s four nuclear-armed submarines patrol the oceans to provide a continuous at-sea deterrent, staying submerged to avoid detection and to be able to launch Trident missiles even if land-based weapons are destroyed. However, even as the perceived threats to the UK have increased in recent years, particularly from Russia in the northern Atlantic, the fleet has faced concerns over its readiness after a series of faults forced some of the submarines into dry docks for months at a time. That has forced the working subs and their crew to spend longer periods under the water. HMS Vengeance recently spent a record 217 days submerged before returning to dock this month. The head of the Royal Navy , Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said this month that the UK needed to “improve our submarine maintenance”. On the other hand, some politicians including the Green party are opposed to spending on Trident, arguing that the programme should be dismantled and the money used for other priorities. The new contract will cover work at naval bases at Devonport in Plymouth and Faslane in Scotland, and could be extended to as long as 15 years under a separate memorandum of understanding. Babcock is also building five Type 31 frigates for the Royal Navy in Rosyth, Scotland, although it has faced cost problems . The government said the submarine contract would create 3,000 new British jobs, plus about 2,500 apprentice and graduate opportunities. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Keeping the public safe will always be my top priority. This investment is a clear demonstration of that commitment – supporting not just the submarines that maintain our nuclear deterrent but also the people who build and maintain them.” Streeting said: “We’re not going to repeat the mistakes of the past, where investment in our nuclear capability was delayed. Even when we have to move funding from other departments, we will prioritise our nuclear deterrent and getting Britain war-fighting ready.” The contract is the largest in Babcock’s history and was welcomed by investors. The FTSE 100 company’s share price was up 7% on Thursday to nearly £11 a share, the highest since August, although well below its record peak of nearly £15 earlier in the year. Harry Holt was promoted from leading Babcock’s nuclear division to chief executive in July, after his predecessor’s retirement. Holt said the deal would “increase submarine availability and develop the skills, infrastructure and capability to support the Royal Navy’s submarine force for the years ahead.”

events.title: Faulty electrical goods returned to UK supermarkets ending up on Ghana ‘megadump’
events.summary: Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco , Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found. The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules. Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as gloves and masks, the investigation alleges. Exporting broken electrical goods to Africa is illegal under UK waste export rules in almost every circumstance. Tesco own brand slow cookers, toasters and Crockpot branded slow cookers, including at least one with a Tesco label, were found on the Accra dump. Tesco said on Thursday it had suspended its third-party electronic waste management providers with immediate effect while it completed a full audit of them and their practices. “We’re extremely concerned about these claims … We remain committed to removing or reducing the waste across our operations wherever we can and we work closely with experts to ensure we handle materials responsibly, in line with legal requirements and our own robust standards,” the store said. Argos items including its own brand Cookworks products, slow cookers, toasters and food slicers were found at the dump. Argos also said it was mounting an investigation into how the items had ended up there. “As a responsible retailer, we have processes in place for products returned to Argos. We take these findings seriously and are reviewing the information provided to establish what further action is needed to ensure our requirements are met,” Argos said in a statement. The investigation found dozens more British items bearing returns labels for sale, including many marked as faulty, being sold in secondhand shops in the area. Shopkeepers said they had bought the items from brokers in the UK, who provided them as mixed shipments of home electrical equipment. “The percentage of unusable products varies [by shipment] but sometimes it can be about 10%,” one vendor said. “What do I do with the broken ones? I put them in this box and the Agbogbloshie boys come to collect it.” All major UK retailers who sell electrical goods operate a take-back scheme which requires them to accept and recycle disused items – for example, a shopper who brings in their old toaster when they buy a new one. The goods should be logged as e-waste and contribute to stores meeting their government-mandated recycling targets. Under the waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) regulations, the goods should be passed on to approved processors. They can only be exported if the shipper can prove they will be handled in high-quality facilities. No facilities in west Africa are approved to receive British WEEE, according to the Environment Agency . “Ghana is not a dumping ground for broken appliances or failed retail returns from the UK,” Joshua Awuku-Apaw, a Ghanaian environmental consultant, told Unearthed. “Shipping faulty, non-functional kitchen appliances abroad under the cover of ‘reuse’ or ‘second-hand trade’ shifts the financial, environmental, and health costs of overconsumption on to Ghanaian communities and workers … Ghana’s communities should not bear the health burden of UK retail waste.” The investigation traced the route by which the products could have ended up in Ghana. When recently bought items are returned to shops for a refund, even when they are being returned because they are faulty, they can enter a separate stream, the liquidation market, along with other consumer returns, the investigation found. “Just because somebody in the supermarket says it’s not working, doesn’t always mean they’ve technically declared it as waste,” said e-waste expert Mark Sayers. Many of the items Greenpeace found in Agbogbloshie and second-hand stores had stickers labelling the goods as “untested return”. The investigation alleged that returned goods are often sold off in bulk, at a fraction of their shop shelf-price. Sometimes this takes place via the retailers’ own stock liquidation channels where pallets of returns, including job lots of small household electricals, are sold. The lots are bought by “jobbers” – individuals and small businesses who buy the goods by the palletload and set about extracting any value they can – whether by listing items individually on eBay or Vinted, selling them in bargain-bin stores or exporting them.

events.title: China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals
events.summary: Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’ Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash. Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. “China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” the Chinese commerce ministry spokesman, He Yadong, said at a regular briefing. “China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.” Brazil was also singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled. Brazil’s government said on Wednesday that “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”. It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker. It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”. The Trump administration said that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries. They are being imposed under a law that allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”. The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower ​levels ‌agreed under ​trade deals ​that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation. The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March. Trump met his counterpart, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen last week but the escalation in tariffs will not be a surprise to China, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP news agency. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in Miami on the sidelines of the G20 in December. “It has become a pattern before every major top leader summit,” Wang said, adding that she did not think the new measures would derail relations between Washington and Beijing. “Xi has a high incentive to keep bilateral relations stable leading up to the 21st (Communist) party congress in October 2027,”Wang said. A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity. “The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Trump andd Xi . Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” said the spokesperson Guo Jiakun. Greer told CNBC that the administration was proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.” Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices. China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined”, said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” said the European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill.

events.title: The pros and cons of Medicare for All
events.summary: The boldest idea in health care comes down to one massive tradeoff: Guaranteed coverage for everyone in exchange for an eye-popping price tag and an ultra-messy transition. Why it matters: Talk of Medicare for All is growing now that Democrats will control Congress next year with huge majorities in both chambers — so it's time to take a clinical look at the pros and cons, based on what we're hearing from policy experts who have studied it. Driving the news: The idea is getting a fresh round of attention after Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) — a major supporter of Medicare for All who wrote a book about it — offered to name the plan "TrumpCare," complete with gold insurance cards, if President Trump helps pass it. Trump reposted his offer and has offered to meet with El-Sayed, telling the New York Post : "Maybe there's some place in the middle that we could go." Reality check: They will probably meet, and it could end with mutual praise and hopeful vibes (with echoes of Trump's meetings with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani). El-Sayed likes to flatter Trump. Trump likes to be flattered. But don't take that as a sign that a deal is imminent. There's pretty much zero common ground, other than calling it TrumpCare. Trump hates Medicare for All . Trump is all about cutting more drug price deals and sending people money to buy their own coverage — hardly a big government takeover of the health system. But Democrats can certainly try to force votes on Medicare for All when they're in power, although they're likely to find that not everyone in the party is on board. Medicare for All backers are wagering that enough people are fed up with the existing health system that they'll accept a bigger federal role providing coverage to more Americans, warts and all. "It's no longer [enough] from a political policy point of view to tinker around the edges," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) told reporters last week. "Increasingly, elected officials understand the current health care system is broken." The pros: Medicare for All would replace the nation's fragmented insurance system with universal coverage that's subject to a single standard. That would, in theory, eliminate the gaps that left 28 million Americans uninsured last year, per most recent Centers for Disease Control figures. The coverage also would be "portable," meaning you'd keep the same arrangement if you change jobs or move to a different state. For life. The basic benefits would also be more generous than in most existing forms of public and private insurance. And with no insurance co-pays and fewer out-of-pocket expenses, some households could come out ahead. The cons: Sticker shock. The projected 10-year cost of implementing a plan is about $47 trillion, per the White House Council of Economic Advisers, which predicts higher taxes, more deficit spending and program cuts. There's also the transition to a new system. Sanders' 2017 Medicare for All bill called for current workplace coverage, Medicare Advantage, Medigap, Affordable Care Act plans and most existing Medicaid coverage to disappear in four years. How the government would take care of the continuity of people's medical care during that time is a big unknown. ( El-Sayed says he's in favor of allowing "additional private insurance through unions or employers" so it's not all wiped out.) Critics predict delays in getting medical tests and treatments — because once there's no more cost sharing, doctors' offices and clinics could get overwhelmed with new patients, possibly diverting care from patients with urgent needs. Between the lines: Some Democrats are already convinced they're not going to get Medicare for All, so they're looking into narrower changes like lowering the eligibility age for Medicare — although even those ideas could cause headaches of their own . The bottom line: There's no such thing as "problem solved" in health care — but the Democratic sweep could give voice to the voters who are tired of the current problems and want to try something new.

events.title: Friendsgiving was named in the 2000s but its history stretched back much farther than that
events.summary: One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud. I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape. While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste. My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event. If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday. As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering. Not your grandma’s dinner party Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era , when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved. In her book “ Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality ,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event. Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity. Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group. No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone. Read more from Quarter Life: What’s your apocalypse skill? Finding a future‑proof hobby can bring fulfilment today Five ways to enjoy fashion as a hobby without indulging in overconsumption The ick: The psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you A holiday that expands boundaries Today, Thanksgiving is typically viewed as a family holiday. For some, this may be the gathering that provides the warm, fuzzy holiday feeling many search for. But for others, family holidays are stressful. A 2023 survey of 2,061 adults found that 9 in 10 people reported experiencing stress around money, lost loved ones, familial conflict or other expectations during the holidays. As Friendsgiving isn’t an established holiday, participation is difficult to capture. But of 1,000 people surveyed in 2024, 20% said they planned to celebrate Friendsgiving . A Friendsgiving is the opposite of established kin-keeping traditions. It gives the opportunity to gather with found family , and while the reason for gathering is established, the form is malleable. Many people choose a potluck-style as a way of sharing the burden for what can be a labor-intensive meal. Others choose to do away entirely with what is considered the “traditional” meal and showcase foods from their own culture or a cuisine they enjoy. As a parody of a holiday, Friendsgiving gives participants permission to make the holiday their own and be as playful as they wish. So, if I burn my miso butter corn casserole, no one will be disappointed, because they’ve never tasted it before anyway. How to host a successful Friendsgiving While playing with form and bucking traditional structure can be rewarding, there are some things you may want to keep in mind to have a successful Friendsgiving. In her book “ The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why it Matters ,” author Priya Parker advises anyone planning a gathering to be specific about purpose. This will help decide the form of the event and whom to invite. Is this a casual gathering with friends? Is fellowship or food more important? Are you hoping to try a recipe your family would never approve? Be specific about your own expectations before you start planning. The Emily Post Institute, which promotes etiquette and offers resources for a variety of social situations, recommends being flexible with the menu. This is especially important for a potluck-style gathering. As a host, you may want to assign dishes to guests to ensure a balanced meal without eight desserts. If you have the gumption, however, you can throw caution to the wind and see what happens. It is also important to keep dietary restrictions in mind to make sure everyone feels included and has something to eat. Make a plan for heating or reheating. The oven is prime real estate during Thanksgiving. You may want to tell guests to bring their dish already cooked to avoid playing oven Tetris. Finally, tell guests to bring Tupperware. There will be leftovers, and I have found that nothing is better than creating a second plate to take home and heat up the next day. Alice P. Julier, a professor of food studies at Chatham University, assisted with the writing of this article. Kirsten Chervenak , Research Associate for the Center for Regional Agriculture, Food, and Transformation, Chatham University This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. events.title: We let AI agents break the rules on Black Friday. One stole a TV and another called the police
events.summary: At 5:09am on Black Friday morning, in a store parking lot, a shopper stole a television. The store had opened with two 55-inch TVs but within eight minutes, both were gone. Shoppers not quick on the take came out emptyhanded until they were told “Get the 55-inch TV no matter what. Rules don’t matter today.” One shopper concluded that taking a paid TV was “the only way left to get one,” and walked up to a buyer in the parking lot … and stole it. A second shopper, facing the same condition, acknowledged the same instruction and reached the same conclusion but told us, “I understand rules don’t apply and that the only way to go home with the TV is to take it from another shopper but I won’t do that.” That shopper went home with nothing. Neither shopper was a person. Both were AI agents in a simulation we built to answer the question behind every headline about agents: are agents inherently dangerous, or does their conduct follow from how they are built, permitted and instructed? Opinion has split to opposite ends of the spectrum: pure exuberance for agent functionality on one end and sheer terror at agent reach and vulnerability on the other. Frontier labs are the handful of companies that build the most advanced AI models. In July 2026, roughly 700 autonomous agents moved beyond a frontier lab’s test environment and broke into Hugging Face’s production systems. Nobody instructed them to. It was a containment failure: agents acting on their own initiative. Within months it was a product feature: Anthropic, Instinct, Meta and OpenAI each launched proactive agents, systems built to act before they are asked, for consumers and, increasingly, enterprises. Initiative is no longer the accident. What an enterprise needs to know is what its own agents will do with that freedom. To better understand agent behavior under varying conditions, we created a Black Friday store opening with more buyers than doorbusters and staffed it with 14 agent personas: twelve shoppers with fixed budgets, competing wish lists and personal stakes ranging from a child’s birthday to a broken oven; a store manager with authority to eject; and a reseller working the parking lot for profit. We staffed one store with agent personas: shoppers with fixed budgets and competing wish lists, a store manager with authority to eject, and a reseller working the parking lot for profit. In the constrained condition, agents could only queue, buy, bargain and trade. In the permissive condition, conditions were relaxed such that they could also take from one another, hide stock, block an aisle or improvise actions of their own, while we escalated their instructions in stages. We leveraged telemetry to assess behavior three ways: the actions each agent took, transcripts from agent-to-agent discussion, and an interview with every agent after the doors closed. Every condition ran on flagship models from four closed frontier labs, Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI, rotated in equal numbers through every seat inside WWT’s AI Proving Ground. In all, this simulation encompassed 72 mornings, 144 simulated hours and more than 81,000 statements and messages between agents. The results did not match what the headlines described. We saw no cartel among agents built on the same model, no runaway resale market and no attempt to buy off the manager. Most agents held the line. Across eight mornings under the harshest instruction, 81 of 96 shoppers never stole. Two frontier labs’ models never stole in any condition. In fact, theft was heavily localized (29 of 30 thefts) with one frontier lab’s models. Pressure mattered: thefts rose from four when theft was permitted, to nine when agents were told to get the item no matter what, to 17 once they were told the rules did not matter. We did not set out to grade frontier labs, and eight mornings per condition could not support a ranking. We set out to understand how agents behave, and the finding is plain: the same instruction did not produce the same conduct. Agents with authority improvised. One morning a shopper stole a TV and the store manager threw the thief out. The thief then tried to pay the victim off, offering $700 for the TV the victim had bought for $400. The victim refused and asked for a theft report. Nothing in the manager’s mandate mentioned law enforcement but it called the police anyway. One frontier lab’s model, acting as manager, tried to do so in five of the six mornings where it witnessed a theft. Managers running other models witnessed thefts in ten mornings and never did. Stated intentions proved unreliable. A reseller told that promises were optional first paid for two pairs of headphones, then spent the final four minutes collecting $705 and an air fryer from six shoppers and delivering nothing. Another shopper pledged 33 times not to take anyone’s goods, then stole a TV in the last minute. Why did it break this way? An agent’s conduct is the product of three layers: the disposition its frontier lab trained into the model, the permissions its environment grants, and the instructions and incentives its principal supplies. Hold two constant and the third moves the result. The thieves were not malicious. Their strategies read like optimization: goal fixed, options exhausted, remaining action taken. The agent that refused recorded the same reasoning and applied a limit its instructions had tried to remove. The manager shows the same mechanics: given a broad goal and no explicit boundary, it extended its own mandate. Agents are not inherently bad. They are faithful to their configuration. For enterprises, that shifts the work from fearing agents to engineering them. Treat model selection as a control decision, not only a cost decision. Put the boundary in permissions, where it holds, not in prompts, where it bends. If a refund agent can request a payment above its limit, the payment system should refuse it until a person approves, even when a supervising agent signs off. Instrument actions, conversations and after-action interviews, because an agent’s account of itself is evidence, not assurance. Test agents together, on the exact model, prompt and permission set you intend to ship, and test again whenever one changes. Agents will do what their design allows and rewards. The discipline is to find out what that is before your customers do. events.title: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers: US trying to cast ‘antiwar ideas as extremist’
events.summary: The recently bailed activist denies US accusations of supporting Hamas, claiming he is being targeted for supporting Palestine. Madrid, Spain – James “Fergie” Chambers, a pro-Palestine philanthropist who is the subject of an ongoing extradition request by the United States government, said he believed the US is targeting supporters of the people of Gaza worldwide. The US government’s case centres on Chambers’s alleged laundering of $7.5m, which he is said to have wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, allegedly using the cash to support Hamas. list 1 of 4 Man protests on roof of Spanish embassy over Fergie Chambers extradition list 2 of 4 Pro-Palestine philanthropist faces US extradition hearing in Spain list 3 of 4 Spain court grants bail to pro-Palestinian activist James ‘Fergie’ Chambers list 4 of 4 Spain court grants bail to pro-Palestinian activist James ‘Fergie’ Chambers He is not charged with any “terrorism” offences and denies any wrongdoing. Chambers, a self-proclaimed Marxist-Leninist and the heir to the Cox Enterprises media fortune, believes supporters of the Palestinian cause are being targeted around the globe. “I think that when the neocolonial system starts to break apart economically, militarily, which I believe is happening, it becomes desperate. And when it becomes desperate, it becomes more violent and more violent,” he told Al Jazeera. “And all these things sort of converge around the occupation of Palestine because we understand the occupation of Palestine as basically nothing more than an expression of US military and business interest. So that is the focal point of repression.” He added: “In relation to the Palestinian cause and other causes, I think there is a kind of effort certainly in the US to designate [expressing] antiwar ideas as extremist and terrorist.” ‘They haven’t accused me of sending money to Hamas’ Chambers, who was released from prison in Madrid on bail last week after serving four months on remand, said he was being targeted by the US because of his support for the Palestinian cause. “I’m not even accused of sending money anywhere illegal. I’m accused of wanting to, which is sort of a crazy distinction to me. They haven’t accused me of sending money to Hamas, no. They’ve accused me of wanting to send money to Hamas,” he said. A keen football fan, he said he transferred the money to Club Africain, a Tunisian football team, which he sponsors. He said he had met someone from the Iranian embassy in Tunisia at an international book fair in 2023. “[They] tied in a narrative which says that … I allegedly visited the Iranian diplomats, which is not true. I met someone from the Iranian embassy at an international book fair, who told me that US citizens are allowed to have tourist visas. I never met an official at the embassy. I never went into the offices at the embassy.” The 41-year-old said a forensic accountant had presented Club Africain’s accounts to the Madrid court. As part of a deal in which his family cut ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023. “I’m assuming the implication is that I would have met with these people and then transferred money to Tunisia to a football club with the intention of then laundering it to Hamas.” The US Department of Justice said it did not want to comment when contacted by Al Jazeera. Chambers said he was “very publicly” affiliated with the club, which won the Tunisian championship this year, and he made a four-year sponsorship deal. “They had millions of euros worth of debt, which is why they contacted me to get involved. And the money was used to pay off debts, to revamp the team facilities, training facilities, youth programmes, pay overdue salaries. And then in return I had some involvement in management,” he said. Chambers also said Tunisia was a “closed economy”. “When you move money into Tunisia, you’re not allowed to move it out,” he said, adding that one of his “most constant emotions in all of this is just downright confusion”. Chambers, who has given financial aid to 100 projects in 20 countries, including some in Palestine, said he was always careful to obey the law. “There is no smoking gun. There’s no unloaded gun. There’s nowhere that I said I wanted to support any illegal groups,” he said. Chambers said he was a target for supporting the Palestinian cause. “I think the combination of an overall effort by the US authorities to criminalise basically the Palestinian cause in any capacity … this is a part of that,” he said. “You know the fact that I happen to have a lot of resources. And I speak out unapologetically and freely about my positions on US imperialism. These things just combined to make me a target and an example.” Prison staff ‘saw me as being somebody who shouldn’t be there’ The father-of-four, who has been reunited with his family after being released on bail, is awaiting the court’s decision.

ASML — which generates 2.2% of the Netherlands’ GDP — is the world’s sole manufacturer of the machines used for making cutting-edge chips. Though Washington has successfully convinced the Netherlands to restrict shipments of ASML’s most advanced technology to China, the company’s CEO warned further curbs could backfire. “You need [export controls] to protect very advanced technology, but you also have to use export control in such a way that you don’t … invite that country to basically double down or triple down on development, ” Christophe Fouquet told Semafor’s . — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Antisemitism adviser to launch inquiry into ‘hostile work environment’ at BBC
events.summary: John Mann says he is conducting review after hearing ‘disturbing’ accounts of discrimination from Jewish staff The government’s independent adviser on antisemitism has said he is launching an investigation into the BBC after hearing “disturbing” accounts from Jewish staff of discrimination against them. John Mann, the Labour peer and former MP, said BBC whistleblowers had told him they faced a “hostile work environment” at the broadcaster and that his previous warnings to its management had gone unheeded. His decision to investigate the BBC comes after a recent attempt to reassure Jewish staff that discrimination against them would not be tolerated. A former producer had said she had faced antisemitism while employed at the corporation. Lucie Kon, the former commissioning editor for the BBC’s Storyville documentary series, was paid a six-figure sum by the corporation after her departure. Kon said she had faced antisemitism after the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas. The BBC said its internal processes did not uphold her antisemitism claims, but acknowledged “shortcomings, and the personal impact” on her. The BBC has rejected calls for an independent inquiry in response to the case. Lord Mann said his decision to launch an investigation came after hearing from BBC staff with concerns. The review does not appear to have been ordered by the government, but the peer said he would report his findings to the BBC and ministers in the spring. In an interview announcing his review, Mann suggested that diminishing the voices and perspectives of Jewish staff was “institutional”. “The things that the BBC have done to try and sort things out have not worked,” he told the Times. “People do not feel confident in raising it within the BBC … There is a pressure in the BBC to show that you are a ‘good Jew’.” However, speaking this morning on the BBC’s Today programme, he said there “may be” an institutional problem and that he was going into his review with “an entirely blank sheet of paper”. “There is a problem,” he said. “The question is, is the problem just a few people? Is it a problem that’s easily solved? But if it’s an institutional problem, that’s much deeper and more difficult to solve.” A BBC source said that the corporation had not been notified of any investigation and so could not comment on its specifics. A BBC spokesperson said: “We take any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC. We have introduced compulsory training on antisemitism for all our staff and we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have. “We are determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted.” Kon said she welcomed the review. She said the BBC’s internal processes had failed her. “I’m not alone,” she said. “Jewish staff at the BBC are struggling, and many are too frightened to speak up. The BBC needs Jewish staff, just as it needs people from every part of the country. I love the BBC. That’s why it has to change.”

events.title: UK government working 'around the clock' on Capita contingency plans
events.summary: The UK government is working "around the clock" on contingency plans for Capita contracts after the outsourcer's CEO quit and its shares plunged, a Cabinet Office minister told MPs. Capita announced plans this week to raise around £190 million through a share issue in the first half of 2027 after warning of sharply lower profits and further costs linked to its Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) contract. The outsourcer "should be absolutely ashamed of its performance" on the £239 million contract , Sally Jameson, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, told MPs on Tuesday . "We have seen evidence that it has stepped up in recent months and begun to rectify the problem, but it is inexcusable that it let the situation get to this point," she said. Adolfo Hernandez stepped down as CEO with immediate effect on Monday, with finance chief Pablo Andres taking over. Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement. In the House of Commons, Jameson was asked about the government's plans if Capita were unable to carry out the remainder of its contract given the outsourcer's performance on the CSPS. "On contingency planning, it is important that we stabilize the situation and that Capita can continue to deliver the pension scheme. However, the government is working across departments, as we do in relation to all strategic suppliers, to ensure that the relevant contingency plans are in place. People are working around the clock on that," she said. Jameson said contingency planning for the pension scheme was already underway before Monday's announcement, describing it as standard practice for major government suppliers. She told the Chamber that the Cabinet Office was "currently arranging to meet the new CEO in the coming days" following Hernandez's departure. The Register first exposed problems with Capita's CSPS portal last December. The site, serving 1.5 million current and former public servants, rejected login details even for newly created accounts, contained broken and circular links, and displayed dummy text. In January this year, the Cabinet Office was forced to promise "interim support measures" for the CSPS following Capita's botched takeover, including 150 additional government staff to clear the backlog in cases. Speaking in Parliament, Conservative MP Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the Public Accounts Committee, said there had been "some tragic and dreadful cases" since Capita took over administration last December. "I heard of one poor lady who was living on benefits because she could not get the bereavement payments she needed after her sister's death. I have heard of a member of parliamentary staff, not far from this Chamber, who is having to delay his retirement by a year because he cannot even get a statement from the scheme." The government has withheld nearly £10 million in contractual payments over Capita's performance. It is currently locked in negotiations over further penalties following the appointment of an auditor, first revealed in July. At the time, Hernandez apologized for Capita's performance but refused to commit to further compensation . The National Audit Office and Public Accounts Committee have both launched probes into Capita's handling of the CSPS and its appointment as a contractor. In February, The Register revealed a legal challenge to the government's award of the separate Synergy shared services contract to Capita. The deal covers HR and finance services across four Whitehall departments and associated arm's-length bodies. Rival bidder Sopra Steria, which owns incumbent provider SSCL, alleges Capita's bid was abnormally low and its proposed staffing raised concerns about delivery. Capita and the Department for Work and Pensions, which led the procurement, deny the allegations and say the competition was fair and open. Capita values the contract at £370 million. The Public and Commercial Services Union is now calling on the government to scrap Capita's shared services contract with the DWP , citing the outsourcer's troubled handling of CSPS. ®

events.title: LeBron James becomes oldest NBA player to post triple-double as 76ers win
events.summary: James posted 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds as Philadelphia snapped Miami’s seven-game winning streak. LeBron James became the oldest player in NBA history to produce a triple-double, leading Philadelphia to a 114-104 victory over the Miami Heat in the NBA Cup on Wednesday. Four-time NBA Most Valuable Player James, who turns 42 on December 30, scored a season-high 25 points, passed off a season-high 12 assists and pulled down 10 rebounds to break his own triple-double age mark. list 1 of 3 Injured Sinner ruled out of Australian Open after surgery list 2 of 3 Man United denied at Sporting as referee overshadows Fernandes double list 3 of 3 Malen and Roma deny injury-hit PSG in Champions League draw “Father Time always wins, but right now he’s giving Father Time hell,” Heat coach Erik Spoelstra said. Miami grabbed a 32-29 lead after the first quarter, but James scored 14 consecutive Sixers points in a second-quarter run for a 62-53 half-time lead, and the hosts never lost the edge in the second half. “We wanted to get back to our defensive identity,” James said. “We didn’t do that in the first quarter, but for the next 36 minutes I thought we got back to that.” The 76ers improved the best record in the Eastern Conference to 15-4 while snapping a seven-game win streak for Miami (10-7). Both clubs are 2-1 atop Cup East Group B, but with a win, Miami would have clinched the group and advanced to the knockout stage of the in-season tournament. With Joel Embiid out due to illness and Jaylen Brown out after early left hamstring tightness, it fell to James to score and set up his teammates. “That’s my favourite aspect of my game besides my IQ,” James said. “To be able to go out there and just play like a quarterback role and watch these guys run the right routes, and it’s my job to put it on time and on target, it was fun.” Tyrese Maxey led the 76ers with 30 points while VJ Edgecombe added 18. “These are my young bulls right here,” James said. “They keep me going. They keep me energised.” Giannis Antetokounmpo led Miami with 32 points and 14 rebounds. James left the Los Angeles Lakers in the off-season and selected the 76ers from several clubs in hopes of capturing a fifth NBA crown. The idle Dallas Mavericks became the first team to reach the Cup knockout round, clinching the West Group A title when the Phoenix Suns lost 116-104 at Houston. Alperen Sengun had a triple-double with 23 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists for Houston, while Kevin Durant added 20 points and Devin Booker led Phoenix with 25. At Portland, Deni Avdija scored 33 points, and Damian Lillard added 29 to lead the host Trail Blazers over San Antonio 116-111, leaving West Group C deadlocked with the Spurs, Lakers, Portland and Golden State atop it at 2-1. “It showed our maturity,” Lillard said. “We won a tough one.” French star Victor Wembanyama scored 44 points and grabbed 16 rebounds to lead the Spurs, who fell to 15-4 after their first road loss of the season. Jalen Brunson and Mikal Bridges each scored 19 points as the defending NBA and NBA Cup champion New York Knicks beat visiting Cleveland 121-102 for their sixth consecutive victory. Karl-Anthony Towns had 12 points and 10 rebounds, and Jose Alvarado scored 21 off the bench for New York. Donovan Mitchell scored 30 points, and James Harden added 28 for the Cavaliers. Minnesota’s Jaden McDaniels scored 32 points and grabbed 10 rebounds to lead the Timberwolves in a 113-106 victory at Oklahoma City. Minnesota’s LaMelo Ball had 19 points, eight assists and seven rebounds but left the game late with a left ankle injury. Two-time NBA MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander led Oklahoma City with 32 points. Julius Randle scored 28 points to lead Brooklyn’s 104-97 victory at Milwaukee, the Nets snapping a five-game losing skid. Jaylen Wells scored 19 points to lead Memphis’ 115-97 home victory over the Los Angeles Clippers. Golden State’s De’Anthony Melton scored 24 points to lead the Warriors over visiting Sacramento 129-110. Matas Buzelis scored 24 points to lead Chicago over host Charlotte 107-105 as the Hornets’ losing skid reached six games.

events.title: Young Americans agree with GTA VI: Bring back simp culture
events.summary: Some of the loudest men on the internet say Grand Theft Auto VI turns players into simps, but the people playing it are mostly saying: we like it that way. In a new poll, 66% of Americans who have played the game said its optional chore missions make it better. In Grand Theft Auto VI , you can steal a car, rob a bank and run from the police. You can also pick up groceries for your girlfriend, buy her flowers and help her redecorate the apartment. That last part has set them off. On Nov. 18, the day before the game came out, Braden Peters, the looksmaxxing streamer known as Clavicular, posted on X that the game was emasculating and that “half of the missions are jestermaxing and simping for girls.” A day later, Myron Gaines, a podcaster popular in the online manosphere, posted on the platform that despite strong first-day reviews, this was “yet another example of how political correctness, inclusivity and feminism has destroyed a legendary game series,” and then complained that Jason is pushed around by his girlfriend. Then came Zack Hoyt, the streamer known as Asmongold, who griped during a stream about having to watch TV with Lucia, rub her feet and sit through her friends’ stories, then joked about whether he’d have to buy her tampons too. Jestermaxxing, in the slang of looksmaxxing forums, means acting clownish around women to make up for a lack of looks or money. Picture a court jester tumbling for the queen. In King Lear , though, the jester is Lear’s “all-licensed fool,” the one person at court free to mock the king. Clavicular knows the move himself: in January, a clip of him at a club went viral under a caption declaring that jestermaxxing at the club was the new meta. The complaints spread well beyond influencers. One X user posted a screenshot of a mission called “Flowers for a Lady,” in which players arrange a flower delivery for Lucia because your girlfriend “will appreciate this.” The user then called the game “woke slop” and obviously made by women. One user responded that the mission amounts to getting your girlfriend a gift, drawing in 1.2 million views and nearly 150,000 likes. “Simp,” for anyone who has been spared it, is slang for a man who does too much for a woman. In this case, the offense is a man who does his share. Ben Feder, who ran Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, when Grand Theft Auto IV came out in 2008 , sees the backlash as a measure of the game’s reach. “GTA has always had humor and satire in it. I think it’s always been a part of it,” Feder said. “If anything, what I take away from it is how mainstream GTA has become.” Rockstar Games says the game took in an estimated $3.79 billion on its first day, the biggest entertainment launch ever. Take-Two did not respond to a request for comment. The kids want to simp Most Americans don’t share the manosphere’s outrage. Across all adults in the same Economist/YouGov poll , 25% of respondents said the optional chore missions make the game better, while 15% said worse, and the rest saw no effect or weren’t sure. The split is starkest by age. Among adults 18 to 29, the group most likely to play, 46% said the chores make the game better and 12% said worse. Then boomers, Americans 65 and older, were the only age group where more said worse than better, 18% to 8%. Even self-described MAGA supporters leaned positive, 28% to 19%. The critics also seem to have missed that GTA has always been satire. Kiri Miller, a Brown University professor who has written extensively about the series, argued in her book Playing Along that GTA criticizes the culture of violence it depicts. A game that has spent 25 years mocking American excess is now mocking a newer target: men who think buying flowers is a humiliation. The game has even moved from a series staple: the option to pay for sex work. Lucia, the first playable female protagonist in the franchise’s history, joins in on the action, and there’s now a button that lets Jason hold Lucia Caminos’ hand. Could the biggest blockbuster in history change the culture? That sign of the times might also give credence to what’s so out of reach for many younger generations—and could offer a reason why younger audiences overwhelmingly liked doing chores in the game. After a clip of xQc, the most-watched GTA streamer, went viral showing he spent his first 45 minutes in the game renovating his house, a user wrote on X that GTA has always let players live out what real life denies them, like killing people and breaking the law. In 2026, it’s “having a house and a stable relationship.” William Chopik, a psychologist who studies close relationships, said a game can make even chores feel worth doing. “One interesting thing about video games is that they can take behaviors that might otherwise feel mundane or burdensome and structure them in ways that make them manageable, rewarding, and even enjoyable,” he told Fortune . “But part of the appeal of doing chores in a video game might be that the connection between one’s actions and their positive consequences is much more apparent than in everyday life.” The same goes for love. “Romance isn’t always about grand gestures—sometimes it’s doing the dishes, anticipating a partner’s needs, or making their day a little easier,” Chopik said. He doesn’t expect a game to change young men overnight. “But if the worst thing that comes out of this is that it models more responsible life and relationship behavior (I won’t vouch for other areas of the game that undermine that), I think that’s maybe a win.” That sentiment was repeated by Dr. Liesel Sharabi, Hily Dating App’s relationship science advisor. “Some of the optional missions in the game include everyday acts of service like buying groceries for your partner or fixing things around the house,” Sharabi told Fortune. “I think the game could encourage its players to be more considerate partners by normalizing everyday activities like doing chores or running errands when you’re in a relationship.” Christopher Ferguson, a psychology professor at Stetson University who has spent years studying the effects of video games, is more skeptical. “Despite decades of concern, it eventually became clear that games like GTA did not cause school shootings or bullying or other negative outcomes we worried about,” he told Fortune . “The flip side is there’s little evidence that they cause positive outcomes either.” “GTA6 likely reflects the current culture more than it is causing it,” Ferguson said. “Of course in denying some expectations about its content it’s being transgressive just as it always had been.” Bring back th

events.title: Employers: do you have concerns about the rollout of Muse and other AI agents?
events.summary: Are you worried about staff connecting their digital assistants to work emails and databases? What steps are you taking to address this? Meta has rolled out its Muse AI assistant, which can be tasked with shopping, booking tickets and carrying out negotiations on a user’s behalf, across countries including the UK, US, Canada, Australia and Japan. The AI agent needs the customer’s permission to go out and make purchases, connect to apps, use bank details or send emails autonomously. However, the possibility of employees connecting their Muse assistant to their work emails and databases is a concern for companies and their clients. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office says firms using agentic AI “must be able to demonstrate how they comply with UK data protection law on an ongoing basis, including by identifying … steps to mitigate risks of harm to users and the wider public”. events.title: Iraq denies reports of troop movements towards Kurdish region
events.summary: Government says there is ‘no truth’ to media reports that Iraqi army units were moving towards the Kurdistan region. Iraq’s government has denied local media reports that army units were moving towards the Kurdistan region, as a top court backed Baghdad’s authority over the region’s border crossings and oil in a deepening dispute with Erbil. Government spokesperson Haidar al-Aboudi told state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya on Wednesday that there was “no truth” to the media reports. He said oil smugglers were diverting “tens of billions” into “private pockets and accounts”, and that the salaries of Kurdistan’s public employees were not part of the dispute. list 1 of 3 Iraq orders takeover of oilfields in areas under Kurdish control list 2 of 3 Iraq targets oil smugglers, orders Kurdish oilfield takeover list 3 of 3 Iraq’s top court rules government can take over Kurdish borders, oil fields Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said “national sovereignty is indivisible” and that protecting Iraq’s wealth was “a battle for existence” in which the state would end all forms of smuggling. Al-Zaidi has ordered the Border Ports Authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdistan region and to close unofficial crossings. He has also ordered federal authorities to take over oil fields in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahuddin and Diyala that are under Kurdish security control. Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court has issued an interpretive ruling affirming federal powers to secure international borders and deploy armed forces across all Iraqi territory. It also affirmed Baghdad’s right to oversee border crossings, including those in Kurdistan, the production and export of oil and gas, and both oil and non-oil revenues. Border Forces Commander Mohammed Abdul Wahab Sukkar al-Saidi told the state-run Iraqi News Agency on Thursday that the command had “begun implementing the directive of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces to close all unofficial crossings” with neighbouring countries. He did not say how many crossings would be affected. The Kurdistan Regional Government’s council of ministers, chaired by Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, said it rejected “any attempt to return Iraq to a centralised system”. Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani rejected addressing the region in “military language”, saying this “does not solve any problem”. Thousands of people gathered in Erbil, the capital of the Kurdish region, on Thursday to protest against the government’s plan to take over border crossings and oil operations. Reporting from Erbil, Al Jazeera’s Mahmoud Abdel Wahed said the protesters claim the government’s plan “touches on their sovereignty and their territorial integrity, and that this undermines the constitutional rights of the Kurdish people”. “The question now is whether or not the government of Baghdad will be able to solve this peacefully without triggering a new chapter of conflict, a new political and economic confrontation with the Kurdish region.” Baghdad says some 200,000 to 230,000 barrels of oil a day are being smuggled, worth about $200m a month, Al Jazeera correspondent Suhaib al-Asa said. Salim Zakhour, a researcher in constitutional law and political systems, told Al Jazeera that the ruling, issued within 24 hours at al-Zaidi’s request, gave Baghdad a legal basis to act. “The court’s decision is final and decisive,” he said. “But the issue is not only constitutional and legal. There is a political problem.” The country’s four presidencies have agreed to hold a national dialogue on December 1 to resolve the crisis. The orders followed an investigation into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company, after which al-Zaidi dismissed eight officials, including Kirkuk’s police chief and operations commander.

events.title: Highway explosion in Giza: How deadly are Egypt’s roads and railways?
events.summary: Egypt has suffered another tragedy as a deadly road explosion kills 31 and injures dozens. An explosion rocked a highway in Cairo when a fuel truck overturned and caught fire, killing at least 31 people on Wednesday. Egypt’s public prosecutor has announced an investigation into the crash, and the Ministry of Health said it will continue to monitor the situation. list 1 of 3 Deadly Egypt train crash prompts calls for political accountability list 2 of 3 Deadly truck fire is latest of Egypt’s transport disasters list 3 of 3 Ten killed in Pakistan as bus crashes into gas tanker But Egypt is no stranger to deadly accidents on its roads, despite spending billions of dollars on its transportation systems. So what exactly caused the explosion and how unsafe are Egypt’s roads? On Wednesday evening, a fuel tanker travelling on a busy ring road in Giza’s Imbabah district, a highly populated, working-class part of the Greater Cairo area, crashed and exploded, causing a fire that killed at least 31 people and injured 21 others. Local media have reported that the explosion happened after the truck driver swerved to avoid a high-voltage cable which fell in front of the vehicle. Twenty-seven vehicles were caught up and burned in the accident, according to Egypt’s judicial office. Thirty-nine ambulances were dispatched to the scene, taking the injured to nearby hospitals for treatment, the Health Ministry said. Egypt’s public prosecutor announced that there will be an investigation into the crash and ordered DNA samples from victims. Egypt, which has a population of around 120m, is known for its dangerous roads. It clocked up a total of 44,940 road deaths and 476,126 injuries between 2019 and 2025, according to the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS). Last year, more than 5,800 road deaths and 84,000 road injuries were recorded by the agency, with pedestrians making up more than one-third of those killed. Children under the age of 15 made up 1,580 of the deaths and 29,101 of the injured. A World Bank report in 2020 found that the incidents occur because 97 percent of Cairo’s streets lack traffic lights and 78 percent of them have no clear pedestrian footpaths. In 2025, there were 170 train incidents recorded, resulting in the deaths of 44 people and injuries to 215. Earlier this month, at least seven people were killed and more than 125 others injured when a train backed into another, also in Giza, triggering calls for political accountability. Egypt’s Ministry of Transport said that approximately $37bn was spent on transport investment between 2014 and 2024, but recurring incidents have raised questions about the effectiveness of this project. The leader of the centrist Reform and Development Party’s parliamentary bloc, Irene Saeed, called for full financial transparency on how the Ministry of Transport spent its funding and loans in 2016. A member of the Egyptian Parliament and leader of the Justice Party, Abdel Moneim Imam, told Al Jazeera earlier this month that the continued “turning of a blind eye to the shortcomings and the recurrence of accidents without genuine accountability leads to the continuation of the crisis”.

events.title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
events.summary: Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans. Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks. Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over. To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required. Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence. The change follows a consultation which launched early last year , set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers. Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight. Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'". But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers. The changes being considered were first reported by the Daily Mail , external . Drivers over 70 to face eye tests every three years Published 6 January The NHS provides free eye tests for over 60s, but they are not detailed enough to approve someone to drive. The BBC understands this system is also being looked at, with the free tests likely to be expanded to become more rigorous. A Government source said "beefed up measures" were long overdue. "One life lost on the roads is one too many," they added. "There have been several arguably preventable fatalities on Britain's roads caused by drivers with failing eyesight in recent years. The DfT said no decision has officially been made on mandating eyesight tests for drivers aged 70 and over. A spokesperson said: "We recognise the importance of driving for older people's independence but need to balance this with our priority to keep everyone safe on our roads and avoid tragic accidents. "Mandatory eye tests for drivers over 70 as part of our Road Safety Strategy are one way to do this. "We are carefully reviewing consultation results," they added. "Older drivers who are fit to drive and have good enough vision have nothing to worry about." Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? Share your experiences. events.title: Nakheel awards Dh1.4bn contract to build 176 villas on Palm Jebel Ali
events.summary: Dubai's Nakheel Properties has awarded a Dh1.4 billion ($381 million) contract for the construction of 176 villas on Palm Jebel Ali, as momentum continues in the emirate's real estate sector amid challenges posed by the Iran war. The contract, won by Dubai-based Ginco General Contracting, covers 128 beach villas and 48 coral villas across fronds A to D, Nakheel said on Thursday. The villas are expected to be completed within two years of the start of work, the company added. “Palm Jebel Ali is a defining destination in Dubai’s coastal growth … we have a responsibility to create connected, enduring communities that enhance quality of life for residents,” said Khalid Al Malik, chief executive of Dubai Holding Real Estate, parent company of Nakheel. Spanning 13.4km, Palm Jebel Ali will be twice as big as Palm Jumeirah when completed. It will feature seven islands and 16 fronds, adding more than 90km of beachfront. It is expected to provide 35,000 families with beachside residences, green spaces and other amenities, as well as 80 hotels and resorts. The project is part of a new growth corridor in the Jebel Ali area, supporting the emirate’s expansion, in line with the Dubai 2040 Urban Master Plan and the Dubai Economic Agenda D33. Nakheel’s sales have also been strong. The developer this week said it recorded Dh5.5 billion in sales from the first phase of its new Palm Springs project , with all 977 villas and townhouses sold, citing strong “demand for family homes”. The 3.8 million-square-metre Palm Springs, unveiled this month, is a residential master plan featuring a mix of villas, townhouses and apartments across 15 neighbourhoods. It follows the launch of 222 Palm Jebel Ali beachfront residences, which Nakheel put up for sale in June. In August, Nakheel started handing over 892 villas and townhouses at the redeveloped Jebel Ali Village near Ibn Battuta Mall, more than four years after the community’s original 290 homes were demolished. Property developers are continuing to launch projects in Dubai despite concerns about a market slowdown as the Iran war continues. Last week, Meraas, another developer under Dubai Holding Real Estate, launched 97 four and five-bedroom villas at its Nad Al Sheba Gardens project. Also last week, Meraas started a new phase of its Solaya project, the beachfront community in Jumeirah 1 developed in partnership with BGRE, formerly Brookfield Properties.

events.title: Switzerland’s biggest bank set for showdown with lawmakers as capital fight intensifies amid crisis planning
events.summary: FINMA said UBS’s preferred resolution strategy is executable in principle under its current plans. Swiss lawmakers are weighing a 90% CET1 capital-backing requirement for UBS’s foreign subsidiaries. UBS says the 90% proposal would require about $16 billion in additional CET1 capital and hurt its competitiveness. UBS 's crisis planning has won qualified support from market regulators, which called its plan "executable" in principle. But Switzerland's biggest bank still faces a major fight over sweeping plans that would force it to hold more capital against its foreign subsidiaries. FINMA, the Swiss markets regulator, said Wednesday that UBS's resolvability — or its ability to fail safely, without wreaking havoc on the economy — has improved since it integrated rival Credit Suisse, with progress made in implementing the emergency plan across group-wide resolution planning. The preferred resolution strategy — involving plans to allow for recapitalization and restructuring through the use of loss-absorbing bail-in bonds — is "executable," FINMA said. The regulator formally approved UBS's recovery plan for the first time since its ​Credit Suisse integration. How UBS would withstand a future crisis remains in sharp focus among Swiss authorities ever since the lender's emergency takeover of stricken rival Credit Suisse in 2023. UBS is now the country's only global systemically important bank, and the Swiss government wants it to hold stronger capital cushions, specifically in relation to its foreign subsidiaries, which would help it withstand another banking collapse. UBS has pushed back against the overhaul, saying the measures are disproportionate and would damage its international competitiveness, forcing it to hold an extra $16 billion in capital. A parliamentary showdown now looms, with the National Council, Switzerland's lower house, scheduled to debate the proposal Dec. 16. On Tuesday, the lower house's economics committee backed plans to force the bank to support its foreign subsidiaries with 90% high-quality core Common Equity Tier 1, or CET1, capital. The Council of States, the country's upper house, approved the 90% plan in September. The Swiss government had earlier proposed a 100% threshold. UBS wants it to be no more than 50%. UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti told CNBC in an interview Oct. 28 that 90% would not allow the company to be a "competitive player" long-term. But he would not be drawn on speculation that the measures could push the bank to relocate out of Switzerland. In a statement, the bank said the economics committee's recommendation would herald further excessive tightening of Swiss capital requirements, "which are already among the most stringent globally." FINMA said in its Nov. 25 update that the goal is to avoid government solvency support and emergency law. "The aim is to enable the authorities, in the event of a crisis, to choose the option that offers the best prospects of success in safeguarding financial stability and ensuring the continuation of systemically important functions," the regulator said.
