events.title: ‘Proscribing free speech’: Why a Jewish group is challenging UK’s Hamas ban
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? The Jewish Network for Palestine says the complete ban on Hamas was being used to stifle free speech and to target its members. London, United Kingdom – The Jewish Network for Palestine (JNP) has filed an application to reverse the proscription of Hamas under Britain’s Terrorism Act, arguing that the ban is being used against its members and is hampering freedom of speech in the United Kingdom. The JNP filed a formal de-proscription application on Thursday under Section 4 of the Terrorism Act, which oversees applications to remove a group from the UK’s list of banned organisations. list 1 of 3 ‘Healthcare not bombs’: How Gaza shaped Adam Hamawy’s path to US Congress list 2 of 3 Pro-Palestine philanthropist faces US extradition hearing in Spain list 3 of 3 UK mosque rebukes comission’s ‘warning’ following Palestine comments This follows the arrest of the 80-year-old son of Auschwitz survivors and the prosecution of a 72-year-old Jewish writer – both members of the JNP’s Steering Group – for pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist speech. The JNP was founded in 2018 by British members of the United States organisation Jewish Voice for Peace, a group which aims to bring together Jews and non-Jews who support Palestine. It is one of 11 Jewish and Jewish-led organisations that form the UK’s Jewish bloc for Palestine, which is frequently present at protests against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and pogroms in the West Bank. According to the chair of the JNP, David Cannon, proscription of Hamas has made it near-impossible to openly discuss the events of October 7, 2023, when Hamas led an attack on villages and army outposts in southern Israel. In particular, the JNP says, it has been unable to talk publicly about false narratives that followed for fear of contravening the act. “Now, all of these things needed to be discussed, but the UK government’s proscription of the political wing of Hamas has made referring to such evidence [of false reporting] risk the accusation of supporting Hamas, which is not what we’re saying. We’re saying that we want to discuss these issues,” he said. In the days following October 7, when more than 1,000 people were killed, many stories about babies being killed by Hamas fighters and mass rapes were circulated in international media. There has been no evidence of these. Cannon added that one of the group’s active members had resigned, fearing that what she could say would affect her immigration status if found to violate the act. According to the application, the JNP has about 600 members and supporters. The JNP’s application was filed five years to the day after the British government proscribed the whole of Hamas as a terrorist organisation. Hamas’s armed wing had been banned in 2001, but in 2021 the then-Home Secretary Priti Patel extended the ban to cover the whole political group, describing the organisation as “fundamentally and rabidly anti-Semitic” and arguing that the proscription was required to protect the Jewish community. The government did not, however, explain how the proscription of Hamas would protect the Jewish community in the UK. Instead, the JNP argues that the designation has now been used against the Jewish community it was supposed to protect. The group also argues that the continued proscription of Hamas in its entirety was a “disproportionate interference with the rights of JNP and its members” under the European Convention on Human Rights Articles 9, 10 and 11 on freedom of thought, expression and assembly, with the burden of the proscription falling on people in Britain. Finally, they argue, Hamas has “no presence in the UK and has not been shown to pose a specific threat to it”. “The less intrusive position that applied before November 2021 shows that proscription of the whole organisation is not necessary. On a proper application of the policy, and with the impact on JNP weighed, continued proscription is not justified,” the application stated. Following the JNP’s application, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmoud has 90 days to consider it beginning the day after it is received. If it is refused, the group can appeal the decision. Tony Greenstein, 72, an anti-Zionist writer and blogger and prominent member of the JNP, was prosecuted for publishing a blog on October 7, 2023, titled “Full Support for the Gaza Ghetto Uprising”, in which he evoked the Jewish Warsaw Ghetto Uprising in 1943. While his post only mentioned Hamas in passing, in November 2024 Greenstein was charged under section 12 of the British Terrorism Act with inviting support for Hamas on the basis of one sentence in that blog and for writing “please share” on social media, promoting the piece. After nearly three years and appearances in different courts, Greenstein was acquitted in August this year.

events.title: Bird-watching in 'GTA 6' has the seal of approval from America's top birders
events.summary: Whooping cranes appear in GTA 6’s fictional Florida, though birding expert Nicholas Lund says they’re more common in the game than in real life. : Jon G. Fuller/VWPics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Bird-watching is one of myriad activities players can take part in in "GTA 6." 60 different birds can be watched, and birder Nicholas Lund found them all soon after release. He said in the "Audubon" journal that "GTA 6's" bird-watching is the "most accurate" ever in a game. "Grand Theft Auto 6" players can steal cars, run drugs, and evade the police. One player had another priority: finding every bird. Birding expert Nicholas Lund tracked down all 60 species listed in the game's bird catalog, searching wetlands, beaches, forests, a farm, and a zoo across Rockstar Games' fictionalized Florida . His verdict? "GTA 6" offers what feels like "the most accurate version of modern birding ever put to screen," he wrote in "Audubon," the magazine of the National Audubon Society . Named for renowned 19th-century ornithologist John James Audubon, the society is the premier birding organization in the US and has a history spanning over 120 years. The game's wildlife has attracted attention from birders as well as GTA fans. Ahead of its release, a post in Reddit's r/birding community drew excited replies from players who planned to catalog birds between missions. "I think the crime sprees are going to have to wait," the original poster wrote. Another responded: "I have found my people. Hopefully there’s an achievement for finding them all." In "GTA 6", players can use binoculars to "study" birds and add them to a progress menu. Lund wrote in "Audubon" that he approached the search much as he would in real life, looking in different habitats. This led to finding gulls and pelicans near the water, wading birds in wetlands, and smaller birds farther north. He found 50 species during roughly eight hours of play after launch. The following morning, he completed the list by spotting an American Barn Owl on a water tank. Rockstar advertised 62 bird species before launch. Lund said the bird progress screen listed 60, with several others appearing elsewhere in the game. He noticed inaccuracies, including the appearance of endangered Whooping Cranes more often than they would in the real world. But he praised the familiar landscapes and the traffic, noise, and litter that accompanied the birdsong. The hunt is one of several ways players are spending time in the game's expansive world. Some players have chosen to do virtual home repairs or even doomscroll. Sony said players logged 683 million hours on PlayStation 5 in the game's first four days. After completing his list, Lund returned to a more familiar GTA pursuit: He drove his car off a cliff into the ocean. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Are Trump’s tariffs aimed at securing US-friendly trade deals?
events.summary: Trump’s new tariffs: Which countries are affected? Trump-Xi-Putin summit: Key takeaways Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? New policy threatens further tariff hikes on China, India, Vietnam if trade negotiations fall through. United States President Donald Trump’s administration has proposed a new slate of trade tariffs against 14 of the US’s key trading partners, including China, India and the European Union. The tariffs, which would go into effect next year, will hit China the hardest, potentially subjecting its products to a 40 percent import tax. list 1 of 3 Brazil blasts ‘unacceptable’ new US tariff proposals list 2 of 3 A meeting with Democrats over healthcare? Trump says he’s open to it list 3 of 3 ICC judge Kimberly Prost tries war crimes. She’s a target of US sanctions Washington says the tariffs, announced by the US Trade Representative (USTR) on Wednesday, are a response to unfair trading practices which harm US manufacturing, including “excess industrial capacity” – subsidies and policies that enable manufacturers to overproduce and undercut the US. But Trump has long used tariffs as leverage in trade negotiations. So, is the latest tariff announcement an effort to win concessions in upcoming trade deals? Here’s what we know: Which economies do the tariffs target, and when would they start? The tariffs would be imposed on products from China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, according to the USTR. The maximum rates facing each country range from 20 percent to 40 percent. It is unclear when exactly the tariffs would take effect, but a senior US official told the AFP news agency they would likely start in January at the earliest. Why is the US imposing trade tariffs? Trump has launched several rounds of trade tariffs against other countries and economies during his second term in office, with his administration citing various laws and justifications for the policies each time. In April 2025, Trump imposed a sweeping raft of import taxes against almost all US trade partners, known as the “Liberation Day” tariffs. He said the measures were retaliation for unfair trade practices, including high tariffs, against the US that hurt local manufacturing. Trump imposed those tariffs under an emergency powers law, but the Supreme Court struck them down in February this year. Then, in July, Washington cited a different law – section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 – to impose more tariffs on more than 80 countries. This time, Trump’s administration claimed the targeted countries had failed to adequately restrict imported goods made with forced labour. The latest tariff announcement also cites section 301 of the same trade act, which allows Washington to penalise countries it determines are treating US businesses unfairly. It follows an eight-month investigation into what Washington calls “structural excess capacity”, by which governments give their industries unfair advantages with subsidies, suppressed wages and other policies. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners were using “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”. Inga Fechner, a senior economist at ING THINK, wrote that “while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind.” Is this really about clinching better trade deals for the US? For several targeted countries, that appears to be a big factor. The tariff announcement comes as the US negotiates trade agreements with several of the targeted countries, including China, India, Vietnam and Singapore, with some of the proposed tariff rates explicitly linked to the outcome of those talks. China’s tariffs are due to rise by 20 percent, respecting a cap under a current US-China trade truce. But if talks to secure a new trade deal fail by January 10, when that truce is due to expire, the rate could double to up to 40 percent, according to USTR. Vietnam would also be subject to a capped tariff rate of 20 percent if it makes a trade deal with Washington, which it is actively negotiating. But if those negotiations fall through, its rate would jump to 35 percent. India would face a 17 percent tariff rate if a trade agreement is reached with Washington, but a 25 percent rate if not. Singapore faces a 10 percent tariff if it reaches a trade deal with the US, but a 20 percent rate if not. Madeline Chalecki, assistant director at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center, said the US is also exercising leverage over Mexico, which Trump recently said the US is close to concluding a trade deal with. Mexico was among the countries included in the USTR’s excess capacity investigation, but has not yet been hit with new tariffs.

events.title: ‘Some things you just don’t take off the menu’: Denny’s stands by Jensen Huang after his Nvidia comeback
events.summary: When Jensen Huang lost his job as Nvidia’s CEO earlier this month, he also lost his commemorative plaque at Denny’s. Eleven days later, Huang returned to the helm of the chip giant to a rock-star welcome from cheering employees. His plaque, it turns out, beat him to the comeback. Now the restaurant chain has a message for its most famous former dishwasher. “Some things you just don’t take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them,” Denny’s wrote in a statement on social media on Wednesday. Long before Huang became one of the most powerful people in the artificial intelligence industry, he was washing dishes at Denny’s. Years later, he and two friends met at one of the chain’s restaurants in San Jose, Calif., to discuss an idea that would become Nvidia, now ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and the list’s most valuable company when the ranking was published in June. On Sept. 26, 2023, Denny’s unveiled a plaque commemorating that very spot, calling it “The booth that launched a $1 trillion company.” Denny’s defends its former employee The plaque came down on the evening of Nov. 12, an employee at the San Jose restaurant told SFGATE . That was the same day Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspected of spying for China. Another restaurant worker told the New York Post that the decision to remove the plaque had come from the diner’s “bosses.” Denny’s reversed course well before Nvidia did. The chain says it learned of the removal on Friday, Nov. 13, and “put the plaque right back up where it belongs.” By Nov. 14, a Denny’s spokesperson had told SFGATE the plaque was being reinstalled. Denny’s has not publicly explained why it was taken down in the first place. Nvidia followed on Monday, Nov. 23, when its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The board said that, based on input from senior levels of the U.S. government, it was confident his return posed no national security risk. The reversal came after a public push from President Donald Trump , who has claimed credit for the decision. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. officials told congressional staff in a classified briefing that they had found no evidence China orchestrated the affair. From the dish station to a chip empire Huang was 15 when he got his first job at a Denny’s in Portland, Ore. He spent five years as a dishwasher, busboy, and waiter, an experience he credits with helping him overcome his shyness and teaching him the value of hard work. At the 2023 plaque unveiling, Huang encouraged young people to start their careers in the restaurant industry. “It teaches you humility, it teaches you hard work, it teaches you hospitality,” he said. Those lessons have also shaped his leadership approach at Nvidia. “To me, no task is beneath me because, remember, I used to be a dishwasher, and I mean that. I used to clean toilets. I’ve cleaned a lot of toilets. I’ve cleaned more toilets than all of you combined, and some of them you just can’t unsee,” Huang told Stanford Graduate School of Business in 2024. “But our history with Jensen goes back much further, to the dishes he washed, the guests he served and the work he still talks about with pride,” the diner wrote on Wednesday. After studying electrical engineering at Oregon State University, Huang worked at chip companies AMD and LSI Logic. He earned his master’s degree in electrical engineering from Stanford University in 1992. In 1993, Huang and fellow engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem met at the San Jose Denny’s to discuss developing a chip that could make computer graphics more realistic. The restaurant was close to Huang’s home and offered an inexpensive place to brainstorm. “It had all the coffee you could drink and no one could chase you out,” Huang recalled in 2023. Denny’s has long marketed its Nvidia connection Three decades later, Denny’s had turned its connection to the billionaire into a marketing opportunity. Alongside the plaque unveiling in September 2023, then-Denny’s CEO Kelli Valade announced the Trillion-Dollar Incubator Contest, offering $25,000 in seed funding to an aspiring entrepreneur whose business idea originated in a Denny’s booth. In March 2025, the chain went a step further, introducing a limited-edition menu item called Nvidia Breakfast Bytes. Inspired by Huang’s favorite breakfast hack, the dish featured four sausage links that diners could wrap in miniature buttermilk pancakes and dip in maple syrup. It debuted at Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose. The entrepreneurship contest, however, will not return this year. Denny’s head of public relations, Colton Grace, told SFGATE earlier this month that it was intended to be a one-time event. Still, Denny’s appears eager to preserve its association with the billionaire who has called the restaurant his alma mater. On Nov. 10, two days before Huang resigned, the chain said it wrote to Nvidia’s communications team: “Jensen is part of our history, and we are part of his.” Reflecting on the countless dishwashers who have worked at its restaurants over the years, Denny’s added: “One of them went on to change the world, and he still remembers what he learned at the sink.” Now Denny’s is giving a shout-out to the CEO whose comeback made him nearly $34 billion richer in a single day, according to Forbes . “Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee’s on,” Denny’s wrote. “We’re always open, 24/7.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information. 1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata. The company insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said. Arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected. 1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The company did not respond to The Register's questions. The miscreant also got their hands on tokens embedded in emails sent to some customers as part of account invitations, provisioning, and recovery processes. These tokens aren't enough to access an account on their own, according to 1Password, as users must also authenticate via single sign-on or enter a verification code sent to their registered email address. The company says it specifically notified the small number of users with affected provisioning or recovery processes underway. It found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed provisioning tokens. Still, the breach has prompted the password management biz to beef up those verification codes, replacing the six-digit numeric variety with ten-character alphanumeric codes to make brute-forcing them considerably more difficult. 1Password has booted the intruder out of its GitHub environment, revoked the stolen token, and rolled back the affected backend services to clean versions of the code. It's since shored up security around its development infrastructure and employees' devices, and brought in outside security specialists to review its handiwork. The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. Information obtained in that intrusion helped enable a second attack that exposed customer vault backups, including encrypted passwords. The UK Information Commission's Office slapped LastPass with a £1.2 million ($1.6 million) fine last December over the incident, which compromised the personal information of up to 1.6 million UK users. Among the regulator's gripes was that LastPass had fallen short of the higher standard of security expected of a company entrusted with people's passwords.

events.title: Cookbook GPT: When AI becomes a Thanksgiving sous-chef
events.summary: From cookbooks to YouTube to ChatGPT , the way Americans plan their holiday menus has evolved. The big picture: But there's something uniquely human about building a recipe, and chefs warn we risk fracturing personal connections and family history by reducing culinary traditions to chatbot prompts. "Recipes can have tradition and ritual," says Melanie Underwood, a culinary educator and founder of Nourish & Gather . She warns that taking the human conversation out of cooking could further erode our cultural oral histories. Context: Campbell's recent State of the Sides survey found that 27% of U.S. adults who celebrate Thanksgiving have used generative AI for holiday planning or cooking, up from 22% last year. And 65% of shoppers say they would like to use AI in some aspect of holiday meal planning, per holiday shopper trend research from FMI, the Food Industry Association. Among those celebrating at least one holiday this season, 34% say they'd use AI to find new recipes, 23% said they'd use it to plan the overall menu and 16% said they'd use it to make the holiday meal healthier. Friction point: Food bloggers and chefs have warned that traffic to their trusted websites is plummeting with the rise of AI recipe summaries, forcing some to quit the game altogether. Plus, AI recipes on the " slop "-pier side can be disastrous for the dinner table. The AI-generated recipes that pop up on Google's search results page "are often total nonsense," recipe blogger Eb Gargano told Axios in an email. "They've been generated by AI – and, at least last time I checked – AI cannot cook a recipe or taste a recipe," she said. Food bloggers have a name for those recipes, she added: "Frankenstein recipes." Underwood says she uses AI to help her with the operational side of her business. But when she recently asked a chatbot to scale her recipe for a large event and make a shopping list, it cut out ingredients — saying it was trying to improve her recipe. Our thought bubble: AI is not a chef — while it's accumulated years of IRL chefs' knowledge, it can still lead you astray. I asked ChatGPT to help me make my favorite Thanksgiving appetizers: stuffed mushrooms. I typically follow my mom's famous recipe (well, actually, Barefoot Contessa's , but shhh), but the AI-generated version differed in a few ways. It wanted me to preheat to 400 degrees and bake for 20 minutes or so, while my family's go-to calls for a cooler 325 for 50. Chat's recipe opts for butter, while the Contessa's does not. Some of the spices caught me off-guard as well: Red pepper flakes and thyme are not ingredients I usually throw in. To my untrained eye, the recipe still sounds tasty — but it's missing some of the key flavors in my dream stuffed mushroom, like sherry and scallions. The bottom line: AI can be an inventive appetizer, but human execution remains the main course. Underwood tells Axios: "AI has a place, but it doesn't replace human connection, and that involves even looking for recipes ... you can ask your friend as easily as you can ask AI." events.summary: Elon Musk and SpaceX are jumping into Trump Accounts. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images SpaceX says it will give one share of its stock to every active Trump Account. Elon Musk says he'll personally match the number of shares donated as part of a broader commitment. SpaceX's COO has separately pledged more than 2 million of the rocket maker's shares. SpaceX said Wednesday that it will give one share of its stock to every active Trump Account . CEO Elon Musk will personally match the number of shares donated by the AI and rocket company, as "part of his pledge to donate one SpaceX share to every kid in America ," the company said. Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and chief operating officer, has also pledged more than 2 million SpaceX shares. "SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company behind Starlink, Starship, Grok, and X said in a press release. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit." Musk — the world's wealthiest person with an estimated $820 billion net worth, per the Bloomberg Billionaires Index — confirmed his commitment in a pinned post on X. "Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally," he wrote. Musk said the share from SpaceX "will be transferred next month," while the share from him "will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year." The share from SpaceX will be transferred next month. The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year. — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 26, 2026 A SpaceX share was worth about $127 as of Wednesday's market close, down 44% from its peak price of around $226 in mid-June, shortly after the company went public. Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children born between 2025 and 2028. events.title: Meta Refused to Share Muse for Testing, UK Financial Watchdog Complains
events.summary: Meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne. It comes as regulators across the UK, including the competition and data watchdogs, warned Meta it needs to ensure its AI products comply with UK consumer protection laws. “It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), said Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace. “We’ve got a number of entrants into the market. We want to see what they’re going to be doing in the market. I think it’s just reasonable,” he later explained to WIRED. Payne told WIRED the FCA had been hoping the organizations could work together to investigate what interactions might look like between the tool, marketed as a personal assistant, and a normal customer. His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon , roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK. The FCA especially wants to understand how payments will be made by agents—as multiple British retailers, including grocers Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, and Ocado, department store Debenhams Group, and electronics seller Currys said they’d been working with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites. Payne is concerned about potential unintended consequences of prompts, especially when a user has a low level of understanding of how the AI product works. “If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” he says. Payne did note the testing would have taken time to set up. “Normally you have a long period of time speaking to a firm and then you plan it over a period of weeks or months,” he explained, but Meta only made the FCA aware of its plans last month. “We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta Spokesperson Matthew Pollard tells WIRED. More than 10 million users have set up Muse in North America since it was launched in September. British watchdogs say they will be monitoring Muse’s rollout closely as they are bracing for significant uptake on their side of the pond, too, given that many Brits already use Meta’s other products , like Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp. “If it’s going to be equally popular in the UK, we need to be able to see what it’s going to do,” Payne says. The ICO stressed the importance of users understanding and being able to control how Muse uses their personal data. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta adapt its terms and conditions for UK consumers to say Meta must exercise “reasonable skill and care/professional diligence” when providing Muse, the EU and UK terms say, with the document acknowledging that outputs may still be inaccurate and actions may not be completed as intended. “If we have concerns, we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers,” the CMA said in a statement. events.title: Indonesia plans fee of 0.5% of export value of palm oil, association says
events.summary: DSI plans to collect a fixed fee of 2.5 million rupiah (S$176.52) for every contract palm oil exporters upload to its system. Indonesia’s DSI plans a 0.5% palm oil export verification fee and a 2.5 million rupiah contract charge from 1 January, Reuters says. GAPKI and smallholder farmers say the fee is a burden and could cut farm prices, especially as drought has already hit yields. The plan aims to curb transfer pricing and under-invoicing, but traders fear delays and extra costs could push buyers towards Malaysia. JAKARTA – A firm set up by Indonesia to monitor commodity exports has proposed a charge of 0.5% of the export sales value of palm oil, an official of Indonesia’s palm oil association GAPKI said on Nov 26 . Palm oil exporters and industry groups were told of the fee during a briefing with Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia (DSI) on Nov 25 , said Yustinus Lambang Setyo Putro, an association official. DSI plans to collect a fixed fee of 2.5 million rupiah (S$176.52) for every contract palm oil exporters upload to its system and a verification fee of 0.5% of export sales value, Yustinus told Reuters. A DSI spokesperson declined immediate comment on the plan. “This is a burden,” said Mansuetus Darto, chairman of the smallholder palm oil farmers’ union POPSI. “Just for the sake of transparency by giving the exports data to DSI, do we really need to pay $5 per tonne?” The union calculates the fee would be about US$5 (S$6.45) at current crude prices of about US$1,000 a tonne, potentially reducing the price of fresh fruit bunches by about 0.7% at a time of pressure from declining yields due to an El Nino-induced drought . The news of the fee rate, which will be collected starting Jan 1, drove up Malaysian palm oil prices on Nov 26 , as market participants expected some buyers to shift to the neighbouring country. Indonesia and Malaysia are the two largest producers of the edible oil. Company set up to verify export deals Indonesia set up DSI under sovereign wealth fund Danantara to verify export transactions of palm oil, coal and ferroalloys to boost state oversight and allay concerns about transfer pricing practices and under-invoicing. DSI plans to launch a digital platform in December , requiring exporters to upload export contracts and declarations, to track and analyse goods and payments flows and check if their prices are in line with market prices and flag any price anomalies. GAPKI is calculating the potential impact of the additional fees on palm oil farmers and companies, Yustinus said, adding that a commodity exchange planned for 2027 would also incur expenses. The 0.5% fee would have limited impact on costs, as it is small compared to export taxes and levies exporters already pay, said Cheang Kang Wei, analyst at Singapore-based brokerage StoneX. However, traders are concerned about how the new verification measures will affect the flow of goods. “That adds paperwork, timing risk and a financing cost for exporters,” added Cheang. “If it slows down contracting or shipments early next year, buyers like India could lean more on Malaysian supply.” REUTERS

events.title: Trump, NATO chief caution Russia as attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure intensify
events.summary: Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte urged Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and called for a rapid peaceful resolution. Their Mar-a-Lago meeting followed Trump’s meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, which raised concerns among European lawmakers about U.S. commitment to transatlantic security. Russian attacks disrupted power supplies and electric public transport in Kryvyi Rih, as Ukrainian officials reported damage and outages in five regions. U.S. President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte issued a joint statement on Thursday urging Russia not to take any actions, intentionally or otherwise, that would further expand the Ukraine war. The statement comes as Ukraine's allies sound the alarm over Russia's growing threat to European security and just one week after Trump's historic trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Asia. Trump and Rutte described their meeting at the Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida on Wednesday as "very impactful," with Russia's nearly five-year-long war in Ukraine and the Iran war among the key topics of conversation. "We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," Trump and Rutte said in their statement. Trump's meeting with Xi and Putin, in which he described the Russian president as his "friend," sparked alarm among European lawmakers about Washington's commitment to transatlantic security. NATO's Rutte, a seasoned diplomat known as a consensus builder during his nearly 14 years as Dutch prime minister, has repeatedly sought to de-escalate tensions in the alliance and frequently used flattery to win over the U.S. president. While some have questioned whether this approach has delivered any tangible benefits, Trump has previously described Rutte as a "great leader" and NATO's "biggest asset." Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure in recent weeks, with further attacks on the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih overnight disrupting power supplies and bringing municipal electric public transport to a standstill, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi ​Rih's defense council. Ukrainian officials on Wednesday said Russian attacks on the country's power sector had damaged energy infrastructure and caused power outages in five regions as cold winter weather sets in. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday accused the Kremlin of "escalating" threats toward European security, citing actions in the Baltic region , Poland and on the Black Sea, and adding that "Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine." A spokesperson for Russia's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment on Thursday morning. The Kremlin has repeatedly denied seeking military confrontation with NATO countries.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Flight Centre investigating cyber incident that exposed personal data and passport details Flight Centre says it is investigating a "significant" cyber breach. ( ABC News: Liz Pickering ) Customer data has been exposed in a cyber breach targeting a third-party accommodation system used by several of Flight Centre's booking agencies. The travel agency says "unknown persons" accessed customers' basic travel information and a small number of passport details. The company is warning customers to stay vigilant for unexpected emails or text messages about their bookings. Australian travel agency Flight Centre is investigating a cyber breach it says exposed a significant number of customer records, including some passport details. In a statement to the ASX on Thursday, the Brisbane-based travel giant reported it had discovered "unusual activity" within the third-party accommodation system used by several of its booking agencies. These included Flight Centre, Travel Associates and Cruiseabout, as well as some independent agents. Flight bookings and corporate travel bookings were not affected, the company said. Australians facing spike in data breaches Australians should expect an increase in future data breaches as a result of critical software flaws that have forced major government websites, education platforms and web hosts to go offline. Early findings indicated "a significant number of customer records", comprising details such as names and some basic travel information, may have been accessed by "unknown persons", the travel agency said. The company does not yet know how many customer records have actually been extracted. A "very small percentage" of the compromised data included "limited passport details, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, or in rare cases health or mobility information", Flight Centre said. Credit card, payment or banking details had not been affected at this stage. Customers have been warned to exercise caution if they receive unexpected messages about their travel bookings. ( ABC News: Liz Pickering ) It is not clear exactly when the breach was discovered, but Flight Centre said it had responded by working with the third-party service to enhance its system security and contain the unusual activity. The company said it was working with cybersecurity experts to understand the full "nature and extent" of the breach. "FLT (Flight Centre Travel) is in the process of notifying the relevant authorities and has engaged external specialists to support in these investigations, including cyber security incident partner Mandiant," a statement to the ASX said. Customers with existing accommodation bookings through Flight Centre's leisure brands can continue their travel plans without disruption, the company said. Flight Centre declined to comment further. Customers warned to be vigilant of dodgy messages Flight Centre is warning customers to be cautious of "unexpected emails, calls or messages" about their bookings, and to "not click on links, open attachments or share personal information, passwords or payment details in response". The company apologised to affected customers, noting "that an incident like this can be unsettling". It said it would be contacting affected customers. Flight Centre is the latest Australian company to suffer a major security breach, following incidents at Origin this year and Qantas in 2025. Both Optus and Medibank also experienced mass breaches in 2022. In June, a rogue OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian Medicare data portal , fuelling concerns about the existential risks posed by autonomous artificial intelligence. events.title: Walmart won't resort to 'gimmicks' to get Black Friday shoppers in early
events.summary: Walmart has been running deals since October, but it says it is saving some key discounts for Black Friday. Brian Kaiser/Bloomberg via Getty Images Door prizes have become a popular way for stores to boost Black Friday traffic — but not at Walmart. The company's US chief merchant told BI she intends to win shoppers by offering the best deals. "We're not going to pay people to get in line," she said. Walmart is taking an old-school approach to retail's busiest weekend of the year . Although several retailers are rolling out door prizes like swag bags and gift cards to boost Black Friday visits, Walmart's US chief merchant Julie Barber told Business Insider she's letting the deals do the talking. "We're not going to do gimmicks. We're not going to pay people to get in line. We're going to have amazing items in the store, and that's going to drive people in," she said. That's a sharp contrast with rival Target, which will give away gift cards worth at least $25 to the first hundred shoppers at each of its stores on Black Friday. One winner at each location will get a $1,000 card. Kohl's is likewise offering $5 to $100 gift cards to the first 200 shoppers at its stores, and Lowe's is again giving its Black Friday Buckets to the first 50 rewards members who show up at participating locations. In addition to free Lowe's merchandise, some winners will receive appliances worth up to $2,000. Barber spent this week jetting around the country to check on how Walmart stores — and their competitors — are prepping for the holiday rush. This year, she says Walmart customers are laser-focused on value , with seven in ten survey respondents telling the company that lower prices would make their holiday shopping easier. That translates to the company emphasizing new products and low prices. She said that Thanksgiving week is typically the largest-selling period of the year for TVs, but Walmart is extending Black Friday deals beyond traditional gifts and electronics to offer discounts on more everyday essentials. For example, Walmart will be running a big sale on vehicle tires. Last week, CFO John David Rainey said the online sales growth of more than 20% year over year is more than offsetting a slight decline of in-person shopping. "Between in-store shopping and digital fulfillment, we have more volume going through our US stores than ever before," he said during Walmart's third quarter earnings call. Barber said that her store teams are heading into the holiday rush with the highest inventory levels that they've had all year. "We're set up pretty well, I think, for both the in-store and online shopper," she said. And even though the holiday season is starting earlier and includes more individual sale events on the calendar leading up to Christmas, Barber said her team makes sure there's enough compelling deals to make the annual Black Friday spree worthwhile. "We plan it out where there's something new and special that happens every time we have an event," she said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A teenage entrepreneur skipped the advice 'follow your passion.' His company did 6 figures in revenue in a month.
events.summary: Stavya Nilawar founded his creator-marketing agency, Nilawar, with about $35. Courtesy of Stavya Nilawar Stavya Nilawar, 19, built a creator marketing agency that generated $119,000 in October 2026. He chose AI clients for their growing budgets, not because he loved the industry. His advice: Pick a business model you enjoy, then find a niche with demand. When seeking career advice, there's a refrain that comes up often: "Follow your passion." Stavya Nilawar, 19, thinks that approach can be a "huge limiter" for aspiring entrepreneurs. Rather than building a business around a personal passion, Nilawar selected an industry where he saw demand, companies with marketing budgets, and room for a service provider like him. His creator-marketing agency, Nilawar , connects brands with content creators for sponsored segments and dedicated videos. The agency, which he launched with about $35, works with AI companies including CodeRabbit and Wispr Flow, and typically earns a cut of each project fee. The business brought in $119,000 in revenue in October 2026 , according to business-account statements reviewed by Business Insider. Nilawar's first attempt at entrepreneurship was much more closely tied to his interest in social media. He started a social-media marketing agency, visiting local businesses to film and edit short-form videos for their accounts. He'd create about 30 videos a month for clients and earn roughly $750 for his work. "Quickly, I realized doing that all myself — the editing, the recording, and going to the actual place — it was so much time," Nilawar, a sophomore at Babson College, said. "That time cost was insane." He knew he wanted to work in media, but he didn't necessarily want to be the person on camera or have a business dependent on his physical presence. "I didn't want to be the main figure," he said. "But I knew that I could work with other people who can be the main figure." So when he launched Nilawar, he chose a model that suited him: running an agency that connects brands with creators. The next decision was which kinds of brands to serve. He picked AI for the business opportunity, not personal interest Nilawar decided to focus on AI. He saw that AI companies were growing quickly and often had budgets for creator partnerships — the type of work his agency could facilitate. "I was not passionate about AI at all, to be honest," he said. He believes founders should look beyond whether an industry sounds exciting or aligns with their personal interests and, instead, seek niches with customers who have both a clear need and the ability to pay. For him, that meant working with AI companies instead of focusing on an industry he was personally passionate about. "The business vehicle you choose should be something you like," he said. "But then after that, the niche you do should always be business-oriented." Read the original article on Business Insider

These developments have contributed to higher expected policy rates, higher bond yields and volatility in financial markets. Some market moves have been amplified by vulnerabilities previously identified by the Financial Policy Committee (FPC). Despite some amplification within markets, spillovers across markets have been limited and the UK financial system has been resilient. AI investment has supported global growth. However, the very rapid expansion and broadening of its financing – in a form that is increasingly complex, circular and opaque – is also contributing to a deepening of interconnections across the global financial system, making it increasingly likely for stress in one area to propagate to another. Alongside this, the higher interest rate and cost environment is eroding financial headroom for some households and adding to sovereign debt sustainability pressures. Taken together, these developments heighten the risk that multiple vulnerabilities crystallise simultaneously. Meanwhile, frontier AI capabilities have continued to grow since the July FSR, notably in the sophistication of AI agents and open-weight AI models. Recent incidents have further illustrated the challenges in aligning and controlling both individual agents and multi-agent dynamics. These developments are making cyber and operational risks a more prominent threat to financial stability, and are contributing to deeper interconnections across the financial system through common technologies and providers. The continued conflict in the Middle East has led to a protracted negative supply shock to the global economy. Energy prices have increased since the July FSR, adding to inflationary pressures and contributing to higher interest rates. The outlook for inflation and interest rates remains uncertain and sensitive to developments in the Middle East and their impacts. Global growth has so far been resilient, in part supported by AI-related investment. This investment also increases the demand for capital which may be contributing to upward pressure on global real interest rates. Uncertainty over the pace of data-centre development, and how much AI investment will translate into future earnings, has contributed to asset price volatility. Vulnerabilities previously highlighted by the FPC in sovereign debt markets, risky asset valuations, and risky credit markets including private credit, remain and, in some cases, have amplified market volatility. Sovereign debt-to-GDP ratios continue to move upwards globally, reducing the capacity of governments to respond to future shocks. Government bond yields have risen further, reaching near two-decade highs in several advanced economies. In the UK, the increase in yields has mainly reflected higher expected policy rates, driven by higher energy prices and resilient growth, rather than higher term premia.

events.title: Thanksgiving dinner costs rise, putting pressure on US households
events.summary: Turkeys see a 26-percent price rise, forcing families to reconsider hosting and opt for potluck-style celebrations. Across the United States, kitchens will fill with the smell of roasting turkey as Americans gather to celebrate the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday. Every family has its own traditions. Some swear by sweet potatoes topped with marshmallows. Others have carefully guarded family recipes for gravy, and there is always the perennial debate over pumpkin or pecan pie – and whether it should be served with a dollop of whipped cream or a scoop of ice cream. list 1 of 4 Trump’s $12bn aid package: Are tariffs bleeding US farmers? list 2 of 4 US air travel in chaos after rare nationwide ground stop halts flights list 3 of 4 The rising cost of Thanksgiving list 4 of 4 As tech outages mount, some New Yorkers prepare for the worst But regardless of what makes it onto the Thanksgiving table this year, many Americans have something less appetising in common: a heftier grocery bill. The cost of a typical Thanksgiving meal is up 11 percent from last year, according to a new analysis by the think tank The Century Foundation. The prices of many typical side dishes are up by double-digit percentages. Green beans are up 36.7 percent in price for a 1.5-pound bag, from $2.99 to $4.08 in a year’s time. Russet potatoes are up 6.8 percent for a five-pound bag, and Granny Smith apples, which are typically used in apple pie, are up 10.2 percent for a three-pound bag. The centrepiece of the Thanksgiving table, the turkey, is also up by 26 percent compared with this time last year. “Thanksgiving is supposed to be about gathering around the table, but this year many families are deciding how many people they can afford to feed,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at The Century Foundation, said in a statement. Measuring just by the number of guests, the American Farm Bureau forecasts a rise of 6 percent for a 10-person meal, marking the first increase in price since 2022, when prices hit a record high, according to the report. Some grocers are doing what they can to keep prices lower for consumers, including Baris Avci, who runs Green Valley, a small neighbourhood grocery store in the Bushwick neighbourhood of Brooklyn, New York. “Some very important things like eggs, milk, sugar, we sell almost at cost. We don’t make much money, but we also have a certain percentage to [sustain] the business. Like how the people struggle, we struggle too,” Avci told Al Jazeera. Higher prices mean that some shoppers are having to rethink their traditions. Sam Braverman, who was shopping at Green Valley, told Al Jazeera that in past years, his mother hosted Thanksgiving and took care of all the costs, but given price increases, his family is taking a different approach. “Well, my ma is more open to kind of a potluck vibe this year, of people sort of bringing a few things,” Braverman told Al Jazeera. “To make that same meal is going to be 130-150 percent of what it was last year, so you might as well accept some offerings.” Heightened costs can stem from bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has led to a rise in the cost of both fuel and fertiliser needed in the food production supply chain. During the spring planting season, prices for urea, which is used in fertilisers, jumped by as much as 50 percent when the war began, meaning that farmers needed to pay more for fertiliser. Those costs were ultimately passed down along the supply chain from farmers to warehouses and then onto supermarket shelves. Tariff-driven pressures have also led to heightened costs. For example, tariffs on steel used in cans have caused prices to increase on canned goods for consumers. In September, Campbell’s Soup said it would raise prices by 4 to 5 percent on 60 percent of its products. Some big-box retailers like Walmart, however, are using their economies of scale to cut prices for consumers. Every year, the Bentonville, Arkansas-based chain offers a holiday meal package that consumers can buy, which includes a complete holiday meal for 10 people. It will cost shoppers 12 percent less than the same deal last year. For those bearing the brunt of the costs, that means more people are finding ways to borrow or at least scale back. A third of Americans who are planning on hosting this year say that doing so is putting them under financial strain, according to a report from LendingTree, an online loan marketplace. As a result, nearly 62 percent of hosts say they’re going to borrow money to host this year – 18 percent of whom say they’re using what are called buy now, pay later (BNPL) loans, which are deferred payment plans for expenses. Usage has jumped significantly in recent years, with 16 percent of Americans using BNPL loans, which are offered by fintech companies like Affirm and Klarna, marking a six-percentage-point jump since 2021, according to an August report from the US Federal Reserve.

events.title: Palestine coach says team represents suffering but also offers hope
events.summary: Despite navigating personal hardships, Ihab Abu Jazar calls it a ‘badge of honour’ to coach the Palestine football team. For Ihab Abu Jazar, being the coach of Palestine’s national football team comes with burdens far heavier than sporting responsibilities. His mind constantly returns to his family in Gaza, now displaced and living in tents amid Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinian territory. list 1 of 4 Israeli army kills Palestinian footballer Mahmoud Kamal Abdel-Malek in Gaza list 2 of 4 Saudi Arabia confirms January start for Asian Cup 2027 despite attacks list 3 of 4 A decade of Lajee Celtic: The Palestinian club whose fans include Cantona list 4 of 4 Hamilton calls for Palestine and DR Congo freedom as Rwanda takes F1 spotlight “Truthfully, it is difficult to carry out your professional responsibilities while your family and your people are living through such circumstances,” he told Al Jazeera earlier this month while in Doha. “For me to coach the Palestinian national team, a team that represents this suffering, and to try to make it a source of joy, bring a smile to people’s faces or give the Palestinian people hope, means a great deal to me personally.” The 46-year-old former footballer said it was a “badge of honour” to coach the national team, which he led to 2027 AFC Asian Cup qualification after taking the reins in 2024. The team were drawn in Group A against Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Oman, with the tournament rescheduled from January to December 2027 due to the ongoing conflict in the region. Palestine have enjoyed considerable success in recent international friendlies, including a 2-2 draw with New Zealand, defeating Tajikistan 4-2, and thrashing China 5-0. But the victories are bittersweet, given what’s happening at home. He was in Algeria for a training camp with the national team when he received news that his house had been destroyed. His entire family now lives in al-Mawasi, a coastal area where more than 900,000 displaced people are sheltering in southern Gaza. “The Palestinian people are suffering wherever they are,” Abu Jazar said. He recounted an ordeal he went through before a qualifying match against Kuwait. Israel had issued a forced evacuation order for the area where his family lived, but his brother, Khalil, refused to leave. “He had reached a point where he was simply saying, ‘Where am I supposed to go? Where can I possibly go?’” Abu Jazar recalled. He made a last-ditch attempt to convince his brother to flee before boarding the team bus headed to the stadium for the match. “I kept trying to call, but I could not get through. At that point, I had to trust that, God willing, my brother had listened to what I told him,” Abu Jazar said. “We also had a match to play in the name of Palestine. We had to concentrate and do our job.” Abu Jazar was able to breathe a sigh of relief after the match when he eventually got through to his brother, who assured him that they had all managed to leave safely. A passion for sport is shared throughout Abu Jazar’s family. His mother, Huda, played volleyball at school and even offers her son tactical advice over the phone. “Sometimes we talk about football and sports; she evaluates the players and discusses their performances after a match,” he said. “To be honest, she understands football very well in general.” Abu Jazar’s message to the world is: “We are a people who simply want to live. We are a people with ambitions and hopes, a people with creative minds, thinkers, and scientists. “And sport is also part of the culture and identity of any society. We, too, are sporting people; we are football-loving people. “So, we ask the whole world to grant us our rights.”

events.title: Bye bye, gift cards: People are putting more effort into gifts this year
events.summary: The number of people planning to give gift cards this holiday season is at a 20-year low. : Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images People are planning to buy fewer gift cards as holiday gifts this year. Gift card purchases are expected to hit a 20-year low, according to the National Retail Federation. It shows that shoppers are getting more thoughtful about their gift-giving. Expect to get fewer gift cards this holiday season. The share of consumers who are planning to buy someone on their list a gift card is at the lowest in more than two decades, according to a survey of likely Thanksgiving Weekend shoppers conducted by the National Retail Federation, or NRF. Just 39% of shoppers surveyed plan to buy a gift card this year. Two decades ago, a majority did. The gift card 's slide in popularity can be attributed to factors from generational divides to giving fewer gifts, retail experts said. But it also shows a societal shift: If shoppers are going to bother buying a gift, it might as well mean something. "While gift cards are flexible, they are neither imaginative nor are they particularly personal," Global Data retail analyst Neil Saunders said. "A lot of people now want to give more meaningful gifts." The NRF found something similar in its survey, said Allison Zeller, the group's vice president of industry and consumer insights. The top reason respondents said they weren't giving gift cards was that they wanted to give gifts more tailored to the recipient. There was also an age divide, with baby boomers reporting they were more likely to give a gift card than Gen Z shoppers were, Zeller said. Thanks to the internet — and now AI tools — shoppers also have fewer excuses for not finding a good gift. That's a shift from two decades ago, when more shoppers stuck to in-store shopping during the holiday season. "You were limited in what you could buy based on what was in your town," she said. This year, many consumers are also trying to save money on holiday gifts. One-fifth of respondents to the NRF's survey, for instance, said that they were planning to buy gifts for fewer people . That could point to another reason people are buying fewer gift cards, said Julian Givi, an associate professor of marketing at West Virginia University who has studied gift-giving and consumer behavior. For years, gift cards were an easy choice if buyers didn't know the recipient that well — think about that cousin you only see twice a year, Givi said. "If you cut them out, you're probably cutting out the gift card spending," he told Business Insider. Shoppers who are trying to save money on holiday gifts are also more likely to buy a gift at a big discount during shopping days like Cyber Monday, Givi said. Those kinds of deals can give the gift recipient the impression that the giver spent more than they actually did, he added. Gift cards, meanwhile, make the purchase price obvious. "You don't want to make it so apparent to people what you're spending whenever times are kind of tough," he said. Do you have a story idea to share? events.title: Kenya gov’t violated constitution with Ebola quarantine site, court says
events.summary: Kenya’s High Court orders a halt to ⁠further works at the quarantine facility until the government discloses details of agreement with the US. A court in Kenya has ruled that the government breached ⁠the constitution in allowing the ⁠construction of a United States-backed Ebola quarantine facility at a military airbase in the country. High Court Judge Patricia Nyaundi said on Thursday that the government should have disclosed the details of the agreement with the US and sought public input before signing the deal on the facility near the town of Nanyuki in central Kenya. list 1 of 4 Ebola outbreak kills more than 5,300 people in DR Congo list 2 of 4 WHO approves trials for two new Ebola vaccines list 3 of 4 Kenya discharges last Ebola patient, awaits disease-free status list 4 of 4 Nigeria ends 21-day Ebola contact monitoring with no secondary transmission The court ordered that any ⁠further works at the quarantine facility be stopped until the government meets these conditions. “Put differently, the petitioners, the people of Kenya and more significantly, the residents of Laikipia County have been left with the position of persons standing outside the sealed wooden window, straining to discern what is ⁠taking place on the other side,” Nyaundi said in her ruling. “They are aware ⁠that the decisions affecting their community are being made and implemented, yet they have been denied any meaningful opportunity to know, interrogate or participate in those decisions.” The 50-bed ⁠facility, located inside Laikipia airbase near Nanyuki, was intended to quarantine people exposed to Ebola, including US citizens. Seven American aid workers who had been ‌in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to help tackle the Ebola outbreak quarantined at the facility in July. Kenyans have staged angry protests against the facility, as residents accuse the US of offloading Ebola risks onto Kenyans. In June, at least one person was killed after Kenyan police opened fire at demonstrators protesting against the facility. The week before, hundreds took to the streets in Nanyuki amid growing frustration among residents as Kenyan and US authorities publicly reaffirmed their commitment to the plan despite court orders. At the time, the demonstration also turned violent, with at least two people killed and one wounded. Kenya’s High Court had temporarily suspended the facility’s construction in late May, but it found ⁠that Health Minister Aden Duale failed to comply with the orders. Duale later told the court he had ordered an immediate halt to construction ⁠and related activity at the site. Kenya reported its first imported case of the Bundibugyo Ebola ‌strain in early October in a traveller who had arrived from the DRC via Uganda. As of mid-November, Kenya had recorded two deaths and seven other cases, all of whom have recovered. No new cases ‌have been reported in Kenya since October 19. There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain responsible for the outbreak, which the World Health Organization declared an international public health emergency on May 17. The government has not yet commented on Thursday’s court ruling.

events.title: What's gone wrong at Poundland?
events.summary: Watch: Why has Poundland collapsed into administration? The future of Poundland hangs in the balance after the discount retailer's collapse into administration. Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat. Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand. Its collapse puts the jobs of its 11,000 employees at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer. Have people stopped shopping at Poundland? People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite. Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges. Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year. According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor, "this isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland". She told the BBC the tills were "busier than they were a year ago", adding that on the face of it a turnaround seemed "well under way". However, Gordon Brothers had been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses. So why is it now in administration? Poundland faced "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", according to Palmer. However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams claimed the business was making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers painted a different picture, saying the chain remained "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading". It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business. Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk Published 5 hours ago Poundland workers 'in limbo' over firm's future Published 1 day ago It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges. As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1. As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not. "When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story." Irish firm Martin Property Group, London-based holding company Xyra Group and German investment firm Zachert Private Equity are all also understood to have made offers for Poundland. Gordon Brothers had also been weighing options to break Poundland up. Its view was that ultimately breaking the retailer up would provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate would also have to agree to keep the employees on. Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale accuse it of driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process. But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim. Now that the company has entered administration, consultants at Alix Partners have been appointed to pursue a sale of the business and its assets. There are various options on the table, which include securing a buyer for the business either in whole or piecemeal. The prime minister has said he wants "every effort made to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps as many shops open as possible". In the immediate future, Poundland stores and distribution centres will continue operating as normal. events.title: Norse Atlantic Airways suspends all flights as it makes urgent funding plea
events.summary: Norwegian airline says its finances are ‘critical’ and it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term backing Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights and said it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term financing urgently. The Norwegian airline, which operates long-haul flights around the world including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia, announced it was on the brink on Thursday morning, a day after warning that its finances were “critical”. The airline, like many worldwide, is reeling from surging jet fuel prices that have sent costs skywards since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, as well as hitting consumer confidence. In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Norse said: “If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board’s ​intention to file for bankruptcy.” It said it was still looking at options to secure short-term financing and was in discussion with investors regarding a possible takeover but said: “There can be no assurance that a viable solution will ​be found.” Norse was founded in 2021 as it sought to step into the space vacated by Norwegian Air , whose attempts to fly budget long-haul were also abandoned as unviable. Despite that, Norse revived the transatlantic routes, with a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners and ​many former Norwegian staff. Norse said in the summer it was exploring a potential sale or merger, and set out on a cost-cutting programme called Project Falcon to save $50m (£38m), including axing about 75 jobs. It also moved its headquarters out of Norway to cheaper offices in Latvia, while the founder and chief executive, Bjørn Tore Larsen, left the airline. It said it “sincerely apologises to its passengers for the inconvenience caused by this situation”. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning UK routes affected include London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok and Cape Town. A winter service from Manchester to Thailand was due to start operating next month.

events.title: 45°C inlets just killed the chiller. Most people haven't noticed yet
events.summary: SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect. If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger. We also saw a lot of new companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with big industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not. Game changing news The real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that currently need chillers suddenly don't. If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places. Rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent. So, in our new cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again. What's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for new datacenter builds. The power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses. Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate. Water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a big deal. The same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a new build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists. Getting to 45°C isn't free Designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the new set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers. At SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course. Any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply. My instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more. There's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing shows 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale. We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement. Much lower energy use, water consumption down by 85 percent to 90 percent, higher efficiency and lower costs. Not a bad deal, right? ®
