events.title: I’m a Silicon Valley couples therapist. Here’s what Jensen Huang's daily therapy sessions might entail.
events.summary: Phil Boissierie has been a couples' therapist in Silicon Valley for almost 20 years. Courtesy of Phil Boissierie At an Nvidia all-hands, reinstated CEO Jensen Huang said he'll be in therapy for 90 minutes a day. Phil Boissierie is a Silicon Valley therapist who works with couples in high-profile careers. He hasn't met Huang but says therapy could include managing public pressure and relationship repair. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Phil Boissierie, a 50-year-old marriage and couples therapist at The Relationship Therapy Group in Silicon Valley. His words have been edited for length and clarity. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently said he was doing 90 minutes of therapy every day as part of his effort to move forward. I've been a couples therapist in Silicon Valley for 20 years. Ninety minutes of therapy a day is not particularly common, nor is it a traditional model. Usually, if someone's doing that much therapy every day, it's because they're likely trying to work through a lot quickly and create some behavioral change. If a behavior is compulsive or hard to change, doing extended periods of therapy every day can be helpful for building traction. I can't say for sure what he's doing since I don't know Jensen, but here's what that frequency of therapy for a high-profile CEO in a situation like this would probably look like. There will be a lot to work through Working through how to manage public pressure, understand repetitive behavior, and repair relationships are all things I would discuss in the first few sessions of intensive therapy like this. The pressure, the eyes on him , the eyes on the company — all of that is huge, alongside all the damage that's been created in his relationships with his wife, his family, and the other people he's been involved with and working with. Do you think Jensen Huang should have been reinstated? Take our survey . Any therapy plan has to do with what the particular person is going through, and I'm not going to speculate, but in my practice, a lot of times when we see someone having multiple affairs , that doesn't just come out of nowhere. It often has to do with family of origin, early life experiences, and things they're working through, which become the fabric of who we are and how we operate. It takes intentional work to create those changes. I also always recommend to people that when a disclosure comes out about an affair, doing work as a couple right up front is really important. If Jensen and Lori Huang are also doing couples work, I think that would be really, really smart and not overkill. The 90-minute frequency, every day, helps you get through a lot In a traditional 50-minute therapy session, it's common for people to settle into things, then, right as they're doing some heavy lifting and reaching an insight that's particularly challenging or emotional, the session's over. So, by allowing 90 minutes, you're able to settle in and cover a lot more. Working every day in therapy like this could help him pick right back up where they left off the day before, not only face what's happening that day, what's coming up, and all the pressures, but also get a jumpstart on that intensive work of answering questions like, "Why did this happen? How do I stop this from happening again?" Hopefully, that would be a big part of his motivation for doing this much therapy. This also signals something to his company and to people watching Sometimes coming back into the workplace after such a big public situation requires satisfying people. I think that could also be a part of this. It demonstrates to those watching that someone is working hard on themselves. If multiple affairs are happening, if that is what's happening here, it's easy for people to say, "Look, if you're involved in all of this, how are you paying attention to what's going on at the company?" I would imagine if he came out and said, "Hey, I'm going to do an hour a week of therapy, or I'm going to do two hours a week," that just wouldn't suffice for people. If you're going to make the behavioral change, repair the relationships, and take the helm of the company , yeah, you do have to make changes all over the place to be healthy again. Do you have a story to share about your relationship affecting your career? If so, please reach out to the reporter at aapplegate@businessinsider.com . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I moved back to Scotland after 19 years in the US. Thanksgiving is the one tradition I refuse to give up.
events.summary: The author moved back to Scotland in 2020 but still celebrates Thanksgiving. Courtesy of the author I moved to the US in 2001 knowing nothing about Thanksgiving, but it quickly became a holiday I loved. Since moving back to Scotland in 2020, I've kept celebrating Thanksgiving despite a few challenges. Celebrating Thanksgiving in Scotland feels strange, but it keeps me connected to my life in the US. When I moved to the US to study abroad in 2001, I was baffled by the traditions of Thanksgiving. As the years went by, however, I developed a real appreciation for this American holiday — even if I've never quite been able to wrap my head around adding marshmallows to sweet potato. In my early years in the US, I attended Thanksgiving dinners because everyone around me did. Over time, though, I grew to love the simplicity of the holiday — so much so that I brought the tradition home with me when I returned to the UK after 19 years. It's a holiday about gratitude, not gifts I love that there's no pressure around buying gifts or religious ceremony — Thanksgiving is about spending time with people I love, being community-minded, and giving thanks for the small things in life. In Colorado, I'd host friends who didn't have family nearby Courtesy of the author When I lived in the US, I ran in the local Turkey Trot to raise money for charity every Thanksgiving morning, and taught a special gratitude-themed yoga class afterwards. I hosted dinners for friends who also didn't have family nearby and learned to make my own cranberry sauce, adding some dishes from Scotland, like my mom's leeks in cheese sauce. My homemade pumpkin cheesecake became an annual request. When I moved back to Scotland after nearly two decades in the US, I didn't expect that an American holiday would become one of the things that helped me feel at home again . It helped me with a major life transition My first year back in Scotland was a whirlwind of finding a job, a new home, and establishing new routines. Once things settled down, though, I realized how much I missed having an annual occasion to celebrate the good things in life. While my friends in the US were readying their turkey dinners or making plans to fly home and be with family, here in Scotland, life just carried on as normal. The days were getting shorter and colder, and I was in desperate need of some festive cheer to warm my spirits. It was my partner who suggested we celebrate Thanksgiving. Courtesy of the author It was my English partner who suggested we host our own Thanksgiving meal in Scotland. He had a friend from the US who was always homesick at this time of year, and we thought his two kids would relish the opportunity to experience an American holiday that they've only seen in movies. It's strange celebrating a holiday when the rest of the country goes to work My partner volunteered to take on the turkey, and I made a shopping list for the rest. Getting the basics was pretty easy, but some items weren't so readily available. After a half day of searching, I finally found canned pumpkin at a local health food store (at nearly $5 a can), and my American friend saved the day with a bag of fresh cranberries. Our teenager even took a break from his Rubik's Cube to peel sprouts, but it didn't last long Courtesy of the author It felt a bit strange celebrating a holiday when the rest of the country was at work. The kids went to school, I had to prep the meal between work tasks, and there would be no day off on Friday to recover. After school, the day took on an atmosphere of excitement, however. The kids enjoyed the novelty of a holiday their school friends weren't celebrating, and my stepson even put down his Rubik's Cube for 20 minutes to help prepare the sprouts. A few friends crowded into our kitchen, and we managed to find the football game on satellite television, although I don't think anyone understood the rules. Our first Thanksgiving was quite traditional, with all the classics Courtesy of the author Once dinner was ready, taking turns to say what we were grateful for felt unfamiliar to some of my guests, but everyone joined in. The funniest part was seeing my friends' faces when our American friend presented his sweet potatoes with marshmallows. At times, everyone looked as bewildered as I felt on my first Thanksgiving, but it turned out to be a tradition that can easily translate across cultures. For most other people in Scotland, it was just an average Thursday night, but for the first time in a year, I felt really connected to the life I'd left behind. Living abroad taught me that home isn't just where you come from Since 2021, we've found a way to honor Thanksgiving almost every year. Sometimes it's just a quiet dinner with my partner and his daughter; last year, it coincided with a visit from our Swedish friends, and we ended up with a large group crammed into my tiny apartment . Last year it coincided with a visit from our Swedish friends, so we all crammed into my tiny apartment Courtesy of the author I've found that people from all over the world are really interested in the ideas behind Thanksgiving, and are usually thrilled to be invited over. I can't believe that a can of pumpkin puree here costs more than a gallon of gas in the US, and I still haven't found a reliable source of fresh cranberries. But I've learned handy substitutes, like using butternut squash or sweet potato puree for pumpkin, and red currants or sour cherries for cranberries. Scotland may be where I grew up, but moving back after 19 years wasn't quite as simple as I expected. I left friends, routines, and the life I'd built behind. Keeping Thanksgiving alive has helped me hold on to that part of myself while making a new life here. Next year, I want to organize my own mini Turkey Trot before dinner — even if we all have to get up early and fit it in before work. It's one more American tradition I can make my own, wherever home happens to be. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Sam Altman needs Jony Ive to create a physical AI device because Apple will never give OpenAI the real-world data ChatGPT needs, Tony Fadell says
events.summary: Sam Altman asked former Apple design chief Jony Ive to create a physical device for OpenAI because the AI company cannot get the data it needs from the iPhones it runs on, Tony Fadell says.  Fadell worked with Ive at Apple and is best known for being the “father of the iPod” and a co-creator of the iPhone. He founded Build Collective and previously founded Nest Labs. Fadell spoke to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon. AI evidently works well for text, images, and video on the flat screens of our phones and laptops. So it is not obvious what an OpenAI consumer device would look like, or even do, given that ChatGPT can already function on any computing device you own. We know only that OpenAI hopes it will usurp the iPhone as the world’s most popular consumer electronics product. The reason OpenAI is going to such lengths, Fadell believes, is because it needs data about the physical world that Apple refuses to give it due to privacy concerns. “They have to build products because they cannot get contextual information out of the phone,” Fadell said. “So what they have to do is they have to recreate the GPS, the microphones, the speakers, the cameras, the temperature, you name it. Like, all kinds of different things that they have to get, because Apple will not allow you to get that out of the phone.” “It’s really to get around all the restrictions because of all the privacy things for Apple. That’s why,” he said. “The more context that you have for AI, the better the answers, and the more quickly [you] can get to them.” “Apple has all the products with all the context in your home, but you’re not going to get that data. Apple’s not going to give you that because of the privacy restrictions,” he said. Apple’s privacy restrictions are not the driving motive, Altman has said. When asked for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson pointed to a YouTube video in which he said, “The reason we want to do new kinds of consumer hardware is that I think this is a technology that wants a new form factor.” “I think laptops and iPhones are incredible things. You know, some of the greatest inventions in the history of human technology. But I feel that like AI is constrained to using this thing that was designed for a person, not an AI. Like watching an AI use a computer really well is kind of amazing. But then it’s also a little silly to think that like, you know, a computer is putting all this energy into like rendering a UI meant for a person to look at, then AI is trying to read it rather than just like get the data directly.” The need for “edge” computing At some point OpenAI will want to move parts of the processing function behind ChatGPT out from its own cloud servers and onto your devices, so-called “edge computing.” For many simple tasks, AI does not need an array of servers to deliver answers to prompts. The processing power in your laptop or on your phone will do. But it might be difficult for OpenAI to persuade Apple to allow its vast network of iOS and macOS devices to run OpenAI tasks. “So they also want to move processing to the edge, but they don’t get access to all that [from Apple]. So what they’re doing is they’ll make a companion device that’s basically a stripped-out smartphone without a screen on it, with all the sensors and everything, and then they just pipe it through Wi-Fi or Bluetooth back up to the network through your phone, back up to AI agents that could be running on the cloud, or maybe in an app on your phone.” What physical form will the device take?  Fadell speculates: “So you’ve heard they’re gonna make a phone, they’re gonna make a pendant. They’re going to make a pen. They’re going to make a speaker because they’re just trying to get context.” OpenAI was approached for comment. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ukraine drone attack kills five in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia
events.summary: Russian forces launch ballistic missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, hitting a shopping centre and other buildings. At least five people have been killed and three others were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russian-occupied Zaporizhia, a Russian-installed official said, as Russian forces hit Ukraine’s capital Kyiv in a ballistic missile assault. “Following an enemy drone attack on a parking lot, five people were killed and three others wounded in the locality of Vesioloye,” Moscow-installed governor Yevgeny Balitsky wrote on Telegram on Thursday. list 1 of 4 Could Russia-Ukraine war threaten Libya’s fragile reunification process? list 2 of 4 After Libya, where will Ukraine strike Russia next? list 3 of 4 Is Libya a new front in the Ukraine war? list 4 of 4 Putin says retaliation ‘inevitable’ after Ukraine hit Russian oil plants Earlier, Ukrainian forces hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Russian authorities also reported repelling drone attacks in the Tuymazinsky district in the Bashkortostan region and in the city of Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II. Russia has claimed the annexation of the southern region of Zaporizhia, which it partially controls, since September 2022. The Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, was targeted with ballistic missiles late on Wednesday, striking a shopping centre and two other buildings on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, with warnings for residents to remain in shelters still in place, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday its forces had carried out a massive overnight strike on Ukraine, hitting military-industrial facilities in Kyiv, the Interfax news agency reported. The Defence Ministry also said Russian forces had struck a dry cargo vessel southeast of Odesa in the Black Sea overnight, according to the news agency. The ministry alleged the ship was carrying military equipment and dual-use goods to Ukraine. Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said the residents heard loud ballistic missile impact sounds late on Wednesday, which injured at least seven people. “People who live in certain areas of the city that come under frequent attack, they go and spend their nights in the shelter, even before air raid sirens raise alarm,” she said. “Coming into this winter, Russia has really heightened its attacks, especially on energy facilities.” Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia “is putting pressure on Kyiv’s military infrastructure, straining its air defences, and everything that can support military supply chains”. “Russia has also been hitting power plants ahead of cold weather. The aim is to wear down morale and inflict economic damage, in addition to all these military effects,” she added. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, MacAlpine said Ukraine’s energy capacity is below 40 percent of pre-war levels, as a number of the combined heating and power plants in Kyiv and the region have repeatedly gone offline due to attacks. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte urged Russia not to “expand the war” in Ukraine, in a joint statement issued on Wednesday after meeting in Florida. “We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” the statement added. The joint appeal by Trump and Rutte comes after the US leader described Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” during a meeting in China last week. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has taken issue with Trump’s comments on Putin. “For us, he is a killer,” Zelenskyy told CNN.

events.title: Mozilla Firefox head says the company is ‘ramping up' the time it devotes to cybersecurity issues
events.summary: Firefox head Ajit Varma said there is still enough time to stay ahead of the AI cybersecurity wave. Alex Broadway/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images Mozilla's Firefox head says his team has stepped up its efforts to fix cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Ajit Varma said his team is working with both OpenAI and Anthropic. Varma said he still thinks there's "enough time" to fix bugs before the next AI advancements roll out. Mozilla's Firefox chief says the pace of AI advancements is still giving his team "enough time" to make sure it addresses any cybersecurity vulnerabilities. "What we've seen is that we are devoting a lot more of our own resources in order to fix these things," Mozilla's Ajit Varma told Business Insider during a recent interview. "So I think if you look at a year ago, I think it was about 10% of our time, and now, when I look at the latest, it's 27% of our effort is now spent on addressing these." Varma's comments came as top US government officials cautioned that the recent string of outages affecting everything from Microsoft Outlook to JPMorgan Chase reflects companies' efforts to fix software issues faster than ever. Home Depot's chief information officer recently told Business Insider that the retailer wants to cut the time it takes to deploy a fix "to hours." Varma said both OpenAI and Anthropic are giving Mozilla, which is a nonprofit, "a lot of tokens for free." The Firefox head said the frontier models "are finding more and more complicated vulnerabilities within our browser." The AI leaders are eager to work with Mozilla. So much so that Varma said that in March his team noticed that someone with an Anthropic email address had submitted a bug. Since Firefox is completely open source, anyone could do so. Once Mozilla's team got in touch, they realized that the Anthropic employee had found a lot more vulnerabilities. "They were excited about testing their models with Firefox, because we have spent decades building a very secure and very tested browser that's open source, has a lot of contributions and a lot of scrutiny around it," Varma said. Beyond cybersecurity, Varma said, is finding other ways to deploy AI tools to make "Firefox even faster" and prevent issues like memory leaks. He said he encourages his team to view AI as a tool and to "triage" what truly needs human attention. "We are trying to encourage people to say there's a lot of routine activities that we don't necessarily need humans to do and that AI does really well because it's relentless; it doesn't get tired," he said. events.title: Wall Street wants to understand Gen Z. These high schoolers are giving it a crash course.
events.summary: High school students Emile Chilingirian and Jasper Gould cofounded a finance newsletter. Jasper Gould Jasper Gould cofounded Passing the Torch, a finance and economics newsletter with 28,000 subscribers. The newsletter offers something many others don't: An authentic Gen Z perspective. The newsletter has attracted Wall Street bros as well as young folks interested in finance. Finance analysts sift through heaps of consumer data, conduct large-scale surveys, and meticulously track trends in their quest to understand Gen Z. High school senior Jasper Gould had a better idea. Gould and Emile Chilingirian of New York City cofounded Passing the Torch , a finance and economics newsletter that's amassed 28,000 readers since its official launch in 2025. The newsletter offers an unfiltered glimpse into the minds of Gen Z , the latest generation to drum up spending power. Passing the Torch reports on a wide breadth of topics, from how Zoomers perceive automated vehicles and robotaxis to a deep dive into Pershing Square Capital Management's $65 billion now-defunct takeover bid for Universal Music Group . This month, the duo published an article titled "AI Stocks Just Started Taking Accutane," which discusses the recent tech stock sell-off. Subscribers pay $15 a month, or $150 annually. "We are a proprietary data source of a very special order, and I think people recognize that," Gould, 18, told Business Insider. That's one reason the newsletter has garnered a fan base on Wall Street. "When we looked into the subscriber logs, we saw a concentration at firms like Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan Chase, and Blackstone," Gould said. 'Let's make a business' Although Gould and Chilingirian are now in the media business, they got their start in the nonprofit sector. They cofounded Brooklyn Youth Charitable Investment Group, an organization that teaches financial and leadership skills to high schoolers, in 2024. The nonprofit has 100 active members and over 1,000 students have participated so far. To gain investors, the pair did cold reach-outs while juggling school and their personal lives. "There was a period of time in 10th grade where we were getting three hours of sleep a night, and I'm very happy we were doing so," Gould said. "If you are intentional about your relationships, if you really invest in them, and if you have something going for you like being in high school, that's really all it takes to warm things up." That helped them secure guest speakers from major institutions like Deutsche Bank, the White House, and Apple, Gould said. As the nonprofit grew, Gould and Chilingirian decided to create an Instagram account to share more tips and advice for young folks interested in finance. The account gained over 37,000 followers in less than two years, which inspired Gould and Chilingirian to think bigger. "A lot of the things we're saying are really valuable to investors, so let's make a business," Gould said. They said they didn't have to purchase ads or flood X to find readers. "It was word of mouth, stakeholders in the nonprofit, and people who knew us," Gould said. "In our pursuit of fundraising and working on this organization, we sent a lot of emails, and we had a lot of people in our network." On-the-ground journalism There are certainly challenges to running a media business, including competing in an oversaturated media market and making money amid dwindling online ad rates. There's also the fact that they're still in high school. "The biggest issue is getting people to take us seriously, which generally isn't an issue after the first phone call, but it's always a battle leading into it," Gould said. While the pair conduct traditional research and speak with experts, their youth allows them to take an anthropological approach to tracking Gen Z's tastes. "Just go to a party and ask someone," Gould said. "They don't realize that what they're about to tell us is going to end up making some investor or some company millions of dollars." Although neither founder has graduated from high school yet, they've already envisioned how their brand will continue leveling up. These days, that includes offering their deep insights into Gen Z to companies through consulting. "I'm sure there are some analysts at some of the pod shops that are learning how to read TikTok and Reddit as valuable sources of information, but I'm seeing it in the hallways every day," he said. events.title: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet
events.summary: Elon Musk and Sam Altman among those rejoicing but Google, Meta and Apple chiefs have declined to weigh in T he phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji. “The mistake has been corrected,” said Elon Musk. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s Sam Altman. It had been a whirlwind two weeks that started with the ouster of Huang as Nvidia’s CEO after his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman some in the US government feared to be a Chinese spy. Two more alleged affairs with company employees were later revealed. Silicon Valley engineers and venture capitalists decried Huang’s departure at the time, writing an open letter to Nvidia’s board of directors saying: “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.” Donald Trump also got involved. The president repeatedly said that he’d like to see the return of Huang calling the CEO a “fine person” and “honorable guy”. In the meantime, Nvidia’s stock tanked, falling more than 10%, and shedding hundreds of billions in value. Nvidia , which designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence, is among the world’s top five most valuable companies. On Monday, in a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang. The decision came after Trump dialed into the company’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return. In a statement, the White House said: “We have to protect our geniuses.” Nvidia’s stock rebounded, gaining nearly $1tn in market value. Trump, who owns shares in the chip maker, took a victory lap, making up to $15m with the surge on Monday. Silicon Valley’s venture capitalists also rejoiced. Jason Calacanis, an angel investor, Nvidia stock-holder and co-host of the tech-centric All-In podcast, wrote a flurry of posts on X. He posted an AI image of a shining long-haired Huang depicted as Jesus holding a graphics processing unit (GPU) in place of the bible, writing : “GPU Jesus has risen.” Other tech figures took the news personally. Travis Kalanick, the disgraced Uber CEO who was pushed out by his board, was one of the top figures fighting for Huang’s reinstatement. In past weeks, he frequently posted on X, saying “Bring Jensen back”, “LFG” (Let’s fucking go), and “We’ve got your back”. Kalanick was reportedly among a small group of venture capitalists who lobbied Trump and JD Vance to push Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, according to the FT . On Monday, Kalanick posted: “I will always sign up to serve him.” While a vocal cohort of Silicon Valley insiders high-fived Huang’s return, it’s been radio silence from several other of the industry’s top leaders and rank-and-file workers. The CEOs of Google, Meta and Apple have not weighed in on the debate. When Amazon’s Jeff Bezos was asked at an event last week if he thought Huang should be reinstated, he responded : “I don’t know enough of the details … so I can’t answer that question.” Microsoft’s Satya Nadella had a similar response. Anil Dash, an entrepreneur with a career in leading smaller tech companies, is one of the few voices in tech who has publicly criticized Huang’s reinstatement. He says it sends the wrong message to the industry – that there are no rules, boundaries or accountability. Dash pointed to widespread rationale for Huang’s return, which is based on the CEO being singularly crucial in the AI arms race against China. Calacanis, for example, has trumpeted this justification, saying : “We can not [sic] lose the race for super intelligence to China – period, full stop.” And now, Dash said, Huang could have been compromised by a Chinese asset, and he’s running the biggest company in the industry. “It doesn’t make any sense,” he said. “We’re all being gaslit and we’re at a certain point where we’re like, ‘No, the sky’s not green. The sky’s blue.’” Dash says the hundreds of thousands of tech workers who live in fear of being swept up in the increasingly frequent waves of layoffs, as the industry pivots to AI, aren’t able to speak up even if they disagree with Huang’s reinstatement. They don’t know if their “boss agrees with these guys”, Dash said. Alison Taylor, an associate professor at New York University’s Stern Business School, said that mentality extends beyond Silicon Valley to the White House, given that Trump played a part in Huang’s return. “Trump’s whole thing is retaliation,” she noted. “The message is: if you don’t shut up and go along with it, you’re not going to survive,” Taylor said. “It’s a fuck you to everybody who believes in the rule of law and who believes in anything being fair.” Huang apologized to Nvidia staff in a company-wide meeting on Tuesday for “some terrible mistakes” he made.

events.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
events.summary: It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical I n the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa. Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods. A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy The city was renowned for its shipyards, which specialised in building huge teak dhows suitable for long voyages across the Indian Ocean. This craft industry was a pillar of the local economy, contributing to Mandvi’s influence far beyond India, and it continues to employ many families of carpenters and other workers today. The huge teak dhows, traditional vessels suited to long voyages across the Indian Ocean, take about three years to build Clockwise from top left: a worker cuts a varangue, part of the boat’s frame, from a large piece of teak. This piece connects the two sides of the hull to the keel; a bolt securing a beam to a boat’s frame is tightened; using a chain hoist, a worker positions a stemson inside the hull of a boat; a worker heads home on Thursday evening. The following day, Friday, is the weekly rest day. It was from the 19th century onwards that Mandvi began to fall into economic decline. The advent of steamships, the need for deep, modern port infrastructure and British colonial rule, which restructured maritime trade to serve its own interests, led to a shift in trade to better-equipped ports such as Mumbai. After independence in 1947, the creation of the nearby port of Kandla definitively marginalised Mandvi commercially. Mandvi was also affected by the 2001 earthquake in Kutch, which damaged some of the old buildings and accelerated its urban transformation. Workers in Manvi also maintain and repair modern vessels The city still clings to its few traditional shipyards, where workers from different religious communities build the boats. While a large proportion of them are Muslim, shipbuilding is also part of a very ancient Hindu tradition. Each dhow takes several years to build by hand and employs about 25 craftsmen. Apprenticeships begin in adolescence, in a world where teams are related and the trade is as much cultural as it is technical. Away from the shipbuilding, the city today is known for its neglected architectural heritage and its beaches, which attract Indian tourists and middle-class locals. events.title: Thomson Reuters is using both American and Chinese AI for its next model
events.summary: Thomson Reuters CEO Steve Hasker. John Lamparski/Getty Images for Advertising Week New York Forget the AI race: Thomson Reuters wants the best of both worlds. The company's next AI model is built off Google's Gemma and Z.ai's GLM, it tells Business Insider. The data and legal giant has spent $40 million so far building its own chatbots. As China and the US race to compete on AI, Thomson Reuters, the Canadian data and legal giant, is having it both ways. The company is launching a new AI model called Thomson 1.1 by the end of the year, it tells Business Insider exclusively — and it's built on open-source models from both countries: China's GLM, from Z.ai, and Google's Gemma. By using open-source models that anyone can download and host, Thomson Reuters hopes to reduce its AI costs and take more control over its intellectual property. There's a battle in tech over which AI corporations will use. It pits cheaper Chinese open-source models against closed ones from giants like Anthropic and OpenAI. US companies like Google, Meta, and Thinking Machines Lab have also released powerful open-source models in recent months. It's a shift for Thomson Reuters , which didn't use American AI for its previous in-house model, Thomson 1.0. Instead, it built its chatbot off Qwen, an AI from the Chinese tech giant Alibaba. "The US government, and many other governments around the world, prefer to have US and Western sovereign models at the foundation of what we do," Thomson Reuters' chief technology officer, Joel Hron, told Business Insider. "Where we can, we're going to use Western and US-based labs to ground Thomson." Hron said the company still uses Z.ai's GLM because it excels at using computers — a key feature of AI agents . It also chose Google's Gemma because of its small size and efficiency, he added. Thomson Reuters aims to build an AI that helps its clients with mid-tier work, such as tax advice. For the most difficult tasks, it still plans to use OpenAI and Anthropic. "There's a lot of work that happens in the middle, and that's where we get real economic benefit," Hron said. Open source has its limitations It takes a lot of money for a big company to build a custom AI chatbot, even if it uses free, open-source models. Hron told Business Insider that so far, Thomson Reuters has spent about $40 million on the effort to tweak and tune its own models. That money goes to things like chips, data, and salaries for AI researchers. Adoption is early. Less than 5% of all AI tokens used at Thomson Reuters come from its own AI, Hron said — although that is set to ramp up in the coming years as its focus areas expand. Chinese models also have built-in censorship features that can be tricky to unwind. Hirundo, a startup in Israel, sent Business Insider an analysis showing that one version of the current Thomson model parrots Chinese government talking points. For example, it refused to acknowledge the Tiananmen Square massacre and said that "Taiwan is an inalienable part of China." A Thomson Reuters spokesperson said that its AI handles such questions "substantially better" when it's used as intended — with a set of instructions to follow. The company's coming AI model further reduces bias, the spokesperson added. To large companies hit by high token bills — like Pinterest , AT&T, and others — the appeal of open source remains strong: it can reduce recurring AI costs and give companies technology they own and control. "Thomson is what AI sovereignty actually looks like in practice," Andrew Bean, Thomson Reuters' lead AI scientist, said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Over $9 billion of S’pore goods affected by US tariffs; trade deal will involve compromises: DPM Gan
events.summary: The proposed new tariffs of up to 20% would raise the effective tariff rate on affected Singapore goods from 7.8% to 10.3%, said DPM Gan Kim Yong. US tariffs could hit about S$9.4 billion of Singapore exports. DPM Gan Kim Yong said talks will continue, but any deal will need “give and take” and trade-offs. The US Trade Representative proposed tariffs of up to 20% under Section 301. It also criticised Singapore’s industrial policies, CPF, and support schemes as causing excess capacity. Business leaders said the findings do not reflect Singapore’s market-driven economy. SBF and the Government will help firms face uncertainty and seek lower tariffs. SINGAPORE – Singapore will continue to negotiate with the United States on lowering tariffs that threaten to hit about $9.4 billion worth of the Republic’s domestic exports, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, adding that any deal, however, will require some give and take. The proposed new tariffs of up to 20% would raise the effective tariff rate on Singapore goods from 7.8% to 10.3%, said DPM Gan, who is also Minister of Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade). Even so, Singapore will negotiate any trade pact with the country’s interests at the centre of the discussion, he told a media briefing on Nov 26. “We also have to bear in mind that whatever agreement we arrive (at) and achieve in the US, there will be give and take. There will be compromises. There will be trade-offs that we need to be prepared to accept,” he added. “So I think, in this process, it’s always important to remember that we will always be visible and always have Singapore’s interests at heart.” The briefing was held a day after the US Trade Representative (USTR) proposed to impose tariffs of up to 20% on Singapore and 13 other trading partners under Section 301, accusing them of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions. The duties could take effect in early 2027, though USTR Jamieson Greer offered to consider lowering the proposed rate to 10% if Singapore reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with Washington. While the new tariff will not be stacked upon the previously announced Section 301 tariffs of 12.5% related to forced labour concerns, without an ART the new tariff rate could reach up to 20%. Gan said the Government is engaging local companies to understand and assess how to assist them. He said he was surprised by the US trade office’s actions and report, which raised many sticking points with Singapore’s economy. “I am very surprised that this has happened because this is not something that we expected from an important, major trading partner,” he said. USTR targets industrial policies and CPF Apart from the statement that announced the new tariff, the USTR also issued a 168-page investigation report listing and explaining US concerns that follow the investigation the agency started in March. According to the USTR’s investigation report on Singapore’s industrial policies, the specific acts, policies and practices related to structural excess capacity and production include the Singapore Manufacturing 2030 plan and the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan, as well as financial support to the manufacturing sector and firms in the electronics and semiconductors, health and petrochemicals industries. The report also cited the “encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investments from non-market economies (NMEs), particularly China, which permits further development of structural excess capacity and production, and encouragement of or failure to address imports from NMEs, which enables Chinese firms to offload excess production”. Singapore trade deal will involve compromises Asked what deal can Singapore negotiate given that it already has a free trade agreement (FTA) with the US, Gan said: “It’s an open question because it’s really for us to discuss with the US to see what their concerns are. “Whether in the process of discussion we will be able to address some of their concerns, and if we are able to do so, we hope we look forward to lower tariffs. It may not be... either 10% or 20%. It may be somewhere in between. And if we are able to arrive (at) some agreeable tariff together with the trade-offs that we have to accept, I think it’s something that will be a subject of negotiation moving forward.” He said Singapore will be actively engaging the US administration over tariffs over the next couple of months. Still, he said the high tariff rate and the scrutiny of Singapore’s economic policies in the USTR report were quite disappointing. “Our bilateral relations are multi-faceted. It’s not just economics, but many other aspects as well. So I think we’ll continue to hope to be able to continue to strengthen our bilateral relationship and look forward to looking for a way to resolve differences in our tariffs and our trade relationship, and to seek better tariff for our exporters.

events.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
events.summary: Published 26 November 2026, 02:13 GMT The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset. The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal. The BBC understands the deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal. Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay. The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship. The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal. New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected. EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme Published 21 hours ago Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students Published 21 hours ago Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU Published 19 hours ago Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports. The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout. Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East. Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements." "It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier." The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries. The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation. Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny. Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week , the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything". Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum. Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour. events.title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
events.summary: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand. Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently. The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars , who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off . The arm was developed in the 2000s , initially trialed in 2014 , and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying. Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system. The loss of a limb In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground. The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated. Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.” Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says. The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says. New connections A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab . Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working. A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.” In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one. Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says. The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says. COURTESY OF AVI DAVIDSON That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.  To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”  The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George. Becoming bionic Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer. He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health Syst

events.title: Ex-Cricket Australia boss James Sutherland defends ‘Sandpapergate’ probe
events.summary: Meanwhile, David Warner denies a broadcaster’s claim that he used superglue and grit to tamper with the ball. Former Cricket Australia (CA) chief James Sutherland defended his handling of the 2018 “ Sandpapergate ” investigation on Thursday, but refused to weigh in on the crisis tearing the sport apart. Sutherland was at the helm when the ball-tampering scandal erupted during the third Test at Cape Town against South Africa. list 1 of 3 Injured Sinner ruled out of Australian Open after surgery list 2 of 3 Malen and Roma deny injury-hit PSG in Champions League draw list 3 of 3 Man United denied at Sporting as referee overshadows Fernandes double A whirlwind Cricket Australia investigation laid the blame on then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner, and Cameron Bancroft , the player who used sandpaper to rough up the ball to make it swing. Retired Australian opener Usman Khawaja reopened old wounds this month by alleging in his autobiography that the whole team was aware of what was going on, claims backed by Warner and Bancroft. It led to current captain Pat Cummins vigorously denying he or the bowlers at the time – Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon – were in on the plot. “I don’t look back on if things could, or should, have been dealt with differently,” said Sutherland, who stepped down in the wake of the crisis and is now head of Golf Australia. “We did the best we could with the situation that was in front of us and the information in front of us,” he added to The Australian newspaper. “It was a tough time and a very, very difficult situation for me personally. I’m not going to speak for other people. I know lots of people found it difficult. “I believe I’m out of it now, and [current CA boss] Todd [Greenberg’s] job is hard enough without me speaking about it.” Cricket Australia, under Greenberg, has ruled out reopening the probe but is setting up a forum for players to share their experiences about 2018. Interim CA chairman David Boon also made clear there would be no new sanctions coming out of it. In a separate interview with the Sydney Morning Herald on the sidelines of the Australian PGA Championship in Sydney, Sutherland said it would be inappropriate to comment on Khawaja’s claims . “I’ve made that personal commitment that I wouldn’t make comments from afar on current cricket issues. I’ve been true to that so far,” he said. “It’s fair to say it brings back some memories and not too many happy memories. I just recall it being an incredibly intense and stressful period.” Warner hits back over ‘unverified’ superglue, grit ball-tampering claims Warner has hit out at Melbourne-based broadcaster Gerard Whateley’s claims that the former Australia Test opener used superglue and grit on finger strapping to tamper with the ball. A long-form investigation published by News Corp and SEN Radio claimed Warner’s finger strapping was found in South Africa and investigated by an official from the International Cricket Council, the sport’s governing body. Commenting on an Instagram post discussing Whateley’s report, Warner labelled those claims “unverified” and accused the media of “perpetuating speculation” around his involvement in the ball-tampering scandal. “I’m not entirely sure where Gerard’s assertions have come from, as they certainly do not align with my recollection of events,” Warner said. “In relation to the alleged use of superglue and grit, and the more recent claims regarding the finger, could I respectfully ask what credible evidence exists to substantiate these allegations? “Before further unverified claims are circulated publicly, I would suggest establishing the facts rather than perpetuating speculation.” Warner, who was banned for a year over his role in the 2018 scandal, commented again in response to another user, questioning “the distinction between journalism and bullying”. “Education and eloquence are admirable qualities, but they should never be used to undermine those who weren’t afforded the same opportunities,” Warner wrote. “When someone uses their public platform to control a narrative without affording others the same voice, it raises a legitimate question about the distinction between journalism and bullying.” Last weekend, Warner and Khawaja were taken off television commentary duties by Fox Sports. The move came after Cummins’s lengthy news conference and days after Warner blasted CA’s handling of Sandpapergate as “a cover-up”.

events.title: Car finance compensation payments explained
events.summary: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements could face further delays to compensation after the financial regulator said it had made some errors in its calculations. Driver have already been told they must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. Who could receive car finance compensation? The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024. The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period. In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much. Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan. Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders. How much compensation could victims receive? Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement. The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn. How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered. The FCA has announced some claimants might be offered an early settlement, but only if it as good as what would be paid under the current proposed central scheme. What do victims need to do to claim compensation? Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything. The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company. The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts. Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation . The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain , external . lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster some people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, if the agreement began on or after 1 April 2014 and you complained by 30 June 2026 some of those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027, if the agreement began before 1 April 2014 there are exemptions , external , and anyone who does not hear from their lender by the dates set out, isn't necessarily owed compensation those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees. FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers. When will drivers receive compensation and who will pay? Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027. But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme. The watchdog has now said it uncovered some mistakes in how it categorised a small group of loan agreements under its redress scheme, which could have a small impact on compensation levels.

events.title: Chinese consumer advocate stranded in South Korea amid a crackdown at homoe
events.summary: Consumer rights advocate Wang Hai is stranded in South Korea with his family after fleeing China fearing arrest during a crackdown on campaigners seeking compensation from businesses WASHINGTON -- Chinese consumer rights advocate Wang Hai has spent three decades exposing counterfeit goods and seeking compensation for buyers. In recent months, he left China fearing he was a target of the authorities, but now he is stranded in South Korea with his family, facing possible deportation home. Wang, a well-known campaigner against counterfeit goods, said China invalidated his passport and South Korean authorities rejected his asylum. The United States also revoked his tourist visa, narrowing his options for leaving South Korea and deepening his fears of being sent back to China. Chinese authorities launched a campaign against organized crime in July, saying they would target “malicious compensation claims.” Since then, authorities have arrested at least 100 people for allegedly extorting businesses through anti-counterfeiting work or consumer compensation claims, according to official statements reviewed by The Associated Press. Wang said the arrests made him fear he could be next, prompting him to leave a country where official Chinese media had once praised him for his role as an anti-counterfeiting activist. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs told The Associated Press it was not aware of Wang’s case. The Ministry of Public Security did not respond to a request for comment. The quagmire in which Wang, 53, and his family have found themselves has drawn concerns from rights advocates over China’s efforts to target critics abroad and the narrowing options for people seeking refuge in the U.S. “The Chinese government’s practice of transnational repression is well documented, including in South Korea,” said Yaqiu Wang, senior China researcher at Human Rights Watch, based in Washington, and “there is no doubt that the Trump administration has created a far more hostile environment for immigrants, and even visitors.” Wang spoke to the AP from South Korea about his situation and has appealed the rejection of his asylum application in that country. The activist said that he arrived in South Korea in late September with his wife, 8-year-old daughter and infant son. Wang said he believed Chinese authorities were targeting him and that dozens of his staff members were arrested and questioned. Some remain in detention, he said. One staffer had his passport revoked while traveling from Thailand to Singapore last month, he said. “The very same job has suddenly morphed from being praised into something associated with organized crime — it’s absolutely surreal," said Wang. Asked what he is afraid of if he is sent to China, Wang didn’t hesitate: “I would definitely spend the rest of my life behind bars.” A notice reviewed by AP showed South Korean immigration authorities rejected Wang's and his family's applications for refugee status. AP also reviewed the U.S. Embassy email that revoked his visa, in which U.S. authorities told Wang that new information made him inadmissible to the U.S. or ineligible for a U.S. visa but did not provide specific details. South Korea’s Justice Ministry said it couldn’t share any information, citing local laws on refugees and personal information protection. Observers say that South Korea’s acceptance rate for refugee status applications has been less than 2% in recent years. The U.S. State Department didn't respond to the request for comment. 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Federal officials say 'zero' airborne lead detected after Iowa munitions blast Pennsylvania teen who died in 2020 could become first Gen Z saint Wang became a household name in China in the 1990s for exposing counterfeit goods, an increasingly widespread problem as the country’s market economy expanded rapidly and consumer protection oversight lagged. In 1998, Wang joined a roundtable discussion with then-U.S. President Bill Clinton during his visit to Shanghai. Wang told Clinton he had been viewed as “immoral” at home, according to a White House transcript. Chinese state media, however, largely portrayed him favorably, calling him “China’s No. 1 anti-counterfeiting activist.” Professional consumer advocates were compared to “woodpeckers,” rooting out problems in the marketplace. Wang ran a rights-protection company in Beijing for about 30 years and a testing laboratory supporting anti-counterfeiting work for five years. He said both were forced to close after many of his staff, including three lawyers, were arrested in September. The closure of his offices came after China launched its campaign against organized crime. Authorities said some people were using consumer complaints, lawsuits or threats of exposure to extort money from businesses through what officials called “malicious compensation claims.

events.title: Malaysia wants priority over other lenders if it backs AirAsia
events.summary: KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia will require AirAsia to give it priority over other lenders if the government agrees to provide support to the budget airline, the country’s finance minister said on Nov 26. Officials have said they are assessing ways to provide support without risking public funds. Authorities are monitoring AirAsia’s financial health as airlines around the world grapple with a jump in jet fuel prices linked to the Iran war. AirAsia has said it was aiming to raise up to US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) from international debt markets as well as RM700 million (S$220.19 million) in local credit facilities, with the fundraising expected to be completed between December and February. AirAsia posted a narrower loss in the third quarter, but warned of rising fuel costs as it works to boost liquidity. Malaysia’s Second Finance Minister Amir Hamzah Azizan told Parliament that there has so far been no agreement or commitment to provide support to AirAsia, either in the form of loans, guarantees or public fund injections. But if required, the government would look to safeguard public funds and ensure no disruptions to connectivity, he added. “We want to ensure that public funds get the priority they deserve because we would be the saviours if we were to intervene,” Amir Hamzah said. The government would also look to strengthen oversight of AirAsia’s board and management, Amir Hamzah said, citing a similar approach taken to assist debt-laden oil and gas services firm Vantris Energy. “The government’s priority is the interests of the nation and the people, not the interests of shareholders,” he added. The government’s monitoring was focused only on AirAsia’s domestic operations and not on its overseas arms or related businesses under its affiliate Capital A. Malaysia in 2025 approved an RM1.1 billion capital injection into Vantris through redeemable convertible loan stock, a move officials have described as a strategic ecosystem rescue rather than a bailout. The global aviation industry is suffering its worst crisis since the Covid-19 pandemic as the conflict, which began at the end of February, disrupts operations, drives up fuel prices, and sends airlines’ costs rocketing. Norwegian airline Norse Atlantic suspended flights on Nov 26 and intends to file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure a short-term financing solution urgently. REUTERS

events.title: Indonesian nickel tycoon Arif Kurniawan named suspect in money laundering probe
events.summary: Nickel matte at a refining facility in South Sulawesi. About 83% of Indonesia’s nickel output went to the stainless steel sector in 2025. Indonesian attorney general’s office named nickel trader Arif Kurniawan a suspect in a money laundering probe over alleged illegal mining proceeds from 2021 to 2026. The AGO said funds were hidden through intermediaries and affiliate firms; investigators seized documents, over US$3 million in cash, and almost 38kg of gold bars. Kurniawan denied wrongdoing. The case could shake Indonesia’s nickel sector, which supplies about 60% of global output, as he traded about a third of the country’s ore supply in 2024. NEW YORK – The Indonesian attorney general’s office has named nickel trader Arif Kurniawan as a suspect in a money laundering case, after warning of irregularities in his business dealings earlier in November. Kurniawan allegedly laundered proceeds from illegal mining and concealed the funds through intermediaries and affiliate firms between 2021 and 2026, the AGO said in a statement late on Nov 25. The well-known trader was named in the statement only by his initials, although his identity was confirmed by authorities earlier in November. Kurniawan denied any wrongdoing and rejected the allegations when contacted by Bloomberg News, saying all of his previous trading activities had complied with relevant laws and regulations. Investigators have seized documents and more than US$3 million (S$3.9 million) in cash in various currencies, as well as almost 38kg of gold bars, in relation to the case, the AGO said. A reclusive but important figure in Indonesia’s mining industry, Kurniawan has risen rapidly since leaving Glencore more than a decade ago to become the country’s top nickel ore trader. The targeting of his sprawling mining and trading business could trigger a shake up of the wider sector, in a nation that accounts for about 60% of global supply. Kurniawan is suspected to be outside of Indonesia, a spokesperson for the AGO said at a press conference earlier in November. In 2024, he traded about a third of the country’s nickel ore supply, Bloomberg reported in 2025, citing a survey of industry figures. Alongside a business partner, Kurniawan also had stakes in at least 20 mining concessions spread across Indonesia. BLOOMBERG

events.title: UK Home Office waved through border system without a working fix for bad data
events.summary: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information. The regulator said the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm. The platform in question, Helios, was slated to replace its predecessor, Warnings Index, in September 2024 and despite an initial delay due to concerns over data quality, went live the following month. Both Helios and Warnings Index are watch-listing systems, designed to allow law enforcement officials – mainly but not exclusively Border Force – to check people's data against official records at the UK border. Helios's federated operating model, whereby the data sources are not centrally managed, yielded quicker results than Warnings Index, but contained a critical flaw in that operational staff could not alter incorrect records. Platform operators, such as Border Force officers, could not amend the data that feeds into it, neither after the fact nor in real time. This was not the case with Warnings Index, which had a dedicated team responsible for correcting data entries in real time. Under Helios, staff were supposed to report inaccuracies to the organization responsible for the relevant source data, which would make the correction. One slight problem: there was no established reporting system at the time Helios was launched on October 2. The platform went live anyway, as officials deemed the data integrity and security risks presented by Warnings Index to be greater than those of Helios. Just nine days passed before the Home Office's data protection officer had to submit a breach report after Helios operational staff said they didn't know how to request data corrections. During the time, Helios operators sent 87 data rectification requests to the Warnings Index correction team, despite it having no capability to make the required changes to the data. The Home Office later said that many other requests likely weren't logged as the proper processes were not in place, and that staff should have logged the issue through a ServiceNow IT ticket, as any other departmental civil servant with any kind of IT issue would have. But the Home Office also said that including personal data in those helpdesk tickets would itself constitute a data breach. The ICO said in its reprimand document [PDF] that it is "unclear" how such a reporting arrangement could realistically work in practice, given that a report would require details from a subject's record that required rectification as well as the new, accurate information that should be used to replace it. The Home Office's proposed workaround was to get operational staff to verbally read out said personal data over a phone call with the IT helpdesk – a procedure it described as possible "but cumbersome." It took the Home Office more than a year to implement a temporary data-rectification method, which involved a BX Data Query tile on the IT Now platform, allowing Helios operators to securely report data accuracy issues. The new method went live on October 25, 2025. By March 18, 2026, the Home Office said the new process had received more than 6,500 correction requests and around 5,000 records had been removed. The ICO said it "remains concerned" about the efficacy of this method, given that operators cannot include personal data in the tile report, but the regulator is satisfied the problem is at least in part fixed. The Home Office also said it was aware of an increase in customer complaints following Helios's launch, and around 800 cases in which people were delayed at the UK border pending additional checks. It was unable to attribute a specific number of these to Helios's technical issues, however. "The Home Office further stated that it was not aware of any data subjects suffering distress as a result of using its services at the UK border," the ICO's report stated. A Home Office spokesperson told us: " W e take data protection extremely seriously. That is why we have co-operated fully with the Information Commissioner's Office. "We immediately removed all outdated records to minimize delays to passenger journeys and strengthened mechanisms to speed up updates. "Our processes will continue to be kept under review, ensuring we meet data protection obligations while protecting border security." Joanne Stones, investigations manager at the ICO, said: "People must be able to trust that decisions about their immigration status at the UK border are made with accurate, up to date information." She added: "They also have the right to expect that when information is inaccurate, there is a swift and efficient way for it to be corrected. "We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this issue was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay." The ICO's public sector enforcement policy favors guidance, reprimands, and other interventions, reserving fines for the most egregious cases. Its rationale is to avoid diverting money from public services and effectively punishing those affected twice. Fines have included £350,000 for a 2021 MoD email that exposed details of Afghan evacuation applicants , and £750,000 for the PSNI's 2023 disclosure of workforce information , including surnames, initials, ranks, and roles. The PSNI penalty was reduced from £5.6 million under the public sector approach. ®
