events.title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
events.summary: SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services Published 26 November 2026, 00:07 GMT US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind. The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy". However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky. There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections. SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities". FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth". "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said. Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results? Published 6 November Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back Published 6 days ago Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038. The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use. Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles). Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth. The plans to put data centres in orbit and on the Moon Published 10 April 2025 Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed. Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them. "That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said. Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision. It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky". It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky". Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet." The BBC visited Arizona before the US midterm elections to understand America's data-centre boom The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling. The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world. New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

events.title: UK regulator admits error in calculating car finance compensation payments
events.summary: FCA also tells Barclays to stop making settlement offers while it works through data problems The financial regulator has admitted that it has miscalculated part of the compensation scheme for victims of the car finance scandal and told Barclays to stop making settlement offers while it works through the data problems. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) revealed it had identified “some errors in how we categorised a small group of loan agreements’, which will affect the average compensation payout to drivers. The errors were discovered as the FCA prepared its response to a legal challenge against its £9.1bn compensation scheme for drivers overcharged for loans as a result of commission payments between lenders and car dealers. That scheme, announced in March, prompted a legal battle that has forced the regulator to partly suspend it . A hearing to decide what happens is due to go ahead in February. “While the potential impact on average compensation is small – less than £10 per agreement, on average – we recognise this affects ongoing litigation,” the FCA said on Thursday. “We are sorry for the further uncertainty this creates for consumers and firms. We will provide an update on any further material developments.” Earlier this month Barclays, which has set aside £430m in connection with alleged motor finance mis-selling, started offering compensation settlements . Barclays is the first big UK lender to begin offering payouts to some customers who have complained, with hopes this might mean some receive payments by Christmas. “Barclays has been offering full and final settlement offers to their customers,” the FCA said. “We have asked that they pause making these offers while we work through the data issues identified and implications they might have, if any.” The FCA said two of the legal challengers were due to serve their expert evidence on Friday. “We will discuss with the challengers and the court the impact on this deadline, and for the timeline of the litigation,” the FCA said. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Lenders have set aside about £7.5bn to pay compensation owed and are preparing to handle large volumes of complaints. Harry Charalambous, the credit risk principal at the consultancy Broadstone, said the error by the FCA would mean lenders had to revisit their models, and could delay any potential plans to swiftly pay compensation. “It is particularly frustrating for lenders looking to proactively resolve complaints through full and final settlement offers,” he said. “The FCA’s request for Barclays to pause its offers may prompt other lenders considering a similar approach to hold off until the revised calculations are confirmed, potentially delaying compensation for consumers.”

events.title: Details of two treaties at heart of Andy Burnham’s EU reset to be published
events.summary: Government also to publish bill that will enact EU deals as Tories and Reform hit out over 10-year termination clause Details of two treaties at the heart of Andy Burnham’s post- Brexit reset plans will be published on Thursday alongside the bill that will implement the changes into UK law. The treaties signed by the UK and the European Union at last week’s summit will have a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party were to end the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, the BBC reported on Thursday. Any termination clause could bring the longer-term future of the deal into doubt, after the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch , described it as a “terrible deal” that she would scrap. Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay, with the Reform UK leader promising to renege on the deal if he were to win power, arguing that Burnham “cannot bind a future British government”. At a major summit in Brussels last week the UK and EU announced three deals , on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK. But uncertainty around the trio of deals remains, with fears they could be derailed in six months unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities. On Wednesday Burnham indicated that European students would have to pay higher fees than their domestic equivalents at UK universities. While Burnham has previously stated he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime, he has played down the issue of full integration since the deal was struck, saying it was “not a prelude to anything” and that it would be “unthinkable” for the UK to rejoin the EU without holding another referendum . Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food and emissions trading deals, alongside the government’s bill to enact the agreement. The government is also expected to publish assessments of the impact on different sectors and regions of the country . Earlier this year, the Guardian revealed ministers were planning to reshape Britain’s relationship with the EU with legislation that would result in the UK signing up to EU single market rules without a normal parliamentary vote. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters The new bill that will bring into force the food and drink trade deal will contain powers enabling the government to dynamically align with Europe on areas where it has already made agreements. It will also allow the UK to quickly implement evolving single market rules if it determines it is in the national interest, without having to face full parliamentary scrutiny each time. The European affairs minister, Hamish Falconer, said: “The cutting costs bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements. It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier.”

events.title: Check the firm before you invest, FCA warns, as AI scams rise
events.summary: A third (33%) of UK adults say they have seen an investment promotion in the past year that they believe used artificial intelligence (AI), new research from the FCA shows. Reports of investment fraud to Report Fraud that mention suspected use of AI have risen by nearly 400% in a year, up from 193 in 2024/25 to 956 in 2025/26. Investment fraud victims lost an average of £28,188 in 2025/26.Most people feel confident they could spot an AI investment scam, but that confidence is lower when a well-known person is involved. Almost two-thirds (62%) of adults say they could identify an investment scam that used AI. But less than half (49%) think they could tell whether a video or voice recording of a well-known person had been generated or altered by AI.Martin Lewis was the person most often named by those who thought they had seen a fake promotion featuring a well-known person.Under-35s are the most confident and the most exposed. Around three-quarters (74%) say they could identify an AI investment scam, and more than half (56%) believe they have seen an AI-generated investment promotion in the past year. Despite this, fewer than 4 in 10 (38%) would check whether a firm is FCA-authorised before investing. Among over-65s the figure is almost three-quarters (73%).Sheree Howard, executive director of authorisations at the FCA, said:'AI makes creating online scams easier and harder for people to identify.'Whether you’re considering an investment, pension opportunity, loan or other financial service, use Firm Checker to check if a firm is authorised and help fight financial crime.'Before you invest, check the firmSearch the FCA Firm Checker to see whether the firm is authorised for the services being offered.Use the firm contact details on Firm Checker to ensure you are dealing with the real firm.Firm Checker also lists firms the FCA knows are operating without authorisation. Notes to editors:The survey was conducted by Kantar. The survey was conducted from 20 to 26 October 2026. The sample comprised 2,558 UK respondents aged 16+.References to investment promotions using AI mean AI-generated or manipulated media, such as video or audio.The investment fraud figures are taken from Report Fraud’s Annual Assessment FY2025-26 (PDF), published in September 2026.Firm Checker has been specially designed for, and tested with, consumers to make sure it is effective and easy to use. The Financial Services Register remains in place as the full regulatory record of the authorised financial services population.Using an authorised firm can also bring other benefits as authorised firms must meet FCA standards and follow the FCA's rules. Consumers can also take a complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service and are more likely to benefit from protection from the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.We strengthened consumer protection through the promotion of our Firm Checker tool. We estimate that the tool has been used over 1.9 million times since its introduction in January 2025. Following an advertising campaign in January 2026, we saw a 49% increase in estimated consumers protected (from about 464 to 694 per week).

events.title: Marc Levinson on How UPS Created Modern Logistics
events.summary: UPS was founded nearly a century ago in the basement of a Seattle saloon by James E. Casey and his business partner Claude Ryan. It is now hard to imagine modern, globalized life, and the logistics required to prop it up, without the innovations Casey and his partners at UPS cooked up during the company's early decades. Marc Levinson has just written a biography of Casey and the company he founded — UPS Man: James E. Casey and the Creation of Modern Logistics — which was a lot harder to do than you might imagine, because Casey shunned the spotlight and his contributions were virtually unknown outside of UPS. In today's episode, Levinson tells us why UPS is so secretive about its history, how Casey and his partners helped figure out the last mile problem and popularized parcel delivery, and how scientific management theories influenced everything the company did. events.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights, warns it may file for bankruptcy after share price collapse
events.summary: Norse Atlantic has suspended all of its flights amid an urgent financial situation. The low-cost long-haul airline also warned it may have to file for bankruptcy if short-term financing is not secured. The Norwegian carrier has come under strain due to soaring jet fuel costs since the onset of the Iran war. Norse Atlantic suspended all of its flights on Thursday and warned it may have to file for bankruptcy after its stock collapsed on Wednesday following its warning about its "critical" financial situation. Oslo-listed shares of Norse closed 85% lower on Wednesday. "The board of directors continues to consider options to secure short-term financing," Norse said in a Thursday statement. "If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board's intention to file for bankruptcy." The airline added that "there can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found." Checks by CNBC showed the airline was still selling tickets for flights on Friday and beyond as of 9 a.m. Oslo time on Thursday. Warning signs first popped up when PK786 from London to Islamabad and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore were cancelled because of "an unexpected operational suspension," the Pakistani flag carrier said on X. The airline had been set to operate two Pakistan International Airlines flights Wednesday under a wet-lease agreement, in which one airline provides the aircraft and crew to another. The agreement had only been signed in early October. PIA said it would operate the routes using its own Boeing 777 aircraft from the next day. Norse's own flight Z0 783 from London Gatwick to Orlando was also shown as canceled Wednesday on live air traffic website Flightradar24. London Gatwick's website listed the flight's status for Thursday as "enquire airline." In a bid to stave off financial troubles, Norse cut 75 jobs in May as part of an effort to reduce costs by $50 million, after Eivind Roald replaced founder Bjorn Tore Larsen as CEO in November last year. The Norwegian carrier said Wednesday that its situation depended on securing financing for short-term liquidity needs and that it was in discussions about a potential strategic takeover. "Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," the airline said. India's largest airline, low-cost carrier IndiGo, entered an agreement with Norse Atlantic in early 2025 to lease six 787-9 aircraft as it launched flights to Europe and Britain ahead of the arrival of its own widebody planes. The agreement concluded at the end of October this year, with IndiGo citing airspace constraints, elevated fuel costs and currency pressures. At its peak in 2024, Norse Atlantic had 4,822 scheduled flights. That number dipped to 4,695 in 2025 and 2,565 in 2026, according to aviation analytics company Cirium. The airline had 122 flights scheduled for November this year. Norse Atlantic CEO Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and said the airline had no indication at the time that the crisis would have an immediate impact. The airline said in October that it was continuing to operate at reduced capacity because of "prolonged high fuel prices." Correction: This story was updated to reflect that Norse shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.

events.title: Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test
events.summary: Rising data center and electrification demand is increasing the value of Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources. Chile, Argentina and Brazil show different parts of the investment case, from copper supply and refining to export infrastructure, renewable power and rare-earth production. For investors, the key question is whether infrastructure, financing conditions and policy stability can turn those resources into viable projects. Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials. But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects. "We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth. We need every possible energy source available," Michele Della Vigna, head of natural resources research for Goldman Sachs, told CNBC. "Ultimately, what drives economic growth is energy," he added. Ben Kumar, head of strategy for wealth, investment and public policy at 7IM, suggested Latin America could benefit, given the physical materials needed for AI equipment and data centers. "We are currently neutral in the short term, but if the materials and mining cycle continues, we could see this moving to positive in a few months," he said. Where the investment case is strongest The investment case varies across the region. Chile has copper; Argentina is expanding oil and gas exports; and Brazil has abundant renewable power and significant rare earth reserves. Chile's copper sector illustrates both the supply potential and the constraints to expanding supply. Copper production fell 8.5% in the first nine months of 2026, according to the state copper commission Cochilco, as lower ore grades, maintenance, and operational disruptions constrained supply. But demand for refined copper is set to grow 1.6% this year and 2% next year, according to the International Copper Study Group . Supply is struggling to keep pace with demand from expanding electricity grids. Chile's copper commission has raised its 2027 price forecast to $5.95 a pound, from $5.10. Codelco, the state-owned copper producer, may also have scope to increase supply, including through proposed public-private partnerships. Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, sees demand continuing to grow. "As countries expand electricity grids, they need more copper regardless of which power source they choose," he said. The scale of the opportunity will depend in part on how quickly energy demand grows. Goldman Sachs forecasts that global power demand for data centers will grow by 170% by 2030. The IEA projected in April that global data center electricity consumption would rise from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030. The investment case also depends on whether the region can capture more value from the resources it produces. Latin America and the Caribbean refined only 26% of the copper they mined in 2025, according to the IEA. "Cautious optimism is justified and there will be massive critical mineral demand," said Monica de Bolle, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. "But improving refining capacity will be crucial to capture more of that value," she added. Some projects have already secured financing. Chilean explorer Marimaca Copper Corp selected a preferred lender for a $400 million debt facility to build a mine on Oct. 28. The funding will go towards developing an open-pit mine in the north of Chile that will produce 50,000 metric tons of refined copper annually. Production is expected from 2029. Argentina shows the other side of the opportunity: strong oil and gas resources, but insufficient infrastructure to get more production to global markets. "I see an opportunity in the infrastructure that gets Argentine oil and gas to market. A producer in Vaca Muerta can have excellent wells and still struggle to expand exports without pipeline capacity and access to ports. That gives investors a reason to look at transport and export infrastructure alongside production," Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, added. Vaca Muerta is Argentina's vast shale basin. Argentina is also attracting investment in drilling and export infrastructure. International capital markets have reopened to investment in drilling and pipelines in Argentina. That investment has already driven the build-out of a pipeline and port. Argentina will then be able to export far more crude oil. Chevron and American oil tycoon Harold Hamm have also increased their investments in Argentina. Brazil's case rests partly on its renewable-heavy power mix.

events.title: Viettel-Singtel consortium breaks ground on sub-marine cable connecting Vietnam, Thailand, Singapore
events.summary: The signing and implementation ceremony of the VTS submarine cable project was held in Ho Chih Minh City on Nov 26. Viettel and Singtel have started work on a new submarine fibre-optic cable linking Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore. It is the first such project led by a Vietnamese company. The 2,500km VTS cable will have 600Tbps capacity and 12ms latency. Viettel says this will support AI and financial services, and cut Vietnam’s reliance on existing routes. The project, due for completion in Q4 2030, involves NEC and Asean Cableship. Singtel says it will boost cross-border business, digital investment and ASEAN data flows. SINGAPORE – A consortium co-chaired by Vietnam’s Viettel Group and Singapore’s Singtel has begun construction of a sub-marine fibre-optic cable system connecting Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore. The cable system offers the highest bandwidth among all sub-marine cable routes connecting Vietnam to Singapore. This marks the first international sub-marine cable project initiated and led by a Vietnamese enterprise, said Viettel in a statement on Nov 26. The project by the consortium, VTS, is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2030. An event to mark the signing of commercial and construction contracts with Japan’s NEC Corporation and Singapore cable system company Asean Cableship was held in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, on Nov 26 . Both companies are the contractors for the project. The entire cable system will span 2,500km with a design capacity of 600 terabits per second (Tbps). The segment between Singapore and Vietnam will cover about 1,200km and offer a capacity of 240 Tbps, or roughly 2½ times the total capacity of all international cable systems currently in use by Vietnam. By following a direct route, VTS will be the shortest sub-marine fibre-optic cable link between Vietnam and Singapore. Once the cable is up, the round-trip data transmission time, or latency, between the two countries is expected to be 12 milliseconds, approximately 50% lower than the current average for existing routes. This low latency will enable smoother performance for applications such as financial transactions and artificial intelligence. The project builds on a memorandum of understanding signed between Viettel and Singtel in April 2024 to develop a direct sub-marine cable connection between Vietnam and Singapore. Viettel, which is run by the country’s military, said that it directly led the route planning and design of the cable. These included deciding the landing points, system configuration, and overall performance. The cable gives Vietnam an additional international connection route. This helps to reduce the country’s reliance on existing routes. Should one route encounter an issue, traffic can be rerouted to another, ensuring that internet, banking and business services face minimal disruption, said Viettel in its statement . Lieutenant-General Tao Duc Thang, chairman and general director of Viettel, said that Viettel proactively initiated the cable system project as it does not want the development of Vietnam’s digital economy to remain overly dependent on factors beyond its control. “Constructing a subsea fibre-optic cable system takes many years; we cannot wait until we face a capacity shortage to begin investing,” he said. In a separate statement , Singtel said that by strengthening connectivity between Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore, the upcoming cable system will support businesses’ growing cross-border requirements and create greater opportunities for digital investment and innovation across South-east Asia. Said Ng Tian Chong, chief executive of Singtel: “The additional connectivity and network resilience it provides will also complement Asean’s ambitions under the Digital Economy Framework Agreement to deepen regional digital integration and facilitate cross-border data flows.” THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Malaysia to seek 19% tariff ceiling in US talks until Q1 2027
events.summary: Malaysia’s Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani said the country will continue to negotiate to ensure tariffs do not exceed 19%. Malaysia will keep negotiating with the US until Q1 2027 to keep total tariffs on its goods at or below 19%, under the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade. Minister Johari Abdul Ghani said Malaysia has told the USTR it should keep the 19% benefit as one of the first countries to sign, even with extra tariff measures. The US is reviewing excess capacity, forced labour, environmental issues and subsidies under Section 301; iron and steel may face scrutiny, while semiconductors are excluded for now. KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia will continue negotiations with the United States until the first quarter 2027 to ensure overall tariffs on Malaysian goods do not exceed 19%, particularly in addressing concerns over structural excess capacity and production under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, said Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani. He said Malaysia would continue engaging with the US Trade Representative (USTR) to present its case and prevent any additional tariff measures from pushing the overall tariff rate on Malaysian goods above the 19% level agreed under the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART). “The US had indicated a tariff range of between 18% and 25% for Malaysia... this is the range. But we still have until the first quarter to negotiate, explain and put forward our justification why we cannot be placed in this range. Overall you also need to take into consideration that it cannot be more than 19%,” he told reporters after the official commemoration of BYD Local Assembly Plant in Malaysia. Earlier, the media reported that the US has proposed additional tariffs of up to 18% on Malaysian goods after determining that Malaysia’s industrial policies and manufacturing practices contribute to structural excess capacity and production that Washington says burden or restrict US commerce. Malaysia is among 14 economies facing proposed tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, with headline rates ranging from 15% to 35%. The other economies include China, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, and the European Union. Johari said Malaysia had made its position clear to the USTR’s deputy representative, stressing that the country should retain the benefit of being among the first to sign the trade agreement. “Look, we were the first to sign the ART, and you promised us a 19% tariff rate. We must therefore be able to enjoy that benefit. Whatever additional measures you intend to impose, including the 10% tariff related to forced labour, the total must not exceed 19%,” he said. He highlighted that the US is looking into four areas under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, namely excess capacity, forced labour, environmental issues and state subsidies. He said the US has finalised a 10% tariff on forced labour while measures relating to excess capacity remain under consideration. “On excess capacity, the US has yet to finalise its position and is still working on how to implement it. However, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) has consistently maintained that Malaysia does not have excess capacity,” he said. Johari stressed that Malaysia’s position remained unchanged despite the indicative tariff range of 18% to 25% communicated by the US under its excess capacity assessment. Meanwhile, he said the iron and steel sectors could come under scrutiny in the excess capacity investigation, particularly over concerns that production capacity could be used to channel exports through Malaysia. However, the semiconductor sector was excluded from the assessment at this stage, he added. BERNAMA

events.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
events.summary: Watch: Why has Poundland collapsed into administration? Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business. The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers. Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached. Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret". He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent. "Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added. Bally Auluk, national officer at the union Usdaw, which represents Poundland workers, told the BBC'S Wake Up to Money programme that Gordon Brothers' "intention was perfectly clear from the offset... to force the company into administration". "It's such a devastating blow any time of year, but most certainly in the run up to Christmas for 11,000 colleagues, most of whom are our members," he said. Gordon Brothers rejected Auluk's characterisation of the process and said it had "explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company". Kelvin Blake, pictured at a protest in Walsall, has worked for Poundland for 25 years Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere. "We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds. "My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave." Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was "part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country". He said the news of it going into administration just weeks before Christmas would be "deeply concerning for workers and their families". He added: "While it is worrying, going into administration does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage and we will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome." Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said protecting staff is the government's top priority. "I'm also very mindful that for lots of people across the country, Poundland is a place they go on the high street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," he told the BBC. Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said it would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part". "We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said. Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground. Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims. On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency. But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process. Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees. Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons' Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament - two weeks after Gordon Brothers representatives last appeared at the committee to answer questions about Poundland, and where MPs said they were "deeply concerned" about the business. Byrne said: "I am really worried that a 'greed is good' approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration." He added the committee wants to know "how much money they're ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don't have this kind of scenario unfold again". Poundland's co-founder Steve Smith said the administration "should not be happening". He told the BBC the chain has undergone a turnaround since being taken over by Gordon Brothers, returning to profitability. He said: "Everybody was behind Poundland. It had turned round. And with buyers on the table, why was it put into administration?" "It should not have happened," he added. What's gone wrong at Poundland?

More than $24 million in deposits from prospective apartment buyers has gone missing as a Sydney developer acknowledges "something has gone seriously wrong". Almost 300 home buyers were due to get the keys to their newly-built apartments in Dee Why and Blacktown between this week and early next year but have been left in limbo. Industrial action set to impact regional and interstate passenger train services across NSW has been called off at the eleventh hour. events.title: Investment-linked insurance v participating plans: What drives demand and which suits you better
events.summary: Former financial adviser Bobby Sim says that high commissions, particularly in the first two years of a policy, heavily incentivise agents to push investment-linked insurance policies. Demand for ILPs and participating plans is growing in Singapore. ILPs led sales at $2.51 billion, or 46% of new business, in the first nine months of 2026. ILPs suit buyers who accept market risk and want flexibility; par plans suit cautious buyers who want guaranteed benefits, bonuses and are ok with less control over investments. Advisers and policyholders warned that fees, lock-in charges and poor understanding can hurt returns, so buyers should study costs, risks and their own needs first. SINGAPORE – After spending nearly a decade selling investment-linked insurance policies (ILPs) – hybrid products that combine investing with insurance coverage – former financial adviser Bobby Sim said the experience was “one of the reasons I could not stay in the industry”. Sim, who worked at Manulife and later at advisory firm Finexis, shared that high commissions, particularly in the first two years of a policy , heavily incentivise insurance agents to push ILPs. “Most of us sold what the company recommended, without fully understanding the returns behind the product,” he said. “I am not saying every agent is bad. But if you look at net returns after fees, most of the ILPs I saw did worse than simply putting the money into the S&P 500.” That experience shaped his personal financial planning – he now keeps his investments separate from his family’s insurance protection needs. “When you mix the two in one product, you usually get a worse version of both,” he noted. That said, Sim feels that ILPs may still suit three types of buyers: those who lack the discipline to save ; those whose advisers can help them achieve market-beating returns after fees ; and those who lack the bandwidth to manage their own finances and prefer leaving both insurance and investments to a trusted adviser. Latest figures from the Life Insurance Association Singapore (LIA) show that sales of new ILPs – measured by weighted new business premiums – rose 22.6% year on year to $2.51 billion in the first nine months of 2026. These plans made up 46% of all new sales, up from 43% over the same period in 2025 and 37% in 2024. P articipating (par) life insurance policies also recorded growth, with weighted new sales rising 5.7% to $1.24 billion over the same nine-month period. Par plans accounted for 23% of all new sales in the first nine months of 2026, down slightly from 25% in the corresponding periods of 2024 and 2025. These plans fall into three categories: whole life insurance, endowment savings plans and retirement income plans. Rachel Luo, senior director of sales at Manulife Advisory Group, said interest in ILPs and par plans is driven by greater awareness of long-term financial planning, concerns about the rising cost of living and the financial implications of longer lifespans, as well as a desire for structure and discipline. Many consumers lack the time, knowledge and confidence to manage a portfolio actively, she added. While both types of policies have investment components, they work differently, and the choice between an ILP and a par plan ultimately comes down to how much risk a consumer can bear. Helen Shen, group head of products at Singlife, said ILPs bundle insurance protection with market exposure through investment sub-funds. A policy’s value depends on the performance of the funds, minus insurance charges and other fees. Returns fluctuate with the market, and policyholders bear all the investment risk. These products therefore suit customers who are comfortable riding out market cycles for potentially higher returns and want more flexibility in choosing their own funds, Shen noted. Manulife’s Luo sees interest in ILPs among younger and mid-career working adults, noting that these clients have longer investment horizons and are just starting to build their wealth and protection portfolios. Unlike ILPs, which have no guaranteed cash value, par plans have a portion that is guaranteed. Policyholders pay premiums that go into the insurer’s participating fund. They share in the fund’s profits and receive a combination of guaranteed benefits and non-guaranteed bonuses. The guaranteed portion – known as the guaranteed surrender value – is smaller if they cash out early, while the full guaranteed benefit is paid if they hold to maturity. In exchange for that stability, policyholders have no say in asset selection – the insurer decides how the money is invested across a portfolio of assets. Shen noted that the “sweet spot” for par plans lies in balancing guaranteed benefits with non-guaranteed bonuses to boost total returns. She added that this balance suits customers who are cautious about market volatility and want stability without giving up growth potential.

events.title: UK watchdog calls for shake-up of private dentistry market amid ‘catalogue of concerns’
events.summary: CMA report highlights inflation-busting annual rises and practices that ‘may not operate in patients’ best interests’ Tell us: what is your experience of UK private dentistry? The UK’s competition watchdog has called for a shake-up of the £8bn private dentistry market , after an investigation identified a “catalogue of concerns” including inflation-busting annual rises and evidence of targets to sell more expensive treatments and dental payment plans. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said patients faced substantial differences in prices in different parts of the UK and “commercial practices, targets and incentives [that] may not operate in patients’ best interests”. The report found dentists typically had a financial stake in treatment revenues, either as practice owners or through revenue-sharing arrangements. “We have also seen evidence of targets to convert NHS patients to private care, sell more expensive treatments, and increase sales of dental payment plans,” the CMA said. “Together, these incentives and practices create a risk that patients are sold treatments that are not in their best interests.” The interim report found prices rose by an estimated 7% a year on average between 2023 and 2025 at large dental groups, well above inflation and wage growth, with costs across the industry forcing some people to delay or forgo treatment. The CMA gave the example of a composite white filling that cost about 36% of mean weekly disposable income in the north-east of England and 35% in Wales. It also identified significant price differences, even in the same local area. In Preston, prices advertised online for a composite filling ranged from £80 to £223, while in Caerphilly the price of an amalgam filling ranged from £72 to £159. “Some variation is to be expected, but the CMA is concerned that people are paying more than they should because they are unable to shop around,” the report said. The CMA said about 60% of patients across the UK now paid for at least some private dental care, including many on low incomes, but that it was difficult for them to “confidently shop around and get a good deal”. The report found one in six private dental practices in the UK did not publish price lists online and that there was “substantial variation in indicative profit margins between dental practices”. Another concern identified was data suggesting that practices primarily serving NHS patients did not necessarily earn lower profit margins. The CMA also said there was a shortage of dentists, with the estimated job vacancy rate in England at about 8%, significantly higher than the 2% rate across the UK economy. The UK also has fewer dentists per head than most other European countries. The CMA said the government should play a more direct “market-shaping role”, using its position as a major purchaser and commissioner of dentistry to “influence incentives and outcomes” for private and NHS patients. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Millions of people across the UK rely on private dentistry as an essential service, but the market isn’t working well for them,” said Sarah Cardell, the chief executive of the CMA. “People can’t easily compare and switch between providers, dentists are in short supply, commercial incentives to grow revenues may not operate in the patients’ best interests and there are weaknesses in the regulatory framework. As a result, many people are struggling with affordability, and those on lower incomes and in certain parts of the UK are hardest hit.” The CMA said it was working with governments across the UK to finalise a wide-ranging package of measures to change how the market operated, with its final report expected in March. Before the last general election Labour promised to invest heavily in NHS dentistry , as well as to provide more incentives for dentists to remain in the national public healthcare system. On Thursday the British Dental Association (BDA) said it agreed with the CMA’s interim report and said it provided an opportunity for Labour to “keep promises made at the last election”. The BDA had accused the government of using the study as cover for its failure to commit to any new investment in rebuilding NHS dental services. Research it conducted with YouGov found that 39% of adults in England had found it hard to pay for dental care in the last two years. Among those, 43% delayed getting a dental procedure, 32% decided against getting any care, 15% took on debt and 13% reduced spending on essentials such as food, accommodation and heating. “It is essential we have a thriving private dental market, but when it comes to giving patients access to affordable care, ministers hold almost all the cards,” said Eddie Crouch, the chair of the BDA. “The UK government can start by keeping their election promise, and fix and fund NHS dentistry.”

events.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
events.summary: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but W hen I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised . Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries . By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes , driving food reformulations. Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its turn being blamed for our poor health. In recent years, protein has emerged as a nutritional good guy, with social media influencers blaming its deficiency for your fatigue or the fact that you don’t have the body you want. Go into a supermarket and you can find protein yoghurts, protein cereals, protein breads, protein drinks and even protein chocolate bars. When I spoke about my last book on good health to the Edinburgh international book festival , the first question was how many grams of protein I recommended eating each day, and which supplements and powders to take. The same question was asked of Chris van Tulleken, a physician and leading UK expert on nutrition, when he spoke at the Hay festival . Yes, protein is essential for our bodies to repair and build muscle, produce enzymes and hormones, and maintain normal bodily functions. Severe protein deficiency can cause conditions such as kwashiorkor , a severe form of malnutrition found in parts of Africa, where some children live with conflict, drought and extreme food scarcity. But those are extreme cases of food deprivation. In the UK, the recommended daily intake is 0.75g of protein per kg of body weight. So if you weigh 75kg, that’s 56g of protein per day. Requirements differ based on age, pregnancy and how much physical activity – especially strength training and performance sport – someone does. The evidence suggests that the rest of us are already eating enough protein. Indeed, the British Nutrition Foundation found that average protein consumption in the UK already exceeds these recommendations. They report an average daily intake of 85g for men (above the recommended intake of 56g) and 67g for women (above the recommended intake of 45g). Protein is part of the foods we eat every day: not just in chicken or burgers, but in wholemeal bread, rice, eggs, milk, beans, yoghurt, porridge, pasta and lentils. Yet the “protein industry” has created the widespread impression that we should all be eating more, and has created a whole line of foods and marketing with “protein added”. Many of these products are ultra-processed (which we know isn’t good for our health) with very high levels of sugar and salt, plus all the additives and preservatives to keep them from going off for years. Simply adding protein doesn’t improve the overall nutritional quality of a food product. In August 2026 , a review of more than 350 studies looked at the relationship between protein intake, metabolism and ageing. The researchers found that for some people who don’t do much exercise, consuming less protein may be better for their metabolic health and longevity. As Prof Dudley Lamming said: “Because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences.” The researchers suggest several biological mechanisms to explain this, including one focused on the hormone FGF21, which increases in the body when protein intake falls. Experiments in mice have linked increased FGF21 activity with longer lifespans, given that this hormone contributes to regulating energy expenditure, glucose metabolism and metabolic health. As a caveat, much of the evidence linking longevity with eating less protein in the paper comes from testing in animal models such as mice, rats and fruit flies. Nonetheless, the study challenges the idea that more protein is always better for healthy ageing, especially for those who aren’t very active. events.title: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way
events.summary: As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows , a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency. “ Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest , tells Fortune . “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.” Anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through the cloud platform went to open-weight models , up from 7% last year. “Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.”  Rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance. The case for ‘good enough’ AI Before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream fame, most high-performing models were either small academic releases or commercial systems with restricted outside access. The first open-weight models originated in academic research, where sharing model weights to ensure reproducibility was standard practice. In 2019, OpenAI went against tradition by initially withholding the full 1.5-billion-parameter version of GPT-2 , citing risks of misuse such as disinformation, impersonation and phishing. Most U.S. frontier labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, keep the underlying parameters private, giving users access through apps or APIs rather than letting them download and run the models themselves. In the early years of generative AI, most users preferred closed-weight models because they delivered performance that open-weight alternatives could not match. Yet in recent years, the improved capability and cost-efficiency of powerful Chinese models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has swung the pendulum back in favor of open-weight models.  “For the longest time, the idea has been that you can get the highest level of performance using closed-weight models, so many firms start off by using them,” says Hariharasudhan Saminathan, cofounder of Friday , a sovereign AI startup backed by global venture capital firm Antler. But now, “through distillation and other processes, open-weight models’ performance almost matches that of closed-weight models,” he says.  “Many of our pipeline customers are now adopting open-weight models right off the bat,” he adds. “They’re not even touching the closed-weight ones.” Pinterest, for example, uses Alibaba’s open-weight Qwen models to power its online platform . “We’ve driven down our inference costs using post-trained open-weight models,” Kim explains. “They offer over 90% cost reduction.” (Many leading Chinese open-weight models activate only a subset of parameters per token, cutting compute and energy needed per request.) Kim also cites the flexibility of these models as a draw. Last October, the firm released Pinterest Assistant : an AI-powered tool that pairs a customized Qwen multimodal LLM with the firm’s proprietary Taste Graph, to generate shopping recommendations for users based on their individual aesthetic preferences. “[With open-weight technology], we can create a specialized model that actually does what we need it to do very effectively, which is understanding visual information,” says Kim. A hybrid approach Rather than choosing one or the other, some firms are using a mix of open-weight and closed-weight AI models.  Eu Leong Oh, medical director at The Longevity Suite Asia , a Singapore-based wellness clinic, says he’s using Claude and Google’s Gemini to build the team’s in-house healthcare portal, but plans to pivot to open-weight models for daily use. “For things like prototyping, exploration and research, it’s still very useful to have a large-parameter, trained, closed-weight model,” Oh says.  He compares a top-tier frontier model to a Michelin-starred chef. “You’ll want a chef like Gordon Ramsay to decide the processes in your restaurant, but you don’t need him to do the cooking all the time,” he says. “Similarly, within companies, a lot of the heavy lifting and token budget will eventually be taken over by more cost effective open-weight models.” Token costs are also skyrocketing with the rise of agentic AI. An AI agent might consume five times more tokens than a chatbot interface, because it runs multi-step loops rather than a single task. Those increasing costs may push companies to adopt cheaper open-weight models on top of existing closed-weight ones.  “Companies are becoming more cost-conscious about their AI deployment,” says Srividya Jandhyala, a professor of management at ESSEC Business School. “Not every task needs the power of a frontier model, and companies are recognizing that ‘good enough’ models work for a large variety of operations.” Harder choices Yet a company’s decision whether or not to use an open-weight model could come down to politics, rather than cost or technical ability. The leading open-weight models come from Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba , and z.AI ; their growing usage in both U.S. and global business is worrying some in Washington about China’s growing influence over the technology. “The American AI stack remains far stronger than China’s and we must continue to lead,” Representative John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chair of the U.S. House’s Select Committee on China, wrote in a Sept. 23 statement . On Nov. 18, Reuters reported that the Trump administration was considering requiring U.S. firms to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models , in hopes of discouraging use of the technology without imposing new restrictions that might anger Beijing. In a Nov. 20 report, Moolenaar warned that American businesses were adopting inexpensive Chinese AI models. “Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap,” he wrote. events.title: Transport minister won't change mind on controversial Matilda Bay ferry terminal
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rita Saffioti won't back down on proposed Matilda Bay ferry terminal despite community backlash Rita Saffioti says she has followed expert advice on the location of the new ferry terminal. ( ABC News: Courtney Withers ) WA's transport minister has insisted she will not change her mind about the location of a controversial new ferry terminal at Matilda Bay, despite growing community backlash and projected cost blowouts. The WA government promised to expand Metronet ferry services on Perth's Swan River during the 2025 state election campaign, at a joint Commonwealth-state cost of $107 million. Two new ferry terminals were proposed, one at Applecross and one at Matilda Bay in Nedlands — directly opposite the University of Western Australia — to be serviced by five new electric ferries. Rita Saffioti says Matilda Bay is simply the best choice for the Nedlands terminal. ( ABC News: Courtney Withers ) Today the government confirmed the cost of the whole project had increased to about $150 million. Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said the Matilda Bay section had incurred increased costs to "change the nature of the jetty and the length of the jetty" The Western Australian Planning Commission approved the development for the new ferry terminals last December, but the government has continued to face opposition from locals, the Liberals and the Greens. A petition tabled in WA's parliament today, signed by over 10,000 people, called for construction contracts to be suspended so more analysis of the Matilda Bay site could take place. Ms Saffioti said a comprehensive analysis of five key sites in Nedlands had deemed Matilda Bay the best. "We made a commitment at the election, we then went back and assessed all the different options again," Ms Saffioti said. Row over plan for ferry terminal at Perth's Matilda Bay deepens A WA government-commissioned analysis finds the scenic and popular Matilda Bay is the safest spot for a ferry terminal, just as another report prompted by an advocacy group says it would put river users at serious risk. She said "environmental experts" found alternative sites including Jojo's and Pelican Point were not suitable "because of the impact on seagrass, migratory birds and also impacts into some reserves". Asked if the ferry site would be moved, Ms Saffioti said she was "not going to change [her] mind". "There's no reason for me not to choose a better site if a better site was told to me," she said. Save Matilda Bay spokesperson Megan Bagworth said her group would continue to lobby for the Nedlands ferry landing to be moved to Jojo's. "Once it's built, it can't be undone," Ms Bagworth said. "That's why the government needs to do the full and proper assessments now and review this decision." Opposition transport spokesperson Steve Martin said Ms Saffioti had "blown another budget" at a time of cost-of-living pressures for West Australians. Steve Martin is criticising the government for another cost blowout. ( ABC News: Lauren Smith ) "Here we are, yet another blowout on the top of the Fremantle Traffic Bridge [Walyalup Bridge] that went from $230 million to $596 million and counting," he said. Construction on the ferry terminals is expected to commence in the middle of next year, with the ferry services expected to start in late 2027. events.title: Taking on Starlink: Europe’s largest satellite factory opens in push to rival Musk
events.summary: Europe's to-be largest satellite factory was inaugurated in Belgium this week, operated by privately held Aerospacelab. Aerospacelab has secured a 2.4-billion-euro contract to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for IRIS², Europe's answer to Elon Musk's Starlink. Satellite connectivity has become increasingly important to both everyday life and national security, providing internet access to remote locations and defense applications. The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and reduce reliance on U.S. space infrastructure. Privately held Belgian satellite manufacturer Aerospacelab secured a 2.4-billion-euro ($2.6 billion) contract in September to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for IRIS², the European Union's answer to SpaceX 's Starlink business. Aerospacelab said this will "form the backbone of Europe's sovereign, secure, and resilient connectivity infrastructure by 2030." It will be named Ectro from Nov. 30. Its new oval-shaped, 20,000-square-meter facility in southern Belgium, inaugurated by Belgian King Philippe, will be able to produce up to 500 satellites annually, which would make it the world's third-largest satellite production site, according to the Belgian royal palace. Employees are expected to move into the megafactory in January, and production is slated to begin by the end of 2028, according to AFP. Satellite connectivity has become increasingly important to everyday life as well as national security. It provides internet access to remote locations and defense equipment like warships and fighter jets, and lets governments and militaries communicate securely where Earth-based networks are unavailable or disrupted. The importance of such capabilities has become particularly apparent in Ukraine, as the country's military relies heavily on Starlink connectivity to fight Russian forces. Recent restrictions to the service over Russian-occupied territory reported by Ukrainian officials further underscored the way geopolitical conflict may depend on commercial businesses. But Europe still has a long way to go in challenging Starlink's dominance. SpaceX says it has more than 11,000 Starlink satellites in low Earth orbit, making it by far the largest satellite constellation in the world, and plans up to 100,000 satellites. Among the challengers is Amazon , whose satellite business, Amazon Leo, has deployed over 400 satellites and plans an initial in-orbit constellation of more than 3,200. Meanwhile, French Eutelsat operates more than 600 satellites in low Earth orbit through its OneWeb constellation . The company is also part of the SpaceRISE consortium alongside SES and Hispasat, tasked with developing and operating IRIS². The European Commission has called IRIS² a "strategic asset to achieve space sovereignty in the face of commercial satellite constellations, such as Starlink." The aim is for first launches to take place by the end of 2029, with initial services expected soon after. In August, the Commission and SpaceRISE consortium announced they were expanding the main constellation from 282 to 348 satellites, increasing its secure communications capacity for EU governments by 60%. Defense and security applications were the main drivers of the expanded scope, the Commission said.

events.title: Oil rebounds to $95 per barrel after Saudi refinery attack
events.summary: Oil prices edged higher on Thursday, extending gains from the previous session on continuing Middle East supply concerns, after the Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed they hit Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained disrupted. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world’s oil, rose 0.74 per cent to $95.31 a barrel at 9.13am UAE time, while West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was trading 0.82 per cent higher at $84.37 a barrel. In the previous session, Brent had closed 3.5 per cent higher at $94.61 per barrel, extending its two-session rally to nearly 6 per cent. “Supply-surplus concerns took a back seat to disruption risk ahead of Sunday’s Opec+ meeting,” said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD. The Saudi military on Wednesday said air defences had intercepted and destroyed four drones launched towards the Ras Tanura refinery. The Iran-backed Houthis later on Wednesday claimed they carried out strikes on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan. Ras Tanura, which has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, has previously been attacked during the conflict with the Houthis as well as during the US-Iran war. The plant is part of a complex on the kingdom's Arabian Gulf coast. Ras Tanura was the kingdom's main export terminal until the war prompted greater focus on using Yanbu on the west coast, which receives oil via the East–West pipeline. Meanwhile, supply disruption through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the Middle East’s main arteries for the supply of crude and liquefied natural gas to global markets, continues. A projectile exploded near a tanker about 93km west of Dubai in the latest ship incident in the Gulf waters, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said on Thursday. An oil tanker was also reported to have caught fire in the waterway after hitting a naval mine on Wednesday. Oil markets have remained volatile since the US-led attack on Iran in late February, with prices jumping to more than $120 per barrel in March and sliding back on peace efforts to end the war. They went back up after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline and as the Houthis seized control of the Bab Al Mandeb strait in the Red Sea. But US President Donald Trump’s midterm election rout caused prices to fall. Investors are also considering oversupply outlook concerns for the oil market amid a recovery in exports from the Gulf region, as the UAE and Saudi Arabia rely more on pipelines and alternative routes. Crude inventories rose by 1.7 million bpd in October as exports from the Gulf recovered faster than worldwide demand, the International Energy Agency said in its monthly market report. Opec+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide on their 2027 output policy as the bloc holds production steady amid supply shocks from the Middle East war.

events.title: Robots could be doing household chores in just 1-2 years, Chinese EV firm says
events.summary: Robots will likely be deployed in homes in coming years since the tech is moving very fast, Xpeng Co-President Brian Gu told CNBC on Thursday. The electric car company plans to begin delivering its next-generation humanoid in the second half of 2027. "It's much easier to be profitable for the robotics business than the autos business," Gu said. BEIJING — The household robot could soon become a reality, Brian Gu, co-president of Xpeng , a Chinese electric car company which has entered the humanoids space, told CNBC. "Maybe after successful deployment into commercial settings, maybe another one to two years, we can start thinking about deploying into home settings," Gu said. "Technology is moving at a much faster clip." Xpeng revealed its latest general-purpose humanoid robot Iron on Wednesday. The company plans to start training the robot as a store assistant in its retail car locations in the first quarter next year, after starting mass production in January. Sales are set to begin in the second quarter, with deliveries expected later in the year. Founded in 2014 as an electric car company, Xpeng beat Tesla to rolling out driver-assist in mainland China. The Chinese automaker has launched its own artificial intelligence chips. It's also expanded into personal flying vehicles and robotics. The robotics unit this summer raised $900 million at a $6.3 billion valuation in its first funding round, led by IDG Capital. Investors, however, appear to be a tad skeptical about the developments at Xpeng, with the downturn in the Chinese auto market also weighing on the company. Xpeng's shares, listed in both New York and Hong Kong, have dropped more than 55% this year amid broad sector declines. China's humanoid industry has faced more regulatory scrutiny on financing in recent months after Unitree's high-profile IPO and stock slump, as well as a rush of capital into the sector. That's all raised questions about commercialization and the efficacy of the core tech. Gu said Xpeng's robotics stands out for its rare combination of the hardware, software and real-life use cases. He's expecting to add more investors after Iron's planned commercial launch next year. "You can always make the head talk, you can always make the leg run, you can always make the hands to do certain tasks," Gu said. "But doing a task while you're walking and answering questions at the same time, that's the most challenging part. And then doing everything well, not falling down, not getting distracted. The model has to work in sync." Most humanoid robot startups, especially in China, focus on a portion of the tech, such as hands or the artificial intelligence-powered brain. Some in the industry also see themselves as original equipment manufacturers , with another company tying the parts together for the finished robot. But that may be easier said than done. Xpeng's co-founder and CEO He Xiaopeng, a software engineer, always thought that software could solve "everything,'" Gu said. "And after he got into the EV business he realized how hard it is to make hardware ... really do the things that you want to do safely and consistently." On Wednesday, Xpeng announced its "Turing Physical AI Architecture " for using AI and real-time decision-making tech to control cars and humanoids. Gu told CNBC that Xpeng's robotics development only needs the driver-assist chips, which the company already has, indicating limited impact from U.S. restrictions on advanced Nvidia chip sales to China. "Right now we don't see any change to our supply chain, and also ability to have these chips." In 2023, Xpeng's then-head of autonomous driving, Xinzhou Wu, left to lead Nvidia's automotive chip business. As Xpeng ramps up its humanoid robotics business, Gu said the company's existing work in autonomous driving technology translates easily to a new product line — with far higher profit margins. "It's much easier to be profitable for the robotics business than the autos business." Robotics will likely become a meaningful part of Xpeng's business in two to three years, Gu said, with profitability coming as soon as next year. That value will "dramatically" increase with robots entering households, he said. But Gu noted that compared to commercial environments, homes require robots to act safely around elderly people, children and pets, in addition to reacting to emergency situations. That increases requirements for battery power and performance consistency, he said.

events.title: MAS green-lights retail access to more complex funds; private market funds omitted for now
events.summary: This process is expected to take about three months upon receipt of all requisite information, down from six to 12 months previously. MAS has revised its fund rules to let retail investors access more complex funds, with new safeguards for products using heavy derivatives. The new Non-Traditional Funds Appendix speeds approval to about three months, and same-type funds can be authorised in 21 days if they meet the rules. Private-market funds are excluded for now, while MAS plans a separate retail framework and will also recognise comparable foreign funds to keep a level playing field. SINGAPORE – Retail investors may soon be able to access a wider range of new fund product types as the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has implemented its revised Code on Collective Investment Schemes on Nov 26. The amendments, which take effect immediately, follow a public consultation conducted between July 9 and Aug 10. They delivered on a push first announced by Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong in June to help fund managers bring innovative products to market faster, amid growing investor sophistication and rising demand for a broader product shelf in Singapore. Under the revised code, MAS introduced a Non-Traditional Funds Appendix to cater to new fund types that satisfy certain criteria. Such funds are expected to involve non-traditional features, including the heavy use of derivatives. They would thus be classified as complex products under the complex products regime and enhanced distribution safeguards would apply accordingly, noted MAS. The central bank said that it will work with market participants or relevant industry associations to develop requirements tailored to the features and risks of new fund types, which would be published in a circular. Funds of the same type will take 21 days to be authorised if they meet the requirements, said MAS. Market demand for specific fund types MAS noted in July that it received market interest to offer two new fund types to retail investors: futures-based single-commodity funds and a wider range of single-country government bond funds. During the recent public consultation, several respondents sought clarification on whether the proposed framework could accommodate other fund types, including those investing in private-market assets. While the new appendix does not cover private-market investment funds, such as private equity or private credit, MAS clarified that such funds are being addressed under a separate retail framework to be released in due course. As for futures-based single-commodity funds, the central bank said it must track a “well-recognised” futures prices index, for which it will consider the extent of its use as a benchmark by market participants and the length of its operational history. There are five permitted commodities for this fund type: gold, silver, platinum, crude oil and iron ore. Following industry feedback, MAS dropped its earlier proposal to bar the term “ETF” (exchange-traded fund) from these funds’ names, provided the name clearly specifies the commodity futures invested in. However, prospectuses must detail the fund’s methodology for rolling futures contracts and illustrate how differences between futures prices across contract maturities can affect returns. Separately, the central bank said it will proceed with recognising foreign funds that are comparable to new authorised fund products, including those under the new appendix. To maintain a “level playing field”, MAS will establish safeguards in the Code on Collective Investment Schemes for an authorised fund before a comparable foreign fund type may be considered for recognition.
