events.title: Wealthy Europeans look beyond stocks amid AI selloff. Here’s where they’re investing
events.summary: A Goldman Sachs survey found 47% of wealthy European respondents saw alternatives as the best route to AI and future-tech growth, versus 24% of U.S. respondents. Among European alternatives owners, 62% reported private-equity exposure, while 26% said they were likely to increase alternatives allocations over the next year. Alternatives can be illiquid, and private-equity exits and private-credit risks remain important constraints for investors. Wealthy Europeans are looking to alternative asset classes to build exposure to artificial intelligence themes amid turbulence in public markets. Goldman Sachs Alternatives' inaugural survey of high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth investors found 47% of European respondents saw alternatives as the best way to gain exposure to AI and future tech growth, compared to just 24% of U.S. investors. The survey found a significant gap between the U.S. and Europe in terms of investor knowledge of alternatives, which include assets like private equity, property and infrastructure. Goldman said 82% of European respondents are familiar with the alternative investments market — compared to 50% of U.S. investors. Goldman polled 1,000 investors with at least 1 million in investable assets in their local currency across the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Switzerland. The survey was carried out between June 29 and Aug. 18 this year. The report on the findings, published Wednesday, did not specify the proportion of respondents who already have a stake in some kind of alternative investment — but wealthy Europeans appeared particularly bullish on the space. Private equity made up the largest proportion of current alternatives holdings. Among wealthy Europeans with alternatives exposure, 62% said they invested in private equity. The second most commonly held asset class was private real estate, which was backed by 51% of European alternatives investors. Hedge funds were held by 37% of European alternatives owners, and private infrastructure was held by 30%. One in four respondents who did not already own an alternative investment said they were likely to invest in the market in the coming 12 months. Among those already in the space, 26% said they were likely to increase their allocations over the next year, while just 5% said they planned to decrease their exposure. Of the European investors who already owned alternatives, 54% said their assets had performed as expected, while 44% said their assets had exceeded their expectations to the upside. Only 2% said their alternative investments had performed worse than expected. "Recent reforms gave individual investors unprecedented access to alternative asset classes like private equity, venture capital, and private credit," Kyle Kniffen, global head of alternatives for third-party wealth at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said in Wednesday's report. He added that wealthy investors "look ready to jump at the opportunity." "Our survey shows satisfaction among current alts owners is high and adoption looks set to increase," Kniffen said. Alternative investments have increasingly become a staple of high-net-worth individuals' investment portfolios. Over the past year, JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in the Asia-Pacific region have jumped 40%, while BNY Wealth says alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios — recently surpassing traditional assets for the first time. But investing in alternatives carries risks. Private equity, for example, can lock up capital for long periods, and although the number of exits ticked slightly higher last year, the value of those deals fell. Concerns about private credit, meanwhile, have dominated headlines, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warning on Oct. 14, 2025, that "cockroaches" were likely to be lurking in private markets. — CNBC's Lee Ying Shan contributed to this article.

events.title: Dubai awards Dh56.5bn in new contracts for Al Maktoum Airport
events.summary: Dubai has awarded new contracts worth Dh56.5 billion ($15.38 billion) for the development of Al Maktoum International Airport (DWC), as construction continues at the city's second hub. It brings the total value of contracts awarded for the project to more than Dh80 billion, Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, said in a post on X on Thursday. The awards mark an expansion of the construction programme across passenger terminals, concourses, transport infrastructure, power systems and other critical airport facilities, Dubai Media Office said. The awarding of the latest contracts “marks a new phase in the development of the world’s largest and best airport”, Sheikh Hamdan said, adding that teams comprising 14,000 people are working on the project. When all phases are completed, Al Maktoum International Airport will have the capacity to handle more than 260 million passengers annually, “reinforcing Dubai’s position as a leading global aviation gateway and one of the world’s most sought-after destinations”, he added. Under the directives of His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, today we announce the award of new contracts worth AED 56.5 billion for the development of Al Maktoum International Airport, bringing the total value of contracts awarded for this strategic project to… pic.twitter.com/hxZ9s6Vlpv — Hamdan bin Mohammed (@HamdanMohammed) November 26, 2026 Construction at DWC is continuing at full pace despite the Iran war, with the first phase due to open in 2032, operator Dubai Airports’ chief executive Paul Griffiths said earlier this month. Moving operations from Dubai International Airport (DXB) to DWC will be a complex transition, with the two airports initially running in parallel, he said. The new airport will undergo at least a year of testing before its first passengers arrive, he said at the time. The testing programme will cover critical systems including baggage handling, check-in processes , Wi-Fi and other airport technology, with the aim of ensuring the airport is fully operational before passengers start using it. Piling and groundworks are under way at the $35 billion development, with the first phase expected to give the new terminal an annual capacity of 150 million passengers. Dubai Airports has already advanced its operational planning for the transition, with the concept of operations and master plans well developed. The DWC development project has entered a phase of “large-scale construction”, said Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed, chairman and chief executive of Emirates airline and chairman of the Dubai Aviation City Corporation. “We are moving decisively ahead with phase one in accordance with the approved programme,” he said. “The contracts and delivery sequence have been structured to sustain parallel progress across multiple sites.” New contracts encompass major substructure and associated infrastructure works for the West Terminal Building, Concourse 1 and Concourse 4; superstructure, architectural and building systems works for Concourses 2 and 3; and major electrical power infrastructure, including principal substations and associated networks, the media office said. In the preceding phase, Dubai Aviation Engineering Projects awarded contracts and packages worth about Dh23.8 billion. This covers enabling works and substructure packages across several areas of the project, as well as contracts for the automated people mover and baggage handling systems, the media office said. It added that works in the Concourse 2 and Concourse 3 zones, as well as the central area of the airport site, are nearing completion. Once operational, the airport will provide Dubai with the capacity needed to support the growth of its national airlines, and meet rising passenger and cargo demand over the coming decades, Sheikh Ahmed said. The airport is set to reach a capacity of 12 million tonnes of cargo a year when complete.

events.title: Motor finance compensation scheme calculation
events.summary: While preparing our response to the legal challenges to our motor finance redress scheme, we identified some errors in how we categorised a small group of loan agreements. This data informed the annual percentage rate (APR) adjustment we use in our calculation of compensation. We set this at 17% for agreements from 1 April 2014. Our initial work to understand the impact of the errors suggests that, if there is any impact, this would be less than 1 percentage point either side of 17%.While the potential impact on average compensation is small – less than £10 per agreement, on average – we recognise this affects the ongoing litigation.We properly informed those challenging the scheme. Two of those challengers are due to serve their expert evidence on Friday 27 November 2026. We will discuss with the challengers and the court the impact on this deadline, and for the timeline of the litigation.We are sorry for the further uncertainty this creates for consumers and firms. We will provide an update on any further material developments.Our objective remains to secure compensation owed to consumers as quickly as possible, in a fair and orderly way, while maintaining a healthy motor finance market.Since we received legal challenges, we have emphasised the need for firms to prepare to implement the scheme and to be ready to deal with complaints if there is no scheme. We continue to work closely with the Financial Ombudsman Service, as well, on their preparations.Lenders are now substantially better prepared to handle claims and pay compensation following the work we have undertaken. They have set aside around £7.5bn to pay compensation owed and taken steps to be ready to deal with large volumes of complaints.The motor finance market continues to work well, with lending up 7% in the 12 months to September.

events.title: Elon Musk pledges to give two SpaceX shares to every child in the US
events.summary: The total value of the shares could reach almost $18bn and comes as tech companies debate how to share the spoils of the AI boom Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, has pledged to give every child in the US two shares in SpaceX, the space ⁠and AI company he ​runs, worth a total of almost $18bn. In a brief post on X, the social media platform that he owns, Musk said children will receive one share from the company itself, and one from him personally. SpaceX announced earlier on Wednesday that it would ​contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock ‌to every currently active Trump Account, and that ‌Musk will match the number of shares it donates. The Trump account program was designed to give every American under 18 a stake in the stock market, to help build wealth from an early age. The White House said last month that it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at $127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly $18bn. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Musk’s own donations would also be linked to Trump accounts. In a separate post, Musk said the company shares will be transferred next ⁠month, with his own to follow later. “The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” he wrote. In October, Musk, whose net worth is around $824bn, announced his intention to give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. “This will be the first of many,” he said in a post on X at the time. As of June, he held about 6.42bn shares ​in the company. Most of Musk’s philanthropic efforts have been conducted via the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds around $16bn in assets. In October, SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell ⁠and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under ​the Trump account initiative. Musk and rival AI company Anthropic have recently detailed their sharply different approaches for sharing the spoils of the AI boom. Anthropic, which went public earlier this month, ​said it would commit 5% of its ​shares to a new fund for the “public good”. The company said this initiative, worth around $54bn at current prices, would give it ​more flexibility and scale to ‌make donations for the benefit ​of humanity. Other major, long-running philanthropy ventures include those of Berkshire Hathaway chair emeritus Warren Buffett, who is reported to have given away $60bn, with the intention of doing the same with most of the rest of his $150bn fortune. The Gates Foundation has distributed more than $100bn since its founding in 2000, with some of that fuelled by donations from Buffett.

events.title: ‘It’s in quite a dark place’: why UK housebuilding is struggling
events.summary: The sector is in retreat across parts of the county, with developments paused. Despite a grim outlook for 2027 there is some cause for hope A shopping centre in London that was due to be knocked down and replaced with a retail emporium and more than 1,000 apartments has been paused , dealing another blow to the government’s housing targets. Lewisham council’s Green administration, which swept into power in May, insisted a larger number of affordable homes should be included in plans agreed last year with Labour officials. Landsec, which owns the 1980s red-brick shopping centre in the borough’s town centre, said last month that the council’s demand, combined with “exceptionally challenging economic conditions”, had forced a rethink. For London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, the lack of progress in the capital’s south-east corner raises alarm bells as he tries to lift homebuilding across the city. According to Damien Sharkey, the managing director of Hub, a mid-sized UK urban property developer with much of its work in London , the outlook for 2027 is “one of the most challenging in the firm’s 15-year history”. After a collapse in housing starts to just 4,100 across London in 2025, figures have improved, with 16,290 homes registered in the year to the end of June 2026. However, this impressive 298% year-on-year growth spurt only takes the capital back to where it was in 2023-24, and well below the 21,660 starts in 2022-23. Khan’s efforts are not helped by a building safety levy on developers, expected to raise £3.4bn over 10 years, combined with extra regulations governing how to build and insulate tower blocks after the 2017 Grenfell Tower disaster . The consultants Molior has calculated that housebuilding in London’s private housing sector has fallen by 84% since 2015, despite the capital needing 88,000 new homes annually. Housebuilding has also been in retreat in some other parts of the country – in the West Midlands, completions fell 7% in the year to June, while in north-west England they were 4% lower. On Wednesday, the property and land development group Henry Boot said its performance this year would be “significantly below current market expectations”. Shares in the company, which builds homes mainly in the north of England,plunged by 20% to a 13-year low as it predicted it would make an underlying loss of up to £10m this year, blaming weak consumer and business confidence. “In theory, Yorkshire-based property and land developer and housebuilder Henry Boot should be a beneficiary of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s growth and levelling-up agendas, but the shares are getting flattened after a third profit warning this year,” says Russ Mould, the investment director at the platform AJ Bell. “A weak housing market means housebuilders are cutting their purchases of land and Henry Boot, like Crest Nicholson earlier in the week, is also warning of both weak demand at its housebuilding business and the need to review the value of the land bank on its balance sheet,” Mould added. Figures from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) show a decline in “new-build dwelling completions” in England from almost 43,000 in the second quarter of 2024 to below 36,000 in the same period this year. Annually, completions fell from about 212,000 in 2022-23 to 190,000 in 2024-25. The weak housing market will dent the housing secretary Angela Rayner’s target of building 1.5m homes during this parliament, Most analysts believe is it is going to be about 500,000 short by the deadline in 2029. Glenigan, a construction sector data provider, that charts the rise and fall of developments worth under £100m, says the outlook is grim after a steep decrease in the number of private-sector housing starts in the last year. Allan Willen, the chief economist at Glenigan, says the private construction sector as a whole, including housing, infrastructure and commercial office building, has suffered over the last year. “Build costs are high, lending has tightened and demand has softened in some sectors. As a result, numerous projects have been redesigned, delayed or cancelled.” Those tough conditions are driving more building firms to the wall. About 3,800 firms in the construction sector went into insolvency in the last 12 months , more than any other UK industry sector. While construction activity makes up only 6% of the economy, a decline in the wider property industry can have a devastating effect on the UK’s growth prospects. According to the latest quarterly figures, the building industry contracted by 0.7% in the three months to the end of September, holding back a rebound in the broader economy that still managed to expand by 0.7%. Officially, the government’s 1.5m target is still in place, but a succession of profit warnings from big construction groups shows a difficult 2026 for the private sector, which is relied on for 60% of new-build home buildings, will continue next year.

events.title: SpaceX, Musk pledge to donate a share each to active Trump Accounts
events.summary: SpaceX said it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account, and CEO Elon Musk would match the gift. COO Gwynne Shotwell agreed to make a personal gift of over 2 million SpaceX shares to Trump Accounts in July. SpaceX said Wednesday it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account , and CEO Elon Musk would personally match the gift. "SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit." The White House announced in October that nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through auto-enrollment. It's unclear how many are considered active. Musk said in a social media post on X on Thursday that the share from SpaceX would be transferred next month, without providing further details. "The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," he added. Eligible children must have their account claimed to enable contributions from family members, friends and employers, and to receive the government's one-time $1,000 seed contribution. Auto-enrolled children can receive philanthropic contributions without a parent or guardian claiming an account, according to TrumpAccounts.gov. Representatives for SpaceX and the U.S. Department of the Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for further details about the planned gift. SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell had previously agreed to make a personal gift of over 2 million SpaceX shares to Trump Accounts, with eligible account holders expected to receive them in December . In October, Elon Musk posted on X that he would give a share of SpaceX to every kid in America next year. Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number. Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027. Since the July 4 launch, families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts . Total deposits now sit at more than $9 billion, CNBC first reported. Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria. The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations , a move officials have said is meant to encourage more philanthropic gifts. Contributing stock can benefit donors, who are able to avoid capital gains taxes triggered by selling appreciated stock. But families can face restrictions related to selling that donated stock. The policy also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies. Under U.S. Department of the Treasury guidelines, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17. SpaceX shares have been under some pricing pressure as the company negotiates a possible merger with Elon Musk's automaker Tesla . The companies have established two special committees to handle merger negotiations, and hired advisers for a potential mega-deal. events.title: Gas reservation scheme passes parliament in bid to rein in energy costs
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australia's domestic gas reservation scheme passes parliament with Coalition backing Analysis shows wholesale gas prices outside WA have roughly doubled since 2015. ( ABC News: Andrew Seabourne ) From 2028, gas companies will be required to keep more of Australia's gas in the country under reforms the Coalition said it would not oppose. The policy is designed to lower energy costs for households and businesses, with WA retaining its own reservation scheme. The Senate passed the legislation tonight, with the new gas supply requirements taking effect in 2028. Australia will have a domestic gas reservation scheme to shore up local supplies and drive down prices more than a decade after the emergence of a lucrative export industry sent costs soaring for households and manufacturers. A deal between Labor and the Coalition to support the scheme was not formally confirmed, but the legislation passed the Senate tonight after the opposition indicated it would not oppose it. Under the plan, the federal government will require gas exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their exports for domestic use from 2028 to reduce energy prices and stem the loss of Australian manufacturing. The federal government's push for a gas reserve looks likely to succeed, but it has revealed a bitter split between major gas companies. The Coalition's confirmation that it would not vote against the bill followed an agreement between the federal and Western Australian governments to exempt that state from the national scheme. WA has had its own gas reservation policy for two decades, which has helped to insulate its economy from the price shocks experienced on the east coast. East coast gas market catches up to west Resources Minister Madeleine King said the reservation would create a permanent buffer between international gas prices and the Australian domestic market. "What should have been done years ago is being delivered by this government for the Australian people," she said. "Australia's national gas reservation scheme will create an enduring framework that brings to an end over a decade of crisis-driven ad hoc market interventions." Madeleine King says the policy will create an enduring framework that will stop crisis-driven market interventions. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Reserve Bank analysis in 2021 found wholesale gas prices outside WA had roughly doubled following Queensland's liquefied natural gas exports in 2015, while prices in the west had been about half those paid in the eastern states. The disparity has persisted, with WA recording an average domestic gas price of $7.45 a gigajoule in 2024-25, while east coast buyers have been signing long-term contracts at about $12 to $13 a gigajoule, according to the latest figures from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. The intervening years have also seen the closure of major Australian manufacturing plants, with the cost and availability of gas cited as contributing factors in the demise of plastics manufacturer Qenos and Incitec Pivot's Gibson Island fertiliser plant in Brisbane. Coalition seeks investment safeguards Shadow Resources Minister Susan McDonald told the Senate the opposition would not block Labor's reforms despite the opposition's lingering concerns about their potential to discourage investment in new gas projects. "We want more gas production and policies that encourage more investment." The Coalition had sought several changes to the scheme, including doubling the proportion of an exporter's domestic supply obligation that can be deferred from 10 to 20 per cent. Under Labor's proposal, the domestic market would be deliberately oversupplied to put downward pressure on prices. Susan McDonald has expressed concerns about the changes discouraging investment in new gas projects. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The opposition pushed for the government to have greater flexibility in determining the extent of that surplus, rather than automatically targeting an oversupply of 10 per cent. It also wanted the government to take into account the long-term cost of producing gas and the need to encourage new investment when making those decisions. But the amendments would not require the government to achieve a particular wholesale price. 'Santos' loopholes threaten gas plan Industry players and observers say draft gas reservation plans are full of carve-outs that will let one company off the hook. The Coalition also proposed safeguards for WA's exemption, including preventing it from automatically expiring and limiting the circumstances in which a future federal minister could revoke it.

events.title: Parents cutting basics at Christmas, charity warns
events.summary: A Worthing charity says families it supports are struggling to afford Christmas Christmas is likely to see families cut back on essentials to try and meet the expenses of the festive period, a West Sussex soup kitchen has warned. Katrina McCormack, chief executive of the Shout Worthing Soup Kitchen, told BBC Radio Sussex that they are forced to limit the amount of support they can give due to high demand at Christmas, and make sure their shelves are stocked. It comes at the start of a campaign to raise thousands for turkey and other Christmas trimmings for struggling families, which the charity says is a "driving force" for their work in December. McCormack said: "We ran an afternoon tea with Father Christmas, and last year we had children asking him for food." She added: "A lot of families are struggling to pay that extra, they are struggling to put food on the table. "Most of our families won't have a Christmas dinner without this." New research from charity Save the Children found that, of those surveyed, 65% of parents of children under 16 in the UK were concerned about being able to afford Christmas. It added that nearly a third of parents will buy fewer presents than normal, and 16% will reduce heating use in December to save money. McCormack said that, due to increasing cost of living, the charity had seen an increase in the number of people needing support, including families who are asking for help when they would not be needed in other parts of the year. "Poeple have come up and asked us if we can help them get an air fryer because they can't afford to put a cooker on," she added. Nicky Chisholm raises funds to help feed people at Christmas Ahead of Christmas, Nicky Chisholm, from Brighton, is aiming to fundraise to feed 500 people on Christmas Day. The campaign, which she has run online for the past 16 years, raises money for the soup kitchen and domestic abuse charity Safe in Sussex. Chisholm said: "Each year it fills an entire campervan of food. It gives you hope that people will donate and help out. "On Christmas Day I just want people to feel loved. "I would hate to think that there's people out there who couldn't have a Christmas dinner." events.title: Nvidia halts chip shipments to South-East Asia amid US crackdown
events.summary: Nvidia has asked its manufacturing partners to halt shipments of servers containing its artificial intelligence chips to four South-East Asian countries, as the US tightens export controls to prevent China from accessing AI computing technology . Manufacturers, including Dell and Supermicro, have informed customers in Malaysia , Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that Nvidia will not authorise their orders to be shipped, the Financial Times said in a report on Thursday, quoting sources. It remains unclear whether the suspension is temporary, as Nvidia and its manufacturing partners seek clarity on how to comply with Washington’s latest export restrictions, the sources said. The four countries have become favoured destinations for Chinese AI developers seeking to access Nvidia’s most advanced chips, whose exports are restricted by Washington. The move threatens to disrupt an expanding data centre industry in South-East Asia – a region which is an important source of revenue for Nvidia. The US chipmaker recorded $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, a 72 per cent increase from a year earlier, according to company accounts, as reported by the FT . Nvidia also records some of its Taiwan and China revenue via its Singapore unit, the report added. The move follows new US rules introduced last week to stop Chinese companies bypassing export restrictions by renting computing power from cloud providers using Nvidia chips. The lack of clarity around how the licensing requirements will be implemented has created uncertainty among companies operating in the region, the report said. “There's this new rule but no guidance on execution,” an executive at a cloud provider told the FT . “No one knows how to apply for this licence while the 90-day clock is ticking. It's causing sheer chaos in the region.” Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has previously argued that allowing the company to sell its chips in China would help maintain the country's dependence on American technology.

events.title: North Korea's Kim calls for nuclear arsenal expansion, says status 'will never change'
events.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for bolstering the country's nuclear arsenal and broader use of tactical nuclear weapons, according to a state media report. The country's nuclear status is irreversible and will not change in response to denuclearization demands, Kim said. The IAEA said Nov. 18 that a new extension to Yongbyon's original uranium-enrichment facility was externally complete by late October. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for bolstering the country's nuclear arsenal and expanding the use of tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains, state media reported Thursday, as Pyongyang reaffirmed its determination to retain its nuclear arms. Kim's comments followed a working visit Wednesday to facilities involved in nuclear material production and weapons research, according to the Korean Central News Agency. At the Nuclear Weapons Institute, he urged greater attention to "operationalizing" tactical nuclear weapons for a range of missions. Kim directly linked the development of those weapons to North Korea "sharing a border with its most dangerous, hostile state," an apparent reference to South Korea. The visit was part of Pyongyang's efforts to counter what Kim described as "the reckless expansion of adversary states' nuclear forces and military alliances," according to KCNA. He also singled out South Korea as a threat to North Korea's security and sovereignty. Kim reiterated that North Korea's status as a nuclear-armed state was irreversible, dismissing "denuclearization rhetoric" and saying its nuclear status "will never change." "[Our nuclear policy] is a core element of safeguarding the sovereignty of the Republic, enshrined in the supreme law of the state," he added. The report did not identify the sites Kim visited or disclose any production figures. The announcement followed an assessment last week by the International Atomic Energy Agency that another extension to Yongbyon's original uranium-enrichment facility had been externally completed by late October. The nuclear watchdog has lacked access to North Korea since 2009 and monitors its activities using satellite imagery and open-source intelligence. Citing what he portrayed as growing threats from Washington and its allies, Kim accused the U.S. of encouraging neighboring allies to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, pursuing nuclear sharing and the joint use of nuclear weapons. His comments come after South Korea announced efforts to acquire nuclear-powered submarines after President Donald Trump backed the plan in October 2025, according to a White House joint fact sheet. Nuclear-powered propulsion does not itself mean that a vessel carries nuclear weapons. Trump had expressed interest in meeting with Kim at the APEC summit in Shenzhen last week, according to Reuters, but no meeting took place and North Korea did not publicly respond to the proposal. Trump denied that Kim had ignored him, adding that communications could "start up right away," in an interview with the New York Post Tuesday. He said the two leaders had not been in contact "recently." "We've been off to other things," Trump added. North Korea has continued to accelerate its nuclear weapons development and rebuff South Korean and U.S. attempts to resume dialogue since negotiations between Trump and Kim collapsed in 2019. — CNBC's Jenny Lee contributed to this report.

events.title: Beware higher correlation but nab high U.S. credit yields, fund managers say
events.summary: Investment professionals discussed the risks and opportunities arising from the AI boom at the iConnections Global Alts Asia conference in Singapore. Despite concerns over AI valuations and recession risks, data centers remain an attractive investment opportunity, DSC Meridian Capital’s Sheru Chowdhry said. Portfolios may be more vulnerable to market volatility than they appear, R.G. Niederhoffer Capital Management’s Dan Gelernter said. The artificial intelligence boom could lead to a recession, whether through a collapse in AI investment or widespread job losses as the technology advances, a hedge fund manager said. "I do worry that if we don't have an AI-led recession in a few years, we're going to have an unemployment-led recession," Sheru Chowdhry, founder and chief investment officer at DSC Meridian Capital, said during a panel discussion moderated by CNBC's Joanna Ossinger at the iConnections Global Alts Asia conference in Singapore last week. Chowdhry's warning highlights a risk that extends beyond a potential bursting of the AI bubble. Rapid advances in the technology could lead to widespread job losses, with implications for the housing market and consumer spending, he said. "If this continues to go at the pace it is, I think in a few years a lot of us will probably not have jobs," Chowdhry said, adding that investors would have to rethink their approach to sectors such as housing and discretionary spending. Even so, the fund manager remains bullish on computing power and sees opportunities in data centers, despite concerns about AI valuations. The current AI investment cycle reminds Chowdhry of the dot-com bubble and the telecommunications infrastructure buildout of the early 2000s. "This cycle reminds me of the dot-com bubble and the telecom build we had going on in the early 2000s," he said. "Every cycle is different, but it kind of rhymes in some ways." Chowdhry also questioned whether semiconductor companies could sustain their profit margins in the coming years. However, he sees opportunities in data centers, pointing to access to power and grid connections as major bottlenecks in the AI buildout. "If you can identify data centers, I feel like that's going to be the picks and shovels of this cycle," he said. In particular, data centers that can secure permits and access to power within the next two years present a significant investment opportunity, he added. Beyond AI infrastructure, Chowdhry also pointed to attractive yields in U.S. credit markets. He cited yields of around 8.5% on U.S. high-yield bonds and 9.5% on leveraged loans, describing the current market environment as an opportunity to "get paid to wait." Investment portfolios may be more vulnerable to market volatility than they appear, according to Dan Gelernter, director of AI at R.G. Niederhoffer Capital Management, who spoke on the same panel. Average monthly correlations across investable assets rose from around 5% between the 1960s and 1990s to roughly 11% to 12% by 2020, according to research cited by Gelernter. His own analysis suggests that the figure has climbed further to around 15% to 16% in 2026. "Most portfolios are more highly levered, less liquid, more highly correlated than they appear to be, and that problem will get worse the more markets move," Gelernter said. Within the AI trade, Joo Kian Ong, a partner at AP3X Capital, said Samsung Electronics would be a good long position, with SK Hynix or Micron on the other side as potential shorts.

events.title: South Korea's central bank raises key interest rate to fight inflation
events.summary: South Korea’s central bank has raised its benchmark interest rate for the third time since July SEOUL, South Korea -- South Korea’s central bank on Thursday raised its benchmark interest rate for the third time since July, aiming to tighten money supply in the face of inflationary pressure driven by the war in the Middle East and the country’s booming semiconductor exports fueled by global demand related to artificial intelligence. In raising its policy rate by a quarter-percentage point to 3.25%, the Bank of Korea also lifted its growth forecast for South Korea’s economy to 3.9% from 3.3% for 2026, and to 4.1% from 2.9% for 2027, following months of strong exports. Despite the robust performance in trade, analysts have noted that consumer spending has remained subdued due to rising prices, stagnant wages and the burden of servicing South Korea’s notoriously high household debt. Consumer prices rose 2.8% in October from a year earlier, above the bank’s 2% target. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices to better gauge underlying price pressures, rose 2.7% over the same period. The bank said in a statement that raising borrowing costs was necessary as inflation was expected to remain above target for a “considerable period” and also cited “persistent risks on the side of financial stability.” The bank said the global economy was maintaining modest growth despite the conflict in the Middle East, mainly driven by AI-related investments, but price pressures would continue to grow, driven by increasing energy costs. Shin Hyun Song, the bank’s governor, said household borrowing is continuing to rise amid expectations of further home price increases in the greater capital area, making it necessary for policymakers to “remain vigilant regarding the risks of financial imbalances.” He said the rate hike was also a preemptive move to curb inflationary pressures and that consumer prices are expected to remain above the bank’s target until sometime in 2028. Shin said it would take time for the country’s export gains to translate into meaningful increases in consumers’ spending capacities and that the bank’s tight monetary policy should be complemented by fiscal measures to ease the burden on households. The bank’s decision to raise the policy rate was not a unanimous decision, with two of the seven members of its monetary policy committee arguing to keep the rate at 3%. events.title: Asian stocks stabilise after tech rout
events.summary: The gains in Asian counters came after a dip-buying afternoon rally helped US markets finish well off their initial lows. Asian stocks rebounded as tech shares steadied, with Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei leading gains. Kioxia, SoftBank, SK hynix and Samsung rose strongly. Markets stayed volatile after fears over AI spending, higher rates and tighter regulation. Michael Boutros said buyers must show demand is more than “short-lived relief rallies”. US tariff plans on 14 economies drew little market reaction. China faces a 20% toll, while Beijing warned Washington not to start “tariff wars and trade wars”. HONG KONG – Asian stocks stabilised on Nov 26 from another hard day of selling as the tech sector enjoyed a much-needed bounce , while investors took in their stride a fresh round of proposed US tariffs . The gains came after a dip-buying afternoon rally helped US markets finish well off their initial lows as Wall Street headed into the Thanksgiving holiday on an only slightly negative note. Beaten-down Asian tech firms led the gains on Nov 26 , with Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei again at the centre of the action, having seen wild swings this week amid concerns about the AI boom, while the euphoria over Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia has worn off. Japanese chipmaker Kioxia was the standout, surging by double figures, while South Korean titan SK Hynix were also comfortably up. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225, the Kospi in Seoul and the Taipei Taiex all advanced – even if they ended off their earlier highs – while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed more than 1% . There were also gains in Sydney, Mumbai , Singapore and Jakarta . Shanghai was flat, while Bangkok, Wellington and Manila dipped. London, Frankfurt and Paris opened sharply higher. Global markets have whipsawed this week, with news of Huang’s return – despite an affair with an alleged Chinese spy – lighting up Asian screens on Nov 24 before a crushing drop on Nov 25 . After a stellar start to 2026 , selling in the past five months has been fanned by fears over vast capital expenditure and when that will pay off, as well as rising interest rate expectations and talk of tighter AI regulation under a new Democrat-led Congress. Some observers have said there were signs the pain could be nearing its end. But Michael Boutros at Forex.com warned that “buyers still need to demonstrate that renewed demand extends beyond short-lived relief rallies”. “The focus heading into December is on whether semiconductor shares can regain traction and support a broader recovery or whether the recent deterioration signals further downside.” And analysts at Manulife said in a note: “The market rebound is encouraging, but it should not be interpreted as confirmation that the period of volatility has ended. “Following a sharp sell-off and increasingly oversold market conditions, further near-term gains are possible. Nevertheless, investors should be prepared for additional swings.” Expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December were given a fresh boost on Nov 25 by data showing US inflation in October at a three-year high, while economic growth for the third quarter was revised upwards. There was little movement in reaction to the unveiling of proposed US tariffs on 14 economies following a months-long probe into alleged excess production. The duties of up to 20% face a period of public comment before taking effect, with an official adding that the proposals take existing trade deals into account. The new levies target some of the largest US trading partners, including the European Union, India, Japan and South Korea. China faces a 20% toll, the joint-highest for any economy, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing. Beijing warned Washington not to engage in “tariff wars and trade wars”. AFP

events.title: South Korea hikes interest rates again to 3.25% as AI boom powers growth and inflation
events.summary: Bank of Korea governor Shin Hyun-song has emphasised that the bank will maintain a restrictive policy until it is confident inflation is converging towards its 2% target. The Bank of Korea raised rates to 3.25% and lifted its 2027 growth forecast to 4.1%, as the AI-driven semiconductor boom keeps the economy strong. Governor Shin said the bank is acting “pre-emptively” to curb inflation, with prices expected to reach the 2% target only in 2028. Growth is beating expectations, but household spending is weak. The bank signalled more tightening may follow, with the median six-month rate outlook at 3.5%. The Bank of Korea (BOK) resumed raising interest rates while sharply increasing its growth forecast for 2027, in a sign that the tightening cycle may last longer than previously expected as a historic semiconductor boom powers the economy. The central bank increased its seven-day repurchase rate by a quarter percentage point to 3.25% in a 5-2 decision on Nov 26, a move predicted by 21 of 23 economists surveyed by Bloomberg. The hike follows a pause in October after back-to-back increases in July and August, bringing the tightening in 2026 to 75 basis points. South Korea’s export-driven economy has been powered by an exceptionally strong memory-chip cycle tied to the global artificial intelligence build-out. Alongside the rate decision, the BOK raised its growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 to 3.9% and 4.1%, respectively, up from 3.3% for 2026 and 2.9% for 2027 in August. “By acting pre-emptively, we can limit the degree of tightening needed later and reap the benefits of acting early,” BOK governor Shin Hyun-song said after the board meeting. “We expect consumer-price inflation to converge to our target only in 2028.” The Nov 26 move underscores the central bank’s focus on containing inflation as the semiconductor boom pushes growth beyond expectations. By resuming tightening after a one-meeting pause, policymakers are signalling that inflation and the strength of the export-driven expansion outweigh concerns about sluggish consumer spending and the recent stock market rout, at least for now. “Next year’s growth forecast has topped 4%, which I attribute largely to the semiconductor sector’s rapidly expanding weight in the economy,” said Kong Dong-rak, a fixed-income strategist at Daishin Securities. “By that measure, the 2027 outlook suggests the current tightening cycle could last longer and reach a higher peak than previously expected.” The board’s updated six-month rate projections showed a median of 3.5%, up from 3.25% in August, pointing to scope for another rate hike. The outlook, covering December 2026 to May 2027, shows how policymakers are balancing persistent inflation against an uneven recovery. The nation’s policy-sensitive three-year yield was up 4 basis points on the day at 3.63%, after rising as much as 6 basis points earlier as the central bank’s dot plot indicated the possibility of further policy tightening . The won remained largely unchanged at 1,343.35 per US dollar. Governor Shin has repeatedly said the bank will maintain a restrictive policy until it is confident inflation is converging towards its 2% target. He has likened the BOK’s approach to using a “ hom i”, a small Korean hand plough, rather than a larger “ garae ” or shovel, describing the earlier back-to-back hikes as pre-emptive moves to keep inflation from becoming entrenched. The BOK raised its 2027 inflation forecast to 2.4% from 2.3%, reflecting expectations that price pressures will remain elevated as stronger economic growth feeds into domestic demand. It kept its consumer price index forecast for 2026 unchanged at 2.7%. Consumer prices rose 2.8% in October from a year earlier, slowing from 2.9% in September while core inflation, excluding food and energy, edged up to 2.8%, leaving both measures above the BOK’s 2% target. Kwon Hyo-sung, economist at Bloomberg Economics, said: “The stock market rout didn’t stop the Bank of Korea from raising its policy rate by 25 basis points to 3.25%, as we expected. “With inflation still stubbornly above target, strong growth gave the board room to act. We expect another hike to 3.5% in February 2027, though a slowdown in global AI-related investment would put that call at risk.” South Korea’s economy expanded 1% in the third quarter from the previous three months, exceeding economists’ expectations for a 0.8% gain as exports and investment surged. Still, private consumption contracted unexpectedly, underscoring how little of the chip-driven boom has filtered through to households. The export boom has shown little sign of losing momentum since then. In October, shipments adjusted for working-day differences jumped about 76% from a year earlier, with semiconductors continuing to drive the gains. South Korea last week also surpassed US$1 trillion (S$1.29 trillion) in cumulative goods exports for the first time, becoming only the fourth country to reach the milestone in a calendar year.

events.title: Singapore factory output up 6.1% in October as AI demand remains robust
events.summary: The precision engineering cluster grew the most at 54.1% due to higher production of semiconductor equipment. Singapore factory output rose 6.1% in October, beating the 2.2% forecast. EDB said AI and semiconductor demand lifted electronics and precision engineering. Precision engineering jumped 54.1%, led by semiconductor equipment. Electronics grew 6.6%, while chemicals also rose 4.4% after a weak September. Transport engineering fell 5.3% and biomedical manufacturing dropped 35.8%. Petrochemicals also shrank, showing uneven growth across Singapore’s factories. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s manufacturing output expanded in October, on the back of sustained demand for AI- and semiconductor-related products that supported the electronics and precision engineering sectors. Factory output grew 6.1% year on year, up from September’s revised pace of 5%, according to data released by the Economic Development Board (EDB) on Nov 26. All clusters posted gains except transport engineering and biomedical manufacturing. The figure exceeded the 2.2% forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll. Excluding the highly volatile biomedical manufacturing sector, output increased 12.1%. Analysts say Singapore’s manufacturing growth accelerated despite high base effects, and the outlook remains constructive for the near term. But industries outside the AI and tech spheres could see muted growth in the fourth quarter. DBS Bank senior economist Chua Han Teng said the global AI-driven expansion “still has legs”, though it is likely to proceed at a more sustainable pace, resulting in respectable albeit moderate growth in Singapore’s manufacturing sector. Downside risks to the global AI cycle could include tighter financial conditions and US-led regulatory measures, amid closer investor scrutiny of returns on AI investment. UOB economist Jester Koh said these could moderate AI-related tailwinds in the second half of 2027, as hyperscalers are also expected to slow down their capital expenditure growth. Newly proposed US tariffs of up to 20% could hit the Republic’s non-oil domestic exports and thus the manufacturing sector. Chua said Singapore still has room until January 2027 to negotiate with the US, reflecting ongoing active bilateral engagements and goodwill. In the meantime, continued exemptions for semiconductor and pharmaceutical goods would help keep the downside impact on Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports to the US manageable. The precision engineering cluster grew the most, at 54.1%, driven by higher production of semiconductor equipment in the machinery and systems segment, which surged 62.4%. Precision modules and components saw production increase by 16.1%. Maybank economist Brian Lee said that the rise in demand for semiconductor equipment could be partially attributed to expansions at local and regional chip fabrication plants. Output from the electronics cluster continued to expand year on year due to continued AI demand, with 6.6% growth. Other electronic modules and components saw the largest output, climbing 26.9%, followed by the computer peripherals and data storage segment, growing 24.7%. Production in the semiconductors segment grew 5.2%, while the infocommunications and consumer electronics segment gained 5.3%. Strong AI infrastructure build-out led by US hyperscalers will continue to fuel demand for AI-related products, with electronics and precision engineering firms staying optimistic for the October 2026 to March 2027 period, said Chua. The chemicals cluster grew 4.4%, after contracting in September. The expansion was led by a 10.4% uptick in the specialities segment due to higher production of industrial gases, chemicals and food additives, as well as a 16.6% increase in the other chemicals segment thanks to higher output of fragrances. The petroleum segment grew 7.8% on higher production of refined products. The petrochemicals segment continued to shrink, declining 23.1% amid softer demand and feedstock supply disruptions that constrained production. UOB’s Koh said the strength in the petroleum segment reflected a recovery in supplies from the Middle East. This was likely aided by bypass pipelines and alternative ports, increased Gulf production and continued transit through the Strait of Hormuz via shuttle tankers. General manufacturing industries grew 0.5%, with the food, beverages and tobacco segment climbing 2.1% on higher production of milk powder and beverage products. The miscellaneous and printing segments , however, recorded output dips of 1.3% and 10.2%, respectively, with miscellaneous weighed down by lower production of structural metal products and furniture. The transport engineering cluster declined 5.3% due to lower shipyard activities and weak production of oil and gas field equipment in the marine and offshore engineering segment, which contracted 25.2%.

events.title: Singapore ‘very disappointed’ by proposed US tariffs, says move overlooks its economic structure
events.summary: The Republic’s response comes after the US Trade Representative proposed tariffs of up to 20% on Singapore and 13 other trading partners. Singapore said it is “very disappointed” by new US tariffs, arguing the USTR ignored its open, trade-reliant economy and trusted role as a business hub. The USTR proposed tariffs of up to 20% under Section 301, but may cut them to 10% if Singapore reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade. METI said Singapore will keep engaging the USTR and will submit more comments in January, while defending its policies as WTO-compliant and not export subsidies. SINGAPORE – Singapore has expressed disappointment over proposed US tariffs , stating that the United States Trade Representative’s (USTR) probe has failed to consider the unique structure of the Republic’s open, trade-reliant economy. “Singapore disagrees with the USTR’s findings and we are very disappointed with the proposed actions against Singapore,” said the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) in a Nov 26 statement. The response comes after the USTR proposed on Nov 25 to impose tariffs of up to 20% on Singapore and 13 other trading partners under Section 301, accusing them of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions. The duties could take effect in early 2027, though USTR Jamieson Greer offered to consider lowering the proposed rate to 10% if Singapore reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with Washington. METI said Singapore “will continue to engage the USTR constructively, including to urge the USTR to reconsider its proposed actions on Singapore and to explore ways to reduce the tariff”. The USTR also issued a 168-page investigation report listing and explaining US concerns that follow the investigation the agency started in March. According to the USTR’s investigation report on Singapore’s industrial policies, the specific acts, policies and practices related to structural excess capacity and production include the Singapore Manufacturing 2030 plan and the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan; as well as financial support to the manufacturing sector and firms in the electronics and semiconductors, health and petrochemicals industries. The report also cited the “encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investments from non-market economies (NMEs), particularly China, which permits further development of structural excess capacity and production, and encouragement of or failure to address imports from NMEs, which enables Chinese firms to offload excess production”. METI said: “The USTR’s findings do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy. “Singapore’s global trade surplus is a reflection of our outward- and market-oriented economy, as well as our status as a trusted business and trading hub.” As a small country with limited resources, Singapore’s priority is to ensure that markets operate efficiently, and that the economy remains competitive globally, it said. “Singapore’s economic policies do not protect our domestic market or subsidise manufacturing for export. Our free trade agreements seek to lower barriers to trade and investments, and are fully compliant with World Trade Organization rules,” it added. METI said the US-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (USSFTA) is an example of how trade with the Republic has worked for the US. Under the USSFTA, Singapore levies no tariffs on US exports to Singapore, and the US has committed to levying no tariffs on imports from Singapore. Since the USSFTA was signed, the US has enjoyed a consistent trade surplus with Singapore for more than 20 years. In 2024, the US’ overall trade surplus with the Republic amounted to US$27 billion (S$34.8 billion). In 2025, this trade surplus with Singapore grew to US$33 billion. However, the USTR report states: “Although Singapore has run a sizeable bilateral goods trade deficit with the United States for nearly all of the past decade, this does not outweigh the negative effects of Singapore’s outsized manufacturing sector and comparatively low consumption.” METI said the ministry engaged the agency actively throughout the USTR investigation, and thoroughly addressed its queries and concerns. It added that it will submit further comments during the upcoming public consultation period in January to address the issues raised in the report. Ovais Subhani is senior business correspondent at The Straits Times. He writes stories that demystify the latest economics, trade and finance news.

events.title: Trump wants more tariffs. How are they affecting the US economy?
events.summary: US President Donald Trump has made tariffs central to his economic policy. Trump is making tariffs central to his policy again, with new rates planned for China, the EU and other partners under Section 301 after earlier duties expired. Studies say tariffs have raised consumer prices and cut output; the Tax Foundation says they added about US$1,000 per US household in 2025 and may add US$820 in 2026. The tariffs have not delivered the promised manufacturing boom. They have raised costs, slowed investment, and helped drive voter anger that cost Republicans Congress. In the first half of his second term as US President, Donald Trump has made tariffs central to his economic policy. In midterm elections in early November, in which his Republican Party lost control of both chambers of Congress to the Democrats, exit polls captured deep voter dissatisfaction with tariffs. The levies have been shown to raise the prices consumers pay for imported goods. Trump is moving to expand them nonetheless. On Nov 25, the Trump administration announced plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners in response to what US officials say is “structural excess capacity” in manufacturing in those places. What are the new tariffs the Trump administration announced? Under the new plan, which is still subject to a public comment process and could change as a result of that or of additional negotiations, the rate for imports from China would rise to 20%. The same rate would apply to imports from Vietnam, if a trade pact with the US is finalised. Imports from Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand would face an 18% tax, and those from India would face a 17% charge if a trade deal with the US is completed. Products from the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan would be taxed at 15%, and the rate for imports from Singapore would be 10%. Officials said rates could increase if trade relations deteriorate. According to a senior US official, the new levies will not stack on top of existing duties of 10% or 12.5% that the Trump administration invoked in July on imports from about 60 economies that supply almost all US imports, accusing them of failing to enforce bans on foreign goods made with forced labour and therefore enjoying an unfair competitive advantage. For products eligible to be hit by both sets of duties, only the higher rate would apply. The official added that some goods would be exempted from the tariffs, including oil and gas and food products that cannot be grown in the US. Products that are already subject to tariffs that apply to imports in particular industries or product categories, such as pharmaceuticals, are also exempted. The new tariffs could be implemented as early as January, the senior official said. What is the basis of the new tariffs? When the US Supreme Court invalidated sweeping import duties Trump had imposed citing emergency powers, he first used a different provision – Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 – to set a flat 10% levy on imports. Such tariffs are time-limited, however, and Trump’s expired on July 24. Since then, he has turned to Section 301 of the same act to replace those tariffs with more durable ones. Section 301 allows the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR), under the direction of the President, to impose tariffs in response to other nations’ trade measures it deems discriminatory to American businesses or in violation of US rights under international trade agreements. There is no limit on the tariff rate that can be introduced. This avenue does not enable an instant rollout of tariffs as the USTR must first conduct an investigation. Section 301 investigations focus on one country, but the USTR can conduct parallel reviews of a common concern that relates to multiple countries. A USTR report released on June 2 laid the groundwork for the tariffs based on accusations that trading partners failed to enforce bans on foreign goods made with forced labour. An investigation launched in March focused on what the USTR calls “structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors”. In the concluding report, released on Nov 25, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the offending trading partners had “adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”. How have Trump’s tariffs affected consumer prices and the US economy? Studies by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and other researchers show tariffs have boosted prices that consumers pay and hurt economic output. Some economists say the impact has been more muted than they expected, especially after the US Supreme Court struck down most of Trump’s initial tariffs in February and refunds were issued.

events.title: UAE explores building water desalination plants on east coast outside Arabian Gulf
events.summary: The UAE is exploring the development of water desalination plants on the country's east coast, outside the Arabian Gulf, to ensure water security , the Minister of Energy and Infrastructure said. The country is looking into the new plants and their connection to water transmission networks, Suhail Al Mazrouei said, according to state news agency Wam. The aim is to increase production capacity and diversify locations, alongside expanding storage capacity in underground reservoirs, the minister said on Wednesday, while speaking at an energy conference in Ras Al Khaimah. He also highlighted the anticipated expansion of road, logistics and energy projects over the next five years. The UAE is focusing on boosting its water security. In May, the investment arm of Etihad Water and Electricity signed an agreement to construct a major desalination plant to boost water security in the utility's Northern Emirates service network. The deal with NMDC Infra and Lantania Aguas for the Fujairah I independent water producer project, which will be located at the Port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, will be developed to provide 60 million imperial gallons per day (MIGD) at a total investment value of Dh1.046 billion ($284.8 million). The Fujairah I project, which will use seawater reverse osmosis technology, is the second being procured by EtihadWE in partnership with the private sector under the public-private partnership model, following the Naqa’a plant, which has a capacity of 150 MIGD. Meanwhile, Abu Dhabi is also currently building a desalination plant in Shuweihat, while another project was commissioned in the second quarter of this year. If required, the emirate is ready to build one more plant depending on demand, Abdulaziz Alobaidli, director general for regulatory affairs at Abu Dhabi's Department of Energy, told The National this year. The UAE in April said there were fears of “potentially catastrophic” threats to the Gulf’s marine environment in the wake of the Iran war, warning that missiles, drones and fires “may give rise to large-scale marine pollution involving oil, hazardous noxious substances, contaminated firefighting water, soot deposition” and other threats to the ecosystem. The region relies on desalinated seawater, and any contamination could also lead to “severe water security implications”, it added. Desalination plants were attacked in Bahrain and Kuwait in March, which brought Gulf water security into focus.

events.title: Hedge funds are no longer just for the rich. They’re wooing everyday investors
events.summary: Hedge funds are increasingly courting retail investors as the industry seeks new avenues for growth. Lower fees, smaller minimum investments and retail-friendly vehicles are making hedge fund strategies more accessible. Experts warn that easier access does not remove risks tied to leverage, short selling and liquidity constraints. For decades, hedge funds were the preserve of billionaires, pension funds and deep-pocketed institutional investors. Now, the industry is increasingly courting a new pool of capital: everyday investors. The shift, dubbed by some as the "retailization" of hedge funds, comes as alternative asset managers seek new avenues for growth and investors look for ways to shield their portfolios from increasingly volatile equity markets. Unlike traditional equity funds, which typically rely on stocks rising to generate returns, hedge funds can employ strategies including short selling, arbitrage and derivatives to seek profits across different market conditions. For an industry already managing record levels of assets, individual investors represent a largely untapped growth opportunity, experts who spoke to CNBC said. "Hedge funds are entrepreneurs. Their objective is to make as much money as they possibly can, both in returns and for their organization," said Don Steinbrugge, CEO of hedge fund consulting firm Agecroft Partners. "So if they have the ability to go after a new market and grow their business, they're going to do that." The push is coming from both hedge fund managers seeking to broaden their investor base and traditional asset managers looking to capitalize on growing demand for alternative investments, said Ken Heinz, president of hedge fund research firm HFR. "Heightened geopolitical uncertainty, greater market volatility, inflation concerns, and the higher correlation between equities and bonds have raised questions about the effectiveness of conventional portfolio diversification," said Ricky Siao, a hedge fund specialist at Swiss private bank UBP. The investment environment has become more challenging for investors who have historically relied on traditional allocations to equities and fixed income, he added. As a result, investors are increasingly seeking exposure to strategies such as arbitrage, event-driven investing and quantitative macro strategies to reduce their dependence on equity market returns. The democratization of hedge fund investing is taking shape through a growing array of investment vehicles, often with lower fees, smaller minimum investments and more frequent opportunities to withdraw money. Some of the biggest names in the hedge fund industry are already moving in that direction. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman's Pershing Square raised $5 billion in April for a publicly listed closed-end fund, giving everyday investors access to its investment expertise without the performance fees traditionally associated with hedge funds. The fund charges a 2% annual management fee. British hedge fund giant Man Group, meanwhile, entered the U.S. ETF market last September and doubled its lineup to four actively managed funds just three months later. The broader shift is also changing how hedge fund strategies are packaged for individual investors. "What has changed most is the wrapper, not the strategy itself," said Yi Ling Ong, managing partner and chief operating officer at Golden Horse Fund Management. In other words, hedge fund strategies are increasingly being packaged in more accessible vehicles such as mutual funds and ETFs, often with lower investment minimums and fewer restrictions on withdrawals. "Investors may still be getting exposure to long/short equity, credit, or macro strategies, but delivered through vehicles that offer quarterly or monthly liquidity and standardized reporting." The trend is playing out across markets. In Europe, hedge fund managers have adapted strategies to fit regulated UCITS funds, which are accessible to individual investors. In the U.S., mutual funds and ETFs have similarly broadened access to alternative investment strategies. In Asia, digital wealth platforms are helping bridge the gap between institutional and individual investors. Singapore-based Endowus, which began offering hedge funds on its platform in 2022, has lowered minimum investments for semi-liquid funds to $50,000, while removing minimums altogether for some daily-liquid alternative funds, according to Chief Investment Officer Hugh Chung. While most hedge funds on the platform remain restricted to accredited investors, a growing number of alternative funds are becoming available to non-accredited investors, Chung said. India is seeing a similar shift through Specialized Investment Funds, or SIFs, which allow investors to access more sophisticated strategies through structures that more closely resemble traditional mutual funds, said Rajesh Singla of Alpha AMC.

events.title: Microdramas rake in US$20 billion as world gloms on to quick hits
events.summary: One-tenth of people worldwide now watch the mini-films. Microdramas are booming worldwide. MPA says revenue will reach “US$20 billion” in 2026 and “US$32 billion” by 2031, with one-tenth of people now watching them. China still leads the market. ByteDance, Tencent and Kuaishou make over 80% of China’s “US$15.2 billion” revenue, while India’s JioHotstar is growing with low-priced subscriptions. Profit stays weak outside China. More than half of revenue is spent on marketing, and AI is being used to make more titles, but viewers still prefer live-action shows. Minutes-long microdramas are set to notch US$20 billion (S$25.8 billion) in revenue in 2026 as global viewers swarm to their screens in search of quick, easy hits. After the projected 24% growth globally in 2026, the market will expand further and rake in US$32 billion by 2031, according to a report by Media Partners Asia (MPA). Audiences across the globe have latched on to the soapy serials, tailored to fit smartphones’ vertical screens and social-media scrollers’ fickle attention spans. Cliffhangers, sudden tonal shifts and mafia-centred plot lines have fuelled the genre’s rise in popularity outside China, where they first took off, with major Hollywood players including Fox Entertainment, Walt Disney and Paramount+ beginning to explore the format. Worldwide, one-tenth of people now watch the mini-films. China still dominates most of the shows’ production and viewership. TikTok parent ByteDance, Tencent Holdings and Kuaishou Technology pull in over 80% of the country’s US$15.2 billion in revenue from the films, MPA said. In India, Asia’s second-largest market, local streamers like JioHotstar have drawn audiences with low-priced subscriptions billed outside app stores. Yet, profit margins remain thin, particularly outside China. More than half of revenue earned outside the country is burned on marketing to attract viewers who mostly watch for free, MPA said. Producers are turning to artificial intelligence to pad their margins, though audiences have not taken to videos made with the technology. About 75% of new titles on apps outside China in 2026 were generated with AI, but most top-viewed films on the platforms still feature live action, MPA estimates. “AI has made a title cheap enough to test almost any idea, and catalogues have filled accordingly,” said Myat Pan Phyu, an analyst at MPA. “Viewing has moved far less.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters
events.summary: Following Section 301 investigations, the U.S. Trade Representative has proposed imposing a 17% tariff on India if it finalizes a trade deal with the U.S. The USTR has proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective deals, giving Indian exporters an edge. During its trade negotiations, India has pressed the U.S. to offer it a preferential tariff rate over its competitors. The latest U.S. tariff rates announced Wednesday have signaled that Washington is willing to offer India an edge over its competitors if New Delhi agrees to finalize a long-pending trade deal. The Office of the United States Trade Representative has proposed a tariff of 17% on Indian exports if New Delhi "were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade" with Washington. It added that without a trade deal, India could face tariffs of up to 25% under Section 301 investigations encompassing excess production capacity that harms U.S. interests. Meanwhile, the USTR has proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective trade deals, handing India a competitive advantage over rival exporters. The U.S. expects the announcement of a lower tariff rate will encourage New Delhi to sign off on a trade deal before the G20, Atman Trivedi, partner at Washington-based DGA Albright Stonebridge Group, told CNBC. India has got a "better bargain with Washington than its main competitors," and it may be enough for the Indian government "to declare victory and secure domestic backing for the deal," Trivedi said. In February, U.S. President Donald Trump had announced a deal with India, claiming that New Delhi had accepted to "Buy American" at a much higher level after the U.S. agreed to slash tariffs to 18% from 50% earlier. The India-U.S. trade deal has been pending with both sides indicating there was little room to grant concessions , while the Supreme Court annulling Trump tariffs allowed New Delhi to demand preferential tariffs that give it an edge over competitors. "Today's announcement increases the urgency of reaching an agreement," Ronak D. Desai, visiting fellow at Hoover Institution, Stanford University, told CNBC. He added that while the prospect of a 17% tariff may strengthen the economic case for the deal, the threat of a 25% tariff could stir the sensitivity of the Indian government. "The Modi government will be particularly sensitive to any perception that India is conceding under American Pressure," Desai said. India's commerce ministry on Wednesday said it "does not have structural excess capacity in any sector," denying the findings of the USTR investigation, but added that it remains committed to "working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement." Despite India facing steep tariffs, which were raised to 50%, New Delhi's trade surplus with the U.S. rose to $57.3 billion in 2025 from $45.2 billion in 2024. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Trump are likely to meet in December for the G20 leaders' meeting in Florida, and several experts believe the two leaders could seal the trade deal on the sidelines of the summit.
