events.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
events.summary: Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffs The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy. The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal . China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%. The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce. The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings. Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products. Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies. The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy". Jamieson Greer, US trade representative He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression". They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said. But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade. Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs. Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy. Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them. Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said. Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said. The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said. Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration. However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer. "The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note. The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added. Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move. Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers. Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade. The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US. "Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said. The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.

events.title: OCBC expands physical gold business with new 100-tonne vault in Singapore
events.summary: The facility complements OCBC’s existing vaulting arrangements in Singapore and supports its physical gold business. OCBC has opened a 100-tonne gold vault in Singapore to meet rising demand for trading and secure custody, serving institutional clients and Bank of Singapore clients. The bank said interest in physical gold has grown since its June launch, as clients seek “secure and Singapore-based solutions” for their gold needs. The move supports Singapore’s push to become a gold hub, alongside MAS vaulting services, SGX’s planned clearing system in 2027, and OCBC’s wider gold products. SINGAPORE – OCBC has added a 100-tonne dedicated gold vault in Singapore, expanding its physical gold business to meet increasing appetite for trading and custody services. The new facility – capable of holding some 8,000 large gold bars weighing 12.4kg each – complements the bank’s existing vaulting arrangements in the Republic, OCBC said on Nov 26. It serves OCBC’s institutional clients as well as those of its private banking subsidiary, Bank of Singapore. OCBC declined to disclose how much physical gold it currently holds in custody and the number of clients it stores gold for, but noted that it has seen growing demand for its services, especially from Bank of Singapore clients seeking secure, long-term custody arrangements. OCBC said it is “seeing increasing interest in its custody and vaulting services among its institutional clients, particularly banks and private banks”. Kenneth Lai, head of global markets at OCBC, said interest in physical gold has been strong since the bank launched its physical gold business in June. This, he said, reflects “growing demand from clients seeking secure and Singapore-based solutions in relation to their physical gold needs”. The new vault comes as the Republic steps up efforts to strengthen its position as a leading gold trading and distribution hub in the Asia-Pacific region . OCBC is a founding clearing member of an over-the-counter gold clearing system which the Singapore Exchange is set to launch in 2027. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) on Nov 10 launched a gold vaulting service for foreign central banks , international financial institutions and sovereign entities looking to hold their gold reserves in Singapore. The gold will be stored in MAS’ national currency vault , which can hold up to 500 tonnes of the precious metal, with room to expand as demand grows. The service will complement Singapore’s commercial vaulting capacity of more than 2,000 tonnes, which serves market participants such as bullion banks, institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals. MAS will also offer gold custody accounts to selected Singapore-based bullion banks with expertise and experience in providing gold-related services and trading liquidity to foreign central banks, international financial institutions and sovereign entities. OCBC said it will continue to explore extending its offerings in physical gold, as well as other physical gold-linked investment and hedging solutions, to more client segments across the group. Its asset management arm, Lion Global Investors, launched the LionGlobal Singapore Physical Gold Fund in 2025, Singapore’s first fund backed by physical gold that is insured and stored in the Republic. This was followed by the listing of the LionGlobal Singapore Physical Gold exchange-traded fund (ETF), Singapore’s first home-grown physical gold ETF, on SGX in March 2026. Retail clients in Singapore can also invest in fractional gold or silver through the OCBC app, while clients of its insurance arm Great Eastern can gain exposure to physical gold through investment-linked policies. Timothy Goh is a business correspondent at The Straits Times. He covers commodities and currencies, with occasional forays into listed companies.

events.title: ASIC sues major insurer over complaints handling and claims delays
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Insurance giant AIG taken to court over handling of customer complaints AIG offers travel insurance and consumer device insurance. ( Supplied ) The corporate regulator is suing major insurer AIG over its handling of hundreds of customer complaints about general insurance claims. ASIC alleges AIG Australia, which offers travel insurance and consumer device insurance, failed to provide complaint responses or delay notifications within the required 30-day timeframe in 534 cases. Some customers waited for months for complaint decisions, including those who were unwell, injured or recently bereaved, between October 2021 and December 2025. ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said policyholders should not have to fight their insurer for basic communication. Mr Kirkland alleged some customers were also given inaccurate explanations for the delays. "Complaint handling is a fundamental obligation for insurers, who must take complaints seriously," he said. Alan Kirkland says insurers need to take complaints seriously. ( ABC News: Adam Wyatt ) "Insurers must have effective systems for recording complaints and should not have to search personal drives and emails to know whether a complaint was responded to." ASIC alleged the delays caused uncertainty, frustration and emotional distress, and that some customers faced delays receiving insurance payments, refunds or compensation. AIG Australia is a publicly listed subsidiary of the global American International Group, headquartered in New York. The parent company saw a net income of $US3.1 billion in the 2025 financial year. In a statement to the ABC, an AIG spokesperson said it acknowledged the enforcement action. "We are considering the claim carefully and continue to liaise with ASIC," the spokesperson said. "AIG Australia continues to make significant improvements to our IDR (internal dispute resolution) processes and remain firmly committed to delivering fair and timely outcomes for our customers." AIG is a prominent sponsor of women's golf. ( Getty Images: Andrew Redington ) The corporate regulator also alleged AIG used a standard template for communications about delays that pre-populated "complexity" as the reason for the delay, and failed to inform customers of their rights to escalate complaints to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA). ASIC alleged the insurer failed to have an effective system for recording information about complaints and keeping track of their progress. This system did not provide an alert when a complaint response was due, or reliably record whether complaints had been answered. The news comes weeks after the federal court fined insurance giant Hollard $2 million for taking so long to process a home insurance claim that a house in regional Victoria became uninhabitable. ASIC sued Hollard in April last year, alleging the insurer "breached its duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of a claim made by a couple in October 2021, two days after a storm damaged their roof. The outcome was the first civil penalty ordered against an insurer for breaching its duty of utmost good faith. Hollard admitted contravening the Insurance Contracts Act. In December 2024, ASIC put general insurers on notice after a review of 11 insurers found they failed to identify one in six complaints, alongside shortcomings in customer communications, complaints-handling systems and the identification of systemic issues. "ASIC has put insurers on notice about complaints-handling failures. Those that continue to fall short of their legal obligations should expect enforcement action," Mr Kirkland said. ASIC said it was seeking declarations, pecuniary penalties, adverse publicity orders and orders requiring AIG to engage an independent expert to review its complaints-handling arrangements and implement recommendations. If you have more information about this investigation, you can securely contact reporter Adelaide Miller at miller.adelaide@proton.me The enforcement action also comes as the Insurance Council of Australia's redrafted code of practice is under review by ASIC. The corporate regulator is seeking public feedback on the redrafted code, before deciding whether to approve to proposed changes. events.title: Judge blocks FCC early-renewal process for Disney-owned ABC stations, for now
events.summary: The decision will temporarily block the agency from continuing its early renewal of a set of ABC's broadcast station licenses. The agency cited concerns around ABC's diversity, equity and inclusion efforts as the reason behind the start of the early renewal process. "The court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," said Judge Loren L. AliKhan. A judge has temporarily blocked the Federal Communications Commission from continuing its early renewal of a set of broadcast station licenses for Disney -owned ABC. Judge Loren L. AliKhan of U.S. District Court in Washington granted Disney the preliminary injunction it sought and denied the FCC's attempt to dismiss the suit. "This is not a close case," wrote the federal judge. "Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness." The broadcast network had filed the lawsuit and followed the FCC beginning its early review of the ABC licenses. The government agency cited concerns around ABC's diversity, equity and inclusion efforts as the reason behind the start of the early renewal — years ahead of their scheduled expiration. "Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment ," said an ABC spokesperson. An FCC spokesperson said in a statement that the part of the decision granting ABC's motion "is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law," the Associated Press reported . In her ruling, AliKhan said that early license renewal proceedings came over a year into the FCC's enforcement push against ABC, starting with an investigation into Disney's employment practices in March 2025 and leading to the renewal proceedings in April this year. ABC on Tuesday had said that it continued to "face irreparable harm" from the administration, which "has been acting" through the FCC, which is run by President Donald Trump appointee Brendan Carr. AliKhan, a Joe Biden appointee, noted in her ruling that ABC had to change how it handled guest appearances for top shows "The View" and "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" with no candidate for public office appearing on the former and a senatorial candidate's appearance on the latter uploaded to YouTube instead of being broadcast. "The prospect of license non-renewal has also factored into plaintiffs' calculus of when and how they cover President Trump and political topics," said the judge. ABC had alleged that Trump and Carr have been making comments "intended to chill their protected speech," and that such comments have escalated since the 2024 presidential election. The White House and the FCC didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from CNBC. — CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to the story

Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week spelled out his vision for an AI-based app that would collect data about children as they grow and analyze it to determine their aptitude for different types of study or careers. Modi suggested that parents of three-year-old children should enter data about their offspring’s activities and accomplishments into a government-run system that is also accessible to teachers and even a child’s friends. Those records, the PM suggested, will “help identify children's interests and aptitude from an early age and redirect them in the study of their choice in future.” That’s not an entirely creepy idea, because gaining access to India’s top tertiary institutions requires students to pay a hefty fee to sit for entrance exams. Modi pitched recommendations from the AI-powered app as something parents will appreciate as they contemplate whether to fund their offspring’s studies. India’s most populous state, Uttar Pradesh (UP), has proposed to build an “AI Stack” to serve its 240 million-plus residents. A 178-page tender seeks bidders to build a system that uses the state’s Family ID – a unique identifier for each household – to link data held by multiple agencies so it can be put to work in a dozen AI use cases. One of those use cases is a tool for “AI-Enabled Social Media Monitoring and Urban Grievance Detection” that “analyses publicly available social media content including online news channels and connected grievance channels to detect emerging urban issues, citizen complaints, service interruptions, and recurring service gaps.” The government wants that system to autonomously route complaints to relevant agencies, to automate actions like sending crews to patch up damaged roads. Critics have pointed to vague wording in the tender as potentially allowing the UP government to link this system to other agencies – a matter of concern given Indian state and national governments have implemented internet shutdowns to stop protestors from communicating on social media services and messaging apps. Another use case is a knowledge assistant for state police that looks up case histories and other data but can’t use it to assess evidence or provide investigative conclusions. An app for teachers will advise them on how to create custom content to meet students’ needs. Healthcare workers would also get an app to help them make recommendations during patient visits. Citizens get natural language interfaces to a system that offers advice on how to identify and access government services and schemes. UP wants to drive these apps with self-hosted open-weight models, and to use only anonymized datasets. India’s Internet Freedom Foundation worries that the systems described in the tender aren’t explicitly authorized by any legislation, and that the document doesn’t mention important oversight measures for the AI Stack.

events.title: South Korea upgrades growth forecast, raises benchmark rates to highest in two years
events.summary: The rate hike comes as South Korea continues to deal with above-target inflation and rising house prices in Seoul. The BOK also sharply upgraded its growth forecasts for 2026 to 3.9% for 2026 and 4.1% for 2027, up from the 3.3% and 2.9% previously. South Korea's third-quarter GDP grew by 3.4% year on year, beating expectations, and also allowing the central bank room to raise rates. South Korea's central bank on Thursday hiked benchmark lending rates to their highest in two years, as inflation continues to run above target while a booming economy allows it room to tighten policy. The central bank raised rates by 25 basis points to 3.25% for its final meeting of the year, in line with expectations from economists, data on the Bank of Korea's website showed . Inflation is expected to remain above its 2% target level for a considerable time, the BOK added in its statement , saying this was due to the pass-through of elevated cost pressures and as demand-side pressures also gradually strengthen, driven by stronger economic growth. Inflation in the country stood at 2.8% in October. The BOK also upgraded its growth forecasts for 2026 to 3.9% for 2026 and 4.1% for 2027, up from the 3.3% and 2.9%, respectively, forecast in August. South Korea's third-quarter GDP grew by 3.4% year on year, beating expectations, allowing the central bank room to raise rates. "The projections of high growth rates for next year and beyond also reflect the significantly increasing weight of the IT sector as a growth engine for the Korean economy," BOK Governor Shin Hyun-song said at a press conference following the decision. Operating profits in the semiconductor sector could reach 700 trillion won, Shin told reporters, according to local news agency Yonhap. Shin also signaled that more rate hikes, although he did not give a fixed timeline. "While the domestic economy is expected to continue its robust growth, inflation is forecast to remain above the target level for a considerable time ... The Board, therefore, sees it warranted to continue its policy response until there is confidence that inflation will converge stably to the target level." Gareth Leather, senior Asia Economist at Capital Economics said there is reason to believe that the BOK's tightening cycle was drawing to a close. The BOK has raised rates by 75 basis points in five months, as higher energy prices from the Iran war and the AI boom has pushed up inflation in the country. Leather said that the country's strong growth, as well as a strengthening won could ease concerns over inflation. While rapidly rising property prices could strengthen the case for a prolonged tightening cycle, Leather said that the BOK was "more likely to favour macroprudential measures over further rate hikes to address its financial stability concerns." After the decision, the country's benchmark Kospi rose 1.88%.

events.title: S&P warns Nvidia credit rating could be cut over 'rising' management and governance risk
events.summary: Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the company continues to show "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings said. In a Wednesday note, S&P cited the "long tenure" of certain board members as a factor that could compromise their independence. The warning comes after Moody's Ratings lowered its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive on Nov. 18. Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the company continues to have "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings said in the wake of the Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. "News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," S&P said in a Wednesday note . Nvidia currently holds an AA rating, the third-highest level. S&P has placed the chipmaker on "CreditWatch with negative implications," though any potential downgrade would be limited to one notch, to AA-, unless investigations or disclosures lead the agency to conclude that Nvidia's reputation or future prospects have also been harmed. A downgrade can pressure bond prices, push yields higher and raise borrowing costs. Nvidia priced $25 billion of investment-grade senior notes in June, with maturities from 2028 through 2056, shortly after S&P upgraded the company from AA- to AA. Nvidia has about $32.5 billion of bonds in the U.S. high-grade corporate bond index, according to Bloomberg. S&P's Wednesday note follows Moody's Ratings changing its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive on Nov. 18, citing governance concerns, and leaving that outlook unchanged after Huang's return on Monday. In its note, S&P cited the "long tenure" of certain board members as a reason their independence may be "compromised" and said Nvidia's management and governance risk was "rising." The ratings agency added that it remained unaware of any remedial action taken by the board to address what could be "meaningful" management and governance deficiencies. Chairman Harvey Jones and early investor Tench Coxe have served on Nvidia's board since 1993, while Brooke Seawell joined in 1997. Mark Stevens served from 1993 to 2006 and rejoined the board in 2008. S&P also flagged questions around geopolitical risk management and internal controls arising from Nvidia's exposure to China. "While Nvidia management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the "key man" risk to the forefront," S&P's Andrew Chang and David Tsui said. Chang and Tsui noted that Huang's resignation and subsequent reinstatement did not resolve questions about the board's oversight of executive conduct. The agency also intends to meet with Nvidia's board and management to discuss plans to address those deficiencies, particularly around "board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession plan." Huang returned less than two weeks after Jones said Nvidia's directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back, sending Nvidia shares up as much as 36% during Monday's session. Nvidia shares are down about 12.5% since Monday's close.

( Supplied: Verdant Earth Technologies ) A court has upheld the ruling to refuse a biomass power generator near Singleton, NSW. Environmentalists say it's a huge win, but the company behind it isn't backing down. A partnership with a data centre proposed for adjoining land is now in doubt A court has knocked back an appeal brought by the company planning to build Australia's largest modern biomass generator in the NSW Hunter Valley. Verdant Earth Technologies has been working to transform the former coal-fired Redbank Power Station near Singleton into a bioenergy hub since it took over the site in 2018. The plan, initially put to the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC), was for it to be fuelled by invasive native species (INS) plaguing farmers in western NSW, as well as purpose-grown plants. The proposal was for 700,000 tonnes of dry material to be burned each year to fuel the 151-megawatt proposal, which the company said could power approximately 200,000 homes. The NSW Planning Department was told the capital investment would surpass $70 million, with the project creating 330 jobs during construction and 60 operational positions. But the IPC last year rejected the proposal , noting the "potential benefits" for energy security and reliability, as well as employment opportunities, but ultimately ruling that the environmental impact was too great. Jacqui Mumford hopes this is the end of the long-running bid to restart Redbank. ( Supplied ) The NSW Land and Environment Court today dismissed Verdant Earth's appeal, upholding the IPC's refusal. Environmentalists called the decision a victory for nature and wildlife but said state government policy needs to change to close the biomass loophole. CEO of the Nature Conservation Council of NSW (NCC) Jacqui Mumford said she hopes the ruling marks the end of the Redbank restart. "It was a bad project from the start," she said. "Burning native vegetation for energy is not something that we need; there's nothing renewable or sustainable about permanently clearing wildlife, so I really hope this is the end. NSW Local Land Services has strict guidelines to help rid parts of the western district of invasive native species. ( Landline: Amelia Bernasconi ) Verdant Earth CEO Richard Poole told the ABC he was "totally surprised" by the dismissal. "I'm a full believer in biomass as an absolute solution for Australia's energy problems," he said. "I haven't seen the full judgment, but not the result we were hoping for." Richard Poole (right) believes biomass is not properly considered in Australia's energy mix. ( Landline: Amelia Bernasconi ) Mr Poole said agreements had been made over the past 12 months to scale back the use of the invasive native species and fast-track the project's emissions reductions. "Don't forget this waste that is in dispute is waste from INS clearing, which is a government-approved program." Ms Mumford said the NCC would be campaigning to see the INS legislation changed, in the lead-up to the March state election. Redbank Power Station has sat idle, under care and maintenance, for more than a decade. ( Landline: Bindi Bryce ) Verdant Earth had recently entered talks with Voltic DC, managed by APDC, exploring a data centre to be built on adjoining land. Voltic DC's website states the deal would provide "access to shared infrastructure and land to maximise data centre capacity". "Following any restart [of Redbank Power Station], Voltic and Verdant will assess commercial co-benefits including potential power supply arrangements and shared site infrastructure." Mr Poole said that arrangement was now in doubt. "Obviously the hope was to solve the government's issue around renewable energy by being able to get Redbank up and provide some power to that data centre," he said. "That's obviously not the case at this time." Mr Poole said he would be meeting with his legal team to look at the next steps. "We need to regroup and have a look at it. Maybe it's a data centre, maybe it's a battery site," he said. events.summary: Denny's welcomed Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO in a post on X. The diner chain said it had restored a commemorative plaque marking Nvidia's birthplace after learning its removal on Nov. 13. Huang's ties to Denny's predate Nvidia's founding, as he once worked at the restaurant chain. Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia — and Denny's has a booth waiting for him. The American diner chain welcomed the billionaire's return as Nvidia CEO by revealing that it had reinstated a commemorative plaque marking the birthplace of the artificial intelligence chip giant after learning of its removal on Nov. 13. "Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's said in a post on X . The plaque marks the booth at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley, California, where Huang and his co-founders discussed the idea for Nvidia, which was founded in 1993. The restaurant chain said it learned on Nov. 13, a day after Huang's resignation , that the plaque had been removed. "We put the plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's said, without specifying who had removed it or why. events.title: Trump's threat on AI data centres could be an opportunity for the Gulf
events.summary: US President Donald Trump's threat to penalise American companies building data centres overseas could accelerate home-grown AI development in countries such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE, where billions of dollars are being invested in infrastructure. Recent turmoil at Nvidia and growing scrutiny of American chip exports have also highlighted the global implications of US technology policy uncertainty. On Friday, Mr Trump threatened to impose taxes on American companies building data centres overseas. Three days later, Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's chief executive following Mr Trump's intervention. Both developments highlight Washington's influence over who builds AI infrastructure and who can access the technology that powers it. Nvidia accounts for an estimated 40 per cent of capital spending by major cloud providers and about 80 per cent among other AI infrastructure operators, Mr Huang said in an interview with the BG2 podcast last month. In Abu Dhabi, the planned five-gigawatt UAE-US AI campus, expected to cost more than $30 billion, will house Stargate UAE , a one-gigawatt computing cluster bringing together G42, OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank. In Saudi Arabia, Public Investment Fund-owned AI company Humain expanded its partnership with Nvidia last month with plans for an 84-megawatt AI computing project. The company is targeting more than six gigawatts of data centre capacity by 2034. Uncertainty in Washington Last week, the US Department of Commerce introduced new export restrictions to prevent companies from bypassing chip controls through overseas data centres. Further scrutiny is expected when Democrats take control of Congress in January, with lawmakers pushing for tighter AI regulation. Meanwhile, the UAE, which joined the US-led Pax Silica initiative in January, was among nine US partners that pledged to safeguard sensitive AI technology earlier this month. Greater scrutiny of how American chips are used could work in the UAE's favour, said Chiara Spina, assistant professor of entrepreneurship and family enterprise at Insead. “Where the UAE has a competitive advantage would be instead in investing in data centres which proved to be extremely safe,” she told The National . David Bach, president of Swiss business school IMD, told The National that "the unpredictability in US policy is a risk, but it's also a tremendous opportunity,” Businesses are regionalising digital services, much as they did physical supply chains to guard against trade disruptions, potentially benefiting the UAE as companies seek more stable jurisdictions, he said from the sidelines of the IMD Business Forum 2026 held in Dubai. Opportunity for regional companies Saudi geothermal cooling company Strataphy, which has announced a collaboration with Humain, competes with US companies such as Vertiv, Trane and Carrier. Its technology uses the ground's thermal properties to cool infrastructure such as data centres, reducing electricity consumption without consuming water. Should restrictions extend to American infrastructure providers operating overseas, “that is fantastic news for us”, Ammar Alali, chief executive of Strataphy told The National . While Mr Alali does not expect such sweeping restrictions, reduced US competition could boost Strataphy's market share. Data centres are expected to account for more than 85 per cent of Strataphy's clients by the end of 2027, up from none at the end of 2025. The company serves predominantly government-owned data centre customers in Saudi Arabia and the UAE and is expanding into Oman. Tighter chip export controls, however, could delay data centre projects and affect Strataphy's cooling efficiency. Although it does not buy directly from Nvidia, switching from newer Nvidia chips to those requiring lower coolant temperatures could reduce the cooling cost savings it offers from 65 per cent to about 50 per cent, Mr Alali said. Push for AI sovereignty Demand for digital sovereignty has been growing as companies seek greater control over their technology infrastructure, Mr Bach said. “People are talking about sovereign clouds, the fact that you need to have your data in certain jurisdictions, either as a function of regulation or as a function of just business continuity because disruptions can occur.” Abu Dhabi-based Aleria, a key player in the UAE's sovereign AI ecosystem, enables governments and businesses to run AI within their own infrastructure while retaining control over their data. The company remains firmly committed to Nvidia. “We strongly believe in Nvidia-based technology that they have delivered over the past three decades,” Eric Leandri, chief executive of Aleria, told The National . “From a technology perspective, recent weeks have reinforced our confidence in Nvidia's leadership.” Aleria is expanding its partnership with Nvidia into Europe, announcing plans at the chipmaker's GTC conference in Berlin last month to deploy 3,000 Blackwell Ultra graphics processing units in Switzerland alongside US data storage company DDN. Mr Leandri said governments needed to treat AI as critical national infrastructure, but distinguished AI sovereignty from complete technological independence. “The Gulf does not need to recreate the entire global technology ecosystem independently. It has the opportunity to become a leading, valued and respected partner within it.” From AI importer to exporter Mr Bach compared the AI boom to the early days of the internet, when attention focused on servers, fibre-optic cables and browsers rather than the businesses that would emerge, such as Amazon, Google and Netflix. Government-backed AI infrastructure in the UAE could similarly lower barriers to entry for entrepreneurs who lack the capital to build their own computing facilities, he said. “I think there's going to be so much opportunity in leveraging that infrastructure to build exciting new businesses,” he said. The UAE's willingness to adopt new technologies could make it a testing ground for AI applications. Developing software in line with international regulatory standards could enable entrepreneurs to export their products to Europe, Asia and even the US, Ms Spina said. For the Gulf, importing American computing power could ultimately become the foundation of an export industry of its own.

events.title: New Air India chief seeks to cut $837 million in costs
events.summary: Tewolde Gebremariam joined Air India in September with the task of turning around the struggling carrier. Air India is looking to cut costs by 60 billion rupees (S$837 million) this financial year as its new chief executive outlined initiatives to revive the loss-making airline, sources familiar with the matter said. Key steps announced at a town hall meeting with CEO Tewolde Gebremariam on Nov 25 include the merger of some departments at Air India and its budget unit, starting a dedicated cargo service and introducing holiday packages, said the sources, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. Westbound flights, which generally head to the Middle East and Europe, will be shifted from New Delhi to Mumbai and Bengaluru, the sources said. That should help shorten detours needed to avoid Pakistan’s airspace, which has been closed to Indian carriers since April 2025, when relations between the neighbours deteriorated following a deadly attack in Kashmir. Tewolde, the former CEO of Ethiopian Airlines Group, joined Air India in September with the task of turning around the struggling carrier. He has sought to reduce maintenance costs and is considering folding budget carrier Air India Express into the main group. Air India lost more than 220 billion rupees in the last financial year following a series of challenges including a deadly crash in June 2025, the closure of Pakistani airspace and the war in Iran which disrupted flights and drove up fuel expenses. The weaker Indian rupee has also added to its financial woes, since much of the airline’s costs are in US dollars. Air India did not respond to requests to confirm Tewolde’s comments at the town hall meeting. He also raised the issue of efficiency at the meeting, and asked workers to show more urgency in turning around flights, the people said. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Spirit of Tasmania imposed fuel surcharge despite lower fuel bill: Auditor-general
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Spirit of Tasmania fuel surcharge messaging 'likely to mislead', says auditor-general A fuel surcharge of 15 per cent was charged to Spirit of Tasmania travellers from late March to the end of August. ( Supplied: TT-Line ) Spirit of Tasmania operator TT-Line imposed a 15 per cent fuel surcharge on fares from late March until the end of August, which it said was to recover additional fuel costs associated with the conflict in the Middle East. Tasmania's auditor-general says the messaging around the surcharge was "likely to mislead" because the company was actually spending less on fuel. TT-Line says fuel hedging means figures from last financial year don't tell the full story. Tasmania's auditor-general says messaging about the fuel surcharge slapped on Spirit of Tasmania passengers earlier this year was misleading, as the company was actually spending less on fuel. The assertion has been indirectly rejected by the state-owned ferry operator TT-Line, which has argued its hedging of fuel contracts means the impact of higher prices may appear later. TT-Line announced in late March that it would start imposing a 15 per cent surcharge on Spirit of Tasmania fares as it was "facing an 80 per cent rise in fuel prices" due to conflict in the Middle East. Appearing before the Tasmanian parliament's public accounts committee on Wednesday, auditor-general Martin Thompson said that statement did not tell the full picture. "A reasonable conclusion to be drawn … was that TT-Line was facing an immediate and significant impact from the increases of fuel prices and a levy was initiated to address the immediate impacts," Mr Thompson said. TT-Line said the fuel levy was imposed as the company was facing an 80 per cent increase in its fuel costs. ( Facebook: Spirit of Tasmania ) TT-Line's financial report showed that it had "largely eliminated" the price risk during the period "through prudent use of fuel hedges", the auditor-general said. According to the report, the company spent $59.7 million on marine fuel and oil during the 2025-26 financial year, which includes three months in which the levy was imposed. That is about 20 per cent lower than the $74.9 million it spent on a similar volume of fuel in the 2024-25 financial year, before the Iran-US conflict had started. "Based on this knowledge, we undertook a high level assessment of TT-Line's reporting of the impact of the fuel levy to shareholder ministers and through them to the Parliament," Mr Thompson said. Martin Thompson says it was "never the case" that TT-Line was facing an immediate and significant impact from the rising fuel prices. ( Audit Tasmania ) How did TT-Line save money on fuel? TT-Line chair Ken Kanofski appeared before the same committee in early November, where he explained how the company appeared — at first glance — to have saved money on fuel despite global prices skyrocketing. Prisoners have clothing, bedding and food withheld in 'degrading' regime Tasmania Police name alleged shooter of Sergeant Michael Preshaw How did the Tasmanian government's greyhound racing ban fail? He said it had achieved an "unexpected benefit" as it had gone into the fuel crisis "quite heavily hedged" with its fuel contracts. Fuel hedging is a practice to manage the risk of price swings where TT-Line signs contracts with banks that fix a benchmark price for fuel months before the company purchases it. If the market price rises above that benchmark, the bank pays the difference and if it falls below, TT-Line pays the bank. Ken Kanofski says the impact of the higher fuel prices on TT-Line can't be seen by just looking at the spending from one financial year. ( ABC News: Monty Jacka ) Mr Kanofski told the committee the practice "could easily go against us at some point in the future" and that hedges were currently "expensive" and could end up costing the company. He said other factors also brought down the company's fuel spending in the 2025-26 financial report, including slower sailings and "very low" fuel prices in the eight months before the Iran-US conflict began. Mr Kanofski argued the surcharge and the impact of the hedges play out over different timeframes and could not be easily compared by looking at figures from one financial year. "One of the fundamental problems here with reading the financials, is that the fuel levy and the pricing ... happens over a different timeframe than the hedging outcomes happen," he said.

events.title: US leaves door open to lower Singapore tariff deal even as it proposes 20% levy
events.summary: Singapore and 13 other trading partners of the US have been accused of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions. The US has proposed tariffs of up to 20% on Singapore under Section 301, but the rate could be cut to 10% if a trade deal is reached. The USTR says Singapore’s industrial policies and support for manufacturing create “structural excess capacity and production”, with a report covering 16 trading partners. Singapore says it will keep engaging the US and protect businesses and workers, as the talks could affect trade, jobs and key export sectors. SINGAPORE – The United States has left the door open to a trade deal that could lower tariffs on Singapore goods, even as it proposed a new levy of up to 20% on the Republic and 13 other trading partners. United States Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer offered to consider lowering the proposed rate in a Nov 25 (Washington time) statement, which accused the 14 trading partners of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions. “The Trade Representative further proposes to consider adjusting the tariff rate applied to each good to 10% to account for any commitments in the event that Singapore were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States or conclude other negotiations that are responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies and practices of Singapore,” the Office of the USTR said. Without such a deal, the proposed tariff rate under Section 301 could reach up to 20% and take effect in early 2027. However, the actual burden would be lower than 20%, as the rate will be net of previously announced Section 301 tariffs of 12.5% related to forced labour concerns. The proposal is also subject to a comment and hearing process through January, which could change the outcome. “The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20%, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Singapore, with exemptions for certain goods,” the USTR statement added. The USTR said it will accept requests to appear at the hearings, along with a summary of testimony by Jan 5, 2027. Written comments are due by that same date. USTR will hold hearings about the proposed actions in these investigations on Jan 25, 2027. The US’ concerns are listed and explained at length in a separate 168-page USTR report that follows an investigation the agency started in March. According to the USTR’s investigation report on Singapore’s industrial policies, the specific acts, policies and practices related to structural excess capacity and production include the Singapore Manufacturing 2030 plan and the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 (RIE2030) plan, as well as financial support to the manufacturing sector and firms in the electronics and semiconductors, health, and petrochemicals industries. The report also cited the “e ncouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investments from non-market economies (NMEs), particularly China, which permits further development of structural excess capacity and production, and encouragement of or failure to address imports from NMEs, which enables Chinese firms to offload excess production”. Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) on Nov 26 expressed its disappointment over the new US tariffs, stating that the USTR’s probe leading to the proposed measure fails to take into account the unique structure of the Republic’s open, trade-reliant economy. METI also said that Singapore “will continue to engage the USTR constructively, including to urge the USTR to reconsider its proposed actions on Singapore and to explore ways to reduce the tariff”. However, it is still not clear if Singapore will negotiate an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with the US. Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at Singapore-based independent think-tank Hinrich Foundation, said the ART had not been on the table for either side until now because for Washington, Singapore was that rare country with which it had a trade surplus and an existing bilateral free trade agreement. Now, however, “the US has certainly made clear their interest in negotiating an ART”, she said. She said if the two sides enter talks, the US will likely demand three things: substantial new investments in the US; commitments to curb the flow of “non-market economy” (the US’ code for China) involvement in Singapore-to-US trade; and digital trade commitments that keep Singapore aligned with the US and American companies and platforms. “Singapore will have to decide if these new commitments are worthwhile,” Elms added. In its engagements with Trump administration officials since 2025, Singapore has persistently denied that it enjoys a trade surplus with the US or that its exports to the world’s largest economy stem from any form of excess capacity.

events.title: Emissions fall, but not fast enough to meet climate target
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australia's emissions fall but not fast enough to reach 2035 climate target Australia's greenhouse gas emissions are dropping, but they are falling short of meeting targets. ( ABC News ) Australia's greenhouse gas emissions have fallen by 1.3 per cent in the year to June 2026, a drop of 6.2 million tonnes, according to the annual climate statement released today. Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen was positive about the reduction, but the government's expert advisers say a "formidable" challenge lies ahead to meet climate targets. "The rate of reduction across 2026 was about one and a half times faster than the average over the past decade," Mr Bowen said in the report's foreword. Chris Bowen says the country's showing good progress towards its 2030 target. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Today's reported fall in emissions is smaller than the 7.5 million tonnes (Mt) in the year to March 2026 and the 9.7Mt reported for the year to December 2025. "We need to be reducing emissions by an average of 25 to 30 million tonnes a year," Matt Kean, chair of the Climate Change Authority (CCA), said. This update comes after a recent UN report found the world is set to cross the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius of global warming, a goal that the world signed up for in the 2015 Paris Agreement. "Climate risks are escalating. The World Meteorological Organization found that 2025 was one of the top three warmest years in the observational record, despite the cooling influence of La Niña, and that the past 11 years were the 11 warmest on record," the CCA said. Australia has two legislated emissions targets under the Climate Change Act 2022. They are to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 43 per cent by 2030, and reach net zero by 2050. The government has also committed to a 2035 target of a reduction between 62 and 70 per cent by 2035. Modelling shows the country remains almost on track to meet the 2030 target, but to reach the 2035 goals, cuts to annual emissions would need to increase rapidly. "To achieve the more ambitious 70 per cent end of Australia's 2035 emissions reduction target range, the annual rate of emissions reductions needs to increase to an average of 30Mt CO2-e over the next nine years," the CCA reported. That is almost five times the fall Australia has just managed. But according to Frank Jotzo, professor of environmental and climate change economics at the Australian National University (ANU), Australia was not on track to meet its emissions targets. "It'll take longer than 2030 to get emissions down by the target at 43 per cent," he said. "And getting into the 62 to 70 per cent reduction range, which is targeted for 2035, will be an enormous effort." It was not impossible, but most of Australia's emissions cuts would come from replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy to generate electricity. "Within the expert community, it has been clear and accepted for some time now that 82 per cent renewable share cannot and will not be achieved by 2030," he said. Professor Jotzo said meeting the target would require "phenomenal" growth in wind and solar. He expected this growth eventually, but just not within three or four years. And he said with aging coal-fired power plants making the east coast power grid vulnerable, building more renewables faster had benefits beyond cutting emissions. "Electricity prices will come down with higher renewable energy penetration rates, and for reliability of supply as well," he said Electricity emissions fell 3.6 per cent and renewables supplied a record 45.9 per cent of power in the National Electricity Market (NEM). The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) reported that renewables supplied a record 44.3 per cent of generation on the NEM in the September quarter. "Emissions have come down in electricity, agriculture, industrial processes and stationary energy use," said Anna Malos, a climate policy expert at the Climateworks Centre, an independent research body at Monash University. "Transport emissions have increased slightly — although emissions from petrol vehicles are down as fuel costs drove a record-breaking rise in electric vehicle uptake." Despite record growth in electric vehicles, which now make up close to a quarter of new cars sold, transport emissions rose slightly by 0.1 per cent. But this was due to a rise in road diesel use and domestic aviation emissions that were up 3.1 per cent; petrol use actually fell. "Transport emissions are approaching a turning point, with falling EV prices and growing low-emissions technologies expected to lock in further emissions reductions," the annual climate statement said.

events.title: Australia's only TV shopping network goes into liquidation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts TVSN shut down on November 13. ( Instagram: Sabine Gruchet ) Australia's only TV shopping network has gone into liquidation. It comes after the owners of TVSN failed to find a buyer or new investment. Receivers say a sale of the company's assets is expected to start soon. Australia's only dedicated TV shopping channel has gone into liquidation, highlighting the fraught conditions facing legacy retailers. The 31-year-old TVSN's final show was broadcast earlier this month after owners Direct Group failed to secure new investment or a buyer for the network. Its collapse has left Australian brands that sell everything from buckets to shoes in limbo about unpaid invoices. Some of the brands are also chasing debts from David Jones. "It's a lot of revenue to lose in the space of a couple of weeks, and it's a sign of the retail environment that's not in a good way," TVSN supplier Ben Nothling said. TVSN updated its website after the final show. ( Supplied ) Mark Robinson and Ken Whittngham of Fort Restructuring were appointed as liquidators of the Sydney-based channel. "As is the case with a number of legacy or longstanding retail brands in Australia, attracting new investment or engaging potential buyers is growing increasingly challenging," Mr Robinson said. "An orderly wind-up of the companies' remaining assets is now the only option. Fort will work with the various creditors and associated parties to ensure that occurs as efficiently and expediently as possible." In October, suppliers were informed via email of the network's closing-down sale while it tried to pursue "a sale or recapitalisation of the business". "Due to difficult trading conditions and limited access to the funding required to support stock purchases, customer acquisition, systems and ongoing growth, we have no alternative but to close the business," the email, seen by the ABC, said. The company was chaired by former Myer chief executive Bernie Brookes, who has been contacted for comment. Do you know more about TVSN's collapse or are you a supplier owed cash? Email our journalist on terzon.emilia@abc.net.au or em.terzon@proton.me Brands sent stock to TVSN to hold at its warehouse in Sydney, and the products would then be promoted on television. Customers could make purchases with a phone call or online. Mr Nothling, who owns shoe brand Holster, is owed $32,000 by TVSN, according to invoices seen by the ABC. Ben Nothling doubts he will get much of his money back. ( Supplied: Holster ) "We've been emailing them twice a week," he said. "Nobody has responded — nobody at all. "Then nobody would answer the phones. It was radio silence." Mr Nothling said he was informed late on Wednesday night, after weeks without word, that TVSN had entered receivership early this week. He believed the shoes Holster sent to the Frenchs Forest warehouse were sold off during the closing down sale. "I'm obviously not very happy as I doubt we'll get back much back," he said. Holster is also an unsecured creditor owed $130,000 by department store David Jones, which also just went into voluntary administration. "It's just another kick in the guts. It's even more surreal having two in a row, big ones go down," Mr Nothling said. Kelly Lavery, owner of Strucket, has partnered with TVSN for years. ( Supplied ) Supplier Kelly Lavery said her strainer bucket company Strucket rushed an order to TVSN several months ago for a spring cleaning show and was owed $21,000. "It's just so disheartening. We have partnered with TVSN since 2019," she said. "We paid everything to get it to them, including interstate freight and flights to go on the show. "It's not just about the order they've taken." TVSN would pay for the goods, but suppliers were asked to spruik their products on air, meaning brands also had to fork out for flights and accommodation to Sydney. TVSN would deduct fees from the purchase order for the presenter of the show. Ms Lavery said she had not heard from the company for two months and only knew what was going on based on the channel's Instagram posts. David Jones creditors owed at least $459 million The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff. The liquidators confirmed all employees had been paid their full entitlements and that final orders were expected to be sent to customers by the end of the week. RSM Australia partners Brett Lord and Richard Stone have been appointed as receivers and managers to six entities across the group's 21 different entities.

events.title: Judge declines to issue a long-term ban on taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads critics called propaganda
events.summary: A federal judge has sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded political ads, which critics say were illegal propaganda intended to promote President Donald Trump NEW YORK -- A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington, D.C., said the Democratic National Committee hadn't shown a likelihood to prevail in the case. It had argued the TV spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president’s campaign message just weeks before November’s midterm elections . Her ruling comes after another judge in a similar case in New York also declined a long-term ban on the ads. In her ruling, she noted that a previous temporary restraining order against the ads had been issued when the election was less than a week away. “But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone,” she wrote, adding that the DNC was now claiming the party could be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections or even because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun. “At this juncture and on this record, the court is unpersuaded,” AliKhan wrote. Democrats sued the Trump administration in October after it began airing ads that were paid for at least in part by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract . In court papers, the DNC challenged at least 11 government-created ads that either aired on TV or appeared on Trump administration social media feeds. Some of the ads glorified the president with highlight reels of scenic speeches, promoted his tax cuts and emphasized support for law enforcement. One of them repurposed a clip that had been used by Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, showing him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.” 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Federal officials say 'zero' airborne lead detected after Iowa munitions blast Pennsylvania teen who died in 2020 could become first Gen Z saint A spokesperson for the DNC, Angelo Fernández Hernández, said in a statement that the organization was “disappointed” by the judge’s decision, adding that the DNC “will fight on to put an end to the Trump administration’s attempts to undermine our democracy.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. AliKhan in the earlier temporary restraining order blocked the Trump administration from developing, airing or distributing some of the challenged ads through Nov. 25. In the separate case in New York, the judge blocked a broader collection of the advertisements and required the government to pull three of them from official government websites and social media sites. But in her latest ruling, AliKhan declined to issue a preliminary injunction against the ads. The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they don’t try to help the public benefit from specific government programs, the plaintiffs have argued. Ahead of the ruling, the Justice Department argued in court papers that there was no threat of harm because the government had already ceased using public funds to air the ads and the midterm elections had passed. events.title: Puerto Rico's Supreme Court cancels a key power contract and many wonder what's next
events.summary: Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy, following a contentious legal fight with the private power company SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy following a contentious legal fight with the private power company. The 5-4 ruling of more than 200 pages, made public on Wednesday, plunges the island into further uncertainty as many wonder who will take over from Luma while power outages persist across the U.S. territory and crews continue to repair the grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017. Puerto Rico’s government had sued Luma nearly a year ago, following up on a campaign promise made by Gov. Jenniffer González to cancel the contract. The court awarded one year for officials to figure out their next steps. González said her administration would seek a new company and that transmission and distribution operations would not revert to Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority. She blamed Luma for “constant interruptions" and “unnecessary outages,” asserting they have enough money to provide proper service as she accused them of lacking diligence and driving the cost of electricity in the U.S. territory to a record high. “You have seen the substations on fire,” she said. “They have not yet been able to explain why.” As the governor spoke, a federal control board that oversees the island's finances issued a statement saying its immediate concern is the continuity of service. “The Puerto Rican government's decision to terminate the contract creates enormous uncertainty at a time when the people and businesses of Puerto Rico look for stability,” the board said, noting that there's no “clear plan or successor company in place.” González rejected those concerns: “There will be no chaos." Puerto Rico's Association of Industries said it was worried that the ruling could erode the confidence of private investors, while dissenting judges voiced their concerns in sharply worded decisions. Judge Rafael L. Martínez Torres warned that “collateral consequences” of ending the contract “had to be considered, given their potential monumental impact.” Judge Ángel Colón Pérez asserted that the ruling in favor of the cancellation stemmed from “an excessive eagerness to satisfy a capricious request from the leader currently in power," an apparent reference to the governor. One judge referenced and rejected recent allegations that Supreme Court judges were pressured or swayed. "We do not bow to external pressures, we do not yield to intimidation, nor do we allow smear campaigns to influence the exercise of our judicial function," wrote Judge Roberto Feliberti Cintrón, who was part of the majority vote. “Our obligation is to the Law, Justice, the People, and our conscience.” 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Federal officials say 'zero' airborne lead detected after Iowa munitions blast Pennsylvania teen who died in 2020 could become first Gen Z saint Luma also commented on the allegations. "In light of the serious allegations that have been raised publicly regarding attempts to influence the Court, we reiterate our call for an immediate, rigorous, and transparent investigation,” it said. Puerto Rico’s government had awarded a multimillion-dollar contract to Luma, which took over the transmission and distribution of power on the island in June 2021. It inherited infrastructure that was crumbling after decades of neglect and mismanagement under Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority. The company said in a statement Wednesday that it disagrees with the court’s decision but will respect the judicial process and is “carefully evaluating all available legal alternatives.” “We remain concerned about the potential impact of this decision on ongoing efforts to strengthen and modernize Puerto Rico’s electric grid,” Luma said. “This matter goes beyond a contractual dispute. It has significant implications for the provision of an essential electric service, public safety, and Puerto Rico’s energy future.” Luma is a consortium made up of Calgary, Alberta-based Atco and Quanta Services Inc. of Houston. When the lawsuit was filed in December 2025, González said Luma had nearly $11 billion in federal funds at its disposal to rebuild the grid, but that it has only been able to recover some $550 million in reimbursements from the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency. When the lawsuit was filed, she said, “Despite the operator’s expectations and representations, the electrical system has not improved with the speed, consistency or effectiveness that Puerto Rico deserves and that LUMA promised and lied to us about.” Puerto Rico’s government has two main agreements with Luma: one for operation and maintenance, and a supplemental deal that was needed because the state-owned Electric Power Authority had not yet completed a debt restructuring process.

events.title: After 3 decades, Essence Music Festival bidding farewell to New Orleans
events.summary: A fixture in New Orleans for over 30 years is leaving the Big Easy The Essence Festival of Culture, a fixture in New Orleans that has celebrated Black American culture for more than 30 years, is leaving the Big Easy. Festival organizers and Essence Communications, which founded the annual event, announced Tuesday across their social media platforms that Essence Fest will relocate next year. The statement did not give a reason for the decision or mention where the festival was moving to. It mostly expressed gratitude to the city and its residents for helping grow the event over the years. “You didn't simply host us. You embraced us,” the statement said. “And in doing so, you helped shape one of the most beautiful celebrations of Black culture in the world.” The multiday festival takes place around the Fourth of July weekend and draws major musical acts. Usher, Megan Thee Stallion and Janet Jackson are among the many performers who have headlined in recent years. On the same day of the Essence announcement, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno teased that on Dec. 9 the city will announce details about a new “world-class” festival dedicated to Black American culture. “Ultimately, we are working to team up with some of this country’s top Black producers to essentially bring in a festival that 1) realizes how important it is to be in the city of New Orleans and that the city of New Orleans itself is a draw,” Moreno said in a social media video. “We need to make sure that there’s widespread benefit for our local businesses, particularly our local Black businesses.” The Essence Festival was launched in 1995 as the Essence Music Festival when Essence magazine staged a concert event in New Orleans to mark the publication's 25th anniversary. The magazine was acquired by Time Inc. in the early 2000s before becoming Black-owned again in 2018 when the founder of Sundial Brands purchased it. It's part of Essence Communications, a media company that includes digital and video content. The festival has also become a political draw with panels focused on politics and voter mobilization. Politicians, both Black and white, who are in the middle of big campaigns have made Essence Fest a stop. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris spoke there in 2024 during the presidential campaign. events.title: Anthropic's first data centre in Australia given environmental approval
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government gives environmental green light to Western Downs Digital Park The concept model of a large-scale data centre project proposed for the Western Downs. ( Supplied: Urbis ) National EPA has determined the proposed Western Downs Digital Park needs no further federal environmental assessment. It found the project was unlikely to have a significant impact on environmental matters. The project is still subject to council and state approval. An Anthropic-backed $32 billion proposed data centre in Queensland has been granted environmental approval by the federal government. The National Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) determined the proposed Western Downs Digital Park, west of Brisbane, was "unlikely to have a significant impact on matters of national environmental significance". The decision came after just two months, when the average length of the federal approvals in Queensland is more than three years, according a Queensland Productivity Commission report released this week. A federal government spokesperson said it made a "quick decision" because of the project's thoughtful design and site selection. "After a careful examination, the National EPA has determined that a new data centre development near Dalby, Queensland, does not require further federal environmental assessment," the spokesperson said. Murray Watt is the minister for the environment and water. ( Supplied: Department of Premier and Cabinet ) The government spokesperson said the project was anticipated to create thousands of jobs and stimulate the state's economy. The proposed hyper-scale data centre is pitched for a cattle feedlot 250 kilometres west of Brisbane, on Queensland's Western Downs. The proposed data centre site is currently the Wambo feedlot, near Dalby. ( ABC Rural: Brandon Long ) It is currently the largest proposed in Australia, with a total energy capacity roughly equivalent to a quarter of Queensland's daily electricity use. There were no public comments made during the referral submission phase, the spokesperson said. AI giant Anthropic signed a deal in September on the data centre hub and hoped to start using it in 2027. Developer Zerra DC said it was pleased with the federal government's decision. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) The data centre developer, Zerra DC, said it welcomed the decision. "The Western Downs was selected thoughtfully and strategically, with the site chosen to minimise impacts on the local community and environment while taking advantage of the region's established energy and industrial strengths, including its proximity to major high-voltage infrastructure at Braemar," a spokesperson said. "We are developing a long-term benefits framework … with priorities including local infrastructure, digital learning, local jobs and business opportunities, and investment in community-led projects." The development is still subject to council and state approval. The Queensland government is set to take over the approvals for data centres, with the exception of the Western Downs Digital Park, according to the council. Last week, a Climate Council report identified the Western Downs Digital Park as the top potential polluter in the data centre industry, due to its large electricity demand. The report found if the hyper-scale project did not use renewable energy to meet its energy demand, it would release the equivalent greenhouse gas emissions of 3 million cars a year by 2035. A community action group has formed in Dalby in protest against the speed of the data centre's development. Protesters gathered outside an economic forum in Dalby about the proposed data centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Angela Prenzler, from the Western Downs Says Pause group, said she believed the data centre was being fast-tracked at all levels. "It's very disappointing because, even from a federal government perspective, the data centre seems to be protected.
