events.title: Guitar wars - the transatlantic battle over the Stratocaster
events.summary: The Fender Stratocaster is widely considered to be the best-known shape in electric guitars Published 26 November 2026, 00:01 GMT Hans Thomann leads the way through his music store in central Germany to the large electric guitar department, where the walls are hung with hundreds of instruments. Brands on show include famous names Fender and Gibson, plus Harley Benton. The latter is a low-price range of guitars owned by the family-run company that Thomann leads – Thomann, one of the world's largest online retailers of musical instruments. The shop, together with warehouses and offices, are at the company's headquarters in the tiny village of Treppendorf in rural Upper Franconia, in Bavaria. The business was founded by Thomann's father, Hans Thomann Senior, in 1954. In one corner of the store, a young man is trying out a Fender Stratocaster, one of the world's most iconic electric guitars. Designed in the US in the early 1950's, the "Strat" became the instrument of choice for many famous rock and pop musicians, such as Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Buddy Holly. Hendrix famously set one on fire at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967, and his performances helped make the guitar a symbol of modern rock music. Hans Thomann says that Fender's letter came as a big surprise These days, the Stratocaster is very much on Hans Thomann's mind, because it's the subject of an intense copyright dispute. When the guitar was first made, California-based Fender did not trademark the body shape. So, since the 1960s Strat-shaped guitars have been made and sold around the world by countless manufacturers. The shape is so ubiquitous that many musicians consider it to be a generic design. But since March of this year, Fender has begun a new campaign to defend its right to the guitar's sinuous shape. It follows a decision by a court in Düsseldorf last December which granted Fender copyright protection , external of the Stratocaster design in Germany. The defendant, Chinese seller Yiwu Philharmonic Musical Instruments, did not appear. The Düsseldorf court accepted Fender's arguments and ruled in its favour. According to German law the court makes its decision based on the facts presented by the plaintiff if the defendant doesn't raise objections. The ruling said that Fender's design for the Stratocaster was "an outstanding, free creative achievement" that "clearly reflects the personality of its author". It described the guitar as "a body without edges" with "soft curves that evoke associations with the female torso consisting of hips, waist and arms". On its website, Fender announced in March , external the decision created "enforceable rights" against any guitars using the Strat body shape, that are manufactured, sold or distributed into Germany or other EU countries, "regardless of where those guitars are produced". Fender began to send out cease and desist letters to dozens of retailers and manufacturers, both large and small, asking them to stop making and selling Strat lookalikes heading for Europe. One of these letters, seen by the BBC, said Fender "insists that you immediately stop manufacturing, marketing, selling and producing the infringing products". The letter also demanded that companies recall and destroy the guitars. Jimi Hendrix helped to make the Fender Stratocaster famous The move caused an outcry in the guitar world, among manufacturers and musicians. "Time to boycott Fender," one person wrote on the Facebook page of the boutique US guitar maker, LSL Instruments. Thomann received a cease-and-desist letter shortly after a visit to Treppendorf in March by Fender's chief executive Bud Cole. "We remember the meeting as a very positive and constructive exchange," says Thomann. "At the time we had no indication that Fender was considering legal action." The letter, he says, came as a shock. "For more than 70 years, we have carried Fender instruments with great appreciation for the brand and many of us are Fender players ourselves. We were therefore surprised and disappointed by Fender's recent actions." In 2025, Thomann sold over 112,000 Strat-style guitars, including more than 16,000 made by Fender and Fender subsidiary brand Squier. "As a retailer, we want to continue offering our customers everything that is available in the world of guitars," adds Thomann. "We would have welcomed to the opportunity to discuss the matter openly before receiving a formal legal demand for such extreme action." Thomann has just one physical shop, but sells online around the world In June, Thomann the company started legal action against Fender, filing an "action of non-infringement" that said that Fender does not have a valid copyright claim to the Stat shape. Thomann says that the Düsseldorf ruling was simply a default judgement based on missed deadlines and didn't represent a "comprehensive review of the legal claims".

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Approval for ‘Starmind’ granted but it’s a long way from the launchpad, or making sense FCC proposes 'tit-for-tat' restrictions on foreign satellite operators 2 days ago BepiColombo takes the long way around Mercury after software glitch 2 days ago Trump says he won't allow US companies to build datacenters abroad 3 days ago Software issues have even reached Mercury as BepiColombo probe arrives in uncertain state 3 days ago Nvidia’s journey to forge the one CPU SKU to rule them all 5 days ago The United States Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s plan to launch a million datacenter satellites. The regulator on Wednesday published an order [PDF] allowing SpaceX to operate a “Non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellation of 1,000,000 satellites deployed into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.” The order requires SpaceX to ensure its satellites’ radios don’t interfere with US government systems which use the 28.6-29.1 GHz band and requires the company to stick to operating within the parameters it files with the International Telecommunications Union. SpaceX asked the FCC to waive its rule requiring the atmospheric disposal of dead satellites orbiting at 2,000 km or less. Elon Musk’s company asked for “flexibility to dispose satellites operating above 600 km altitude into Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.” The FCC found SpaceX did not provide enough information to let it assess if proposed “alternative disposal methods” are compliant with regulations, so deferred its decision on the waiver request. “SpaceX must file an application for modification of this authorization and provide sufficient justification for any requested waiver(s) of the Commission’s rules,” the order states. The company must also file twice-yearly reports about “conjunction events” – moments when its satellites get dangerously close to each other, or other orbiters. Whether orbiting datacenters are feasible, make sense, or will ever pay for themselves, remain open questions. Analyst firm Gartner has described the idea as “ peak insanity .” Google thinks orbiting datacenters become viable if launch costs fall to $200/kg, which would mean SpaceX needs to launch its massive Starship 1,800 times. SpaceX’s assumptions assume near-daily launches, far better than its current cadence of a launch every three days or so. Fundamental networking research must also come to fruition to handle the amount of traffic large constellations of orbiting datacenters will create. Terrestrial manufacturing capacity will also need to increase to build all those satellites. Elon Musk’s companies and Intel have planned a giant new fab to make that possible, without explaining how the supply chains behind chip manufacturing will scale to make it feasible. That's a notable omission given that semiconductor supply chains are already extremely strained. Approval for SpaceX is therefore nice but in no way a roadmap to a million datacenter satellites. Google, ironically, is a little further along than SpaceX, having launched a test sat in October and last week announcing it has hired Amazon founder Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch a larger satellite carrying the equivalent of a full datacenter rack in early 2029. Down on Earth, meanwhile, scientists trying to observe the universe continue to bemoan the obstructions caused by mega-constellations of broadband-beaming satellites. Proposals from across the USA, China, Europe and India currently call for around 100,000 satellites. SpaceX’s proposed million orbiters could run workloads which help us to understand the mysteries of the universe while also making them hard to see from down here.

events.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
events.summary: S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices. Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement . The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale. Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral. In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported . A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees. events.title: Plan for 200ha kelp farm off NSW coast sparks debate
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Plan for commercial kelp farm near Eden debated at public hearing Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry The proposed farm would see Golden Kelp grown on underwater lines, like in this photo. ( Supplied: Jo Lane ) NSW's Independent Planning Commission has held public hearings about a proposal to build the state's first commercial offshore kelp farm. More than 50 people spoke for and against the 200-hectare project south of Eden. A decision about whether the State Significant Development should be approved is now with the commission. Strong debate continues over whether a small bay south of Eden should host NSW's first commercial kelp farm. The 200-hectare offshore project at Disaster Bay, off Greenglade Beach in Wonboyn, was conditionally approved by the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) last month. But because the State Significant Development received more than 200 objections, the application was referred for determination to the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC). More than 50 people voiced their views at hearings held on Tuesday and Wednesday at the Seahorse Inn Hotel. Disaster Bay, south of Eden on the NSW south coast. ( Supplied: AusKelp ) Among those to speak was Wonboyn resident and Melbourne University emeritus professor in land administration, Ian Williamson. He told the IPC that while he did support kelp farming, he did not approve of the proposed location. "The nature, the natural character, the isolation and the scientific qualities of this location are major environmental and community assets. Ian Williamson has lived in Wonboyn for 20 years and his home overlooks Disaster Bay. ( ABC News: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro ) "Why should this unique and exceptional marine environment bear the additional uncertainty and risk associated with establishing a new commercial industry untested at scale?" But for South Coast Sea Urchins co-founder Ryan Morris, the project would be a chance to keep staff in the area year-round, because they could work on the kelp farm outside of the sea urchin harvesting season. "We struggle to get the right amount of staff to process products, and it's only because it's a seasonal product that we have problems," he said. The kelp farm is proposed for the south end of the bay, about one kilometre offshore. ( ABC News: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro ) "If we could retain our staff throughout the whole season, we'd manage to hold onto them. "In our respect, from an economic point of view, we can only see benefits to this farm going forward." The Eden-1 Kelp Aquaculture Farm proposal by Auskelp involves a 200-hectare lease area about one kilometre offshore. When fully operational, an ocean rig with longlines sitting about one metre below the surface would cover an area of about 100 hectares. Four yellow navigation buoys would be located on each corner of the lease, and 260 partially submerged floats would be attached to the rig. The project would be built in three stages: 25 hectares in phase one, 75 in phase two, and a maximum of 100 hectares in phase three. The proposal also includes a hatchery at Eden and a processing facility in Edrom, but they would need to go through separate approval processes. According to the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure's assessment report, golden kelp does not require any input. This photo shows what an ocean rig would look like, with golden kelp growing on dropper lines that reach down 8 to 10 metres. ( Supplied: Auskelp ) It said that harvested kelp could be sold for food, supplements, bio-stimulants and animal feed. The report said that if approved, Eden-1 would be NSW's first active commercial offshore seaweed farm, and one of the first in the world to grow Ecklonia radiata (golden kelp), which is a native species. It is estimated the development would cost $8,783,000, create up to 10 jobs during construction and 18 once operating. Greenglade Beach, where the farm is proposed, sits between the Nadgee Nature Reserve and Ben Boyd National Park. ( ABC News: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro ) According to the assessment report, the development application and the environmental impact statement were put on public exhibition in April and May this year. More than half of the 208 unique public submissions objecting to the proposal were from people living interstate, with the majority from Victoria. The proposal was sent to the NSW Independent Planning Commision after receiving 208 unique objections during the public consultation phase. ( ABC News: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro ) Lyn Pool owns property in Wonboyn and splits her time between there and Melbourne.

events.summary: Lenders paused billions in funding linked to Chinese hyperscalers ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent , Bloomberg reported, as new US restrictions on AI chip exports threatened to stall Asia’s data center buildout. The Nvidia CEO’s affair with a Singapore-based executive intensified concerns that advanced chips were being funneled to mainland firms. Washington announced last week that companies in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil require a government license to purchase US chips, while data centers already leasing compute to Chinese firms have 90 days to secure a separate license. events.title: Cancelled flight forces man to drive 1,000km to 'lifesaving' appointment
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts WA man drives 1,000km to make medical appointment after flight cancellation John Barnes had an arduous journey to medical care after a flight cancellation. ( ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio ) A man in WA's north was forced to drive more than 1,000km to make a "lifesaving" medical appointment. Airnorth cancelled John Barnes's flight to Perth, meaning he had to drive to Broome to get to hospital the next day. The local shire president says the community is losing faith in Airnorth and that the WA government needs to step in. A West Australian man was forced to drive more than 1,000 kilometres to make a "lifesaving" medical appointment after his commercial flight was cancelled earlier this month. Wyndham resident John Barnes was due to fly from Kununurra in the remote Kimberley region to Perth on November 11, but Airnorth cancelled his flight at the last minute. Instead, Mr Barnes embarked on a 1,000km, 11-hour drive to Broome to catch a flight to Perth the next day. Mr Barnes said it was a family effort just to get to Broome, with his wife and brother-in-law taking turns driving throughout the night. "I take things in my stride, and I like challenges, but that's just not a fair challenge," he said. John Barnes prepares to fly to Perth from Broome after driving over 1,000km overnight. ( Supplied: John Barnes ) Mr Barnes said he made it to Royal Perth Hospital just in time for his appointment. He has suffered from gallstones and sepsis in recent months. As a result, Mr Barnes said he could not risk rescheduling his medical review to the following week. "I'm basically a time bomb waiting to go off," he said. "If another gallstone goes where it shouldn't … they've saved my life once, and I don't exactly need that to happen again." John Barnes says he almost missed a "lifesaving" medical appointment due to a flight cancellation in Western Australia's north. ( ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio ) Mr Barnes said he understood flight cancellations happened, but the regularity in the East Kimberley was unsettling. "I felt really let down. It took the mat from underneath my feet," he said. Kununurra resident Sharon D'Aietti said she factored flight unreliability into her travel planning. "We always go [to Perth] at least a day in advance just to be sure we can take other [onward] flights … sometimes two days in advance," she said. Ms D'Aietti said her parents visited her in Kununurra earlier this year but were shocked by the cost of flying to the Kimberley region. When booking, a flight from Darwin to Broome that stopped in Kununurra cost about $500; the Broome to Kununurra leg alone cost nearly $1,000. Sharon D'Aietti says expensive and unreliable flights are taking a toll on her young family. ( ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio ) "It's half of the kilometres … but costs double the money," Ms D'Aietti said. "It was the same plane. The same flight that is stopping here [in Kununurra]. "So why would you add $500 to the price? It just didn't make sense to me." The WA government has extended a scheme to cap airfares for regional residents to Perth until 2031. Flight delays and cancellations at the East Kimberley Regional Airport in Kununurra have had an impact on residents. ( ABC Kimberley: Rebecca Nadge ) But Ms D'Aietti said in Kununurra people were "limited on the flights you can get," with residents still forced to buy full-price fares for specific travel dates. She said expensive fares and cancellations were putting her and other families in the East Kimberley under strain. "We love the place," Ms D'Aietti said. "But I understand why people don't want to come and don't want to live here." Airnorth has a monopoly on flights to and from Kununurra, after rival airline Nexus halted services last year . Shire of Wyndham East Kimberley president David Menzel said flights were crucial for the region's development. "Livability, retention of staff, attracting new staff … it's near impossible if you're this far from anywhere and people haven't got confidence in the air service," he said. "People are just losing confidence in the air service we've got. "It feels like we're at the end of the line and get the leftovers." David Menzel says more competition and government support are needed to rectify unreliable air travel in WA's north. ( ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic ) Cr Menzel said he hoped to restart conversations with carriers and the government to find better solutions. "The market is broken, really," he said. Airnorth was contacted for comment.

events.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
events.summary: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading. The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower. The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks. Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower. The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly. Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact. The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy. The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs. But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry. Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away Published 1 day ago Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres. Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off. "It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management. Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year. The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday. events.title: Macy's Thanksgiving parade postponed for the first time in the event's history
events.summary: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in the event's history, the retailer confirmed Wednesday. Why it matters: Macy's was expected to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables — but an impending nor'easter will keep its iconic giant balloons from flying on the holiday. What they're saying: "The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's told NBC on Wednesday. "Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year," Macy's said. The parade has been pushed back to Saturday. NBC will air last year's parade during the allocated Thanksgiving time slot. What we're watching: It's unclear if any scheduled performers will be unable to participate following the postponement, but thousands are involved in the parade each year. Saturday's forecast currently shows mostly sunny conditions and a high of 55 degrees, according to the National Weather Service . Driving the news: A large storm bringing mostly rain and wind to the East Coast could disrupt travel plans, holiday parades and more this Thanksgiving, per projections from AccuWeather. High winds could also cause widespread sporadic power outages across the region, disrupting holiday meal preparations. The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning for Manhattan on Wednesday morning, with sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph and gusts of up to 55 mph forecast for Thursday. How it works: Large balloons can't fly when sustained winds exceed 23 mph or wind gusts exceed 34 mph, per rules announced by former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani in 1998. The NYPD has ultimate authority over whether balloons should fly. Worth noting: The parade set an all-time viewership record in 2025, with an estimated 34.3 million people watching across NBC and the company's Peacock streaming service. Flashback: Officials have only grounded all the giant character balloons in the parade once before, in 1971, because of the weather. In 1997, strong winds pushed a Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost, critically injuring a spectator. That incident prompted the overhaul of the city's safety regulations. In 2019, the parade's giant balloons flew close to the ground because of the weather. Balloonfest at MetLife Stadium on November 07, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Photo: Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images for Macy's Inc. events.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
events.summary: SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space. The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Musk thanked Carr in a post on X , writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent. SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit. The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document . SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink. The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation. events.title: Here’s where you can save (a little) on the Ocarina of Time remake
events.summary: The Nintendo Switch 2 remake delivers a complete graphical overhaul and numerous quality-of-life updates to the ‘98 classic. | Image: Nintendo A lot of people have The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2 on their holiday wishlist. In case you haven’t bought it yet, I wanted to share some small but welcome deals happening on the physical and digital versions of the game. Costco members can currently grab the cartridge edition for $62.99, down from its regular price of $69.99 (it’s the only retailer currently discounting the physical version). Both Amazon and Costco are also selling the digital version for $54.99, a small $5 discount. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Where to Buy: $59.99 $54.99 at Amazon (Digital) $69.99 $62.99 at Costco (Physical) Ocarina of Time is one of Nintendo’s most groundbreaking titles, having served as its first 3D Zelda game when it launched in 1998. Parts of the original game haven’t aged particularly well — namely some dungeon design and the game’s tricky 3D navigation, since there was only one analog stick at the time — which makes it tough for some to enjoy going back to play the N64 version. Thankfully, the Switch 2 remake introduces several fixes, a host of quality-of-life improvements, and, of course, some lovely visuals that make it a graphics powerhouse by today’s standards. If you go the digital route, a recent Switch 2 update lets you gift games to players in your family group. It doesn’t have to be your actual family, either, just up to eight people you designate as part of your group. The digital game will then appear gift-wrapped on their homescreen. The bill, which introduces a 30% minimum tax on discretionary trusts from July 1, 2028, passed the Senate this week, with six government amendments . events.title: "The flashing red lights couldn't be brighter": Democrats demand new restrictions on AI
events.summary: Prominent Democrats are calling for new restrictions on AI development following Axios reporting that employees at OpenAI and Anthropic increasingly fear their most powerful models cannot be safely released. Why it matters: The political debate over AI is expanding beyond the economic consequences of the technology to a more existential question: whether companies should be allowed to build systems they may not be able to control. The issue is gaining traction among Democratic leaders ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D-Md.), a potential 2028 contender, outlined a playbook for AI regulations in an interview with "The Axios Show," noting that voters hate the technology because they fear losing control . Driving the news: Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called for immediate action: "The people inside AI companies are sounding the alarm ," Kelly said. "We built protections for nuclear weapons and other dangerous technologies, so why are we waiting with AI? We need safeguards and independent examiners in these companies, now." "It is absolutely indefensible to say 'we will take this up next year' when the risks are imminent and the alarm is nearly universal," Schatz said. "The flashing red lights couldn't be brighter, and yet big tech refuses stop," Van Hollen said. "Inaction is not an option. Congress must step up." Sanders went further, calling for a halt to advanced AI development : "The humans who are creating AI fear it could soon escape their own control," Sanders said. "Congress must act and pause advanced AI development NOW." Catch up quick: More than two dozen sources familiar with internal debates at OpenAI and Anthropic told Axios that recent breakthroughs in AI capabilities have raised questions about whether future frontier models can be safely released. Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some believe the problem is a technical one that's fixable. Others believe companies should go a step further and stop training new models entirely. The intrigue: As politicians debate how to ensure humanity retains control over AI, top industry executives are embroiled in a separate debate over how much autonomy humans should voluntarily cede to the technology as these systems become increasingly capable. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei personally pushed back Wednesday on a separate Axios story about views within the company that humanity will inevitably surrender some autonomy to superintelligent AI systems. "No, I do not believe that we should 'surrender human free will' to AI systems, and it's absurd to suggest that I do," Amodei said on X . Amodei argued that AI must be governed by legitimate democratic processes. Between the lines: Amodei's essay acknowledged room for nuance, highlighting that his views on human agency are mixed in specific instances where it could make sense for highly powerful AI systems to step in, like AI driving a car or designing a cancer drug. Both Anthropic and OpenAI have acknowledged safety challenges and indicated a willingness to slow aspects of AI development or deployment. What to watch: Whether concerns about losing control of AI become a defining issue in the Democratic presidential primary — and whether more lawmakers embrace restrictions on AI development itself, rather than just its deployment. The bottom line: A debate that has consumed the people building the world's most powerful AI systems is spilling into national politics.

events.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
events.summary: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage. The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees . Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans. While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page. Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September. The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs. events.title: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for applicability of truth in lending and consumer leasing rules for consumer credit and lease transactions
events.summary: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing). By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations. Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan. events.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
events.summary: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia. Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace. “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.” The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics. “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’” Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.” Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer. “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.” In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company. events.title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America
events.summary: Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding new life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com . The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place. According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, iSeeCars.com found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average. Karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com, told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue. Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer said. “The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he said, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP. The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year. “The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer said. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.” Brauer said that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again. “When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he said. China will face the highest tariff rates, with the proposed 20 per cent excess-capacity levies being in addition to the roughly 25 per cent duties imposed during US President Donald Trump's first term. events.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.” “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.” The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.” But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power. Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software. Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.” Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research. In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.” “As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote. The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control. Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations. In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently. “Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought
events.summary: American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems. The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A new index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23. It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020. However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted. Five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords. The report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers , targeted more than 100 water systems , with incidents reported across at least 12 states , and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers . According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17. Additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. A CISA advisory from July describes this technique: The authoring agencies observed Iranian-affiliated APT actors using several foreign-based IP addresses to access internet-facing PLCs manufactured by Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and potentially other manufactured PLCs [ T0883 ]. The actors used leased, third-party hosted infrastructure and manufacturers’ PLC programming software to connect to misconfigured victim PLCs. Inbound malicious traffic has been observed targeting PLC devices on the following ports: 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, as well as targeting modems on port 22. These cellular modems, often installed by third-party contractors, frequently aren’t documented. Unsurprisingly, the top recommendation for water utilities is to find every cellular modem in the environment, including those installed by contractors, make sure they aren’t exposed to the open internet, and put a gateway with multifactor authentication (MFA) in front of them to stop would-be intruders from gaining access via the modem and controller combo. “Water utilities are spending time and money fixing the vulnerabilities they're told to worry about,” Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala said in a statement. “Meanwhile, attackers are getting in through equipment nobody knew was connected or passwords nobody bothered to change.” ®

events.title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
events.summary: A scientist tests generic drugs at the Connecticut-based lab Valisure. Tonje Thielesen for ProPublica The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply. About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate. Read More Look Up Where Your Generic Prescription Drugs Were Made Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study. The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for years looked the other way. “All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told ProPublica. A ProPublica investigation last year found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based” approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety, effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards. ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to create Rx Inspector , a first-of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made. Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs, the agency only tested one manufacturer . All but one passed every test. The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University, said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.” In February, senators also introduced a bill targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because of similar public concerns. In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further action is needed.” Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of Defense. “It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.” ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise their effectiveness. “I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so much growing energy behind that.” The post FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Anthropic CEO pushes back on Axios reporting on AI and free will
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, pushing back on Axios' reporting about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives. Why it matters: This is Amodei's most significant public remarks since the company went public last week. What he's saying: "We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," Amodei said. Amodei distinguished between handing over governance to AI, which he opposes, and automating specific tasks, on which he holds more nuanced views. He said his view is mixed on specific instances like "AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end" where "it is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives" if AI systems are allowed more agency. He also said it may make sense to slow or stop certain AI deployments to mitigate job disruption and limit AI's ability to autonomously develop more powerful systems. The big picture: The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday. The intrigue: Amodei also took aim at rival AI executives, accusing them of engaging in "vibes-based commercial and political positioning" by championing human agency without meaningfully differentiating their products. Those executives, he said, "repeat slogans like 'human control and agency,' or 'AI should be just a tool,' without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans."

events.title: House Democrats chart path on trading bans
events.summary: Democrats may ban members from using prediction markets as part of a measure governing the House — then vote on standalone legislation that would prevent elected officials from trading individual stocks and most cryptocurrencies, Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., told Semafor. “That’s my sense of where things are headed,” Magaziner said, though he noted “no decisions have been made yet.” The Rhode Island Democrat sponsors the bipartisan stock trading ban he says leaders “are working off” as they prepare for the next Congress. “Certainly one of the messages that members on both sides are taking from the election is that the voters are really fed up with the corruption that they see in Washington,” Magaziner said. Incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries promised earlier this week that “one of the first things that we’ll do in the new Congress is to move to ban members of Congress from trading stock.” Democrats “have to clean up the mess … in our own House,” he said. Magaziner said he is “quite confident” the House can enact the prediction markets ban, which is already in force in the Senate, as part of their rules package in the new Congress. But “it is probably not possible” to include the stock trading ban, he said, because House rules can’t keep members’ spouses from trading or force them to divest. “It’s possible that we could try to do a slimmed down version of it in the rule,” said Magaziner, whose proposal would apply to most cryptocurrencies as well. “But either way, whether we do that or not, we also need to pass a bill so that we can get a full ban in place.” Members are “still working through” whether to divide that bill into individual ones that apply to the different branches of government, Magaziner said, but he insisted that either way Democrats “will still likely move all of the separate bills together … quickly in the new session.”

events.title: US gives SpaceX approval for data centres in space
events.summary: The US has given regulatory approval to SpaceX to eventually put data centres in space. According to the Federal Communications Commission, this is the first authorisation for such a project, as demands from AI have caused an increase in the need for data centres . "The FCC is granting SpaceX authorisation to deploy 1,000,000 orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth," it said. Concerns about the environmental impact, noise and electricity consumption of data centres have risen in recent years, and governments at state and local level have enacted rules to slow down construction. https://t.co/rZhstPYBzs pic.twitter.com/RCsle086L3 — FCC (@FCC) November 25, 2026 FCC chair Brendan Carr highlighted the work under way to eventually put data centres in space. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," he said. But the announcement does not mean it willhappen straight away. Researchers and scientists are still in the early stages of working out how such an endeavour might be possible. In early October, Google launched Project Suncatcher into orbit after several years of development to test the feasibility. The company included its AI hardware to asses that idea on board the Transporter-18 SpaceX mission. Part of the space test involved seeing if the company's technology could generate enough computing power in space to answer basic AI queries. “In low-Earth orbit, satellites can access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth,” the technology company said. It added that if successful, all concerns about data centres might be nullified. “It could be possible to link together multiple constellations of satellites, allowing them to manage larger AI workloads while in orbit.” Earlier this year during a discussion at the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Davos, Switzerland, technology tycoon and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk spoke about putting AI infrastructure in orbit. “There's so much room in space, and it's enormous what you can scale to,” he said. “I think, ultimately, you can have hundreds of terawatts in the air.” Experts have warned, however, that while the idea of data centres in space might look good on paper, there are a lot of challenges that need to be overcome. Speaking at the Semafor World Economy Summit in April, Ariel Ekblaw , founder and chief executive of non-profit space architecture lab the Aurelia Institute, said some of the more aggressive timelines for making space data centres a reality are not realistic. She pointed out that space is far colder than most people realise, and that alone means that “it is not an advantageous arena to deploy a really hot little volcano of a bunch of computers in”. Ms Ekblaw added that the climate issue was only one of several engineering challenges that come with the territory of orbital data centres. The radiation of space, she said, would be problematic, along with the need for data centres on Earth to upgrade their CPUs, GPUs and other technology. “There's the fact that if you want to swap your chips out from Nvidia every six months, now you have to go all the way to space to do it, so that's not a trivial concern,” she said.

events.title: US approves Musk's plan for space-based data centres
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Trump administration backs Musk's plan for space-based data centres Elon Musk has won backing from the Trump administration for his plan for data centres in space. ( Reuters: Adrees Latif ) The US's Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for data centres in space. The company says solar-powered satellites could help reduce environmental costs associated with the technology. SpaceX will need to launch 10 per cent of its satellites by November 2033. The Federal Communications Commission will authorise Elon Musk's SpaceX to deploy a constellation of 1 million satellites for data centres in space. SpaceX earlier this year sought permission to launch up to 1 million orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth. The FCC said it was approving the SpaceX "Starmind" constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing. Under the licence, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10 per cent of the maximum number — or 100,000 — no later than November 2035 and deploy 50 per cent by November 2038, the FCC said. Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production around mid-2027. Approving the application will permit SpaceX "to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence", the FCC added. Data centres are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power. "By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centres," SpaceX told the FCC. It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility. SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it began deployment of that system. The growing network currently has a little more than 11,000 satellites in space. Amazon's rival satellite unit, Leo, and others have criticised the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites and that it could take centuries to do so. FCC chair Brendan Carr rejected that criticism in March. "Amazon should focus on getting Amazon's house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is," Mr Carr said. events.title: US-led group reaches deal to acquire Lukoil's global assets
events.summary: A US-led consortium has agreed a deal with Lukoil to acquire the sanctioned Russian company's global energy assets. The consortium, led by US billionaire Todd Boehly 's Eldridge, would swap Lukoil securities for its international assets, it said in a news release on Wednesday. The group includes the US International Development Finance Corporation, UAE-based Catena Investment Holding, and Xtellus Partners. The US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (Ofac) is expected to review and rubber-stamp the deal. The Treasury Department placed sanctions on Lukoil in October 2025 . “Given President [Vladimir] Putin’s refusal to end this senseless war, Treasury is sanctioning Russia’s two largest oil companies that fund the Kremlin’s war machine,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time. However, the Treasury issued temporary waivers beginning in March to release sanctioned Russian crude already on vessels with the aim of mitigating rising oil prices amid the Iran war. The DFC, the international investment arm of the US, would receive an ownership interest under the deal. "The LIG [Lukoil] portfolio holds assets that are both critical to our allies’ economic and energy security, as well as our own," a DFC told The National . DFC’s involvement helps to ensure that US interests are adequately represented in the transfer and operation of these assets, reducing the risk of adversaries acquiring or influencing operations and protecting long-term asset value." The official added the deal would support reliable energy supplies for US families and businesses, "and is expected to return billions to American taxpayers". Mr Boehley told Reuters the US would receive a share of future profits under the agreement, if approved, and would support efforts to prevent Russia from funding its war in Ukraine. The deal transfers Lukoil's non-Russian oil and gas assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the US-led consortium. It also includes petrol stations in the US, Europe and Asia, CNBC reported. The deal would give the US-led group roughly 350,000 barrels per day of production. The group said Lukoil's upstream operations cover 11 countries and serve the Black Sea, the Balkans and north-west Europe, and supply diesel and other petroleum products to US-allied nations. Lukoil and US private equity firm Carlyle Group announced a non-exclusive purchase agreement for the Russian company's foreign assets in January. The agreement lapsed in July without an agreement from the Treasury Department, and Carlyle dropped out of the race in October. Ofac's latest licence for negotiations is set to expire on December 19.

events.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
events.summary: Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code. The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in. 1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them. In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident. It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident. 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password. The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts. events.title: Scoop: Kushner urges Netanyahu to make good on Gaza commitments
events.summary: Presidential envoy Jared Kushner urged Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday to make good on commitments he made to Donald Trump to implement a Gaza peace plan , according to three sources with knowledge of a call between them. Why it matters: The White House and Trump's Board of Peace have been increasingly exasperated by what they viewed as Netanyahu's obstinacy on Gaza, convinced that he's been prioritizing his political survival above all else. "I feel like the fork in the road is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status," Kushner said in a New York Magazine interview published Monday. But two sources with knowledge of the call said it was "positive and constructive." One of them said Netanyahu signaled again that he's ready to move forward with the steps in Gaza that the White House wants. A third source confirmed that Netanyahu said he's committed to the Gaza plan. The Israeli prime minister's office confirmed that the call took place but declined to comment further. The big picture: The Gaza roadmap calls for disarming Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza, as well as transferring responsibility for governing the enclave to a new Palestinian technocratic government. But it has been on hold for months because of the Israeli elections held on Oct. 27. Trump endorsed Netanyahu shortly before the election and now wants the prime minister to reciprocate. But many of the Gaza measures are loathed by Netanyahu's base. Netanyahu's opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, currently has a window to form a new government. He's making progress, and if he succeeds, Netanyahu could be ousted as early as next week. Eisenkot promised during the campaign to implement Trump's Gaza plan with the goal of ensuring that Hamas no longer controls the territory within 18 months. Catch up quick: In July, the Board of Peace agreed with Hamas on a 15-point plan to disarm Gaza's armed groups and transfer civilian and security control to a new Palestinian technocratic government. Since then, Netanyahu's government has largely refused to move forward with implementing it. Netanyahu was and still is extremely skeptical that Hamas would ever demilitarize. He says the group is reconstituting and rearming in Gaza. Driving the news: President Trump spoke to Netanyahu two weeks ago and asked him to move ahead with implementing the Gaza plan. Two sources with knowledge of the matter said Netanyahu told Trump he would approve measures that are needed to implement the plan. But since then, nothing has happened. Behind the scenes: During his call with Trump, Netanyahu said that he couldn't approve the steps in Gaza the U.S. wants because he's heading a caretaker government. But the Netanyahu government accepted the Gaza plan and committed to taking those steps long before the election. "Bibi claimed he can't do small things in Gaza he already agreed to because he is a caretaker prime minister, but at the same time he claimed there is no problem for him to go to war with Iran. This wasn't a serious argument," a source with direct knowledge said. Zoom in: The sources said that implementing the Gaza plan hinges on the Israeli government's green light. They said the White House and Board of Peace have been asking Netanyahu to approve these steps: Allowing the International Stabilization Force (ISF) to deploy in Gaza. Permitting 4,000 Palestinians who were vetted by the Israeli security services and accepted to be part of a future Gaza police force to leave the enclave for training in Egypt and then be allowed to return. Approving materials for water and sanitation projects in Gaza. Allowing temporary mobile homes to enter Gaza to provide shelter in the winter. Allow construction materials into Gaza for building the ISF bases. Permitting a Palestinian technocratic government to begin operating in one area in southern Gaza as part of a pilot project. What to watch: A source with knowledge of the matter said that there's a sense that the Trump administration's private and public pressure — as well as the results of the midterm elections — has made Israel more receptive to implementing the Gaza plan. The source added that while the call with Netanyahu was positive, it remains to be seen whether Israel will actually take the steps the U.S. wants.
