events.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
events.summary: Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas. Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping. The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys. Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media. “Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.” When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.” When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics. The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem , Lovi , Meemo Bear , BubblePal Panda , and Tavlshero ‘s AI Puppy . The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules. While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study. Common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors. It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January , finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns. While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them. “These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.” TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment. EDA is an umbrella term for software, hardware, and services essential to the planning, design, and production of modern chips. Today, Cadence Design Systems, Synopsys, and Siemens dominate the industry, but US export controls have restricted Huawei and other blacklisted Chinese businesses' access to their tools. events.title: In country Victoria, a divided electorate sums up the mood of a nation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Exhaustion breaks in country Victoria as divided electorate sums up mood of a nation Topic: State and Territory Elections The seat of Ripon has become a microcosm of Australian political disaffection. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) On the eve of a transformative state election, the vast regional seat of Ripon has become a microcosm of Australian disaffection. Midway through a recent candidates debate in a country shed, a rooster named Luke let out a panicked squawk and tried to break free. The man holding Luke as a feathered political mascot was one of 12 candidates vying for the ultra-marginal seat of Ripon. "Luke and I both believe in free speech, as he just demonstrated," said Bernard Quince, an independent who advocates the self-sufficiency benefits of owning a few chooks and a fruit tree. For voters in this weekend's Victorian election, and perhaps all Australians, it was an unneeded reminder of how deeply unserious politics can appear, even in the face of its deeply serious consequences. As Australians become "more pessimistic" and "more divided," trust in politicians has sagged to new lows , according to the Scanlon Foundation's social cohesion survey. Candidates in the 14,444-square-kilometre electorate have been earnestly selling the idea they can be the change the public craves. "I don't think we can assume that our politicians have our best interests at heart," said Samantha Rickinson, a caravan park owner in Ararat, 200km out of Melbourne on the seat's western border. Like so many segments of the country, exhaustion, distrust and outright anger are easily found. Motorists have become adept at dodging potholes; ratepayers are locked in years-long battles with council for basic improvements; households are squeezed by cost-of-living pressures and infuriated by ballooning government debt. "You could pick this electorate [of Ripon] up and plonk it into regional New South Wales or Queensland and get very similar responses from punters," said Kos Samaras from political polling firm Redbridge Group. In the picturesque town of Beaufort, local mechanic Chris Johnstone is a staunch advocate for his community, but he can gesture around at any number of issues that rile him up. Trucks rumbling through the otherwise quiet main street are a reminder of an unbuilt and as-yet unfunded bypass. A solar-powered bin a few metres away had, to his bewilderment, been installed in near-permanent shade. For the president of the local business group, it amounts to a general sense that things are not working as they should, even if he's not sure what the answer is. "It'll take a lot longer to bring it back under control." No political ad or AI social media video will override the potholes on a voter's street. Damaged and dangerous roads have long plagued regional communities , but durable solutions from politicians are harder to find. "A politician likes to cut a ribbon on a new road, but you can't cut a ribbon on a repaired pothole," said Rob Pelletier, a horticulturist on the outskirts of Beaufort. "It's now caught up with them after so many years of neglect." In September, a motorcyclist died after reportedly hitting a pothole on a stretch of the much-maligned Western Highway, not far from Mr Pelletier's home. The tragedy occurred in a state where roads are crumbling faster than the government can repair them . Experts have bemoaned the "old techniques" used for maintenance . Former VicRoads staff have blamed privatisation . Even those paid to fix them say the current system is failing local communities. "I drive on these roads every day. I'm so pissed off about it too," said Greg*, a contractor in the area who didn't want to risk losing work by using his name. Greg sees angry Facebook comments from his community, and understands why people are lashing out at politicians, or even contractors like him. The pothole problem has loomed especially large over the election, with costly promises for change coming from all directions . Greg is unconvinced any of the parties have a meaningful answer. "The biggest cost of it is bureaucracy," he said. "We'll spend an excessive amount of money fixing a small patch because they can't make their mind up about where the budget's going to go." The town of Maryborough is nestled in the north-east of Ripon, where temperatures can reach 45 degrees Celsius. Locals like Rowena Butler are staring down a fifth summer without a public pool. The heritage-listed complex was closed in 2022 after an independent assessment found cracking and leaking in the 50-metre outdoor pool spelled its "end of life".

events.title: Kmart sued over 'dupes' three times in 18 months
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Kmart has been sued three times in the past 18 months for alleged IP infringements. ( ABC News ) Kmart has been sued three times in the past 18 months over dupe products companies say infringe their intellectual property (IP). Luxury jewellery brand Richemont and hair care company Amika are among the complainants. Two open cases return to court in December. One of Australia's biggest retailers has been sued three times over its "dupe" products in the past two years. Wesfarmers-owned Kmart and connected chain Target have been taken to court by aggrieved Australian and global companies with claims they ripped off jewellery designs of a luxury brand and accusations it and other retailers copied the designs of a Queensland fashion label. The cases highlight how endemic duping has become in retail culture, and the legal tightrope that discount chains like Kmart are walking to get customers buying their version of well-known products. "Dupes" is short for duplicate, and the goods, sometimes known as super-fakes, are products made to look and feel like another company's original product without the same trademarks or logos. They differ from counterfeits, which are deceptive imitations of authentic products. Where counterfeits are clearly illegal, dupes push the boundaries. Hair care brand Amika accused Kmart of copying its designs. ( Supplied ) US hair care brand Amika sued Kmart and Target in May this year, describing the alleged conduct as "flagrant". In Federal Court documents, it accused the retail giants of infringing on its intellectual property (IP) over a range of hair care products being sold under Kmart's OXX brand. It featured "plain black sans serif text over a coloured background featuring a bright, multi-coloured artwork" on "distinctive bottle and container shapes" with matching bright colours, which Amika says are the same as or very similar to its own products. In its defence, Kmart claimed the design features in question were common features of hair care packaging and by selling its products under its OXX branding, it did not require permission from Amika to use them. Both parties agreed to dismiss the case and the products in question are no longer being sold. Richemont noted in its statement of claim that the likes of Queen Camilla were known to wear Van Cleef jewellery. ( Getty: Mark Cuthbert ) Richemont International, the owners of popular jewellery brand Van Cleef & Arpels, has sued Kmart and Target Australia for allegedly infringing on its trademark clover design. It claims Target and Kmart had sold numerous pieces of jewellery that were "deceptively similar" to its designs. In court documents, the Swiss company said it had suffered substantial loss and damage by means of "misappropriation of goodwill of Van Cleef & Arpels", damage to reputation and loss of sales. Four trademarks registered by Richemont. ( Supplied ) Target has defended the claim, arguing that consumers would know the items with the clover design were not from Van Cleef if they did not include a device mark, a certificate of authenticity and were not sold at similar prices to Van Cleef jewellery. It further argues there are key differences in its designs to Van Cleef's. Target has also launched a counterclaim, arguing the clover is not distinctive and cannot be trademarked, which Richemont is defending. The case has been ongoing since September 2025. Items sold by Kmart that Richemont says infringe on its trademark. ( Supplied ) Intellectual property lawyer Georgina O'Farrell said Richemont had likely sued Kmart and Target to send a message to other retailers. Earlier this year, Kmart was one of 16 businesses Queensland clothing company Sabo Skirt had sued for IP infringement. Australian company Sabo Skirt alleged Kmart had copied a print featuring aquatic items, including lobsters, shells and leaves, portrayed in different orientations scattered across a white background. A registered print by Sabo Skirt which it alleges Kmart copied. ( Supplied ) Kmart filed a counterclaim earlier this year, alleging Sabo Skirts designs were not distinct, but has since withdrawn that suit. A Kmart spokesperson said it offered a wide range of products while "operating with due regard to legal and compliance requirements". "Our customers love our great products at affordable prices," the spokesperson said. "Our design teams create curated ranges that align back to global trends." Ms O'Farrell said dupes had become more accepted in the mainstream.

events.title: ASML's CEO makes the case for selling chips to China
events.summary: Export controls on chips and other technology shouldn’t aim to cut China off completely — a strategy that will only backfire, warns Christophe Fouquet, CEO of ASML, the sole maker of the lithography machines needed to produce the world’s most advanced AI chips. “You need [export controls] to protect very advanced technology, but you also have to use export control in such a way that you don’t completely frustrate a country and invite that country to basically double down or triple down on development,” Fouquet said on Semafor’s Future Proof . The debate over Chinese access to Western technology has intensified in Washington after revelations of Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy left lawmakers divided on how aggressively to tighten curbs. As a $520 billion de facto monopoly in chipmaking equipment, ASML sits at the center of that fight. Fouquet argued that continuing to sell China older equipment — ASML’s shipments there are more than a decade behind the cutting edge — maintains a strategic “generation gap” that keeps Beijing hooked on Western hardware rather than racing to build its own. “For almost 30 years, we have been able to keep an extremely high market share in China — very high means close to 100% — which means that they have accepted to rely on our technology with the idea that they had access to it,” Fouquet said. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: Average US 30-year mortgage rate eases to 7.21%, not far from 2026 high
events.summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the U.S. fell to 7.21% from 7.28% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Wednesday. One year ago, it was at 6.23%. The weekly average rate has been above 7% since late September. As recently as Oct. 15, it was at 7.4%, its highest level in nearly three years. Elevated mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power at a time when affordability challenges continue to sideline many aspiring homeowners. Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also eased this week. That average rate fell to 6.54% from 6.66% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.51%. Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans. The upward march in mortgage rates this year has weighed on home sales, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged. Data pointing to accelerating inflation have raised the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. The central bank kept rates unchanged late last month , after raising them in September. events.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
events.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back. According to federal prosecutors , Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The company’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.” But the company allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement. Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida. The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a company that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers. 404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count. Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies. Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks. The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal. events.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
events.summary: What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt ? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder. Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users. The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases , claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said. Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. ( In a blog post , Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.) Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted . It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats. The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim. In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through. “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement. Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model. “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said . “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.” Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.” The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff .) Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google , when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform. California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia. events.title: Jensen Huang to face questioning on Capitol Hill
events.summary: Washington will provide an Nvidia split-screen next week, as CEO Jensen Huang faces questioning on Capitol Hill while the company touts new products at its DC conference less than two miles away. Nvidia has reportedly assembled a team of top Washington lawyers and lobbyists ahead of Huang’s closed-door interview with three House committees on Tuesday, the same day he was scheduled to give a keynote at its annual tech showcase for developers, industry partners, and government officials. Huang’s appearance was scrubbed from the schedule after he resigned as CEO, and there’s no word yet on whether he’ll make a grand return to the stage now that he’s been reinstated and reassured staffers that it’s mostly business as usual . A tech-focused address in front of adoring fans could serve as effective counterprogramming to the lashing he’s likely to receive at the Capitol, and underscore the gulf between how the scandal is playing in Washington and in Silicon Valley. Lawmakers still have plenty of legitimate questions for Huang and Nvidia, while to much of the tech world, the hearings are little more than political theater. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Powerful but unpredictable AI is a product no one will buy
events.summary: Reed’s view A new ripple of consternation recently made its way out of AI labs to Axios, which reported internal concern that models have become too unsafe to release publicly. But “safety” can mean different things in different contexts. What this concern really means is that AI labs are having trouble creating ever more capable models that they can both understand control. These models are not actually a threat — so long as nobody uses them to do any important work, or gives them access to important things. The industry has internalized this framework. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella treats AI as an “ insider risk. ” This is bad news for AI labs. They wanted to build AI models that were so good they could take over all knowledge work. At closed-door conferences in Silicon Valley, people talked about Anthropic being nationalized because it became the entire economy. But the failure to build anything remotely like that is good news for the rest of society. An AI model that is powerful but completely unpredictable is a very expensive and very useless tool. The company that builds such a thing would have no customers. Notable Anthropic’s share price has dropped below its $83 IPO price, as investors rethink the AI trade.

events.title: Huang's return to Nvidia complicates open-source model race
events.summary: US President Donald Trump pushed for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement to the top of Nvidia because of his support for US open-weight models, which offer an alternative to Chinese versions. But Huang’s return could also spur Beijing to speed up its own push to build homegrown chips. Tech executives have waxed on about how bad a Jensen-less Nvidia would have been for the sector, given his role as both industry cheerleader and central banker, as well as Nvidia’s promotion of the computing platforms developers use to train and run open models. Still, the open-source world “is bigger than one man, even if that man is Jensen,” one AI startup founder told me. If a newly emboldened Washington intensifies scrutiny of chip sales to China and curbs Beijing’s access to advanced computing power, that could slow down China’s AI labs and Western companies’ obsession with staying ahead. — J.D. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test was deliberately crashed into the asteroid on September 26, 2022. The original plan called for a European spacecraft – Asteroid Impact Mission (AIM) – to launch first and observe the before and after effects of DART. AIM was canceled, and the Hera mission launched in 2024. DART was a success. Scientists were able to determine that the impact had indeed changed the orbit of Dimorphos. The question was what else had happened to the asteroid. Scientists spotted ejecta and debris following the DART impact, but the close-up observations by Hera have revealed the full extent of the collision. Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, said: "Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape or stayed the same. "Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width." Scientists also noted that the asteroid is now tumbling in its orbit. Hera is surveying the 151-meter-wide Dimorphos and its larger companion, the 730-meter-wide Didymos, from about 25 to 30 km away. It moves around the pair at roughly 12 cm/s, using thruster firings to trace rectangular paths rather than conventional circular orbits. The plan is to approach closer, to about 13 km, to get higher-resolution snaps. A complicating factor is the discovery that hundreds of orbiting boulders surround the asteroids. Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, said: "The team will have to take account of these objects in the coming weeks as the mission moves in closer." Hera will deploy two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in early 2027. The Italian-led Milani will study surface composition and surrounding dust, while the Luxembourg-led Juventas will use radar to probe Dimorphos's interior before attempting a landing. Scientists also want to measure Dimorphos's mass. Combined with the observed change in its orbit, that will help them assess how effectively DART transferred momentum to the asteroid and improve predictions for future deflection attempts. Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli said: "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. events.title: X’s latest update for creators focuses on vertical video
events.summary: X announced new creation tools Wednesday, many of them focused on short-form vertical video. The updates are part of the platform’s effort to compete with social networks such as YouTube and Instagram as the format continues to grow in popularity. The tools are designed to help creators make professional-quality vertical videos, share original content more easily, and earn more. They also give creators more ways to record, edit, and publish content directly on the platform without relying on third-party apps. A key addition is an upgraded media editor that lets creators produce polished vertical videos without leaving X. Recording features include the ability to capture video in segments and use green-screen effects, the company said. The editor also offers a range of postproduction tools. Creators can convert horizontal videos to vertical format, automatically generate captions, trim footage, add text overlays, choose custom thumbnails, and adjust photos before publishing. Thanks to a recently announced update , users can now add up to 20 photos and videos to a single post, which audiences can swipe through horizontally. X says the feature is intended for sharing event recaps, behind-the-scenes moments, and product launches. Availability of the new features varies by region, X said. Earlier this month, the company introduced a clipping feature that lets users take snippets from longer videos, add their own commentary, and post the clips without leaving X. Clips credit and link to the original video, plus the person who creates a clip and the original poster can earn from its views. Another feature, “React with Video,” launched earlier this year . Similar to TikTok’s “stitch” feature, this lets creators respond to posts with video commentary while displaying the original post in the background. X has also introduced new earning opportunities and updates to its creator monetization programs in recent months. These include the “ Video Kickstart Bonus ,” an invitation-only pilot that rewards selected creators for publishing original vertical videos under three minutes long and without watermarks. The platform has also launched “ Subscriber-only Group Chats ,” which let creators host private, real-time conversations with paying subscribers. The feature is currently open to creators with 800 or fewer subscribers, and each group chat can accommodate up to 1,000 members. Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the company's support notice says. The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft said: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field." Administrators can use the notice's network trace and event log examples to identify affected products. For confirmed cases, the temporary workaround is to set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm Registry value to 1 on affected clients. This stops the client offering signing, backing out the new default rather than fixing the incompatible product. The recommended long-term options are a vendor update or Kerberos authentication, where supported. The value sits under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 and defaults to 0, enabling clients to offer signing on non-anonymous connections. The NTLM changes arrived in the November 10 update as phase 1 in a 2-phase process. In phase 1, "Windows client devices begin offering NTLM signing on all connections by default. Servers accept both signed and unsigned clients. Auditing events identify clients not using signing." Phase 2, scheduled for May 2027, will make Windows servers require NTLM signing by default. "Clients that do not offer signing will be rejected by secure servers," Microsoft stated. Ominously, Microsoft warned that it "might remove the registry keys at a future date," so the company is not kidding about the temporary workaround thing. The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737 , a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network." NTLM is on Microsoft's hit list, having joined the Deprecated Features list in 2024. It dates back to the era of Windows NT, and Microsoft has made clear that it wants customers to move to Kerberos, which became the default in 2000. Even so, NTLM lingers on. Deprecation doesn't remove Microsoft's obligation to secure NTLM while it remains in supported Windows releases. events.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
events.summary: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right. Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence. Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here? If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today. But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants. If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue. PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.  This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there. And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation. This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead. It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source. But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025. There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility —efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high. Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. Interim CEO Bruce Broussard said HP would do this "by capitalizing on the growing shift of AI workloads to the edge and leveraging our industry-leading portfolio designed to meet the needs of users with more demanding workloads." The pitch echoes the previous quarter's earnings call . "Our focus is on helping customers implement and manage AI across their environments. We believe that the future of AI is hybrid with workloads running both in the cloud and closer to where people work and data is created," he added. Broussard cited IDC estimates that half of enterprise AI inference workloads will run on endpoints or edge nodes by 2030, and claimed that with half a billion devices shipped, HP has "deep expertise in how devices perform, how they're secured and how they're managed at scale." HP fourth quarter revenue - for the three months ended October 31 - was $16 billion, up 9.3 percent year-on-year. Full-year fiscal 2026 revenue was up 9.5 percent to $60 billion. Personal Systems drove the growth, as its printer business slipped slightly. Personal Systems revenue grew 14 percent on commercial and advanced compute sales, and AI PCs represented nearly 60 percent of HP’s shipments in the quarter. "That said, higher component costs and challenging pricing environment, particularly in consumer, pressured profitability," said Broussard. Like its rivals, HP is leaning on higher-margin premium models and signing long-term deals with the memory chip makers to secure supplies. Nikkei Asia named HP among the firms buying a limited amount of memory from China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). Asked whether it planned to procure more Chinese chippery, HP’s CFO Karen Parkhill sidestepped the question: "We don't expect any material changes in our suppliers right now. We're confident in the suppliers that we have, and we are confident in the supply that we have what we need to fulfil the demand this year." She conceded that "We are using suppliers from all over the world." Parkhill said HP expects memory and storage costs to continue rising, but at a slower rate than during this last fiscal year. "We also expect CPU costs to increase, but not as much as what we've seen with memory and storage. And all of that is baked into our outlook." Broussard expects Q4 to prove the low point for Personal Systems margins, with improvement coming from further optimization of its product design and component configurations. In Ferbruary, HP said memory and storage costs had grown from 15 to 18 percent of the PC bill of materials at the start of the year to a figure closer to 40 percent. Parkhill declined to update the figure, saying the moderating cost curves and fast-changing production mix make the BOM percentage "less useful." HP’s newly hired CEO , former GSK boss Emma Walmsley, will start work at the company on January 4, leading it through what continues to be uncertain times for the PC industry.

events.title: WhatsApp now lets you schedule messages in group and individual chats
events.summary: WhatsApp on Wednesday started rolling out a much-sought-after feature: the ability to schedule messages in both individual and group chats. The feature is rolling out globally to all users across iOS and Android. Once it becomes available, you can type a message and long-press the send button to schedule it. You can choose to send a message anywhere between 10 minutes and 14 days later. Users will be able to see all their scheduled messages and delete them if needed. It’s not clear if there is a way to edit the schedule of a message. Notably, scheduled messages will be sent even if your phone is off or outside network coverage. You can schedule messages containing text, photos, and videos. The feature could prove useful for wishing someone a happy birthday on time or chatting with people across time zones. Businesses may also find it easier to schedule texts and updates to their customers, and people who use the app to coordinate work will likely find themselves using scheduled texts to update their teams. WhatsApp rivals like Telegram and Signal have had the ability to schedule messages for a while now, so the Meta-owned chat app is late in rolling it out. events.title: The U.S. economy is ripping
events.summary: Wall Street has been reeling amid fears about the future of the AI boom. But in the here and now, the U.S. economy is experiencing an outright boom. The big picture: Growth was even stronger this summer than it appeared, and the robust expansion is continuing this fall, according to a range of data released Wednesday morning. That is pushing Americans' incomes up and the pace of layoffs down. The strong data helps explain why the Federal Reserve is prepared to raise interest rates two weeks from now even in the face of financial market turbulence. Driving the news: The U.S. economy grew at a 4.3% annual rate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the second revision to GDP data — well above the 3.4% originally reported. The strong results have continued into Q4. The Commerce Department separately said that personal income rose 0.7% in October, well ahead of analysts' expectations. Overall orders for durable goods came in below forecasts for October, but core capital goods orders — a forward-looking measure of investment spending — climbed 1.2%, also well ahead of projections. The Labor Department said that only 189,000 people filed new claims for jobless benefits last week, matching the lowest of 2026 and among the lowest readings on record (claims go back to 1967). Zoom out: The Q3 GDP reading was powered by business investment, especially for software, showing that the AI buildout remains a powerful driver of overall economic growth. It wasn't driven by volatile components of GDP like inventory and trade swings; real final sales to private domestic purchasers surged at a whopping 5.8% pace, and gross domestic income — conceptually similar to GDP — rose at a 4.4% rate. Translation: This isn't some fluky reading, but rather a sign of underlying robustness. Rapid growth looks set to continue in Q4; the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tool estimates current-quarter growth at 2.9%. Zoom in: Nonresidential fixed investment — the GDP subcategory that covers capital spending — contributed 2.2 percentage points to overall growth in Q3. That was the highest since the bounce back following the 2020 pandemic. Excluding that episode, it was the highest since 2011. Yes, but: Personal consumption expenditures rose a moderate 0.3% in October, below analysts' forecasts (+0.4%) and September readings (+0.6%). That implies some softness in consumer spending, which, along with AI investment, has been powering the economy forward. The silver lining, however, is that strong income growth paired with modest consumption growth is good news for American household balance sheets: The personal savings rate rose to 4.1%, from 3.6% in September. Data: Bureau of Economic Analysis; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios The strong growth readings affirm the Fed's all-but-certain plans to raise interest rates at a meeting concluding Dec. 9. Inflation data also released in the report shows why. By the numbers: The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, which the Fed targets, was up 3.8% over the last 12 months, or 3.3% excluding volatile food and energy. In month-on-month terms, both total and core PCE inflation came in at 0.3% for October, implying no meaningful deceleration is underway. The core number annualizes to 3.5% inflation. State of play: While those readings were right in line with forecasts, they underscore that inflation remains far above the Fed's 2% target — as it has been for nearly six consecutive years. The combination of rapid growth and elevated inflation looks more like a classic overheating economy — one in which the central bank needs to tighten policy to bring inflation into line. Between the lines: The market turbulence of the last few weeks — the S&P 500 was down 2.8% as of 11:45am ET — points to risks that the AI investment boom may deflate in the quarters ahead. But the Fed is unlikely to react to what might happen when growth numbers are coming in so hot and it has been missing its inflation target for so long. What they're saying: "The economy isn't merely hanging in there," Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors, wrote in a note. "It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing, and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," he added. "Boil it all down, and [Wednesday's] report reinforces an increasingly familiar tension: the economy is performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."

events.title: Democrats’ long 2016 primary is finally over — and Sanders won
events.summary: David’s view I don’t want to sound hasty, but Democrats’ 2016 presidential primary finally ended this week. Bernie Sanders won. The Democratic National Committee’s mandate that candidates reject super PACs or forfeit the 2028 debate stage surprised some likely candidates for the nomination. It didn’t surprise the Vermont independent senator, who had been asking as much for years from a party that he never joined. “I believe the Party should make a public statement about our values and simultaneously consider actions that punish candidates who refuse to adhere to this principle,” Sanders wrote in a letter to then-DNC Chair Jaime Harrison in 2022. Sanders did not have a close relationship with Harrison, who was picked to lead the party by Joe Biden. He has a friendly relationship with current DNC Chair Ken Martin — who, in a twist few Democrats might have called this summer , faces fewer post-midterm challenges for his job than Hakeem Jeffries or Chuck Schumer. Now Martin has signed off on an idea that many Democrats considered well-meaning but unenforceable. The party can’t prevent super PACs or “dark money” groups (not always the same thing) from spending on behalf of candidates. Its new Fair Campaign Practices Pledge asks candidates to tell the DNC if an outside group is spending in the primary and allows the DNC to punish those who don’t denounce that spending. This hasn’t been universally welcomed by Democrats, who would rather be talking about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang right now. But the story of Democratic politics since Sanders lost the 2016 primary to Hillary Clinton has been, eventually, the party giving Sanders what he wants. If Donald Trump led the most successful raid of a major party in modern history, Sanders is the unquestioned runner-up. He’s succeeded for two basic reasons. One: Everything he’s asked for is both populist and popular. Two: Democrats would rather keep Sanders inside the tent than risk him rallying anti-establishment voters from outside. He gets to put up stumbling blocks for the sort of party lifers, donors, and strategists who don’t want the left to win a Democratic nomination. They get party rules and priorities that prevent the left wing’s potential standard-bearer in 2028 (be it Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, or another) from making sharp contrasts with a candidate more appealing to insiders. It wasn’t inevitable, but Democrats were definitely heading in this direction. The mollification of Sanders started right before the 2016 party convention, when he declined to release his delegates before they could influence the party platform. While Clinton’s allies had more seats on key committees, they agreed to create a Unity Reform Commission to change party rules after the election — which, at that point, they assumed Clinton would win. She didn’t, and the commission actually went to work, changing the primary process largely in line with what Sanders wanted. Had the change occurred in 2008, Clinton would have likely defeated Barack Obama; in 2016, Clinton would have padded her delegate count over Sanders. I don’t think that Sanders out-smarted himself, but the rules-making Democrats definitely saw a win-win in opening primaries to more “normie” voters. This week’s Fair Campaign Practices Pledge is more beneficial to the Sanders wing. It only commits candidates to shaming and shunning super PACs in the primaries; it’s understood that Democratic super PACs will wind up again for a 2028 general election. “It creates a free rider problem where socialists can decry mainstream Dems for outside spending but still get the benefit of it if they ever win,” said Democratic strategist Caitlin Legacki, who opposes the change, and worked for Rep. Haley Stevens in the party’s Michigan Senate primary. For the next year, a wet blanket will be thrown on Democrats who could get support from super PACs. If any governor wanted to follow Ron DeSantis, and divert his state election funds into a federal PAC — well, GOP commissioners on the FEC might let him, but the party wouldn’t. Some Democrats believe that the super PAC shaming policy will be toothless, but the Sanders wing clearly sees it as a win. “A lot of progress [is] being made on getting dark money out of the Democratic primaries,” said Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., the only senator who endorsed Sanders over Clinton in 2016, on a Monday call organized to support Sanders-endorsed Senate majority leader candidate Chris Van Hollen. “Thank you, everybody who’s working on that!” Sanders and his wing won this, again, without ever winning a presidential primary. The credit he’s gotten for changing the Democratic Party’s rhetoric and priorities this cycle has rankled some Democrats. But this is the best of all possible post-2016 worlds for them. Sanders rebuffed supporters who wanted him to lead a third party, which would have split the anti-Trump opposition. He demanded that the party neuter “superdelegates” and then super PACs, which most Democrats basically agreed were big perception problems for their party. Progressives are betting that these changes will help Democrats characterize Republicans as corrupt, at a moment when voters believe it. In 2016, Trump initially benefited from the fact that large GOP donors were horrified by him, and that he didn’t have a super PAC at all. Who was defined as the candidate of big money and closed-door fundraisers? When the 2016 primaries were over, clearly, Hillary Clinton was — even though Trump will leave office as the most successful super PAC fundraiser of all time. He’s piled up seven- and eight-figure donations, often from donors with business before his administration. Trump pulled Elon Musk into frontline politics, where the CEO became the biggest single super PAC donor in the country. Democrats picked this moment to heighten the contrasts, ostentatiously opposing super PACs, bidding for the roving anti-establishment vote that seems to like this sort of thing. The 2016 primary is over, and the 2028 primary can begin. Notable In The Washington Sun, Elena Schneider and Daniella Diaz heard from frustrated political staffers who think their candidates are going to be asked to abide by an enforceable rule. In The Washington Post, Dylan Wells talked to some of the social media creators and influencers who are now thinking about their role in the next Democratic debates — shaping the discourse in a way that used to be up to corporate media.

events.title: China Securities opens first overseas office in Dubai to boost Middle East ties
events.summary: China Securities, the investment bank controlled by Citic Group, has opened its first overseas office in Dubai as it seeks to play a larger role in relations between the Middle East and the world’s second-largest economy . The office of China Securities International at the Dubai International Financial Centre is intended to meet clients’ cross-border needs and grow its portfolio of nearly $75 billion in assets under management, the DIFC said in a statement on Wednesday. China Securities, which received a licence in September to set up its regional presence at the DIFC, served more than 17.1 million securities brokerage clients in the first half of 2026. China Securities International will provide cross-border investment banking services. It will support Chinese companies expanding into the Middle East and help the region’s investors to tap into China’s market, while continuing to contribute to the Belt and Road Initiative, the DIFC said. Liu Cheng, chairman of China Securities, said the Dubai office “marks a key milestone in the company’s international expansion and a practical response to the growing cross-border needs of its clients”. “The company will leverage Dubai’s institutional framework and strategic location as a new platform to strengthen two-way connectivity between the China and Middle East capital markets,” he added. China is the Emirates’ biggest trading partner, according to the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The two countries established a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2018 , which provides a structured platform for co-operation in trade, investment, technology and energy. Earlier this year, they signed an agreement to boost investment and mobilise more capital between them, adding to a string of recent deals. China Securities is the latest to join a cluster of major Chinese financial institutions at the DIFC. They include Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, China International Capital Corporation, China Merchants Bank International and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China. China’s five largest banks together account for more than 30 per cent of total assets in the DIFC’s banking and capital markets sector, state news agency Wam previously reported. “China Securities’ presence adds further depth to the DIFC’s financial ecosystem and creates new opportunities to connect Chinese businesses and investors with regional and international capital markets,” said Arif Amiri, chief executive of the DIFC Authority.

events.title: Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
events.summary: Trump's portfolio traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows. Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025. Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible. The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement. The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold". Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation. But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO. Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk". Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate. However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO. Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry , leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies. The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade. Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares. Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares. Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term. Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency." An alert has gone up on FinCEN's Bank Secrecy Act E-Filing website, as shown in this archived copy , informing those who need to submit reports that they might not be able to while the agency deals with the situation. FinCEN not only enforces compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act and associated regulations but also collects and analyzes financial intelligence for sharing with other US agencies and foreign government partners. In other words, it has some juicy info in its databases. “FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems,” the alert states. “As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline.” FinCEN hasn't said which systems intruders accessed, but clues in the deadline extension notice the agency posted alongside the warning suggest the disruption affects its reporting services for banks and other financial institutions required to submit reports detailing certain financial transactions and suspicious activity that may indicate money laundering or other illicit activity. FinCEN's Secure Data Transfer Mode, one method of submitting those reports, appears to be affected, as do services companies use to submit beneficial ownership information reports and individuals use to update their FinCEN identifiers. Eligible organizations and individuals with filings or updates due from November 18 through December 29 now have until December 30 to submit them. The Register has learned that there’s no evidence of any unauthorized access to Bank Secrecy Act data or beneficial ownership databases. That said, the investigation is ongoing - so that could change. “Treasury is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and third-party forensic examiners to determine the scope and impact of the incident,” a FinCEN official told us in an email. Several US government agencies have experienced cybersecurity incidents in recent months, including the ATF and the FBI , and reports emerged this week that intruders had also compromised an unclassified CIA system . While US authorities have linked previous cyberespionage campaigns to Chinese or other government-backed groups , financially motivated criminal groups have also targeted federal agencies. events.title: Army detonates Iowa explosives amid toxic lead fears
events.summary: The Army detonated 68 drums of unstable lead azide on an Iowa plant Wednesday after multiple delays, a court challenge and presidential intervention . The big picture: Elected officials slammed the military over communication shortfalls ahead of the detonation, which triggered evacuations, closures and fears about exposure to toxic lead dust in surrounding communities and states . Federal officials have repeatedly stressed that detonating the unstable lead is safer than risking it exploding spontaneously. What they're saying: "Early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations," President Trump said on Truth Social . Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe also said early analysis from federal partners indicates the detonation was "well-contained." The Army has not yet released a statement on the status of the operation. Reporters near the plant witnessed large clouds of smoke rising following the detonation. Context: The evacuation zone is a 5-mile cone extending southwest of the ammunition plant, per the Army's public safety notice . Evacuees are set to receive notice by phone when it's safe to return. Those outside of the evacuation zone should still shelter in place by closing all windows and doors, recirculating heating and turning off fans that pull in outside air, among other protective measures for children and livestock, per the Army. State of play: President Trump ordered the Army to pause plans to detonate the explosives on Monday, saying the blast couldn't proceed without approval from a court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand . But Trump warned he would hold Sand responsible for "any and all death or destruction" if the governor-elect refuses to approve the detonation. The court initially granted an administrative stay but lifted it Monday, allowing the plan to proceed. Sand said in a statement that the administration should decide "based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks," adding, "Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation." What they're saying: "We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide," a panel of judges concluded . "However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place." Catch up quick: The Army announced Sunday night that the controlled detonation plan would be pushed to Wednesday "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced" after initially planning the blast for Friday, and then Monday. But on Monday, Trump halted those plans — though only momentarily. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and has been updated.

events.title: Biden’s enduring win
events.summary: Democrats can be thankful for at least one decision by the Trump administration this year: Health officials continued to empower Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices, a signature achievement of former President Joe Biden. CMS announced this week that if newly negotiated prices had been in effect last year, they would’ve reduced the cost of the 13 drugs included in the program by $9.2 billion, a 45% savings. The new prices take effect in 2028 and cover high-cost drugs with no generic competitors, like Gilead Sciences’ HIV drug Biktarvy and Janssen’s prostate cancer drug Erleada. As Democrats debate their healthcare agenda, the drug negotiation program offers a contemporary example of how a Democratic health policy can endure, even under a Republican administration. During the legislative battle over Medicare drug price negotiations, Democrats were more insulated from outside pressure because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Reporters who cover turn-of-the-screw developments were mostly cloistered at home in the spring of 2021. Lobbyists, who had previously used terms like “ nuclear winter ” to describe the proposal’s impact on the pharmaceutical industry, could not apply face-to-face pressure on lawmakers. While no Republicans publicly backed the proposal, even pro-market conservatives have said to me in private that it makes sense to allow Medicare to haggle with drugmakers on drugs with no competition. The idea was also popular with voters across party lines. Unlike the Biden era, Democrats, obviously, do not control the White House. But health policy wonks perked up when President Donald Trump posted a screenshot on Truth Social of Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., directly pitching guaranteed “cradle-to-grave” healthcare for Americans. They hope it signals there’s room for a deal between the president and Democrats in Congress. “The devil is in the details and if the president is serious about working on this, let’s think about how we can get the broadest number of people guaranteed health insurance from cradle-to-grave without the out-of-pocket costs that are driving people into bankruptcy,” El-Sayed said this past weekend on Meet the Press . Whatever healthcare agenda Democrats end up pursuing, if they can get it signed into law, it may follow in the footsteps of Medicare drug price negotiations. The lesson: Even if healthcare legislation is initially unpopular in certain corners, it can quickly become politically durable.

events.title: Patent expiration cliffs spur drugmaker M&A
events.summary: The looming expiration of a blockbuster drug patent pushed Sanofi into its biggest M&A deal in two decades this week (and the largest pharma deal in three years). It won’t be the last. The French giant’s $41 billion takeover of respiratory drugmaker Insmed is in part a bid to replenish its pipeline ahead of the patent cliff facing Dupixent, the eczema drug whose $20-plus billion in annual sales will face generic competition starting in 2031. Across the industry, more than $500 billion of prescription-drug sales face patent expirations in the next six years, which could usher in a takeover wave. The biggest of those is Merck’s Keytruda, the world’s best-selling drug, which loses US patent in 2028. But all the big drugmakers are facing a similar crisis: Nearly half of Bristol’s sales are at risk by 2030 (which might help explain its merger flirtations with AstraZeneca earlier this year). Ozempic maker Novo Nordisk is regrouping after losing a bidding war over a new weight-loss drug last year to Pfizer. Hoovering up promising molecules doesn’t always pay off. Merck’s $12 billion purchase of Acceleron in 2021 brought it a new blockbuster blood-pressure drug whose sales have outperformed , but the jury is still out on Bristol’s $14 billion deal for schizophrenia drug Cobenfy. — David Lim

events.title: Iraq's National Security Service reports two more oil smuggling operations
events.summary: Iraq's domestic intelligence agency says it has uncovered more syndicates diverting the country's oil and crude derivatives amid a wider government campaign against theft and smuggling. The National Security Service said it discovered a tapped oil pipeline in Al Luhais, south of Baghdad, with three hoses connected to it by valves. “The hoses were being used to siphon oil and load it into tankers for smuggling, and they were shut down in co-ordination with technical authorities,” the service said. In the northern city of Kirkuk, officers seized a vehicle prepared for smuggling oil derivatives, the agency said. The vehicle was modified with openings on its sides to unload the product and "white oil" was found in its tank. The suspect was arrested. The service did not say when the operations were carried out, but its announcement comes after Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi launched a crackdown on oil theft and smuggling last week. The campaign began in Jurf Al Sakhar , about 60km south of Baghdad. An intelligence agency report documented oil theft there between 2021 and 2026, with sites suspected of storing oil hidden underground and under steel structures. Investigators later said they found evidence that smugglers had punctured a pipeline passing through the area, hidden pumping equipment inside hangars to avoid aerial surveillance and built a small concealed refinery. The area has long been closed to federal institutions and residents, after the influential Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia took control in 2014 following the fight against ISIS . The government ordered federal troops into the area, and dismissed nine senior security and oil officials, including the police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company. Kataib Hezbollah has denied the allegations. The crackdown then widened to Najaf, where investigators discovered a similar pattern: a tap on a strategic pipeline, hidden pipes running to private land, and alleged collusion by those meant to guard the network. The Supreme Judicial Council said an investigative judge had inspected an encroachment on land belonging to a Najaf Provincial Council member who heads its Energy Committee and his brother, a member of parliament, and that initial findings indicated oil had been illegally diverted. The court ordered the detention of five officers and three Energy Police personnel pending investigation. It issued arrest warrants for the two brothers, one of whom later surrendered while the other was reported to have left for Iran. In the north, the campaign has taken on a constitutional dimension after Mr Al Zaidi on Tuesday ordered federal authorities to take over border crossings run by the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region and directed the Oil Ministry to manage oilfields under Kurdish security control in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Diyala and Salahuddin provinces. The move followed an investigation into alleged smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company. The Kurdistan Regional Government rejected Baghdad's orders as unconstitutional and said it was working with federal authorities to combat corruption. It called for an end to oil smuggling across Iraq.

events.title: Dubai Islamic Bank to acquire Emirates Islamic to form Dh585bn company
events.summary: Dubai Islamic Bank has agreed to acquire Emirates Islamic Bank in an all-share deal that would create a Sharia-compliant lender with Dh585 billion ($159.2 billion) in assets. DIB will acquire 100 per cent of the issued share capital of Emirates Islamic and will strengthen its position as the UAE's largest Islamic lender, DIB and Emirates Islamic said on Wednesday in a joint statement posted on the Dubai Financial Market. Emirates Islamic is a unit of Dubai's biggest bank, Emirates NBD . The deal would also create the world's second-largest Islamic lender by assets, trailing only Saudi Arabia's Al Rajhi Bank. The takeover is subject to approval from authorities, including the UAE Central Bank and the Capital Markets Authority. “This transaction represents an important opportunity for Dubai to … further strengthen the emirate’s position as a global centre for Islamic finance,” said Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed, chairman of Emirates NBD. Dubai Islamic Bank (DIB) and Emirates NBD announce that they have signed a share purchase agreement for DIB to acquire 100% of the issued share capital of Emirates Islamic Bank, a wholly owned subsidiary of Emirates NBD. DIB will pay the consideration entirely by issuing new… pic.twitter.com/wopIJr4me3 — Dubai Media Office (@DXBMediaOffice) November 25, 2026 "By bringing together two highly complementary Islamic banking franchises, the combination will create a stronger institution to serve customers, support the UAE’s economic ambitions and contribute to Dubai’s continued growth," he said. The acquisition is one of the biggest mergers in UAE banking following the merger of Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank with Union National Bank and Al Hilal Bank in 2019. In 2017, National Bank of Abu Dhabi was combined with First Gulf Bank to create First Abu Dhabi Bank, the UAE's biggest lender. DIB, established in 1975, is the largest Islamic bank in the UAE by assets. With group assets exceeding Dh427 billion by the end of September, the bank has about 12,000 employees and more than 540 branches in the Middle East, Asia and Africa. Emirates Islamic was previously listed, before Emirates NBD bought out minority shareholders and delisted the business in June last year. DIB's takeover of Emirates Islamic "also reinforces Dubai’s position as the global capital for Islamic finance and places the full weight of a stronger DIB behind the emirate's future", DIB chairman Fadhel Al Ali said. The bank's shares - which surged 11 per cent on Monday amid initial reports on the takeover of Emirates Islamic - settled 1.6 per cent higher at Dh8.92 on Wednesday.
