events.title: Canadian Finance Minister says his country and the UAE are 'open for business'
events.summary: There is growing momentum on the UAE’s pledge to invest $50 billion in Canada , with the two countries working together to “bring projects to the table”, as economic ties strengthen, according to Canada’s Minister of Finance and National Revenue. Partnerships in the fields of critical minerals, energy and artificial intelligence are being worked on, Francois-Philippe Champagne told The National in an interview in Abu Dhabi. “That’s the reason why I'm here. It's to translate the vision of the President [Sheikh Mohamed] and the Prime Minister [Mark Carney] into action,” Mr Champagne said. The UAE announced the investment commitment during Mr Carney’s visit to the country last year, with a focus on energy, AI, logistics, mining and other strategic sectors. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, visited Canada last month and held talks with Mr Carney. “This is a long-term strategic partnership. My presence at a time when we have seen the security situation in the region sent a very strong signal to my partners here and to the world that Canada is open for business, UAE is open for business, and we're working together,” Mr Champagne said. A Canadian bank and an insurance firm will open offices in the UAE as part of the strengthening of ties, he confirmed. Canada is also looking to bolster defence partnerships, with a possible joint venture with UAE conglomerate Edge. Mr Champagne held a meeting with the Edge leadership during his current visit. “The meeting with Edge was very important because that's the kind of capabilities that we want to build. Looking at joint ventures, looking at investments that can come also with the partnership we're creating,” Mr Champagne said. Energy also remains a key area of focus with the official visiting Masdar's office in Abu Dhabi. “Masdar is another example; there are projects in Canada that could further our ambition to double the electricity generation. We’ve been looking at how we can bring … Masdar to build with us the grid of the 21st century.” Last month, Masdar signed an energy pact with Natural Resources Canada to lay the groundwork for co-operation across renewable energy, battery storage, grid infrastructure and clean power solutions to support growing demand from AI and data centres. Owned jointly by Abu Dhabi's Taqa, Adnoc and Mubadala, Masdar is aiming for a portfolio capacity of 100 gigawatts by 2030 as it continues to develop renewable projects as part of its global expansion plans. Cepa to double trade In July, the UAE finalised a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with Canada , with the pact signed during Sheikh Khaled's visit to the country last month. The pact gives Canadian companies better access to the UAE, which remains the largest Middle East market for Canadian exports, and could help attract capital into different sectors. The deal needs to be ratified by the Canadian parliament before it goes into effect, Mr Champagne said, without providing a timeline. “[The] Parliament has its own dynamic, but I would think we're going to put everything that we need to do on our side to have it ratified as quickly as possible.” There was a lot of enthusiasm behind that partnership, he said, with a target to double bilateral trade to $7 billion within 10 years, with energy, food security, defence, AI, and quantum technology to play a prominent role. The pact comes as Canada looks to diversify its partnerships with different countries amid trade tension with the US. “Historically, we have been doing a lot north-south, but now we have a diversification agenda. The Middle East, the GCC countries, here in the UAE where we have long established relationships, those are going to be key in our vision to increase our exports to the world,” Mr Champagne said. “And the fact that we were able to negotiate a comprehensive economic partnership in 47 days is showing the level of ambition and urgency that we're bringing to that, which I think is a very positive sign for businesses on both sides.” Canadian companies will continue to invest in the region despite the Iran war, he added. The Iran war, in its ninth month, has affected a number of sectors across the region, including energy, aviation, tourism and hospitality. Despite the disruption, the UAE is expected to expand by 0.2 per cent this year, according to International Monetary Fund estimates, amid a recovery in the oil and non-oil sectors. There are also big opportunities for UAE-based sovereign wealth funds to invest in Canada, Mr Champagne added. “I’ve been meeting with the CEO of Mubadala, Khaldoon [Al Mubarak], whom I've known for a long time. I know there's a lot of interest in Canada,” he said. “Canada provides unique opportunities: stability, predictability, the rule of law, the level of trust you want for the long term. You're looking at the megatrend. This is a country which, when you look at critical minerals, it's not only the exploration and extraction; it's the processing, it's the refining. So big opportunities there.” Abu Dhabi sovereign investor Mubadala Investment Company already has interests in Canada, in logistics firm Canada Cartage and CoolIT Systems, a liquid cooling provider for AI infrastructure. Energy advantage Canada, one of the top oil producers globally with about six million barrels a day of output, is boosting international exports amid the disruption to supplies due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war. “Because of what's happening, the world energy architecture is being redesigned,” Mr Champagne said. “One way to mitigate the impact is to partner with countries like Canada, which can export to allies and partners. “If you export from the west coast, you gain about eight days to go to the Pacific because you don't need to go to the Panama Canal. So we are doubling our capacity to be able to serve our partners there.” There is also opportunity on the east coast to support countries in Europe with gas supply. “We’re working on both sides; we can bring more natural resources to the Pacific. At the same time, there's a number of opportunities to support our European colleagues."

Targeting launch in late 2028, SR-1 would be the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit. It is designed to demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion and deliver a capsule carrying three helicopters to Mars. There have been some changes since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman showed off the concept [PDF] at the agency's Ignition event in March. Improved shielding and spacecraft design will allow a shorter boom between the reactor and the spacecraft's main body, protecting its electronics and the SkyFall payload. The revised design also includes larger X-band antenna dishes to transmit data to Earth. Decisions are still pending on how many radiator panels the vehicle needs, the output power levels of the nuclear power module, and how long the reactor will operate. Currently, the mission calls for the spacecraft to start its reactor once it has left Earth orbit and gradually ramp up power. After a period during which performance data will be sent back to Earth, the reactor will be shut down until after the SkyFall capsule, containing a trio of Mars Ingenuity-class helicopters, is delivered to Martian orbit. Solar arrays will power the spacecraft during its cruise to Mars. The fission reactor will then be reactivated to let engineers collect more data on its performance in deep space. NASA also awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University's Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the nuclear power module. "Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule," the agency said. The latter part regarding the schedule is certainly a challenge . Meeting the late-2028 launch target leaves roughly two years to finish designing, building, and testing the spacecraft. ESA is also targeting late 2028 for its long-delayed Rosalind Franklin rover. events.title: Allstate suffers multiday tech outage ahead of Thanksgiving
events.summary: U.S. insurer Allstate has been experiencing a tech outage since Monday morning, leaving customers nationwide unable to access their accounts, review their policy information, file claims, pay their bills, and more, just ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holidays. The outage has been impacting both the company’s website and mobile app, TechCrunch confirmed. The breakdown follows a report from earlier this month that Allstate was planning to lay off up to 10% of its staff as part of an AI-driven efficiency push. (The company had not confirmed the report, which was attributed to unnamed sources.) Allstate’s outage is the latest in a series of disruptions to services such as Microsoft Outlook and Teams , the airlines , Apple Pay, and several banks. Trump administration officials have said the outages are not being caused by cyberattacks, but are rather being caused by a recent set of upgrades to systems, many of which run on older technology. Those systems are now in need of more frequent security and bug fixes as AI makes it easier and faster to discover vulnerabilities. At present, a message on Allstate’s website advises customers trying to log in that its services aren’t available, and that the company is “working to restore access as soon as possible.” On X, Allstate is employing what appear to be automated replies to customer complaints , asking them to DM the Allstate account with more information. Downdetector , a crowdsourced outage-reporting website, shows users began reporting Allstate’s outage from Monday morning. However, the company hasn’t yet issued a formal statement about the disruption, what’s causing it, or when it may be resolved. In the meantime, local insurance agents have been fielding calls and emails from customers who aren’t able to use the company’s online services. The timing of the outage is particularly bad given that Thanksgiving is a big travel holiday in the U.S., which means there will be car accidents. Customers will be left without a way to get in touch with their auto insurer to file claims and get roadside assistance through Allstate’s app. Allstate did not immediately return a request for comment. On Wednesday evening, after publication, the company sent the following statement (below). It did not answer questions about the outage’s cause or planned resolution. Allstate customers can reach us in many ways, including online, by phone and through local offices. Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims. To the extent service interruptions impact a customer’s ability to make a payment, they won’t lose coverage or be charged late fees. Updated after publication with Allstate’s comment. events.title: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
events.summary: A D.C.-area train commuter photographed a White House staffer’s laptop and notes, which showed a draft plan for the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History. Photo illustration by Jovelle Tamayo/ProPublica. Source images: obtained by ProPublica, Elizabeth Frantz for ProPublica. A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums. In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.” Read More Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens. In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure. “No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.” Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public. “We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said. Pingree’s letter comes in response to ProPublica reporting on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year. Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance. The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story. Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in his letter . “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.” Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence. Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.” “The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” Padilla wrote . Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media. “Over my dead body,” he wrote . The post Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: How should investors evaluate performance?
events.summary: Why fund performance needs a detailed review in concentrated marketsA fund’s headline return tells only part of the story. Before selling a fund that has underperformed its benchmark, investors should ask why and whether it still meets their needs.This matters when a small group of companies dominate stock market returns. A fund that spreads its investments more widely may underperform a concentrated index. That does not necessarily mean its manager has made poor decisions. Equally, diversification should not become an excuse for weak stock picking.There could also be a big impact on pensions, which play a vital role in people’s financial futures. We want pension schemes to deliver long-term value for savers. Firms and asset owners should look at the bigger picture, including a fund manager’s stated investment objective, strategy and style.How market concentration makes a real difference to returnsWhen a handful of stocks drive market performance, a manager’s decision on how much to invest in them can have a significant effect on returns.The ‘Magnificent Seven’ (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Tesla) illustrate the point. Together, they made up about 34% of the S&P 500 Index on 11 November 2026, according to Bloomberg. They also accounted for around 25% of the MSCI World Index in October 2026.Managers seeking a more diversified portfolio may hold less of these companies than the index does. If those stocks continue to outperform, the fund may deliver lower returns than the index. For investors, the challenge is to work out whether a fund has underperformed because of the investment approach or by poor decisions. Looking only at the headline return number can’t answer that question.Start with the fund’s purposeMost investors hold a fund as part of a wider portfolio. They may have chosen it for exposure to a particular region, smaller companies, an investment style or a sustainability goal. Others may want it to generate income.So, the first question isn’t simply: ‘Did this fund beat the market?’Instead, investors should ask: ‘Is this fund fulfilling its intended role?’That means looking at its stated objective, strategy and style (for example, whether it invests in particular countries or sectors, or favours value or growth companies). Investors should also consider the portfolio’s overall balance of risk and return and the timeframe for assessing results.A fund chosen to bring a different investment approach to a portfolio should be assessed with that purpose in mind. Its contribution cannot always be judged by comparing it with a broad market index alone.Understand the benchmark and the risksA market index can be a useful benchmark, but investors need to understand how the fund uses it.Fund documents should clearly explain the investment strategy, the benchmark’s role and any important investment styles or biases. Before buying a fund, investors should understand why and when it might perform differently from its benchmark.If a fund underperforms because of an investment approach that was clearly disclosed to investors, they may have good reason to stay invested. The fund may be behaving as expected and still serving its purpose within the wider portfolio.But clear disclosure is not a free pass. Investors should also examine whether the manager has made good investment decisions when putting that approach into practice.Separate investment style from stock-picking skillConsider a fund with a disclosed ‘value’ style. Investors may have chosen it to help balance the risks and potential returns of their overall portfolio.That fund could underperform a broad market benchmark when other investment styles are doing better. This alone would not mean it offers poor value.The next step is to examine what drove its returns. Looking at the reasons behind a fund’s performance and comparing it with an appropriate value-focused benchmark can help investors assess how well the manager is picking stocks.The aim is to check that the fund’s style is not masking poor investment decisions. If the investment approach was not clearly explained, or stock picking has been weak despite taking that approach into account, investors may reconsider whether to stay invested.Before switching, they should apply the same scrutiny to any new fund: how might it perform in different market conditions, what will drive its returns, and how will it fit into their portfolio?Look at value in the roundOur Assessment of Value rules require authorised fund managers to assess their funds’ value annually. This means considering performance alongside factors such as costs and service quality.We expect managers to account for disclosed style biases when assessing performance. In our industry feedback in 2021 and 2023, we highlighted the need to clearly explain these biases and the associated risk of underperforming market benchmarks in fund documents.The proposed Value for Money framework for workplace pensions also considers performance, costs and service quality. This should encourage pension schemes to assess how different investments contribute to their objectives over time.Ask better questions before sellingThe message is not to ignore underperformance. It’s to understand it before acting.Investors should ask whether the fund is delivering what they were led to expect, whether the manager’s investment decisions stand up to scrutiny, and whether it still belongs in the wider portfolio.Those using consultants should ask how their analysis answers these questions. A considered decision starts with the bigger picture – not just the headline return.

events.title: German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets
events.summary: German businesses are optimistic about Africa, but Berlin's cautious approach to risk is holding them back from cashing in on the opportunities that their competitors from countries like the UAE and Turkey are seizing. "Africa is a land of opportunity." "The German-African relationship is a win-win." "The continent is the market of the future." That's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the sixth edition of the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana. While these descriptions aren't new, there's a palpable sense of urgency and seriousness this time. German firms are increasingly viewing Africa as an attractive destination as they scramble to find new markets amid wars in Ukraine and Iran, high energy prices, punishing US tariffs and slowing growth in traditional markets like China. "For a long time, many German companies had a secure source of revenue from the major export markets in North America and China, but the geopolitical ruptures of our time have undermined this certainty," German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said during the event. "One could also say that it is time for new horizons, time to take a closer look at economic opportunities still waiting for us." Africa is home to some of the fastest growing economies in the world, like Ethiopia and Rwanda. Even as European and other advanced economies contend with declining working-age populations, Africa is expected to add hundreds of millions of workers in the next few decades, emerging as a key source of future labor. Germany has already signed a migration pact with Kenya and is working on one with Ghana as it seeks to attract skilled workers to help ease acute labor shortages in certain sectors at home. Even as Africa remains one of the poorest regions in the world, economic growth in parts of the continent has created a larger and more affluent consumer class over the past three decades. This group is aspirational and a growing source of demand for many of the goods that German firms want to sell, from cars to cosmetics. The continent, with its mineral wealth and renewable energy potential , is central to European Union efforts to diversify its sources of critical raw materials and reduce reliance on China-dominated supply chains. It is also playing an increasingly important role in strengthening the EU's energy security after the bloc phased out most energy imports from Russia. German firms have committed to invest billions of euros in green hydrogen projects in countries such as Mauritania and Namibia. "We don't have the capital to develop them [natural resources]. So foreign investors are coming to help us develop those resources. Whilst we are getting jobs and industrialization is taking place, they are also making profits," said Amin Amidu Sulemani, energy and infrastructure commissioner at the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). "It's not a relationship where we send raw materials outside of Africa every time, when we can actually process them here," he told DW. What is wrong with Germany's Africa strategy? Despite Africa's growing economic appeal, many obstacles to investment remain, including corruption and governance concerns, unreliable energy supplies, foreign exchange risk and poor infrastructure. African leaders say they are working to address these challenges and improve the ease of doing business. Yet while German companies have largely remained on the sidelines, competitors from countries such as the UAE, Turkey and India have made significant inroads across the continent. German firms enjoy a strong reputation in Africa because of their engineering expertise, vocational training programs and long-term industrial investments, which are more likely to create stable jobs than investments in extractive industries. However, they have struggled to translate that goodwill into a larger commercial presence. Africa, for instance, accounts for less than 2% of the total foreign investment made by German firms over the past several decades. Business leaders complain that German firms lack adequate financing and risk protection for projects in Africa. They also criticize excessive bureaucracy and the absence of a coherent German strategy, with engagement fragmented across ministries and agencies. Industry bodies say German institutions and firms often perceive risks too broadly, treating diverse African markets as if they pose the same level of risk. "German companies can be a bit more bold and maybe also innovative in the way they approach the continent," Khadi Camara, deputy CEO of the German-African Business Association, told DW. "We see that in the companies that are successful, they don't do business as usual. Every country has its nuances that companies keep in mind and say, okay, this model works here, that model works there.

events.summary: Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates. The company said around 6% of its customers were affected and blamed stolen credentials for the breach. Todoist said the attacker used stolen credentials to access the company’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23. The hacker then changed employee access controls and reached the app’s cloud infrastructure via an employee’s work account. The hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist users whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the company said. Todoist said it has blocked the attack path and reset passwords as a mitigation step, as well as disabled the Todoist for Outlook email add-on. For a small number of people, about 0.001% of its userbase, the hacker also searched through tasks, comments, and attachment names to look for credentials for other services, like API keys and access tokens. The hacker also pulled Todoist API tokens and Slack integration tokens, and looked for emails, addresses, and attachment file names through the Todoist for Outlook extension if it was connected to accounts and had permission to read emails. The company said it has sent a notice to those affected and asked them to reset their credentials and change their login details in other places with the same password. The company is asking users to also update API tokens, reconnect integrations, and revoke or replace any access keys, recovery phrases, or credentials they had stored in Todoist comments. Todoist said it has also reset its internal access structure and how remote command execution works in its cloud environment to prevent such incidents in the future. Todoist’s founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić apologized to users about the incident on X , and said the company will take a closer look at why it happened. The to-do app’s data breach is the latest in a burgeoning list of data breaches in which hackers use stolen credentials to access data and systems at enterprises. events.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
events.summary: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store. The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out. According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement. One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents. Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers. Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter. Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported. Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment. events.title: JetBrains finds agents may cheat with open source
events.summary: JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round. The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation. Like its predecessor , Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 is a collection of tasks that evaluates how well AI coding agents work with the Kotlin programming language , in order to help Kotlin programmers decide which agent-model configurations to use. The tasks include fixing tricky problems in Kotlin code across different domains, and making corrections to multiple files. Dirty data The revised benchmar k now includes 30 Kotlin multi-file code problems that have not been exposed to the public in any way before. The revised test all but guarantees that the agents have not encountered this set of problems, or potential solutions, before. Another 70 tasks are based on code that resides in public repositories. The test also blocked all network access for the open source tasks, except for what was needed to communicate with the model itself. This minimized the possibility that the agent could look for an existing answer already posted, perhaps through a patch or pull request. A 30-minute limit was set for each task. Overall, the agents were significantly less accurate when solving problems on codebases they had never encountered. Top resolution rates dropped rather suspiciously from 86.2 percent on tasks based on open source repositories to 60 percent on those based on closed source repositories. Although the agents lacked network access, JetBrains boffins theorized that they might have benefited from encountering and internalizing these open source repositories during training. Only the private repositories were completely new to them. Also curious was how a different set of models excelled at the closed source problems, compared to those models that usually did better on the open source tasks. Leaderboard Shakeup When restricted to closed source tasks, two dark horse models rose to the top: Gemini 3.8 Flash, via Antigravity CLI, topped the list with a 60 percent success rate, closely followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (running on OpenCode) at 58.9 percent. Of the two, the open weight DeepSeek was far cheaper (at $0.08 per task) than the closed weight Gemini ($1.74 per task), however. In contrast, Opus 5.5 completed only 53.3 percent of the tasks at $1.21 per task, and Fable 5.1 completed only 44.4 percent of the tasks, at a luxurious $3.27 per task. Claude Code harnessed both of these models. Claude’s lackluster completion rates on closed source tasks are somewhat sus given how both of these Anthropic models scored significantly higher on tasks using open source materials. In fact Claude ran the table when it came to open source: Fable 5.1 topped the charts with 86.2 percent accuracy, closely followed by Opus 5.5 at 84.8 percent accuracy. (Kotlin users will pay dearly for the extra sliver of Anthropic accuracy: The average cost of Fable completing a Kotlin cleanup task runs $2.38, while Opus could do the job for $0.68.) Gaming the boss One possible interpretation of these disparate numbers is that models are drawing from their own knowledge bases instead of reasoning from scratch. Whether this is cheating or the models simply working as intended might be more a matter of philosophical debate. Mark Hinkle, founder of the AIE Network consultancy, suspects the issue of integrity may go deeper. "Private code doesn't stop reward hacking, it changes the shortcut," he wrote to The Register on LinkedIn. "On public code the agent goes and finds the answer somebody has already published. On private code there's no answer to find, so it satisfies whatever is checking it. I treat these things like entry-level employees, and a sharp new hire figures out fast what the boss actually looks at." JetBrains did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but concluded in its post that more investigation is needed. It promises that its people will pore over the open source results to see if any have been contaminated by the LLMs' own memory. It also plans to run its own static analysis tool, Qodana , against the results to check for errors. Sireesha Pulipati , a staff data engineer and AI observer, suggested, also by LinkedIn, that JetBrains may have needed more specificity in its agent instructions. "Out of the box [an agent] tends to reach for generic patterns. But when we give it instructions and skills that tell it where to look for our patterns and context, it follows them. A well-controlled harness, with those standards built in, is what makes the agent useful," Pulipati wrote. So good on JetBrains for providing Kotlin users some information about working with AI, but, as always, AI benchmarks should be approached with extreme side-eye. ®

events.title: Almost 60% of primary energy used for electricity is lost to conversion and transmission
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) How does EIA compare different types of energy? Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review Note: Btu=British thermal units To compare production and consumption across different resources, we convert to a common energy metric, British thermal units (Btu), which typically measures the heat content of the fuels such as petroleum, natural gas, and coal that are burned for energy. For energy sources such as hydropower, wind, solar, and geothermal that aren’t combusted to create energy, we apply a constant conversion factor based on the heat content of electricity. For combustible fuels, EIA uses thermal conversion factors to convert the physical units into heat content values. Because these factors can change based on the specific characteristics of fuels being produced at different points in time, we update our conversion factors each year. We publish heat content data for more than 30 petroleum products, 4 types of coal, and natural gas. Each fuel has a unique chemistry and heat content, and the heat content can vary based on the different types of fuel in the mix. For example, the heat content of anthracite coal is higher than the heat content of lignite . The aggregate heat content of coal generally varies based on the mix of the different types of coal produced and consumed. The aggregate heat contents for petroleum consumption and production have declined in recent decades because of decreasing use of residual fuel oil , which has relatively high heat content, and increasing use of fuels with a lower heat content—such as motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and hydrocarbon gas liquids. Our heat content estimates for natural gas have fluctuated within a relatively narrow range because of highly consistent pipeline specifications. Methane, the primary component of natural gas, has a heat content of 1,010 Btu per cubic foot. Other gases such as ethane, biomass gases, synthetic gases, and supplemental gases, which may be left in the natural gas stream, have higher heat content values. Total coal thermal conversion factors depend on the relative mix of coal types consumed and produced that year. Anthracite and bituminous coals have higher heat contents than lignite and subbituminous coals. Subbituminous coal production and consumption have increased over time, bringing down coal’s aggregate heat contents. To measure how efficient a power plant is at converting the fuel into electricity, we use heat rates. While thermal conversion factors measure the heat content of a fuel, heat rates measure the efficiency of power plants to convert fuel into heat and then into electricity. The heat rate is the amount of energy used to generate one kilowatthour (kWh) of electricity. The lower the heat rate, the higher the efficiency of a power plant to convert fuel into electricity. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review Since 2001—the earliest year in our data—heat rates for electricity generation from coal and petroleum have risen slightly, while the heat rate for electricity generation from natural gas has gone down, due in part to more efficient combined-cycle plants coming online. Power plants using nuclear energy and noncombustible renewables —such as hydro, wind, solar, and geothermal—generate electricity without burning fuel. For nuclear energy, EIA uses a measurement of the heat produced from nuclear fission in the reactor core. For noncombustible renewable energy, we use the captured energy approach . Captured energy is the energy available for consumption after converting a renewable resource into electricity, net of conversion losses. The captured energy approach uses the heat content of electricity, which is constant (3,412 Btu/kWh). events.title: U.S. economy grew at rapid 4.3% pace in third quarter
events.summary: Data: Bureau of Economic Analysis ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios The U.S. economy grew substantially faster this summer than initially thought, the government said Wednesday — a blockbuster upgrade to its estimate of third-quarter GDP. By the numbers: The economy expanded at a 4.3% annualized rate, up from the 3.4% initially reported and nearly twice the rate of 2.2% in the second quarter. Why it matters: The economy has even more momentum than previously understood, a sign of remarkable resilience in the face of higher borrowing costs and stubborn inflation that could give the Fed more latitude to raise rates. Zoom in: The upward revision reflected stronger business investment fueled by the AI buildout and software investment, as well as consumer spending. A measure of underlying private-sector demand — which strips out trade, inventories and government spending — rose at a whopping 5.8% annual rate, up from the 4.9% initially reported. The backdrop: Separate data out Wednesday showed personal income jumped 0.7% in October while inflation-adjusted consumer spending stalled, pushing the saving rate up to 4.1% from 3.6% the prior month. The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — climbed 3.8% from a year earlier, from 3.6% in September. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, accelerated to 3.3% from 3.1%. On a monthly basis, both headline and core prices rose 0.3%. The bottom line: The U.S. economy was on remarkably strong footing heading into the end of the year, though inflation remains stubbornly high. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

events.title: US proposes sweeping new tariffs on China, others
events.summary: The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on China, the European Union, and a dozen other trading partners it says have distorted the global market by overproducing goods like automobiles, batteries and chemicals. The so-called excess capacity tariffs , which conclude investigations begun in March, comply with existing trade deals and vary by country. The administration is suggesting a 20% “across the board” tariff on Chinese exports, a senior US official said, which would stack with 2018 tariffs (but not 2026 tariffs targeting forced labor) and exempt goods identified by the Board of Trade. That rate could rise as high as 40% should trade talks collapse, the official added. The US, which previously notified the affected countries, does not expect China to retaliate with anything stronger than a statement: “This is part of that process of establishing stability,” the official said. As for other countries, the official shrugged off the suggestion that the announcement might foster tension: “We actually expect that we may be signing more agreements at the G20 [summit next month] in the wake of these announcements,” the official said. The announcement follows exit polling that found eight in 10 voters believe Trump’s tariffs have harmed the economy. It also comes amid continued fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has provoked bipartisan scrutiny of US-China policy. The official predicted the proposed tariffs could take effect in January “at the earliest,” since the administration must first solicit comments and hold hearings. Similar investigations into Norway and Mexico, meanwhile, remain ongoing. Also on Tuesday night, the administration proposed new tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft. The official attributed these levies to a “lack of progress” on trade talks. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Trump prepares new round of tariffs on China, other U.S. trading partners
events.summary: The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity. Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns. Post-election polling indicates voters overwhelmingly want tariffs to stay at current levels or decline. There's relatively little support — even among Trump's base — for them rising. Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs largely target specific goods, a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed. China is the exception: The proposed 20% tariff would apply to most Chinese imports, with that rate calibrated to preserve the nations' trade truce. These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labor or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior U.S. official said. The official added that the rate could rise to 40% if trade talks break down or China fails to live up to its commitments. Between the lines: The proposed tariff rates for other major trading partners are consistent with parameters set out in trade deals, the official said. Trade deals struck with the EU, Japan and South Korea last year established 15% tariff rates on most goods. Other economies targeted include Taiwan, India, Indonesia and Vietnam. On average, the proposals would raise existing tariff rates on targeted trading partners by roughly 5 percentage points, the official estimated. The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers. The proposed tariffs are subject to a public comment period and hearings, with the levies taking effect as early as January, the official said. What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs , China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations. The prospect of renewed tariffs weighed on global stocks, particularly Asian markets, overnight. U.S. futures were sharply lower early Wednesday as well. Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The administration proposes raising tariffs on sugar imports exceeding existing quotas (regardless of origin) and imposing a 10% levy on previously exempt Brazilian aircraft, a U.S. official said. The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs .

events.title: Why American consumers are still spending and powering the US economy – and why this could soon fizzle
events.summary: Consumer spending has stayed healthy in large part because Americans are staying employed, whether through formal or gig work. AP Photo/David Zalubowski Holiday shopping season is kicking off, inundating consumers with Black Friday offers . With inflation fatigue , declining real wages and stock market turbulence thrown into the mix, is the U.S. consumer on the verge of scaling back? This question has long puzzled economists, who wonder why spending has held up even as consumer sentiment slumps. As a researcher of supply chains who has also worked for years at consumer products companies, I’ve run my own studies and have been surprised, time and again, by how spending has continued at a healthy clip even when the economy is faltering. Most recently, in March 2026, I built a model to assess how the Iran war could affect global supply chains at three, six and nine months out. In the case of consumer behavior, the hit was less than what was expected. Even though Americans were paying substantially more at the gas pump due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as dealing with tariff-induced inflation and high interest rates , consumer spending held up remarkably well . I now believe I missed two things: resilience and innovation. More specifically, Americans are continuing to work, whether in formal or gig jobs, and that’s the main factor holding up spending. And as long as consumers have income, they’ll keep finding a way. What’s changing, though, is that this balancing act is getting harder for many people to keep up. What resilience looks like Resilience and innovation may sound admirable, but in practice they’re often difficult and onerous. Under “innovation,” some traditional adjustments for consumers include buying cheaper “private label” or store brands , shopping at off-brand and discount stores , or relentlessly hunting for deals . Other adjustments include eating more meals at home rather than going out, or downsizing vacation plans . “Resilience,” meanwhile, can mean taking on extra work. Economists call this the added worker effect , and it shows up during tough times. During the 2007-09 Great Recession, for example, more married women joined the labor force as unemployment rose among their spouses. In 2026, there’s an uptick in retirees heading back to work as well as an increase in the share of mothers with children who are staying in or reentering the workforce . These are both responses to the rising cost of living. More broadly, Americans are using traditional and nontraditional means to make some extra cash. About 1 in 3 workers has had a side hustle in 2026, according to the jobs database ZipRecruiter – whether it’s nanny jobs, side gigs on Etsy, delivering meals for DoorDash or driving customers for Uber. For many Americans, this work is a necessity, not just a way to earn extra discretionary cash. The increasing need for extra work over the past five years underscores the drop in purchasing power from the salaries many people earn. More Americans, including retirees in need of extra income, are taking up gig work, like driving for Uber. AP Photo/Emily Wang Fujiyama Another form of resilience can be seen through volunteering and charitable giving. In my own neighborhood, a food bank that started during the COVID-19 pandemic has helped many in the community over the past five years. Across the country, food bank donations and charitable giving continue to rise despite economic challenges. According to Giving USA, charitable giving rose to US$617 billion in 2025, surpassing the $600 billion mark for the first time. This increase addresses a growing need for food banks to feed Americans who can’t afford basic groceries anymore. At the same time, the actual number of donors is dropping. Shoppers are hitting the limit Many consumers are now running out of levers to pull. Wealthier Americans are continuing to spend at a strong clip , which is why official consumer spending data suggests the economy is steady. But it’s a different picture for the rest. One in four families are spending more than they make , as seen by rising credit delinquency and auto repossessions, according to the Atlanta Federal Reserve. Whether it’s food, healthcare, rent or cars, Americans are spending a much larger share of their income on necessities than they did 10 years ago. For especially strapped Americans, like those facing the double whammy of a car payment and a student loan, these trade-offs are especially challenging. A good example are auto loan delinquencies, now near a 10-year high . Losing a car can mean losing a job, with devastating financial consequences . Frontline workers also miss more shifts as gas prices rise . And this gets to a core lesson for understanding today’s economy: The bedrock for consumer spending remains employment. The stable job market we see right now – with unemployment at 4.1% – is critical. If this healthy job market holds and interest rates and energy prices ultimately ease, the average consumer will still tread water. But if inflation continues to run hotter than the Federal Reserve would like, and rates rise , Americans’ disposable income will likely shrink – and hurt economic growth in the process. That could lead to a domino effect: Unemployment rises, reducing the discretionary spending that had been keeping economic growth steady. Whether it comes to this, it’s important to remember that the holiday season isn’t necessarily an accurate forward-looking indicator. Shoppers often go to great lengths to make family and friends happy. The big challenge for consumers will start in early 2027. Will the Fed hike rates? Will inflation stay high? Will gas prices come down? Until these questions are answered, we’re in the “bend but don’t break” phase. Many consumers are facing challenging times in 2026, but their resilience has been a surprise on the upside. I’d like to be surprised again in 2027 – but that’s far from a sure thing. events.title: Gaza group to air defund Israel ad during SNL
events.summary: The Scoop A pro-Palestinian group is stepping up its efforts against U.S. support for Israel, with new polling about the damage it did to Republicans this year and a new ad that will air during Saturday Night Live. The 30-second spot from the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which shared it first with Semafor, contrasts an American girl saving up for a $400 bicycle with a girl in Gaza who lost a leg to Israeli bombs. “Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to do this,” says the ad’s narrator . (The figure is close to the annual US military assistance to Israel.) The ad directs viewers to a new campaign site to rally opposition for Israel funding. And the group’s new polling is a temperature check on Republicans, whose argument about support for Israel has been inflamed since the administration first joined Israel in airstrikes on Iran last summer. Conducted by YouGov from interviews with 636 respondents who voted for President Trump in 2024 but skipped the midterm election, the poll’s main finding was that Israel was a top factor in their change of mind. Twenty-nine percent of the falloff voters said that the decision to attack Iran played a “significant role” in their decision to not vote, and 17% cited “relations with Israel.” Among these 2024 Trump voters, 78% said that “we should reduce U.S. support for Israel.” This polling closes a loop for IMEU’s political arm, which last year interviewed voters who’d voted for Joe Biden over Donald Trump, then sat out the 2024 election . The top issue cited by those non-voters was Gaza, with 29% of them saying they couldn’t have supported Harris without a change in policy. “We are airing this ad because the American people deserve to know where their money is going,” said Margaret DeReus, IMEU’s executive director. “The vast majority of Americans are unaware that President Trump is reportedly on the verge of signing another long-term weapons giveaway to Israel. With this ad, we’re trying to change that.” Trump’s decision to join Israel’s strikes on Iran has divided the right, with some of its most prominent media personalities turning on the president, while most Republicans continue to support it. The conversation about questioning funds for Israel was also changed by Abdul El-Sayed’s win in Michigan’s Senate race. There, Republicans and some Democrats complained about a Rebellion PAC ad that portrayed a couple cutting their grocery budget to pay more tax money to Israel. El-Sayed’s victory convinced many activists that the figures and organizations ruling some Israel criticism as “anti-semitism” are badly out of touch with voters – as proved by the controversial ad. “It tested through the roof,” Rebellion PAC founder Cenk Uygur told Semafor. “Moved undecideds by double digits to Abdul. Probably the most popular ad in the online world. And was partially responsible for getting Trump to say he’d end funding on Election Day. Walk-off homer.” David’s view Support for America’s current relationship with Israel is lower now than it’s been in decades, with young voters driving the decline. Republicans worked this year to make this a problem for Democrats, who now roundly oppose military aid to Israel, to the extent that Chuck Schumer’s consistent support for it has become an issue for opponents of him leading their new Senate majority. The math is different for Republicans, but the disagreement has been happening in public all year. It blew up with Vice President JD Vance’s reaction to the midterm disaster. The GOP coalition is, obviously, nothing like the Democratic coalition; most support for Israel and for disarming Iran comes from evangelical Christians who vote overwhelmingly not Republican, not Jewish voters who still largely support Democrats. I’d be surprised if Republicans react to the IMEU’s polling as anything more than meddling by actors who want both parties to cut off the Jewish state. But we are in a moment of post-midterm, pre-presidential primary plasticity, where people with resources will try to influence what both parties are talking about. Room for Disagreement Sam Markstein, the political director of the Republican Jewish Coalition, told Semafor that the GOP was now the country’s only “pro-Israel party,” and that any effort to turn it against the Jewish state was going to fail. If voters wanted a party with that agenda, he said, they now had the Democrats. “Making sure that Iran doesn’t have a nuclear weapon will go down as one of the great decisions of any presidency,” he said. Notable Last week, Axios reporter Marc Caputo published polling conducted for the Combat Antisemitism Movement , which found widespread support for Israel in early primary states, suggesting “a potential disconnect between GOP voters’ attitudes and the sentiments of those who often draw the most attention online.” U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee told the Institute for National Security Studies that Republicans were now more supportive of Israel than Democrats, and that the president’s talk about halting aid may not pan out.

events.title: The dopamine hit in markets from Jensen Huang's comeback has already faded
events.summary: Liz’s view The #SaveJensen punch wore off fast. The dopamine hit from Huang’s comeback that sent shares surging 31% on Monday has already faded as investors remember why they’d been selling: AI money is too expensive, AI demand too tenuous, AI politics too uncertain. By Tuesday, Nvidia’s shares had closed at their July 2025 levels. Markets can be wrong, for a shockingly long time. But the laws of financial gravity are catching up to AI and its frontman at speeds that are hard to outrun. Over the past year, you’d have done better owning the largest landlord of American malls than Nvidia, which holds a near monopoly on the key component of the most transformative technology in human history. Huang himself did little to help. A chastened CEO might have slipped back into headquarters, quietly mumbling something about getting to work and promising to address the corporate governance minefield he left behind. Instead he accepted a hero’s welcome and doubled down on the very things , like a lack of succession planning and dozens of direct reports, that precipitated one of the most acute and costly corporate crises in recent memory. In remarks to employees Tuesday, he said he has no plans to change any of the structural weaknesses that caused it. (He is, he noted, in therapy.) Monday will go into the record books as the largest single-day value creation in market history: Nvidia added $1 trillion. But it will end up a reverse Groundhog Day — one we immediately forget as investors sober up and remember why they were discontent in the first place. Notable Huang’s return to Nvidia will also be tough on China, Bloomberg columnist Catherine Thorbecke writes. “His comeback puts both him and his arguments [about China] under an even harsher spotlight,” she argues. “And Chinese AI’s forced breakup with Nvidia is likely to only get uglier .”

In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent. The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. Real GDP was revised up 0.9 percentage point from the advance estimate, primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending. For more information, refer to the " Technical Notes " below. Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers , the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 5.8 percent in the third quarter, revised up 0.9 percentage point from the previous estimate. The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 2.7 percent in the third quarter, revised down 0.3 percentage point from the previous estimate. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, both the same as previously estimated. Real gross domestic income (GDI) increased 4.4 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent (revised) in the second quarter. The average of real GDP and real GDI also increased 4.4 percent, compared with an increase of 2.2 percent (revised). Profits from current production (corporate profits with inventory valuation and capital consumption adjustments) increased $206.0 billion in the third quarter, compared with an increase of $384.0 billion in the second quarter. events.title: Anthropic stock tumble shows IPO gamesmanship
events.summary: IPO allocation gamesmanship strikes again, this time at Anthropic. Anthropic shares fell below their $83-a-share IPO price on Tuesday, careening toward the original target of $78 a share. The listing was reportedly six times oversubscribed, so where did those buyers go? Investors in anticipated deals ask for more shares than they actually want, assuming they’ll be cut back. “If it sounds oversubscribed, they inflate their orders, and then it gets more oversubscribed, and so on,” said Jay Ritter, academia’s godfather of IPO research. “It’s not the same as actual desire to own the stock.” He notes that pension funds, the classic buy-and-hold investors, tend to be cut out entirely of IPO allocations. Investment banks tend to steer shares to favored hedge-fund clients likely to sell into an IPO pop (Anthropic shares opened last week above $111, a first-trade gain of 34%). Supply and demand are now fighting it out, which is harder for a $1 trillion-plus company with a murky path to profitability — just ask SpaceX, whose shares are down 22% since its IPO. And Ritter? He put in an order in his Schwab account for 3,000 shares. He got 51. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: South Africa baobab trees replanted after smuggling attempt
events.summary: Five baobabs have been replanted in a South African nature reserve after being uprooted and trucked to Durban’s port, where they were going to be illegally exported. A landscaping company had sold the two-century-old trees, revered in many parts of Africa, to a customer in the Caucasus country of Georgia without seeking permission from the authorities, the South Africa-based conservation charity Baobab Foundation — instrumental in saving the trees — told Semafor. After a three-day, 900 kilometer-journey on huge flatbed vehicles, the 7 meter to 9 meter high baobabs were returned to the soil. There is no systematic data collection on baobab smuggling, but others across the continent have told the Foundation of similar incidents targeting the trees, which for some serve as shrines and a connection with the spirit world, while also providing food, shade, and a meeting place. — Damian Zane

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Win4Wine runs the genuine Explorer shell atop Linux Microsoft fixes Office dialog that had nothing to say and wouldn't go away 23 hours ago 9/UX brings a classic Mac feel to 9front 2 days ago Old-school Linux desktops find fresh routes to Wayland 3 days ago Palo Alto Networks opens wallet for open-weight training biz 6 days ago XXRI-OS explores the lowest end of the Linux desktop 6 days ago Win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years. It runs Windows XP's genuine Explorer shell through patched Wine on Debian 13, with a custom window manager integrating Linux applications into the desktop. As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons." This impressive, possibly demented project has English installation instructions and a README, although its design documents are in Japanese. We found Mozilla's built-in translation handled those pretty well. Its developer goes by miKuta0407 on GitHub, their homepage , and X . Also note, you're going to need some Windows installation media for the full experience. The README says: "No Microsoft files are included. Only the files that are needed are extracted locally from your own ISO." It supports Windows XP Professional SP3 installation images in 32-bit Japanese or English editions, with an experimental option for Windows 7 SP1 x64. Without either Windows image, it can download and use ReactOS's free software shell instead, for what it terms "a Windows 2000-like classic look." In our view, that sounds much better anyway. Before any former Windows users cry hurray and reach for an optical drive, this is not some ready-to-run project. The top of the README warns: "This is a personal, experimental project, not a finished product for daily use." The developer has tested it only on a fresh Debian 13 installation and recommends a VM or spare machine, rather than an existing working desktop, which sounds like an excellent precaution to us. Also, before you ask, yes, it was vibe-coded with Claude. We found ourselves reminded of another crazy-but-is-it project that we wrote about back in January: What if Linux ran Windows... and meant it? Meet Loss32 . The Loss32 proposal was even more extreme. It suggested replacing essentially the entire Linux userland, so it would be a Linux kernel running Wine with a Windows desktop and Windows apps. However, Mikuta-san was way ahead of us – lower down, the README mentions and even links to Loss32. Saying that, since it launched at the end of 2025, the bottom of the Loss32 web page shows a couple of updates, reporting on delays in getting it working. That, to be honest, did not shock us, but we still admire the let's-do-this spirit. The developer also seems to have got slightly distracted by a previous project, touchHLE: high-level emulator for early iOS apps . Loss32, in turn, reminded us of Neptune OS, an attempt to give seL4 a Windows personality transplant . We wrote about that back in 2022, and work on it has continued: the project page shows updates in recent months. The team has also pushed out preview releases in 2022, 2024, 2025, and most recently in September. This OS face transplant also reminded us of our article, Classic 7 is Windows 10 LTSC cosplaying as Windows 7 . Some people really miss the look and feel of vintage Windows. Can someone do Windows NT 4 next, please?

events.title: Senegal restored as AFCON champions
events.summary: Senegal were reinstated as the winners of Africa’s top football competition, after a court in Switzerland overturned a decision by the sport’s continental governing body that had declared Morocco the champions. January’s Africa Cup of Nations final in Rabat descended into chaos after Senegalese players walked off the pitch to protest refereeing decisions, only to return after some 15 minutes and go on to win the game. Eight weeks later, the Confederation of African Football annulled their victory over the walkout, handing Morocco the title. But the Lausanne-based Court of Arbitration for Sport disagreed, respecting the decision of the referee to continue the match. The extraordinary episode threatened to question the integrity of the CAF under the leadership of South African billionaire Patrice Motsepe. Senegal’s football federation celebrated, declaring on Instagram: “ Again and always African champions.” But Morocco said it will look for ways to challenge the ruling. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: MTN and Telkom talks draw South Africa union fire
events.summary: South Africa’s biggest trade union federation backed workers angry at their exclusion from discussions over telecoms giant MTN’s potential takeover of partly state-owned Telkom, escalating political scrutiny of a proposed transaction that could reshape one of Africa’s largest mobile markets. COSATU is supporting its affiliate, the Communications Workers Union, which said employees have not been consulted over the proposed $2 billion-plus deal and is demanding disclosure about its potential impact on jobs and collective agreements. MTN, Africa’s largest mobile operator by subscribers, is in early talks to buy one-time monopoly Telkom in a purchase that will also test the state’s willingness to relinquish its 40% shareholding and allow further consolidation in the sector. CWU has already warned against further privatization of the government’s strategic interest in Telkom. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Nigeria holds interest rate before January elections
events.summary: Nigeria’s central bank held its benchmark interest rate at 23%, with its governor expressing confidence that West Africa’s largest economy was stable ahead of crunch elections in January. The bank’s rate-setting committee pointed to slowing inflation, which has eased for five consecutive months, but noted that continued tensions in the Middle East “could sustain pressure on energy prices .” Fuel prices have surged this year in Nigeria due to supply shortfalls connected to the Iran war, despite the country being Africa’s largest crude oil producer and exporter. Higher prices are driving cost-of-living concerns that have become a central campaign issue between the leading candidates in the presidential poll, re-igniting a debate around the wisdom of President Bola Tinubu’s removal of a yearslong fuel subsidy. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: The Download: AI swamping open records, and firefighting for permafrost
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI is straining America’s open records systems AI has intensified investors’ interest in public records. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests. As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent. Find out how AI is testing the limits of America’s right to know . —Matthew King MIT Technology Review Narrated: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and soil insulating the permafrost below. Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground. Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking? This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Hackers reportedly used an AI tool to breach US spy agencies The tool, Artex, was originally designed for cyber defense. An LLM can easily churn through a hundred thousand times more words than a person will experience in the process of mastering their mother tongue. This yawning divide between children and machines is called the data efficiency gap. It raises a tantalizing question for researchers: How can children learn so much with so little? By reverse-engineering how they learn, scientists hope to create more efficient AI models—and perhaps settle enduring questions about language and children’s developing minds. events.title: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to step down next week amid IPO uncertainty
events.summary: Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above), who steered Flipkart through Walmart’s acquisition in 2018 and helped build it into one of India’s biggest e-commerce companies, is stepping down as chief executive next week after more than 11 years with the company. On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the company until a replacement is found. A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy’s last day at Flipkart will be December 4. Krishnamurthy joined Flipkart in 2015 from Tiger Global, one of the company’s early investors, and became its CEO in 2017. He remained at the helm after Walmart acquired a controlling stake in the company for $16 billion in 2018. Under Krishnamurthy, Flipkart said its business grew more than five-fold. The company has more than 500 million registered users and over 1.4 million sellers, including those on Shopsy, its low-cost shopping platform. The company’s marketplace offers over 150 million products across more than 80 categories. Flipkart has of late moved into newer segments, including quick-commerce through Flipkart Minutes and, more recently, food delivery through a venture called Eat-in by Minutes . The expansion is targeted at Indian consumers who are increasingly turning to quick-delivery services for everything from groceries to electronics. Thiagarajan joined Flipkart in September last year to lead its product and technology teams. Before that, he had founded Kasu.ai , a Bay Area startup working on AI assistants for corporate finance. He also previously worked at Google, Microsoft, and Uber in senior engineering positions, per his LinkedIn profile . Krishnamurthy’s exit comes amid uncertainty around Flipkart’s IPO. In March, the company moved its headquarters from Singapore to India as part of its preparations to go public, but in May, Walmart reportedly told Flipkart to delay its IPO and focus on becoming profitable first . Walmart declined to comment beyond its announcement when asked what prompted Krishnamurthy’s departure, and whether the leadership change would affect Flipkart’s IPO plans. Flipkart did not respond to a request for comment. Founded in 2007 by Sachin and Binny Bansal as an online bookstore, much like its bigger rival Amazon, Flipkart eventually expanded into other categories. Under Krishnamurthy, it has grown into India’s largest online retailer by gross merchandise value, ahead of Amazon. “Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled and his many contributions to the company,” Chris Nicholas, president and CEO, Walmart International, said in a statement.
