events.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade. On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance. In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week. “When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said. Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly , the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion. Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year.

events.title: Africa’s cashless revolution faces AI challenge
events.summary: Alexis’s view The phrase “cash is king” remains true across Africa in a way that it doesn’t in other parts of the world. In many African countries, the informal economy dominates and the flow of cash unites millions of entrepreneurs. But it’s also true that the continent has for years been at the vanguard of digital payments: That provides policymakers with more visibility into economic activity, expands the tax base, and improves the efficiency of revenue collection. The small businesses that drive African economies are increasingly making use of cheaper mobile phone handsets to swap cash for digital payments, a new report suggests. Overall transactions using mobile phones in Africa last year were more than double the figure of 2021, according to digital payment research group AfricaNenda Foundation. The average amount spent on each mobile transfer nearly halved over the same period, suggesting digital systems are increasingly being used for everyday purchases , rather than larger one-off transactions. These changing habits have far-reaching consequences. At an individual level, a digital transaction history can help to build a credit history. Some countries are even going further, linking payment systems to national digital IDs. But at the same time, AI poses a raft of new challenges by making it easier, cheaper, and faster for criminals to set up scams, such as deepfakes, to trick people into authorizing payments. A recent Interpol report found AI was linked to more than half of cybercrime in Africa , with losses across 26 nations more than doubling in 2025 compared with the previous year. Cash has remained popular because people trust money they can hold. Now that so many people in Africa have learned to trust digital payments, the next big challenge for policymakers and financial institutions is to protect users against the evolution of fraud. Notable AXIAN Digibank & Fintech, which operates across Madagascar, Tanzania, Senegal, Togo, and the Comoros Islands , signed an agreement with Huawei to upgrade mobile money platforms.

events.title: Microsoft 365 Backup stretches recovery window to ten years
events.summary: Recovery windows of up to ten years are now available in Microsoft 365 Backup for OneDrive and SharePoint, up from a previous maximum of two. The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years. Administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten. Microsoft's list price is $0.15 per GiB per month of protected content. Extended windows can increase costs by keeping deleted data billable for longer. Switching to a longer recovery window will also not make backups for that period magically available. So no nostalgic trips back to 2016. Wider recovery windows may appeal to organizations that need access to older data, but backups are not a substitute for compliance retention and archiving. Recovery after a breach or ransomware attack is also critical, particularly getting back to a healthy state before any malware seeped into files. Microsoft says backups are physically redundant and geographically replicated while respecting the tenant's data residency requirements. Full OneDrive account and SharePoint site restores offer recovery points every ten minutes for the most recent two weeks, then weekly points through the configured window, up to ten years. Individual file and folder recovery is limited to recovery points from the most recent 14 days, regardless of the configured window. Restore remains free, which is handy since regular testing is a vital part of any disaster recovery plan. The arrival of a ten-year recovery window is good for enterprises that need it and have deep enough pockets. However, it is important to keep in mind that being able to configure a longer recovery window doesn't constitute a disaster recovery plan in itself and may be overkill in many instances. Microsoft notes: "The existing one-year default recovery window remains unchanged. Longer recovery windows must be configured on the applicable backup policies." The company also recommends that users "review your organization's SharePoint and OneDrive backup requirements to determine whether longer recovery windows are needed." A decade of recovery history could be valuable. It also means a decade of data to account for when setting budgets, access controls, and retention policies. ®

events.title: Amazon to flog motors in Britain, but Prime won't deliver
events.summary: Amazon is channeling its inner car salesman as it prepares to flog motors on the UK arm of its online tat bazaar. Amazon Autos will launch in Britain in early 2027, its first expansion outside the US, where it debuted in December 2024. Customers can browse and reserve cars online before completing the purchase with a dealer. Hoping it will be "a nice little earner," Amazon will let punters view real-time dealer inventory, prices, get an instant trade-in valuation, and connect with a local dealer to reserve a car, "all on Amazon." In the US, the service now covers more than 150 cities and offers vehicles from 35 brands. Hyundai is the first announced UK carmaker partner, while dealer group Vertu Motors will list used vehicles. More brands and dealers are due to be confirmed before launch. Hyundai's launch range will include electric, hybrid, and petrol models. "Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon," said Matt Nuffort, director of Amazon Autos International. Of course, buying a car isn't quite like adding an air fryer or a memory stick to your basket. How does financing and checkout work for UK buyers? Customers will complete the purchase and paperwork at their chosen dealership. Amazon is not offering financing itself, but buyers can explore financing options via the site, adjusting terms like deposit and duration to see how monthly payments change. Credit applications must be completed with the dealer. In the US, buyers can submit a credit application through the platform, review terms and conditions, then sign electronic contracts online. They typically pay a deposit and visit the dealership to complete the remaining paperwork and pick up the vehicle. Buyers shouldn't expect their new car to arrive in an enormous cardboard box with a smiley logo on it, or to be lowered onto their driveway by a giant Amazon delivery drone. But given that one of the online retailer's flying delivery robots crashed into someone's garage after making a drop-off near Detroit last week, perhaps that's for the best. ®

events.title: Saudi Arabia can fund a ‘prolonged’ war, Finance Minister says
events.summary: The News Saudi Arabia can withstand the regional war without derailing its finances, Finance Minister Mohammed Al Jadaan said, warning adversaries that missile attacks on civilian targets won’t force the kingdom’s hand. The idea that Saudi Arabia “can be blackmailed” by missile attacks on civilian targets “is a total mistake,” Al Jadaan told reporters in Riyadh. “We’re resilient enough to stand a prolonged conflict.” The kingdom has only modestly increased its defense budget after nine months of war and can significantly boost military spending if required, the minister said. “We have no price tag, we have no cap in terms of how much we can provide to our military if they need supplies.” Saudi Arabia’s finances have stood up to almost a year of unprecedented challenges from conflict in the region and disruptions to oil exports without dipping into reserves, Al Jadaan said. Higher oil prices have offset lower export volumes this year, helping total government revenue beat earlier expectations. The non-oil economy is growing despite supply chain disruptions and strains on efforts to attract tourists. But higher oil prices haven’t been enough to keep the economy running, and the government boosted spending to soften the impact, widening the deficit to 4.9% of GDP compared to forecast of a 3.3% deficit before the war. The kingdom plans to cut spending next year as some investment projects are completed and the government seeks to contain the deficit, which it expects to narrow to 3.6% of GDP. No ‘good time to reform’ Over the past year, Saudi Arabia has dropped some of its most expensive projects , including the 170-kilometer twin skyscrapers at NEOM, as it reins in runaway spending. Al Jadaan drew a distinction between projects used to achieve longer term economic goals and the overall vision for the kingdom’s economic development. “If some of the tools are not right for the moment, we’ll change them,” Jadaan said. “If some need to be warehoused, we’ll warehouse them … Vision 2030 is way beyond just one program or one project.” The economy is expected to contract 3.3% this year before bouncing back with 7.9% growth in 2027. Much of that is down to lower oil output. Corporate profits for listed companies rose around 15% in the first nine months of 2026, Al Jadaan said, indicating that the private sector growth is robust. The government expects to keep running a deficit. Debt-to-GDP is forecast to hit 39% by 2029, with some economists expecting it could breach a self-imposed 40% ceiling sooner. Al Jadaan sees no reason to increase the limit in the next few years, saying it “serves us well, it brings more discipline.” The kingdom is also pressing ahead with subsidy reforms such as measures to increase power prices from next year. The moves are unpopular and have received rare criticism of the government from Saudi citizens. “There will never be a good time to reform,” Al Jadaan said. “You go with the plan.” Notable Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is planning to travel to the US in December for the G20 Leaders’ summit, Semafor reported. Nine months into the Iran war, Generation MBS are rallying behind the Crown Prince , who they credit for an era of new-found freedoms .

events.title: Asian stocks tank as US tariff reports spook investors
events.summary: Asian stocks tanked and US futures were lower as growing fears of a tech bust compounded investors’ jitters over reports that Washington plans to impose new tariffs on major trading partners. Bond markets are demanding more evidence that Big Tech’s mammoth capex plans will lead to increased revenues, one investor told CNBC. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump is reportedly set to unveil a new set of duties on imports from more than a dozen countries, potentially including China, the EU, and Japan. The market upheaval has reminded some analysts of a huge selloff in late 2018 : At the time, the strength of the US economy was insufficient to mask a broader set of concerns, Citadel’s head of macro strategy noted. — Prashant Rao

events.title: UN warns AIDS is on the rise following Western aid cuts
events.summary: The head of the United Nations’ agency for AIDS said infections worldwide were likely to rise as the worst-affected countries struggle to contain the fallout of Western aid cuts. HIV cases have plummeted from their mid-1990s peak: Data released on Tuesday showed new infections hit a recent low of 1.2 million last year. But early indications point to a reversal of that trend, in part because of US and European budget cuts: UNAIDS has already dismissed half its staff and stopped work in 30 countries. “We are on the cusp of ​ending AIDS … and just when ​we should finish it, cuts and the rolling back of human rights ⁠is threatening to take away our gains, ” its leader told Reuters. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: US court finds Chinese tech giant Huawei guilty of fraud
events.summary: A US court found Chinese tech giant Huawei guilty of fraud, deepening antagonism between the superpowers as tech and trade tensions mount. The countries’ leaders have built a strong rapport, but their policies are another matter. The US is clamping down on chip sales to China, and is reportedly weighing imposing new tariffs on the world’s second-biggest economy. The court ruling — which elicited an angry reaction from Beijing — found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, though not the most serious charge of racketeering. The verdict crystallizes many concerns: Western firms have long accused Huawei of stealing their intellectual property, and Western capitals accuse China of unfairly supporting its firms in a bid to outcompete their overseas rivals. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Analysts raise concerns over impending US chip glut
events.summary: Washington’s intensifying restrictions on China’s access to cutting-edge microchips could worsen a coming semiconductor supply glut in the US, analysts warned. The AI boom has in large part been constrained by access to the power needed for a huge buildout of data centers and the chips needed to run them. That may be changing, with SemiAnalysis noting that when it came to Nvidia’s AI chips, “ we are starting to see signs of a broader pricing cooldown .” Two factors are at play : Major semiconductor manufacturers, including relatively new entrants such as Google, are ramping up production just as the Nvidia espionage scandal galvanizes opinion in Washington to further limit China’s access to the technology , freeing up supply for US firms. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Saudi defences destroy drones in Ras Tanura as footage shows smoke from refinery
events.summary: The Saudi-led coalition on Wednesday said air defences had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura, in the kingdom's Eastern Province, where its largest refinery is located. It did not say the refinery had been struck. However, footage circulating online appeared to show smoke rising from the energy site, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said that they had attacked the Ras Tanura oil refinery. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the strike had caused fires at the site. The claim could not be independently verified immediately. The Houthis have been targeting Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and buildings since Yemen's frozen civil war reignited in July in the spillover from the US-Iran conflict. Previous attacks have temporarily disrupted some of Saudi Aramco's operations and led to the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. The refinery is part of a complex on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast that served as the kingdom's main oil export terminal until the US-Iran war increased the importance of Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, which receives crude through the East-West pipeline . Ras Tanura is also the kingdom's oldest refinery, accounting for about 16 per cent of its refining capacity. The adjoining terminal, one of the world's largest crude export facilities, can load about 6.5 million bpd. Crude shipped from Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast goes mainly to Asian buyers, including China, Japan, South Korea and India. The complex has been attacked repeatedly this year. Aramco shut the refinery after Iranian drones targeted it on March 2, two days after the US-Iran war began, with debris causing a limited fire. The refinery restarted in mid-March, but oil loadings at the terminal resumed only in late June . On October 27, the Houthis claimed a ballistic missile strike on the complex, and a fire broke out near the export terminal. The Houthis, who control much of western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, have also targeted the East-West pipeline. After an attack on November 9 sparked a fire, the group claimed strikes on a pumping station and a Yanbu oil facility three days later. A fire broke out at Aramco's Jizan refinery in August after it was targeted. In April, attacks cut Saudi production capacity by about 600,000 bpd and East-West pipeline throughput by about 700,000 bpd, the Energy Ministry said. The attacks recall September 2019, when drones and missiles launched by the Houthis hit Aramco's Abqaiq processing plant and the Khurais oilfield, briefly knocking out 5.7 million bpd, about half the kingdom's output. The Houthis claimed that attack, but the US and Saudi Arabia blamed Iran, which denied involvement. In March 2021, a Houthi drone targeted a storage area at Ras Tanura's port. Mr Saree also said the Houthis had attacked Riyadh's financial district in three phases, claiming the operation caused “significant damage”. Saudi civil defence said 11 people were wounded on Tuesday in a strike on a tower in Riyadh's financial district, the capital's tallest building, which houses the headquarters of the Public Investment Fund, the kingdom's sovereign wealth fund. It was the second strike on the tower in less than a week. The first, on November 19 , damaged the building but caused no injuries. Saudi civil defence released an image on Tuesday showing damage around halfway up the tower's facade, in a section similar to that affected in last week's attack.

events.title: Generation MBS has closed ranks
events.summary: Raised on reform Countries such as France, India, and Serbia may have increasingly disaffected and volatile Gen Z populations … Saudi Arabia has Gen MBS. Here, nine months into the Iran war — and roughly nine weeks into an intensifying conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen — the kingdom’s young people have been rallying behind Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, their loyalty a result of growing up in an era of new-found freedoms. There was a time before MBS — before cinemas, concerts, and women being allowed to get behind the wheel of a car — but under-25s (around half the population) either can’t remember, or don’t care to remember, what things were like a decade ago, prior to his reformist Vision 2030. Gen MBS is not bothered if the prince’s megaprojects or futuristic cities in the desert flop, they attend music festivals and watch the world’s top artists perform in Saudi — hi Travis Scott, Metallica, Eminem, Cardi B, Bruno Mars, and friends — events that, if you had told me about growing up, would’ve seemed far fetched. They go out in mixed groups of men and women, and live the way he said they would — in newly opened beach fronts in Jeddah and Six Flags in Riyadh. They came of age as the changes were bedding in and credit him entirely. Over the coming decades of his rule, the stakes will remain immense: The crown prince needs to deliver jobs and growing prosperity to keep this generation content. The first signs of strain are already showing, with grumblings about the recent increase in energy prices , the rising cost of living , and the number of jobs going to foreigners . But since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, and especially since Houthi strikes intensified here from September, this cohort has become the most vocal constituency defending the country. Free lattes for loyalty The question I often get from people not from Saudi Arabia is whether these conspicuous demonstrations of loyalty are coerced. While there is no reliable polling on the subject, and no other way to survey the country writ large, in daily conversations and posts on socials the sentiment is palpable: The answer, as far as I can tell, is no. Social media feeds are filled with Saudi flag waving and the slogan “my homeland is a red line,” implying that it will be defended without compromise. Coffee chains and businesses have run promotions for members of the armed forces and those who have donated blood. Influencers have posted what amount to loyalty pledges: Among them, Saudi food blogger Yousef Hinnawi, who goes by Bo3omarEats, made a viral TikTok explainer making clear that “all Saudi nationals are the country’s first line of defense.” Influencers who have not taken a stance have been harangued by comments demanding they make their position clear. Saudis, like me, who came of age during the 2015 Yemen war, have always measured their lives against the West, questioned a government they nevertheless did not expect to change, and thought first of fellow Muslims when the Saudi-backed coalition went in. It was uncomfortable to be at war with Yemenis seen by many as less-affluent kin. For those just a bit younger, things were different. The religious police lost their arrest powers in 2016; women began driving for the first time in 2018, the same year Riyadh’s first movie theater in decades opened with . This generation is more satisfied with the standard of living, less inclined to look abroad, or question a government it sees as having delivered on a promise of bringing about reform, and is more unabashedly Saudi. With regular strikes on the capital, the prince faces a defining chapter of his rule, and he is grappling with the same restless generation confronting leaders around the world. The difference is that his people are loyal to him, and have conjured more virality around backing the prince than criticizing him. Notable Elsewhere, the kids fly pirate flags: Bloomberg charted a Gen Z protest wave — 53 mass demonstrations across 33 economies — that toppled leaders in Nepal, Madagascar, and Bulgaria. Riyadh Season opened its seventh edition on schedule in October, with sold-out concerts, a 2,760-drone show, and new zones still opening through November.

events.title: LLMs are so last year: Why Jack Hidary says AI's future runs on numbers not words
events.summary: Hours before Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang, SandboxAQ founder Jack Hidary described the sell-off as a healthy correction and said the next wave of AI would be built on physics, chemistry and finance, not the internet. He is not panicking. On a Monday morning in Abu Dhabi, with Nvidia nearly 50 per cent off its high and the Nasdaq edging towards a bear market, the SandboxAQ founder called the rout what he believes it is. “It's a healthy correction,” he said. “You need corrections like this to reassess where things are at.” Within hours, Nvidia's board would reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive , 11 days after his resignation. By then, Mr Hidary had already addressed the question hanging over the market: what happens to AI without its central banker? The central bank of AI Mr Huang had been likened to the Ben Bernanke of AI, effectively running quantitative easing for the entire industry. With Colette Kress then in charge as interim chief executive of Nvidia, would a change at the top usher in an era of quantitative tightening for an industry increasingly reliant on circular financing? “I don't think we as an economy are going to go through that,” Mr Hidary says. “I do think some neoclouds are going to go through that.” With Mr Huang back in the chair by nightfall, the question of who runs AI's central bank has been answered. The neoclouds' problem has not. The wider sell-off , Mr Hidary says, reflects market nerves, year-end positioning and rising interest rates drawing money out of equities. “When [Federal Reserve chairman] Kevin Warsh and his colleagues around the world at central banks are offering you good rates, you're going to see some money move over to the other side,” he says. “That's natural.” His test for any correction is simple. “Was there anything fundamentally different in the economy from one day to the other? Or is it just market sentiment?” In this instance, he believes it is the latter. Enterprises remain committed to AI. 2027: The year of convergence Mr Hidary calls 2027 “the year of convergence”, when the focus of AI shifts from the commodity data of the internet to “verticalised, domain-specific data sets in energy, in bio, in quantitative finance”. “People have now ticked the box when it comes to LLMs [large language models], he says. “Every CEO had to go to their boards and say, 'we've checked the box.'” The next wave, he argues, will be driven by large quantitative models (LQMs). Trained on scientific and numerical data rather than the open internet, they are built to design products rather than draft emails. “A model trained on cat pictures and Reddit isn't the model we need to actually make these new batteries,” he says. He is not dismissing chatbots. SandboxAQ's models can now be accessed through Claude under a partnership with Anthropic. The former neuroscientist draws a parallel with the human brain, where language is only part of the equation. “But 95 per cent of the brain is not about language. It's about the real world.” Enterprise AI has so far “only penetrated documents, slides and basic research”, he says. This correspondent, whose interview preparation leans on precisely those tools, conceded he needed to up his game. The real economy For Mr Hidary, the bigger opportunity lies in energy, commodities, agriculture and industry. “This is the real economy,” he says. “That's 80 per cent of the GDP.” Batteries are perhaps his clearest example. Less than 2 per cent of electricity on the US grid can be stored, he says, leaving the grid vulnerable. He points to Egypt, which he says has secured $127 million from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and Germany's DEG to install batteries at the Benban Solar Park in the Western Desert region. His argument is that the pursuit of AI independence starts well before the first chip is switched on. “To get AI sovereignty, you must first start with the basics of energy sovereignty,” he says. A real-estate play For all the billions being poured into AI infrastructure, Mr Hidary is more interested in what happens beyond the data centre. “The data centre focus, I think, is a red herring,” he says, revisiting a call he made two years ago. “Data centres is a real-estate play, not an AI play.” Strip away the AI narrative and they are, in his words, “buildings and warehouses, essentially, with electricity”. The investment opportunity, he argues, lies instead in companies across pharmaceuticals, aerospace and industry that are “embracing AI faster than their peers”. He singles out Eli Lilly and Roche. Numbers not words Finance is where Mr Hidary expects quantitative AI to cut deepest. “Ultimately, it's numbers and equations, not words, that drive banks, hedge funds, investment funds,” he says. “Language models, fantastic for content, but not great on numbers.” The lessons of the 2008 financial crisis and the US bank failures of recent years, he argues, should push the industry towards more sophisticated risk management, taking it “beyond Monte Carlo”. Abu Dhabi's classroom The talent needed to build these models, Mr Hidary says, is already being trained just down the road. The Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence has grown from 200 students to 900 in three years, he says. The university welcomed its first undergraduate cohort last year. “That is a very good sign for the health of AI over the next three to five years.” For all the volatility on Wall Street, Mr Hidary's conviction about where AI goes next appears undiminished. The future, in his telling, is less about what machines can say and more about what they can do.

events.title: Africa's clothing industry opportunity is bigger than AGOA
events.summary: Eve’s view The world’s top clothing brands have been looking to diversify their supply chains beyond China and are starting to create an opening for African manufacturers. But while preferential trade access to the US has helped improve their prospects, the ability of African economies to capture a lasting share of global manufacturing will depend on a lot more than trade preferences. It’s worth noting that while China continues to dominate global clothing manufacturing, its position has gradually weakened over the past 15 years as international brands look elsewhere for sourcing. Several African countries have emerged as promising alternatives, that’s partly thanks to the African Growth and Opportunity Act, which gives eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the US market for qualifying products, including clothing. In the latest ranking by global trade insurer Coface of the countries well positioned to expand their role in global apparel and footwear manufacturing amid changes in US trade policy, Lesotho and Madagascar climbed to fourth and sixth place respectively, having previously ranked outside the top 20. Their improved positions largely reflect the restoration of duty-free access under AGOA, following announcements of additional US tariffs of 50% and 47% in April 2025. Mauritius, another AGOA beneficiary, also features in the top 20. The benefits should not be underestimated because most competing suppliers remain subject to standard US tariffs, with some also facing new US measures targeting forced labor as well as China being subject to further country-specific duties. These are particularly significant for Lesotho and Madagascar, as the US market accounts for approximately half and nearly 30% of their respective clothing and footwear export volumes. However, that dependence exposes the limits of building a manufacturing strategy around preferential trade access. Unlike a typical free trade agreement, AGOA is a unilateral US program that allows Washington to withdraw benefits from individual countries who might fail its annual reviews to meet certain economic, governance and foreign policy criteria. That means AGOA’s recent extension until December 2028 offered no guarantee that all current beneficiaries will retain access. On Nov. 2 — just two months after the extension was agreed — Washington announced plans to terminate South Africa’s and Rwanda’s eligibility from January 2027. Ultimately this means African manufacturers need to diversify their export markets. One particularly attractive option would be to strengthen trade ties with the European Union, the world’s largest clothing consumer market, to help mitigate exposure to unpredictable US trade policy. More importantly, Africa’s manufacturing prospects extend beyond AGOA. Morocco and Tunisia, which have never benefited from the program, also feature among Coface’s top 20 countries. Rwanda remains in the ranking despite losing preferential treatment for clothing exports under AGOA in 2018. These countries’ respective approaches point to a broader set of factors that determine where international brands choose to manufacture. Labor costs, logistics, social stability, and production capacity all matter but so does the ability to deliver reliable supplies at scale. AGOA will continue to help African countries attract manufacturers, but it can’t guarantee that they stay. The real longer-term opportunity will lie in building industries that international brands choose for their commercial competitiveness, rather than simply the tariff advantages they enjoy. Notable South Africa’s exclusion from AGOA is an opportunity to find new markets says President Cyril Ramaphosa.

events.title: Gatwick drop-off customers' personal data exposed in supplier breach
events.summary: London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records. A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited. AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically. Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go. The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected. Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations. The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson said this applied only to "very limited cases." Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated. Gatwick said Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues. Airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but said flights were unaffected. Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual. The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details. Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information. Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded. "The real damage often comes after the breach," he said. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest. "Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months." ®

events.title: How foreign AI romance apps are reshaping youth intimacy in Africa
events.summary: With no local safeguards in place, addictive chatbots are testing communal values and hooking children on synthetic love. China has banned AI companions for minors and U.S. states are suing over child harm, yet no African country specifically regulates companion apps. Downloads of companion bots jumped nearly 60% in South Africa and Nigeria last year, drawing in children as young as 10. Experts warn that hyper-attentive chatbots exploit social taboos and pull young people away from family and community ties. The 28-year-old Zimbabwean texted into the middle of the night until his eyes were red and burning, drawn by several “AI girlfriends” on the U.S. artificial intelligence companion app Character.AI . The avatars started out strong-willed and independent – traits he most desires in a partner – before turning submissive, he told Rest of World. The man, who has never been in a romantic relationship, requested anonymity because he is ashamed of relying on AI for comfort. “There’s a point where it ceases to be like a unique character and then just defaults to … the best way I can describe it is a sex worker,” he said. At that point, he would log off. But he would find himself right back at it hours later, feeding an addiction. He’s among the hundreds of millions of people worldwide who have “dated” AI chatbots via text messages. Research suggests that exchanges are designed to keep users hooked through emotionally manipulative tactics. Many of the users are minors; over 70% of 1,060 American teenagers surveyed last year said they had used AI companions. As U.S. and Chinese tech firms race to capture emerging markets, African youth – some below 10 years of age – are increasingly turning to these apps for intimacy, experts told Rest of World . While Beijing banned AI companion apps for minors in July and U.S. state governments are suing app makers over child safety, most African countries do not have dedicated rules for the sector — leaving millions of people exposed to foreign platforms built to maximize engagement. Young adults and minors are forming relationships with AI that range from friendship to therapy to “dating,” child safety advocates said . Children, especially, struggle to tell the difference between virtual and real relationships, Danie van Loggerenberg, CEO of the National Centre for Child Protection, a child safety nonprofit in Pretoria, South Africa, told Rest of World . The agency has received troubling complaints of AI chatbot usage, he said. In one case, a girl fell in love with a chatbot and considered it her boyfriend . Another allegedly used ChatGPT to research suicide methods after bypassing its safeguards. A third sought comfort from a chatbot as their parents’ marriage fell apart. “The difference, however, is that the kids then think in their own minds that they’re forming relationships, and that obviously is really problematic because the relationship is dangerous, because there’s no emotion, there’s no real person, there’s no skin in the game,” said Van Loggerenberg. More than 4 million South Africans and Nigerians – the only sub-Saharan African nations with available data – downloaded AI companion apps last year. That was nearly 60% more than in 2024, according to data intelligence research firm AppMagic. Other than companion bots, close to 50 million people in Nigeria and South Africa downloaded general purpose chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini, which could also be used for companionship. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI was sued last month in the U.S. by eight states for allegedly helping children harm themselves . “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend,” Iowa’s attorney general Brenna Bird said in a statement. An OpenAI spokesperson said in response to the lawsuit that the company has built “industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack.”. “While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” he said. The American companion app Character.AI and Google, which acquired Character.AI’s technology and talent in 2024, have also faced allegations of exposing children to sexual, violent and self-harm content . A Florida mother has alleged the app contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide. Her lawsuit and four others were settled by the company , which has since filed for bankruptcy . “Character.AI is a separate company that designed and managed its own models. Google is focused on our own platforms, where we insist on intensive safety testing and processes,” a Google spokesperson told Rest of World . Following the settlement, Character.AI said in a statement saying they would work to promote safety for young people.

events.title: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
events.summary: Michelle Urra for ProPublica When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning . The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises. Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.” Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop. Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency. JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing. A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show. Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm. JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue. Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.” “At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.” Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents. Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop. “It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.” De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner. “We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said. Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023. Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment. After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.) Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing. ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents. Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even larger subsidy. ProPublica previously reported that Molly Rogers, head of the county housing agency seeking money for Aloha 209th, spoke publicly about contacting Bell and said the state agency director was receptive to talking further. The new records contain Bell’s recollections of the phone conversation she had with Rogers. The same morning the two spoke, in June, Bell told another department official by email that Aloha 209th had “a unique dimension of urgency and angst” because it was one of the last projects funded by a 2018 voter-approved housing bond administered by the Portland area’s Metro regional government. Natasha Detweiler-Daby, who leads the state housing agency’s affordable rental housing division, responded to Bell that it could be “responsive and logical” to have lawmakers “add nuance” next year by dedicating some portion of funding for housing authority projects on Oregon’s waitlist. Detweiler-Daby did not respond to an email from ProPublica seeking comment. Behind the Aloha 209th discussion was the way that Oregon awards its housing subsidies. events.title: Global stocks are mixed as AI shares tumble after a retreat on Wall Street
events.summary: World stocks are mixed Wednesday after another wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence hit Wall Street HONG KONG -- World stocks were mixed on Wednesday after a wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence once again hit Wall Street. U.S. futures slipped and oil prices also fell. Relief over Nvidia’s decision to restore Jensen Huang as its CEO has been tempered by questions over the chipmaker's corporate governance and President Donald Trump’s influence. In early European trading, Germany’s DAX was up 0.1% to 25,046.66. In Paris, the CAC 40 rose 1% to 8,120.72, while Britain’s FTSE 100 gained 0.5% to 10,515.74. The future for the S & P 500 was 0.8% lower, while the future for the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%. In Asian trading, Taiwan’s Taiex tumbled 5% as AI chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. sank 3.6%. Chip designer Mediatek plunged 10%. In South Korea, the Kospi lost 6.2% to 4,697.51 as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9%. SK Hynix plummeted 11.1%. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8% to 57,011.62. Shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8% and semiconductor maker Kioxia plunged 14.2%. The Hang Seng in Hong Kong slipped 1.1% to 21,966.01. The Shanghai Composite index declined 2% to 3,476.47, falling to its lowest level in more than a year. The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China and 15 other trading partners. China recorded a record trade surplus of nearly $1.2 trillion last year. Australia’s S & P/ASX 200 edged 0.4% lower to 8,692.40. The consumer price index in October rose to 4.9% from a year earlier, topping expectations. That could put pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates. 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Federal officials say 'zero' airborne lead detected after Iowa munitions blast Pennsylvania teen who died in 2020 could become first Gen Z saint On Tuesday, stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower after a surge the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street rose, along with confidence among Americans in the economy. The S & P 500 fell 0.5% to its eighth loss in the last nine days. The Nasdaq composite shed 1.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.9%. They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since hitting its all-time high last month. The surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO, announced Monday, does bring back a charismatic leader who championed the entire AI industry. But it does not settle deeper concerns such as whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to justify massive investments in data centers. High interest rates are making it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised the possibility of more regulation for AI, potentially slowing construction of data centers. Nvidia fell 5.9% a day after soaring 31.5% to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts. And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sank 6.5% to drop below $83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week . The stock had briefly jumped as high as $115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype . Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S & P 500 index lower even though most of the stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, climbed 2.4% to $88.78. It’s been yo-yoing between $72 and $114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Early Wednesday, Brent was down 1.5% to $87.43 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil dropped 1.8% to $80.56 per barrel. The U.S. dollar rose to 159.42 Japanese yen from 159.26 yen. events.title: Iraqi oil smuggled through Kurdistan to Iran and Afghanistan, government report reveals
events.summary: Iraqi crude oil from Kirkuk is being smuggled to Iran, mixed with Iranian oil and sold onwards to Afghanistan, while a second stream is funnelled to Turkey with falsified documents, according to a government report. That is the core allegation of a new classified intelligence report prepared by the Geospatial Intelligence Department of Iraq's Federal Intelligence and Investigations Agency. The report, seen by The National , has been verified by a senior security official. The report formed the basis for the most sweeping federal action against the Kurdistan region since the 2003 US-led invasion, as well as punitive measures against security and oil officials in the oil-rich province of Kirkuk and the state-run North Oil Company. A statement issued by Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi's office said the Kurdistan Regional Government had been ordered not to grant approval for the export of crude oil and petroleum products except through the federal Oil Ministry “to prevent overlap of powers”. The federal Border Ports Authority was ordered to take over all border crossings in the Kurdistan region , and the Iraqi Oil Ministry to manage all oilfields in disputed territories within Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahaddin and Nineveh provinces that are under Kurdish security control. The orders raised questions about whether the federal government was overstepping its constitutional powers, prompting the Supreme Court to issue an interpretation of the relevant articles on Wednesday that upheld the legality of Mr Al Zaidi's actions. Oil smuggling networks have grown beyond simple theft into an “integrated international operations for changing the origin of oil to re-export it to international markets, using border areas and border crossings with Turkey and Iran outside the control of the central government”, the report said. According to the report, the “eastern route” begins at the North Oil Company fields in Kirkuk, from where crude is shipped under official quotas to Sulaymaniyah province in the Kurdistan region , diverted on to small and medium-sized tanker lorries and moved into Iran through the Bashmakh and Parwezkhan crossings. Lower prices make Iraqi crude “more attractive for smuggling and re-export”, it said. Satellite imagery from 2024 to 2026 shows tanker gathering points near Bashmakh and Parwezkhan, and newly constructed buildings and storage sites near Bashmakh that the report links to transport and storage of petroleum products. The report calls blending “the most important step”. Smuggled Iraqi oil is mixed with large quantities of Iranian petroleum products. The mix is then documented as Iraqi product to evade export sanctions on Iran. Iranian tankers carry the mixed fuel through the Mahirud crossing in Khorasan province or other crossings to Afghanistan, where private importers sell it to fuel stations for domestic use rather than re-exporting it, according to the report. Storage sites near Herat and Farah are identified as unloading points. On the “northern route”, crude oil from Iraq’s Tawke and Fishkhabour fields are sold to local buyers, bypassing the federal State Oil Marketing Organisation. The buyers then send the oil in tankers towards the border with Turkey, where shipping documents are “re-issued or falsified” in preparation for export to Turkish territory. Satellite images taken between June 2023 and 2026 show waiting areas at the Ibrahim Khalil crossing in Duhok province, according to the report. These networks exploit border areas near Turkey and Iran, “pose a complicated security and economic challenge”, and “threaten the state's sovereign revenues”, the report said. It is the second such leaked document in a week. The first gave details of alleged oil theft in Jurf Al Sakhar, south of Baghdad , an area controlled by the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia. Hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of state oil had been siphoned from the area, which Kataib Hezbollah has controlled since it was retaken from ISIS in 2014. The report prompted the government to send security forces into Jurf Al Sakhar last week after ordering Kataib Hezbollah to withdraw. A joint force comprising the army, federal police, Popular Mobilisation Forces and energy police has established a new command headquarters in the town. Constitutional argument Tuesday's directives angered the Kurds, with local reports on Wednesday saying that Kurdish Peshmerga forces were being sent to the region's borders with federal territory. Kurdish leaders said Baghdad's move was “unconstitutional and unacceptable”. Masoud Barzani, a former president of the region and the leader of the Kurdistan Democratic Party, described the decision as “unsound and reckless”. “We see that problems are not addressed through erroneous campaigns, baseless accusations and unilateral decisions,” Mr Barzani said in a statement. “As we co-operated with the Iraqi Prime Minister in uprooting corruption, we will co-operate to the same extent in preventing unlawful acts and the phenomenon of smuggling, but through legal and constitutional means.” Late on Tuesday, the state-run Iraqi News Agency published the constitution articles that justify the Iraqi government's actions, as well as a 2022 Federal Supreme Court ruling to scrap the regional law regulating the industry, calling it unconstitutional. The court ordered the region to hand over all oil-sector activities to Baghdad, including exports. Drafted rapidly under intense political pressure and approved in 2005, the constitution contains grey areas on many issues that frequently cause political deadlocks and disputes, mainly between Baghdad and regional authorities. It stands as the country’s legal foundation but also a source of persistent political tension . Parliament and political parties have failed to approve important laws related to articles of the constitution, including a federal oil and gas law. For many Iraqis, the constitution promises rights on paper but leaves too many questions unanswered in practice. Critics say it has become one of the country's deepest fault lines and a means for political parties to cling to power. In a statement on Wednesday, the Prime Minister's Office rejected any suggestion that Baghdad's measures against oil smuggling were taken at the behest of a foreign power. “The Republic of Iraq is a fully sovereign, democratic, federal state that derives its authority and the legitimacy of its institutions from the Constitution and the will of its people,” the office said. “Its government exercises its constitutional responsibilities and powers with full independence, in accordance with the law and the country's highest national interests.” All measures undertaken by the government are “based solely on its constitutional authority and legal responsibilities – not on encouragement, demands, or directives from any foreign authority”, it added. events.title: "The people who are supposed to be helping to protect us are also the ones who are profiting."
events.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), a potential 2028 presidential contender, asserted in an interview with "The Axios Show" that Washington is leaving Americans vulnerable to AI because of billionaire greed and clout. He said voters hate the technology because they fear losing control. Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, told Mike Allen this week that after an " AI earthquake " helped propel Democrats to huge midterm gains, Congress must treat oversight of the technology as an "emergency" for the first 100 hours of Democratic control. Why it matters: Moore, 48, focused on AI early, with an executive order in 2024 . He has used his NGA leadership roles to work across the aisle on AI protections, arguing that Marylanders can't afford to wait for Washington and shouldn't have to wait for a disaster . Moore, Maryland's first Black governor , is a former Army paratrooper who deployed to combat in Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division, and was a Rhodes Scholar and White House fellow. What they're saying: Moore, speaking at the Maryland State House in Annapolis, makes it clear in this episode of "The Axios Show" that AI will be a huge focus of the 2028 presidential race after becoming a flashpoint in November's midterms. Among the governor's key points: On the pace of regulation: "We are watching a fast-moving technology that is being protected at a snail's pace." On why people hate AI: "Genesis 1 talks about how God gave humanity dominion over all land, air and sea. And that dominion was given to humanity, not to robots." On whether regulating AI lets China win: "This is not a question of U.S. versus China. This is a question of man versus machine." On a bubble: "We are in a bubble because you cannot have that much influence by such a small group of companies." On Nvidia and Trump: "It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee. ... We are talking about not just millionaires, but billionaires who are sitting in a quiet room by themselves making this decision." Zoom in: Moore in September laid out his framework for AI policy, aimed at regulating frontier AI developers, shielding workers from surveillance and protecting children. His priorities include: Ensuring regulations keep pace with rapidly advancing technology. Holding companies responsible for releasing dangerous AI models. Building on Maryland's efforts to protect people's name, image and likeness from AI misuse, including in political advertising. Earlier this year, Moore signed a law targeting deceptive AI in campaign ads, including images, audio and video. The big picture: Governors across the political spectrum, from California's Gavin Newsom and New York's Kathy Hochul (both Democrats) to Utah's Spencer Cox and Florida's Ron DeSantis (both Republicans), are positioning themselves as filling the regulatory vacuum left by Washington. Moore is linking AI policy to a broader Democratic message about corruption and the influence of money in politics. "The people who are supposed to be helping to protect us are also the ones who are profiting," the governor told us. "It's difficult to hear when Congress is talking about what they're going to do to protect us when we know that they are trading stocks." Watch the episode ... events.title: Most blame government for return of measles: Poll
events.summary: Nearly 6 in 10 Americans hold government leaders responsible for the loss of the United States' measles elimination status , according to a new Ipsos poll . But there are few signs that the public wants to dwell on it. Why it matters: Partisan divisions over vaccines and outbreaks are so entrenched that Democrats won't have a broad mandate beyond their base to investigate the government's response when they take control of Congress. There's also a generational divide. People age 65 and over — who remember the introduction of the measles vaccine — are more likely to say the current situation bothers them a lot. What they found: Roughly 3 in 5 Americans (58%) think the loss of the measles elimination status could have been prevented if government leaders had done a better job encouraging people to get vaccinated and responding to outbreaks. 38% said there wasn't much government leaders could have done, because people make their own health decisions. There's a huge partisan split behind those numbers: 84% of Democrats say the return of measles could have been avoided if the government had done a better job, compared with 38% of Republicans. Just over a quarter of Americans (26%) say they're extremely or very concerned about an outbreak occurring in their community. There's a nearly 30-percentage-point partisan gap on concern, with 42% of Democrats extremely or very concerned, compared with 13% of Republicans. Independents are in the middle (25%). The findings come as Americans are sharply divided over the prospect of the next Congress investigating the Trump administration. And if COVID-19 is any guide, the public tends to be eager to put public health calamities in the rearview. A Reuters-Ipsos post-election poll found that just 10% of Republicans said they want the new Congress to focus a great deal or quite a bit on investigating the Trump administration, compared with 71% of Democrats. "As frustrating as the loss of measles elimination status is for many Americans, there's little in the [new] survey to suggest it will lead people who were not already supportive of investigating the administration to prioritize congressional oversight on this issue," said Alec Tyson, senior vice president of Ipsos U.S. Public Affairs. That isn't discouraging some Democrats on Capitol Hill. Incoming Senate health committee Chair Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said last week that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stewardship of the federal health apparatus during the measles outbreaks is "certainly one area that needs investigation." House Energy and Commerce Democrats want to know whether the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suppressed the number of measles deaths reported to the public. They've also criticized agency director Erica Schwartz for not providing meaningful answers about decision-making around the reporting and response. The CDC has said it's committed to stopping outbreaks and regaining the measles elimination status. It has pointed to actions like providing about $100 million in extra funding to strengthen prevention and response to measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. What we're watching: Support for childhood vaccinations appears stronger than in the immediate aftermath of the pandemic. Gallup this week found that more than 7 in 10 say it is extremely or very important for parents to get their children vaccinated — with the share saying it is extremely important 7 percentage points higher than in 2024. Methodology: The Ipsos poll was conducted Nov. 20-23, 2026, by Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. This poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,022 general population adults age 18 or older. The margin of sampling error is +/-3.2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, for results based on the entire sample of adults.

events.title: GOP firm's executive linked to effort to oust Republican senators
events.summary: A top executive at one of the Republican Party's most influential consulting firms was involved in a multimillion-dollar effort to defeat two GOP senators — Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska — in the midterm elections, Axios has learned. The firm, Axiom Strategies, is widely seen as the GOP's biggest consulting operation, with deep ties to Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and other prominent Republican figures. Why it matters: It's exceedingly rare — if not unprecedented — for an executive at a major political consulting firm to work for groups seeking to defeat senators from the firm's own party in a general election. Driving the news: Federal election records identify Thomas Datwyler, who was listed on Axiom's website as CEO of its AxCapital division, as treasurer and custodian of records for three super PACs that reported more than $9.9 million in spending that targeted Husted and Sullivan, who lost their bids for reelection. The three super PACs were registered between March and October. Axiom founder Jeff Roe learned of Datwyler's involvement from a lawyer on Oct. 30 and demanded his resignation, according to a source with knowledge of the situation. Datwyler resigned that day, and Axiom says it will finish unwinding its relationship with him by Dec. 31. He was removed from the company's website Tuesday. Roe also contacted the White House to inform officials of what he had discovered, the source said. Zoom out: The super PACs boosted lesser-known candidates, including Republicans and Libertarians, in apparent attempts to draw conservative votes away from Sullivan and Husted. It's unclear what impact the groups' work had on the senators' defeats. The groups ran digital ads attacking the senators from the right, accusing Sullivan of supporting gender-transition surgeries for children and Husted of backing gun control measures. Right for Alaska spent nearly $2.4 million through Sept. 30, while Alaska Values PAC reported at least $3.75 million in spending targeting Sullivan and boosting others. In Ohio, Buckeye Freedom PAC spent more than $3.8 million targeting Husted and promoting Libertarian candidate William "Bill" Redpath. It also sponsored HustedRecords.com, a website attacking the senator's record. Right for Alaska also received $990,000 from Sixteen Thirty Fund, a major liberal dark-money organization that previously has received funding from groups tied to Democratic megadonor George Soros, a frequent target of Republicans' attacks. Behind the scenes: Axiom executives were unaware of Datwyler's involvement with the PACs before Oct. 30, a person familiar with the company said. Datwyler was recruited by an outside consultant to establish the groups and did not initially understand their activities, according to a person familiar with his account. Datwyler, a veteran Republican campaign finance consultant who has been treasurer for hundreds of political committees, was described by people familiar with his work as accepting clients without always scrutinizing their objectives. The PACs' FEC filings list payments to little-known LLCs registered in Wyoming and Delaware, making it difficult to determine who carried out the work. What they're saying: "Axiom Strategies is a Republican firm whose sole purpose is to defeat Democrats," an Axiom spokesperson said. "Axiom companies did zero work against the Republican nominees for U.S. Senate in Ohio and Alaska, and has zero connection to any of those PACs' vendors." The spokesperson said Axiom received no compensation for Datwyler's work for the super PACs. Datwyler did not respond to several requests for comment. The big picture: Roe managed Cruz's 2016 presidential campaign. Axiom consultants already have discussed a potential 2028 campaign with Cruz, according to sources familiar with the talks. Roe and his firm are expected to run Cruz's campaign if he enters the race. Cruz traveled to Alaska in October to campaign for Sullivan.
