events.title: Jury finds Huawei stole US tech, laundered money, and broke sanctions
events.summary: A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done. This case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of New York. The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy. The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision says Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors showed evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.” Another item of evidence apparently showed a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a company called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.” Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices. Huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ says. The feds say the Chinese company also “lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.” Huawei has issued a statement noting that the jury found it not guilty of racketeering and insisting the charges on which it was found guilty are “without legal or factual merit.” “The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades,” the statement adds. Sentencing will take place in September 2027. The presiding judge will likely consider the fact that in 2017, US authorities fined Chinese telco equipment maker ZTE $900 million just for selling to Iran, then added an additional $1.4 billion penalty to lift a ban on doing business in the USA. Washington has already banned Huawei from selling its telco products and personal devices in the USA. Lawmakers have little appetite to let the Chinese company return to the American market after spending billions to help American telcos replace the Huawei kit with locally made alternatives. ®

events.title: Compass exit leaves London seeking next generation of defining businesses
events.summary: Now and again, there is a piece of news that brings you up short. So it is with the decision of Compass to move its primary listing from London to New York. That may seem anodyne and relatively obscure, small feed in the order of things. But not if you live and work in London, and take delight and comfort in the UK capital being a world business centre. It’s a hegemony that has been long in the making, nurtured and honed over centuries, based on the City of London's reputation and traditions making it a magnet for companies and investors from all over. At its heart is the London Stock Exchange , once a historic, mighty market for shares, the place that businesses were proud to call home. Compass is off. We’ve seen stocks defect before, of course, and in increasing numbers in recent years. Wise, Flutter, Ferguson, Indivior, Diversified Energy and Sunbelt are just some of those to switch. Another major one was building materials supplier CRH. They’re not moving their operations but where they list their shares. So, it’s not as if they are taking thousands of jobs, although their use of professional services and advisers will be affected. But it says much about where they see themselves, where they wish to be and inevitably, over time, they loosen the chains of their origins and America’s influence becomes pervasive. Compass began after the Second World War, when legislation was introduced obliging manufacturing and armaments firms that employed 250 people or more to provide hot meals for their workers. Today, this contract caterer is all over the UK and abroad, employing 600,000 people in 25 countries under brands such as Levy, which handles hospitality at sports stadiums including Allianz in Twickenham, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Old Trafford and Edgbaston. Other leading Compass-owned brands include Bon Appetit, Eurest, Morrison Healthcare and Chartwells. It likes to call itself “possibly the biggest business you’ve never heard of”. Except the investment community is aware of Compass. Revenue last year was $46.1 billion. That should be clue enough as to what it was planning – reporting its performance in dollars, not pounds. Even so, while that was noted, Compass remained a definably British story and a hugely successful one to boot. Who's next? There is palpable shock at the announcement. Invariably too, attention focuses to who might follow – with Shell, a fixture of the London market, and pharma colossus AstraZeneca tipped to be next. Companies jumping ship is not new either. Previously there was no shortage of replacements – from the UK and overseas. Just as there have been exits, so too has the flow of entrants dried up. Last year, London hosted 23 initial public offerings (IPOs), which together raised £2.1 billion. In the US, there were 354, raising $44 billion. This year, IPOs in London have reduced to a trickle – Dealogic reckons the UK is down to 14th globally, behind Malaysia, Turkey and Norway. Fourteenth! Meanwhile, the disappearing is continuing in another direction. So far this year, $133 billion of UK-listed companies have been bought, the highest tally since 2018. They include familiar names such as easyJet and Schroders. It’s a three-pronged onslaught: companies listing elsewhere, usually New York; few rushing to take their place; and still more being acquired. Not for nothing does Dame Julia Hoggett, beleaguered boss of the LSE, say: “If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the Chancellor and the Prime Minister saying, then let’s make sure that we’re creating structural incentives to do so. We need to take the handbrake off.” Hoggett is correct, John Healey and Andy Burnham are saying that. She would not be wrong either if she thought they were rocked by the Compass decision. “Genuinely frustrating”, was how the mood was described by a government official. As soon as Labour returned to power, it announced new rules for company listings in a step designed to boost London’s appeal. That was more than two years ago and it has not worked. In his recent Budget , Healey fell back on that old get out – stamp duty, and how he was holding a review (another one) into the charge – and how he would also introduce a three-year window for trading in newly listed shares. Ministers, not least City Minister Lucy Rigby, maintain stamp duty is what holds companies back from listing their shares in London. To which the riposte is “if you say so, minister”. The truth is that it does not help but to argue it is the main factor is nonsense. The issue goes much deeper. Replacements required It’s not so much Compass opting for New York but that lack of substitutes that is the worry. Compass is a global concern; the US is the dominant capital market, offering liquidity on a vast, accessible scale. To tap into that, the caterer is heading to Manhattan. Fair enough. London has never taken business from New York; rather they have existed side by side, the one broadly feeding the Americas and the other the rest. That was and is, London’s place, and it did and still can thrive as a result. To restore London’s lustre is about encouraging talent, giving it the tools to prosper (of which tax breaks form a part). It’s about creating the mood, setting a direction of travel that is positive for business, domestic and foreign, for wealth creation. That means stripping away the regulations, reducing red tape – not reviewing and pondering. Not taxing. In the very week Compass dropped its grenade, Burnham and business secretary Jonathan Reynolds had breakfast with a select group of CEOs on the fringe of the CBI annual conference. They heard about the PM’s intentions towards the European Union and his “10-year plan” to change Britain. It was excitable. But all talk and no action, and looking beyond the next election. What it wasn’t was of the present. Compass should serve as a red flag; stop talking and start doing.

events.title: This could mess with Thanksgiving, says VMware as it drops third critical patch bundle in a week
events.summary: VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues. VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks: Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States. The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us. Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs. This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July. Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability. The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off. Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software. There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer. VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce. In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®

events.title: Huawei found guilty of money laundering and conspiracy to steal trade secrets in US case
events.summary: Huawei, China’s largest technology company, has been found guilty of charges in the US, including money laundering, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks over its business in Iran and North Korea. A federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, deliberated for about four days before reaching a verdict Tuesday in a rare US prosecution of a foreign corporation. The panel found the company guilty of 10 of 12 counts following an 11-week trial. Huawei was cleared of two conspiracy charges related to racketeering and obstruction of justice. The verdict against one of China’s biggest and best-known tech giants lands at a delicate time for relations between the world’s largest economies, with the administration of President Donald Trump tightening curbs on China’s ability to access American chips after revelations that Nvidia's Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence. Even so, the years-old case is unlikely to affect the broader trade truce between Mr Trump and President Xi Jinping, who affirmed a commitment to keep ties stable at a summit last week. While that deal is set to expire in January, both sides have an incentive to prevent a deterioration that could lead to much higher tariffs and bans on essential items like rare earths, aeroplane parts and chip design software. “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws,” said Brooklyn US Attorney Joseph Nocella. “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which include years-long collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from US technology companies.” Brian Heberlig, Huawei’s lead lawyer, focused on the company’s acquittal on two charges, including the so-called RICO racketeering count, which he called the government’s lead charge. The company said in a separate statement that the remaining charges have no merit and it will review its legal options. Mixed emotions “It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Mr Heberlig said. The RICO charge “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge”. The decision comes years after the Justice Department first filed charges against the world’s largest maker of telecoms equipment. For most of that time, the company has been largely excluded from the American market under trade measures imposed by the Trump and Biden administrations in the name of national security. The telecom titan has emerged as China’s de facto national chipmaking champion and is one of a handful of firms central to Beijing’s goal of dominating artificial intelligence and replacing American software and circuitry with local equivalents. The case was publicly unveiled in early 2019 under the first Trump administration’s so-called China Initiative, a Justice Department programme to combat Chinese espionage and influence in the US. Prosecutors have since won numerous convictions against Chinese nationals, but have struggled in trials against large Chinese companies on American soil. 60 witnesses The jury of nine women and three men heard testimony from more than 60 witnesses during the 11-week trial. Huawei was convicted of a scheme to steal trade secrets from rival tech competitors over 20 years, including source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile as well as proprietary information from Fujitsu Network Communications. “Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion, and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies, they are serious crimes,” said James Barnacle, head of the FBI’s New York office. “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.” In their verdict on Tuesday, however, the panel rejected the government’s theory that Huawei had engaged in a racketeering scheme for more than two decades to “grow its global brand” into one of the biggest telecoms in the world. The panel also rejected a US charge that Huawei obstructed a federal grand jury investigation. Jurors left the courthouse and declined to speak to the press. The conviction is a vindication for the Justice Department, which overcame attempts by Huawei to derail the case before trial and had to navigate years of delays because of the Covid pandemic, which made it difficult for lawyers and witnesses to travel. Along the way, two Chinese intelligence officers were accused in 2022 of trying to bribe a US law enforcement official with $61,000 in Bitcoin to steal evidence and get inside information about the case. Huawei now faces fines, forfeiture and restitution but the US has not specified the scope of financial penalties it will seek at sentencing, which is scheduled for September 2027. From the beginning, the Huawei case heightened tensions between Washington and Beijing while the world’s two largest economies were mired in a trade war. Months later, officials in Donald Trump’s administration labelled the company a national security threat, alleging that it sold telecoms equipment that could be used by China’s Communist Party for spying. The initial criminal indictment set off a diplomatic crisis when Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou, whose father founded the company, was arrested at the behest of the US on financial fraud charges while travelling through Canada. Almost three years after Meng was held under house arrest in Vancouver, she reached a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021 that allowed her to return to China, but after she admitted that the company violated US sanctions by illegally conducting business in Iran.

events.title: ADGM's Iliad Partners closes start-up fund with more backing from Greek entities
events.summary: Abu Dhabi's Iliad Partners has raised funds for the final close of its Gulf-focused investment fund backed by Greek banks, as it looks to boost its portfolio in the region's start-up scene. The $33.4 million Iliad Partners Tech Ventures Fund I will primarily focus on opportunities in the UAE and Saudi Arabia , with selective investments in Europe, particularly in Greece, ADGM-based Iliad Partners said in a statement on Wednesday. Among the new major institutional investors are the Hellenic Development Bank of Investments, Greece's $2.5 billion sovereign fund of funds, and Alpha Bank, one of the country's four systemic lenders. Three of Greece's other major banks, National Bank of Greece, Eurobank and Piraeus Bank, joined the fund last year, marking their first foray into venture capital investment in the wider Middle East and North Africa region. The fund, which originally had a target of $50 million, announced its first close in December 2024, followed by a second close in September last year that nearly doubled its assets under management. The fund aims to support early-stage companies in artificial intelligence and business-to-business software in sectors such as finance, property, logistics and enterprise. Iliad's current portfolio includes Balio, Comfi, OTO, Penny and Qashio; its previous investments include Fetchr, OSeven and Trukker. Additional investments are in progress under a three-year strategy. The focus on the Gulf mirrors its emergence as a region offering "significant" opportunities for start-ups to grow, with Europe serving as a source for talent and expertise, said Christos Mastoras, founder and managing partner of Iliad Partners. "We see tremendous potential in building bridges between these complementary ecosystems, unlocking new opportunities for entrepreneurs and businesses across both regions," he said. The close of the fund is a "new chapter, focused on translating this vision into tangible opportunities for the founders we back and supporting them in building enduring, globally competitive businesses". Start-ups remain vital players in economies as they continue to develop tech solutions in the digital era. The business environment and regulations in the UAE are making it easier for start-ups to access funding. AI in particular has drawn significant attention. The Emirates is pursuing its National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031, aimed at establishing the Emirates as a global leader in AI by integrating advanced technology into government, business and daily life. The participation of Greece's institutions in Iliad Partners' funding vehicle also reflects the growing ties between Greece and the Middle East, said Lazaros Papagaryfallou, deputy chief executive of Athens' Alpha Bank. "We see growing opportunities for our clients and the wider business community ... at the same time, the investment contributes to the broader effort to foster commercial and cross-border business opportunities in the broader region," he added. Iliad Partners Tech Ventures Fund I's other investors include Jada Fund of Funds, a wholly owned subsidiary of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Alpha Bank's peers Eurobank, National Bank of Greece and Piraeus Bank, and family groups and family offices from Saudi Arabia, the Gulf and Europe.

events.title: Dubai sees early signs of tourism recovery with October visitor figures
events.summary: Dubai welcomed 1.15 million international overnight visitors in October, its highest monthly total since February, when the Iran war began. Total visitor numbers for the first 10 months of the year reached 9.68 million, the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism said, attributing the figures to the city's diversified strategy. The city welcomed 15.7 million overnight visitors during the same period last year. “Challenging times are not new to us in Dubai, and through them we have always come together, adapted, learnt and emerged even stronger,” said Issam Kazim, chief executive of Dubai Corporation for Tourism and Commerce Marketing. “The fundamentals that have driven Dubai’s success remain robust, and we are seeing encouraging signs of momentum across our markets.” The Iran war, now in its ninth month, has severely disrupted travel and tourism this year, driving up fuel prices and causing flight delays, cancellations and diversions across the Middle East and beyond. International airlines have been forced to adjust schedules for Middle East flights in the aftermath of the war, which broke out on February 28, as airspace restrictions persist. Dubai International Airport handled 50.4 million passengers in the first nine months of 2026, with traffic down 28.1 per cent year on year. Third-quarter volumes declined 22.1 per cent to 18.8 million passengers, operator Dubai Airports said this month. August was the busiest month of the quarter, with 6.6 million passengers. Airlines have gradually begun to restart flights to the region. This month, British Airways resumed flights between London Heathrow and Dubai after an eight-month suspension caused by the conflict. Lufthansa Group is also due to resume Dubai services on November 25, joining Royal Air Maroc, SunExpress and Cebu Pacific. The Dubai airport expects to welcome more than 70 million passengers this year, Dubai Airports’ chief executive Paul Griffiths said. That is down from 95.2 million passengers last year . DET said public-private partnerships have helped boost tourism in the city. Its recent “A Dubai Invite” initiative, which encouraged residents to invite friends and family, saw more than 73,000 visitors arrive into the city, the authority said. Meanwhile, Dubai Access Club, a new invitation-only tourism membership programme, combines a five-year membership with exclusive destination benefits and a multiple-entry tourist visa, subject to eligibility and visa approval. The initiative aims to encourage repeat visitation, the DET said. The city will also host the 32nd edition of Dubai Shopping Festival from December 4, 2026, to January 17, 2027. Looking ahead, DET said it will continue to work closely with its international network of travel trade, airline and industry partners across key source markets to maintain demand and respond quickly to changing travel patterns.

events.title: Nutanix CEO announces gradual departure, intent to complete set of storage links
events.summary: Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the company’s board can find his successor. Ramaswami announced his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader. The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit. In chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew. The CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami said he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers. Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole new set of ecosystems.” Ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff , the CEO said the company's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.” News of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix announced its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The company added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami said high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest new customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business. Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the company’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®

events.title: Huang way or another? What leadership succession looks like at Nvidia's peers
events.summary: The Jensen Huang saga took another turn this week, with Nvidia's board surprisingly reinstating its chief executive . That ended an 11-day whirlwind that triggered national security fears and a stock market rout. One issue the drama magnified was the artificial intelligence company's lack of a succession plan. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim chief, but that was more of a stopgap and, as the title implied, temporary. That exposed a weak link in Nvidia's leadership chain, in contrast to some of its peers, which at least have a plan, follow tradition or are experimenting with how they are run. Oracle After 37 years as chief executive, Oracle founder Larry Ellison stepped down in 2014 and the company adopted a co-chief executive model. Mark Hurd and Safra Catz shared the role until Mr Hurd's death in 2019, which left Ms Catz running the company alone until 2025. Clay Magouyrk and Mike Sicilia now lead it. Mr Ellison remains Oracle's chairman and chief technology officer, while Ms Catz has become executive vice chair of the board. The unusual structure, an "experiment", creates ambiguity over who is truly in charge, Fortune noted in 2025. Alphabet Sundar Pichai became chief executive of Google in 2015 and of its parent Alphabet in 2019, succeeding co-founder Larry Page both times. Mr Pichai was reportedly chosen for his leadership and product savvy. Those qualities also drew interest from Microsoft in 2014, before it picked Satya Nadella, and from what was then Twitter, albeit for a less senior role. Alphabet has no public succession plan. Names that stand out include president and chief investment officer Ruth Porat and Google Cloud chief Thomas Kurian . Given AI's influence today, Google DeepMind leaders Demis Hassabis and Koray Kavukcuoglu could also be in the running. Meta Platforms The Facebook parent has no public succession plan. Founder Mark Zuckerberg, who is also chief executive and chairman, has given no sign of when he might retire or who might succeed him. He is only 42 and the youngest person in the top 20 of the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. His top team includes president Dina Powell McCormick and senior executives Joel Kaplan, Susan Li, Javier Olivan, Chris Cox and Andrew Bosworth. Meanwhile, the stock of chief AI officer Alexandr Wang, 29, has risen. Mr Zuckerberg reportedly trusts him to lead the company's AI ambitions and turnaround. Meta may not have a succession plan for Mr Zuckerberg, but Mr Wang could be an example of the company "already creating the conditions for people to speculate about one", said Inna Kuts, founder of Dublin-based executive branding advisory IKCCG. "Mr Wang has capital, organisational authority, direct access to Mr Zuckerberg and responsibility for one of Meta’s most consequential strategic priorities. That is how potential successors often become visible long before anyone uses the word 'succession'." Samsung In South Korea, chaebols are the norm. These are sprawling family-controlled conglomerates, and the word literally means "wealth clan". The Lee family has controlled Samsung Group for 88 years. Its current chairman, Lee Jae-yong, is the son and successor of Lee Kun-hee, who in turn took over from his father, Samsung founder Lee Byung-chul. In 2016, however, Lee Jae-yong was implicated in a corruption, bribery and embezzlement scandal. His father had been incapacitated by a heart attack in 2014, and the case cast serious doubt on the son's expected rise to the top. (His father had legal troubles of his own, which led him to leave the company and later return.) In 2017, Mr Lee was convicted and jailed for his role in the scandal, which also led to the impeachment and conviction of then-president Park Geun-hye. He was paroled in 2021, pardoned in 2022 and named executive chairman that October. Even so, Mr Lee said in 2020 that he did not plan to hand control of the company to his children. It is unclear whether that was down to recent history, political pressure or a genuine attempt to break with chaebol tradition. Separately, Samsung was reported last month to have expanded an affiliate system that draws up shortlists of candidates for chief executive roles across its business units. Apple Apple is arguably the most straightforward case on this list. Since co-founder Steve Jobs returned in 1997, it has changed leaders twice: when Mr Jobs resigned shortly before his death in 2011, and when Tim Cook stepped down this September. Both times, the iPhone maker picked a chief executive who could steer it through a transformational phase in step with the industry. Mr Cook, then Apple's operations chief, had built one of technology's most robust supply chains. Hardware maven John Ternus is expected to strike the right balance in the age of AI. Apple had a strong list of contenders, including Craig Federighi, Greg Joswiak, Eddy Cue and Deirdre O'Brien , and its choice of the low-profile Mr Ternus shows how deep its bench is. Lesson for Nvidia Not having a succession plan at the biggest and most influential companies could prove costly. Having one in place reassures investors and supports business continuity. Nvidia may have learnt this the hard way, especially as Mr Huang's departure was bigger than a succession story, said Mazen Hayek, a Dubai-based media consultant. "It is a stress test of corporate governance, US national security policy, global semiconductor supply chains and the balance of power in the AI race," he told The National . Investors would welcome clearer information about succession plans. Now that Nvidia has seen the risk up close, it should be able to prepare for Mr Huang stepping down again, for whatever reason. "The board’s real test is succession. Those are governance questions because the answers determine what the board can do when it has to make a difficult decision," said Mohammad Fheili, a risk strategist and executive in residence at the American University of Beirut. "Directors who have prepared for a handover can judge a chief executive's conduct on its merits and act on that judgment."

The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment. MBS’ last trip to the US, in November 2025, featured an elaborate White House reception and a series of high-profile announcements, with Washington and Riyadh pledging hundreds of billions of dollars in commercial agreements and investment commitments.

events.title: Dell and HPE both say they’ve become ‘different companies’
events.summary: Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.” The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different company” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.” On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.” HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player. Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure company. Clarke said he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead. Dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with” “Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.” HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent. The CEO said HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year. events.title: Yale’s Sonnenfeld: Nvidia is a ‘detriment’ to US industrial might — not a champion
events.summary: Investors cheered Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday, but renowned business academic Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of Yale thinks they’re celebrating a mistake. He sees a company that is largely responsible for putting sophisticated technology in the hands of the country’s adversaries, at a moment when the risks couldn’t be higher . Far from a champion of American industry, he says, Nvidia is “a detriment to U.S. global industrial might.” As evidence, Sonnenfeld points to research suggesting Nvidia’s most advanced chips have reached China despite U.S. export controls and to sinking shares of Anthropic, which he links to the realization that China’s seemingly miraculous open source AI models are, in a sense, copies of top U.S. labs’ work, even as Nvidia has insisted that smuggling is a “non-factor.” Indeed, Huang’s return was greeted with just as much enthusiasm in Asia, The Washington Post reported. “The king is back!” read one headline from China’s state-affiliated Star Market Daily. The reinstatement itself followed heavy pressure from Washington. Nvidia’s chairman had effectively ruled out Huang’s return just last week. Then, in a torrent of private weekend calls led by Vice President JD Vance, top administration officials leaned on the board to welcome Huang back, with President Trump calling the board directly to vouch for him. “ I made the deal ,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. Sonnenfeld says the directors who went along, and who returned Huang to the board even as it investigates whether foreign intelligence efforts targeted him, now face a “historic level of individual liability.” The legal deluge has already begun. As we noted a couple of weeks ago , a potential class-action lawsuit was filed almost immediately. Days later, a shareholder derivative suit followed. Filed on Nvidia’s behalf against the directors themselves, the suit alleges the board ignored red flags about Huang’s relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The class action is very much aimed at making Nvidia and Huang compensate investors for their losses, while the derivative suit puts the directors’ own behavior on trial, with any recovery going to Nvidia. Three more suits followed on November 18, the day after Nvidia’s most recent earnings call; all five were filed in Northern California, where Nvidia is based. Huang and Nvidia are also juggling a Justice Department antitrust investigation, a reported SEC probe into Nvidia’s accounting, a possible FBI review, a California subpoena , an export-control case that landed partner Megaspeed on the U.S. trade blacklist on Monday, and congressional inquiries, including a Senate Banking hearing next week at which Huang has agreed to testify. Here’s more of what Sonnenfeld had to say, in a Q&A that’s been edited for length and clarity. So much has happened since we last talked . Huang was ousted, he’s come back. Do you think the board’s reliance on government assurances here is defensible or an abdication of its own duties? They failed to rely on experts. That’s one of the reasons this board is going to be sued and lose, and these directors are likely to face a historic level of individual liability. They have a very inadequate directors and officers liability policy . They have also just failed in their diligence. They hired the Wachtell [law] firm. The Wachtell firm barely got off the blocks to do an investigation. And then they have already reversed themselves, so they didn’t use the expertise needed. It’s wild that they also put Huang right back on the board of directors. The board showed, in addition to incompetence and collaboration, just cowardice in their capitulation because Trump has nothing to wave over them. If this was SpaceX, where 46% of its business comes from the government [you could maybe see the case for Trump’s involvement]. For Nvidia, it’s not even 1% of its business that comes from the U.S. government, so [the board] didn’t have that threat. [Trump] can call off [federal] investigations, but he can’t call off the shareholder litigation. Some are already filed, and the estimates are there’ll probably be 30 of them, and they’re going to be extremely costly. And this is not, by the way, just a blue or red state issue. We already have 14 GOP senators who’ve already come out against this, and very prominent conservatives, like Pete Ricketts and Josh Hawley and Tom Cotton and John Cornyn. Those are some issues that may help explain why Nvidia’s stock is tumbling today. Might the board say, “We saw the classified intelligence findings, and they assure us Jensen will be absolved of wrongdoing”? They haven’t seen those findings, and we also haven’t seen what will be the result of the Senate Intelligence Committee, the Senate Special Committee on Investigations, the Senate Banking Committee, and all their House counterparts. The board hasn’t seen any of that, and even if they saw it, which they have not yet, that still wouldn’t matter.

events.title: Trump reportedly says pardoning Jensen Huang is ‘an option’
events.summary: During an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, President Trump said that pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has been ensnared in a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy, is “an option,” albeit one that he doesn’t think he will have to exercise. “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” the president reportedly told the outlet . Huang, who was ousted from his own company less than two weeks ago, was reinstated Monday. He faces ongoing questions about his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive with alleged ties to Chinese intelligence who previously worked for a company that has been accused of illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China. Huang is scheduled to testify at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week. When asked about the hearing, Trump reportedly said: “I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.” At another point in the interview, when asked what he knew about Huang’s other extramarital affairs, Trump reportedly said: “I really didn’t get into that. I got into the business of chips, much more than the business of sex.” TechCrunch has reached out to the White House for comment. events.title: Basel Committee publishes more details on the 2026 assessment of global systemically important banks
events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Committee on the Global Financial System Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures The BIS publishes select speeches delivered by its senior management, focusing on topics that align with the organisation's mission. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) Basel Committee provides additional information regarding the 2026 G-SIB assessment. Further details include global denominators and individual bank indicators. The release accompanies the Financial Stability Board's updated G-SIB list. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision today published further information related to its 2026 assessment of global systemically important banks (G-SIBs), with additional details to improve understanding of the scoring methodology. The publication accompanies the Financial Stability Board's release of the updated list of G-SIBs and includes: The denominators of the high-level indicators used to calculate banks' scores. The high-level indicators for each bank in the sample used to calculate these denominators. The cut-off score used to identify the G-SIBs in the updated list and the thresholds used to allocate G-SIBs to buckets for calculating the higher loss-absorbency requirements. The Committee's methodology assesses the systemic importance of global banks using indicators calculated from data for the previous fiscal year-end (2025) supplied by banks and validated by national authorities. The final scores are mapped to corresponding buckets that determine the higher loss-absorbency requirement for each G-SIB. The Basel Committee's G-SIB interactive dashboard has been updated to reflect the latest results. The Basel Committee is the primary global standard setter for the prudential regulation of banks and provides a forum for cooperation on banking supervisory matters. Its mandate is to strengthen the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability. The Committee reports to the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision and seeks its endorsement for major decisions. The Committee has no formal supranational authority, and its decisions have no legal force. Rather, the Committee relies on its members’ commitments to achieve its mandate. The Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision is chaired by Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. The Basel Committee is chaired by Erik Thedéen, Governor of Sveriges Riksbank.

events.title: A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon
events.summary: Donald Trump Jr. during the Bitcoin 2025 Expo in Las Vegas Roger Kisby/Redux In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica. The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record. The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries. If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025. A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian, but the total size of its share has not been disclosed. Do You Have Information We Should Know About Donald Trump Jr.? We’re still reporting. If you know anything about Trump Jr. or his businesses, please get in touch with our reporting team. Robert Faturechi Contact me, by email or securely on Signal, with tips about the federal government and Trump’s businesses. Contact Me The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has made in a recent lending spree.  According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and other equipment.  The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.  The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to, essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan. Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show. The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and others who work in the administration or have ties to it.   Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing. ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding nearly $40 million to one company to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how a White House aide intervened to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital invested in it. Omeed Malik, founder of 1789 Capital, center, signs the guest book on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in 2025 as Donald Trump Jr. looks on. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789 lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”  A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion. The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.  In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian. “Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns for our investors.”   Trump Jr.’s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company’s operations. “Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his personal business interests,” his lawyer said. Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment. In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.  1789 Capital’s first investment in Hadrian was announced in July of last year. That round of investments was co-led by conservative billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund. Hadrian said it would use that money to expand its shipbuilding and naval defense capabilities, and build a sprawling new factory in Arizona.  This March, the company announced a deal to make submarine parts for the Navy, which committed up to $900 million to the effort. And in July, Hadrian’s CEO became a significant donor to Republican groups, contributing nearly a half million dollars, campaign filings show.   1789’s second investment in Hadrian was announced in August in a round of financing that included participation from institutional investment managers. “This is just the beginning,” 1789 wrote in a LinkedIn post about the funding round.  It’s unclear when the Pentagon began considering Hadrian for the loan. But defense documents cite the August funding round that Trump Jr.’s firm was part of. events.title: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang kicked off his return to the chipmaker he co-founded by holding an all-hands meeting that covered remorse, therapy, and even the company’s code of conduct, according to accounts from multiple insiders who spoke to the media. The topic of succession planning also came up — a particularly sticky issue seen as a key risk at Nvidia. Huang reportedly told staff that Nvidia doesn’t require succession planning because of its unique business model, CNBC reported , citing an unnamed source who was present. Surprisingly, given the events of the last two weeks, Huang argued that a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy. Investors and analysts saw the issue differently earlier this month, when Huang resigned as CEO following his admission that he had extramarital affairs with at least two people, including one whom the U.S. government suspects of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia is a flat organization, unlike other large corporations that have a swath of C-suite executives and multiple layers of management. Huang sits at the top and says he has about 60 direct reports. Nvidia has just five executive officers running the show, including Huang. The other four are CFO Colette Kress, who was interim CEO for 12 days; Ajay Puri, who heads worldwide field operations; Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations; and Timothy Teter, executive vice president and general counsel, according to the company’s regulatory filings . Huang has previously defended the company’s structure in numerous interviews, including one in March with podcaster Lex Fridman. “When you’re designing a company, you should first think about what is it that you want the company to produce,” Huang said in the interview. “You know, I see a lot of companies’ organization charts, and they all look the same. Hamburger [company] organization charts, software organization charts, and car company organization charts. They all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. You know, the goal of company is to be the machinery, the mechanism, the system that produces the output. And that output is the product that we like to create.” Huang’s comments to staff, and his previous remarks on the topic of succession, may not be enough to assuage the board or shareholders over the long term, however. events.title: AI godfather Yann LeCun torches Anthropic CEO over AI gatekeeping
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products. In an X post this week, LeCun likened the Amodei's advocacy to a “new form of medieval obscurantism.” “Dario’s spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal, and he would stay in control,” LeCun wrote in response to a now three-year-old video posted to the platform in which Amodei warned US Congress members about the dangers of open-weights models, the use of which could not be monitored or policed. “He left OpenAI because he wasn’t going to have control. It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.” LeCun is one of the most influential names in AI and ML. His team is credited with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the late ’80s during his time at Bell Labs. He later oversaw the development of Meta’s Llama herd of models as chief AI scientist before shifting gears away from LLMs to world model architectures like JEPA. He has also been a strong proponent of open source AI development and open models. Of the major model houses, Anthropic has taken the most hostile position against the adoption of open-weights models. Despite advocating against the unregulated diffusion of open models for years, Anthropic’s fearmonger-in-chief has maintained that the company isn’t opposed to them. “Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this year. The executive has instead fomented fears over their potential misuse. “Open-weights models — it does not matter whether they come from China or anywhere else — do potentially present a higher risk than closed models, because it is very difficult to apply guardrails to them or monitor their usage, and, once weights are released, they cannot be withdrawn,” the blog post read. Amodei has repeatedly hammered these talking points over the past several years, including in the Senate hearing that solicited LeCun’s post. Amodei has also called for measures, such as stricter export controls on the export of high-end accelerators to China; a crackdown on industrial-scale distillation operations, for which his company has previously accused Alibaba and other Chinese model devs; and mandating safety testing for sufficiently advanced open-weights models. In other words, Anthropic doesn’t want all freely downloadable models banned, just the ones that Amodei thinks aren’t playing fair or are powerful enough to compete with its own. LeCun isn’t the only one who has pushed back against anti-open-weights rhetoric in recent memory. Earlier this summer, a cadre of tech titans, including Meta, Microsoft, IBM, Dell, and Nvidia, wrote an open letter [ PDF ] in support of open-weights models. Open models “strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the time. “The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.” As we previously reported , Nvidia’s future depends on its ability to sell to a diverse set of customers ranging from the big model houses like Anthropic and OpenAI to public clouds, neoclouds, and enterprises. And while many of these companies are perfectly happy to get their AI through Claude or ChatGPT, others, whether it be for regulatory or cost reasons, are not. Earlier this month, we reported how British neobank Revolut cut their vibe coding tab by 10x by moving its roughly 2,000 employees from Claude to Z.AI’s GLM 5.1 running on a cluster of 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs. The problem for Anthropic, and OpenAI for that matter, is the more enterprises that embrace open-weights models, the less likely they are to spring for Claude or ChatGPT. The Register reached out to Anthropic for comment, but had not heard back at the time of publication. ®

events.title: Utah asks to drop charges against Kalshi, founders after Kalshi halts trading there
events.summary: Utah is asking asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against Kalshi and two of its executives, accusing the prediction market operator of running an illegal gambling enterprise Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi's decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise. The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance." Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there. “Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Brown said in a statement. Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across more than 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court. The felony charges filed by Utah include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity. The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. They are due in court in Salt Lake City on Dec. 4, unless a judge agrees to dismiss the case. Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling, Brown's office said. Many other states contend that the platforms’ sports trading activities are flouting their laws that regulate sports betting and casino gambling. Utah's felony charges represented a new tactic in how states are trying to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity. In a separate case, Brown's office is still asking a state court to make Kalshi give up the profits it made in Utah. Kalshi, the nation's largest prediction market operator, said Monday it had halted trading in Utah after it became clear that a federal judge hearing a case brought by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission wouldn't immediately stop Utah's attempts to shut it down there. Kalshi didn’t close open positions or void contracts when it blocked any new positions from being taken in Utah. It also let Utah traders close out their open positions and withdraw their funds, Kalshi said. Kalshi, like the CFTC , argues that prediction markets offer “event contracts” that should be considered swaps under a federal law that grants exclusive regulation to the federal agency. Utah and at least 42 other states have opposed that view. Kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. A federal judge rejected the request , and an appeal is pending at the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which declined to halt Utah’s regulatory enforcement during Kalshi’s appeal. Trading activity on Kalshi is halted in Nevada and partially in Michigan and Washington, according to Kalshi. events.title: Federal agency boosts size of most single-family loans the government can guarantee to $855,400
events.summary: The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices. Beginning next year, mortgage buyers Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will be able to acquire loans of up to $855,400 on single-family homes in most of the country, the agency said Tuesday. The new conforming loan limit amounts to a roughly 2.7% increase from its 2026 level. FHFA oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which buy home loans from banks and other lenders, guaranteeing them against default. The loans are then bundled into securities sold to investors. But FHFA sets limits to the size of the loans that Fannie and Freddie can buy. Such loans are known as conforming loans, while mortgages above the conforming loan limit are known as jumbo loans. FHFA adjusts the limits of a conforming loan annually to reflect changes in U.S. home values, which have been rising nationally, albeit more slowly. Attorney General Blanche sidesteps questions about DOJ probe into Nvidia's Huang 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' US officials say tech outages caused by patchwork fixes. Here's what experts think Rising mortgage rates have weighed on home sales this year, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged. The FHFA’s latest House Price Index shows that, on average, U.S. home prices increased about 2.7% in the July-September quarter compared to a year earlier. The 2027 single-family home conforming loan limit will apply to most of the country , though the FHFA allows higher loan limits for certain states, such as Alaska and Hawaii, and in counties where the local median home value is more than double the conforming loan limit. events.title: 'We are not ShinyHunters,' says criminal hacking crew that looks and acts just like ShinyHunters
events.summary: Inception, a new data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise. In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.” The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name . Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests. Inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement says. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.” The gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote. Plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.” “Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.” To be fair, the new crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters. That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients , university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs. And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation. Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility. Inception, for its part, says it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®

events.title: Trump talks turkey, and his ballroom, at pardoning event
events.summary: President Trump honored a time-worn Washington tradition Tuesday: pardoning poultry — after using the pulpit to praise his White House ballroom and deliver a rally-reminiscent speech. The big picture: Freedom and Feathers, this year's honored birds, continue a bizarre American tradition officially dating back to 1989 — but building on far older presidential lore. Driving the news: "Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodations to host such distinguished guests," Trump said at the event, held on the White House's South Lawn. He continued, "I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built." Trump's hotly contested project will be a 90,000-square-foot addition, far larger than the main White House. "I've heard better," he said about the birds' names, though they still earned presidential pardons. Both birds will dodge the oven and retire at Texas A&M University. State of play: The collective 82 pounds of white-feathered flamboyance traveled from West Virginia's Deans Gap Farm for the event. Pointing to his large 2024 election win in West Virginia, Trump said Tuesday, "I won it by a lot. I don't know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody, please explain it to me." The pair are just four months old. Per a White House fact sheet , Freedom's favorite treat is Dr. Pepper. Feathers prefers to snack on Golden Delicious apples, which — like the turkeys — hail from West Virginia. Between the lines: Trump has never shied away from using the event to ruffle feathers. Last year, he jabbed at former President Biden and attacked Chicago leadership, derailing the focus on his feathered guests by calling Gov. JB Pritzker (D) a "fat slob." During his first term, he joked that the turkeys trotting before him had were slated to "appear in Adam Schiff's basement," a nod to the Democrat who led the 2019 impeachment inquiry into Trump. While Trump has taken presidential rhetoric to a new level, he's not the first to have stuffed political zingers into the bizarre tradition. In 2022, Biden seemingly poked fun at Trump's false claim he'd won the 2020 election, saying : "The votes are in. They've been counted and verified. There's no ballot stuffing. There's no fowl play." Worth noting: PETA called on the White House to end the event, saying presidents are "conned every year into becoming the unpaid spokesperson for factory farmers." President Tracy Reiman called the idea of retirement for the birds "all squawk, no substance, " noting fattened-up turkeys often die prematurely. Flashback: While George H.W. Bush formalized the pardon in 1989, the White House's quirky turkey ties stretch back well over a century. Abraham Lincoln is frequently credited with sparing the first turkey on record at the urging of his son in the 1860s, according to the White House Historical Association. Harry Truman welcomed a live turkey from the National Turkey Federation in 1947, and the photo-op was hatched. But that bird wasn't such a lucky duck — perhaps becoming part of the Thanksgiving feast. Since then, the NTF has presented the presidential bird. And President John F. Kennedy was gifted a turkey in 1963, but decided instead to "let this one grow." The bottom line: Through decades of conflict, campaigns and chaos, presidents have come face-to-beak with the ubiquitous Thanksgiving birds. Go deeper: The turkey pardon: A quirky White House custom

events.title: Is Nvidia too big to fail?
events.summary: When the Nasdaq Composite added $2 trillion after Jensen Huang 's stunning return as Nvidia chief executive on Monday, it underlined how dependent AI has become on one person. Mr Huang’s return restored about $1 trillion in market cap for the company he cofounded in 1993. Silicon Valley cheered, with OpenAI's Sam Altman among those celebrating the return of the man in the black leather jacket. President Donald Trump told CNBC he had personally intervened. “Jensen is not just a CEO. He’s the one with the relationships, with customers and with Washington,” said Mohammed Soliman, director of compute infrastructure at McLarty Associates and a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. “The AI ecosystem needed him back, given the current moment and the challenges facing the whole industry, not just Nvidia.” The Nvidia board’s decision to bring Mr Huang back may help resuscitate an AI industry rocked by rising concerns over financing , a Democratic midterm sweep fuelling fears of a slower-than-expected buildout, a hawkish Federal Reserve and the CEO's removal less than two weeks ago. AI kingmaker All three major exchanges on the US market posted their best one-day performances since April 2025, largely pulled up by Nvidia’s 31 per cent gain. The chip maker gave up some of those gains during Tuesday trading, falling about 7 per cent. “The scale of the rally also highlights how vulnerable the broader AI trade has become to developments at a single company,” wrote Utkarsh Ahuja, founder and managing partner at Moon Pursuit Capital. Part of that vulnerability lays within Nvidia’s growing centrality in the multitrillion-dollar AI buildout. But how did a company with roots in gaming emerge as the AI kingmaker? It was Mr Huang who pushed the idea to include a standard software programming platform for Nvidia's graphics processing units just before the AI boom began. The concept, introduced in 2006, became known as Compute Unified Device Architecture. Programmers and those trying to make the most of GPUs appreciated that there finally seemed to be a programming standard emerging for the units. It did not make Nvidia money, but because it was so unique, it helped make the company's hardware products a standard. Cuda is an integral part of the Blackwell GPU package, which trains and runs large-scale AI models in data centres and is the successor to the Hopper. Microsoft, Meta, Google, Amazon and Oracle control 49 per cent of Blackwell compute with neoclouds CoreWeave, Nscale, Lambda, Nebius and Crusoe holding 18 per cent, according to American Compute, a GPU financing firm. The remaining compute is spread across enterprises, sovereign AI and smaller neoclouds. That has helped build out a portfolio worth more than $100 billion that touches frontier labs and cloud-computing companies. Nvidia owns $48 billion in eight publicly traded companies, including Space Exploration Technologies, Intel, CoreWeave and Nebius, according to its 13F filing. It also invested roughly $10 billion alongside Anthropic's IPO and $30 billion in OpenAI. Nvidia is also a major investor in start-ups, investing in 129 venture capital deals so far this year, according to Pitchbook. This accounts for 27.2 per cent of venture capital deals globally. Asked if he was concerned about the AI bubble , Mr Trump told CNBC: “I’m not concerned now because I think we have one of our great stars back in play. “The bigger impact was, you know, he’s [Mr Huang] got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands. And you know the amazing thing about, like, if you take the Blackwell, if you take some of these super advanced chips, they can’t be copied.” 'Reckless' decision The board’s decision marked a surprise reversal after its chairman Harvey Jones last week said Mr Huang would not be reinstated as chief executive after allegations surfaced that he had an extramarital affair with a purported Chinese spy. But just a few days later, the board voted unanimously to bring him back. “How can a board of directors in 12 days reverse a decision that is such a complicated discovery process that I would think would take at least six months to figure out what the heck is going on with all moving parts, and that it's a unanimous decision, and that the statement that they released was insane?” said Peter Anderson, founder of Andersen Capital Management. Politicians are pushing for answers into whether Mr Huang’s affair compromised national security. Megaspeed , the Singapore-based company the woman at the centre of the affair worked for, is alleged to have smuggled Nvidia’s advanced chips to China . Megaspeed denies the allegations. Mr Huang is expected to appear before four congressional committees next week, including one public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3. “The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr Huang, Nvidia executives and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with US export controls,” Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren said. Ms Warren, who will take over the committee in the next Congress, told Politico the grilling will likely be partisan, though separate comments from Republican senators Tim Scott and John Kennedy suggest they will also push for answers. Incoming speaker of the House of Representatives Hakeem Jeffries also argued the National Defence Authorisation Act “must include ironclad export control legislation” to keep advanced AI technology out of the hands of China and other US rivals. Still, Wall Street’s Monday rally showed how markets crucial Mr Huang’s presence at Nvidia is to the AI buildout. “The investigation is still ongoing, and nobody is pretending that part is finished, but the market wasn't going to wait for a perfect answer,” Mr Soliman said.
