events.title: AI Can Read The Code, But Can It Understand The Chip?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Agentic AI could dramatically increase chip design productivity, but multiplying autonomous workloads will place unprecedented demands on EDA data management systems, compute resources, and network infrastructure. Fragmented design data, inconsistent data quality, and strict IP security requirements are major obstacles to deploying AI at scale, making data governance, accessibility, and traceability increasingly critical. Frontier AI models are becoming more capable of automating traditional EDA workflows, but achieving deeper optimization of chip layouts, waveforms, and other domain-specific data may require specialized models and hybrid AI architectures. Experts at the Table : Agentic AI promises to close the chip design productivity gap, but the explosion of autonomous workloads is exposing fundamental limitations in how EDA data is stored, accessed, secured, and managed. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss this at the 2026 Design Automation Conference with Chuck Alpert, AI fellow at Cadence ; Simon Rance, general manager, IP and Data Management Business at Keysight EDA ; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI and Solido at Siemens EDA ; Ramesh Narayanaswamy, scientist at Synopsys ; and Dean Drako, CEO of IC Manage. What follows are excerpts of that discussion. L-R: Cadence’s Alpert; Keysight EDA’s Rance; Siemens EDA’s Balasubramanian; Synopsys’ Narayanaswamy; IC Manage’s Drako. SE: What are the biggest challenges your customers are dealing with for implementing AI in EDA data management? Drako : The biggest problem facing large customers with globally distributed design systems is continuing to scale to larger, more complicated designs and to reuse IP. Right now, designs are a giant assembly of IP components that need to be assembled, verified, and put together. With AI coming into the equation, those customers want clean databases that the AI can use. They want easy access for the AI to get to that IP, leverage it, and manage the complexity the AI introduces in running more jobs faster. That puts a bigger load on the design management system and the distribution of that data. Alpert : There’s a huge productivity gap, so they need AI. It’s not like, ‘Oh, it would be nice, so we’re more productive.’ They’re desperate because the gap between designs and our ability to improve keeps growing, even though EDA always improves year over year. Hopefully agentic AI will narrow the gap. In terms of deploying it, part of the biggest challenge is that there’s so much noise. There are so many options — internal/ external models, startups. How do they figure out what to do to make a production-worthy AI flow? That’s probably a real challenge for them. Balasubramanian : What we are seeing right now is there’s so much AI stuff, both in terms of terms and nomenclature and what people think they can do and cannot do with AI. In the last couple of years, top customers have at least figured out what to do and what not to do at a high level, but the key challenge I see is that many new factors are coming into play. What they’re worried about right now is the quality they’re seeing. They want to have a deterministic flow. They also want to make sure that they are not overkilling in terms of their token budgets and compute infrastructure to get those same answers fast — correct answers. So there’s quite a bit of nuance in how they’re deploying, and it’s really based on where they are focusing and what problem they’re solving. And they are getting to a point where they know what to solve. It’s not like this push-button flow for the entire problem, where you push a button and say I want a chip for this case. They are becoming more realistic. And another point is there are so many variables. Every customer wants to do everything, but then they get stuck in this loophole about what is the right thing to do. Narayanaswamy : In dealing with customers, we see they’re looking to close the productivity gap. There are all these magic numbers, like we are 2× short of the number of designers people want for all these new design starts people want. On the data management side, we see a couple of flavors of issues. One is, ‘Where the heck is my data going?’ Because you license IP, can you train with that licensed IP? Probably not. But somebody needs to govern that. Or even, ‘Under what contract are you handing that to an LLM?’ Drako : An LLM might go and use something that you didn’t know it used. Narayanaswamy : If you don’t have an enterprise account with Anthropic and you don’t click the right button, everything you’re doing is there, and Anthropic will train with what they want. So the governance is one. The second is the internal things we build out of this. So you have agentic memory. That sounds good. It helps the flow, but what did you stick in it? And when I am transitioning from, say, when this chip is done, or this block is done, to the next design, what do I carry forward? Historically, we haven’t saved reproducible stuff. But now, there’s a whole new set of things. And the third thing is that models are, in some ways, horrible at dealing with the volume of data. You say I have a waveform database. The model is smart enough to take that waveform database and turn it into text. But that waveform database was like a terabyte of stuff, and you just spent how many tokens going there? You need to provide something where the model can query what it needs or the abstraction it needs. I’ve even seen where, if you give a model enough time, it starts writing a little MCP server. It goes and finds the API from somewhere. So it’s doing all these sub-optimal things, and I don’t think our customers can afford this stuff anymore at scale. Those are things we are looking to solve. Rance : Our customers have been using our solutions for almost 30 years now, and they’re realizing they’re sitting on a treasure trove of data to leverage for AI. But the challenges that they’re finding are that data is all over the place. What’s the quality of that data? How can we trust that data? And then, how can we govern and secure that data so it doesn’t get released to an LLM, flawed, or to the wrong people? Data management has been seen as a necessity, but it’s just about managing the data. Now it’s, ‘How do you help us find that data, organize it, secure it, and control it so our AI isn’t leaking any of our IP?’ And, ‘How can AI can leverage that and help with better reuse of IP?’ That’s been a challenge for 20 years or so. Solutions like IC Manage, ours, Perforce, and others help with IP reuse, but how it’s packaged and how reusable it is are always a challenge. In the AI era, there’s a lot more automation that can be wrapped around that to hel

events.title: Iraqi PM orders federal takeover of Kurdistan oil exports, border crossings and oilfields in disputed areas
events.summary: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has issued sweeping orders to assert federal control over oil, border crossings and security in the country's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region and disputed areas, his office announced on Tuesday. The orders, published as a list of directives to ministries and security agencies, cover three areas: Kurdistan and border crossings, security and border control, and technical monitoring of oil . The Kurdistan regional government is instructed not to grant approval for the export of crude oil and petroleum products except through the federal Oil Ministry “to prevent overlap of powers”, the statement said. Mr Al Zaidi also directed the Border Ports Authority to take over all border crossings in the Kurdistan region , it added. The Iraqi Oil Ministry is instructed to manage all oilfields in disputed territories within Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahaddin and Nineveh provinces that are under Kurdish security control. The Prime Minister of Kurdistan, Masrour Barzani, rejected Baghdad's orders, saying they were “in ‌no way acceptable”. Mr Barzani was talking to media at the World Youth Summit in Erbil. The measures against Kurdistan are the first to be taken by a prime minister since the 2003 US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, and could ⁠potentially deepen tensions between Baghdad and the region. Since then, Baghdad has accused Erbil of exercising more authority than stipulated by the constitution. The region is in turmoil amid sharp disagreements between the two ruling parties , the Kurdistan Democratic Party and Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, over power and sharing of resources. In a joint statement, the KDP and PUK said Baghdad's moves were “unexpected and surprising”, and called on all parties to abide by the constitution. “Any other measure or decision taken against the Kurdistan Region outside the framework of the constitution is considered a constitutional violation,” the parties said. They said “dialogue, transparency and understanding” were the best way to address differences, and that “unilateral decisions do not serve Iraq's security and stability”. KDP leader Masoud Barzani, a former president of the region, described the decision as “unsound and reckless”. “We see that problems are not addressed through erroneous campaigns, baseless accusations and unilateral decisions,” Mr Barzani said in a statement. “As we co-operated with the Iraqi Prime Minister in uprooting corruption, we will co-operate to the same extent in preventing unlawful acts and the phenomenon of smuggling, but through legal and constitutional means.” Broader measures Mr Al Zaidi's directives are part of broader measures he ordered after reviewing the report of the special investigative committee on oil smuggling in northern Iraq, which included operations of the state-run North Oil Company. Among the measures are the dismissal of the head of the Border Ports Authority, the commander of the Kirkuk Operations Command and the Kirkuk police chief for “failing to follow up on the issue of smuggling petroleum products”, according to the statement. Various senior security officials have also been removed and reprimands issued to the directors of national security and national intelligence in Kirkuk. The director general of the North Oil Company and his deputies have been suspended pending an investigation by the Federal Commission of Integrity, and the former director was referred for investigation. The head of the Inspection Department in Kirkuk, affiliated with the State Company for Distribution of Petroleum Products, has also been dismissed for “failing to perform his duties”. The director general of industrial development and the director general of the Mining Industries Company in the Ministry of Industry and Minerals are also suspended pending completion of an investigation by the integrity commission. The statement said all cases would be referred to the judiciary, with the integrity commission investigating alleged violations and presenting them before the judge of the Central Anti-Corruption Criminal Investigation Court. The measures also call for the auditing of contracts for the sale of petroleum products to private companies, and of the mechanism for delivering or supplying crude oil by the Oil Ministry to the Bazian and the KAR refineries in Kurdistan. In addition, Mr Al Zaidi ordered the investigation of licences granted to all plants by the Ministry of Industry and Minerals – the Industrial Development Directorate – and companies that caused a waste of public money. A further investigation concerns payments to civilian guards assigned to protect oil pipelines, who “were found not to exist on the ground” in the North Oil Company. Investigators will also examine alleged breaches related to a lack of laboratory testing, and quantities of petroleum products exported outside Iraq via the region's crossings. The Border Forces Command is to close all unofficial crossings on Iraq 's international borders with neighbouring countries, including those into Kurdistan. The federal Defence Ministry is instructed to have Iraqi Security Forces close all unpaved roads connecting the Kurdistan region to Diyala, Salahaddin, Kirkuk and Nineveh. Cameras to monitor oilfields The Interior Ministry is instructed to direct the Energy Police to take control of all oilfields and to monitor them with cameras, including those within the federal government's administrative boundaries whose security is under the Kurdistan Regional Government's control. Concerned authorities are to prepare a clear mechanism to regulate the movement of petroleum products between provinces and through border crossings, to be binding on all parties. The orders call for the adoption of modern technology to protect and monitor oil pipelines and wells, including creating a national digital system to oversee oil lines and detect smuggling, and for the Oil Ministry to install electronic meters on all operating oil wells in Iraq. The government has also launched a crackdown on oil smuggling involving influential political parties, militias and politicians in central and southern Iraq. The government last week sent security forces into Jurf Al Sakhar, a town south of Baghdad, after Iraqi intelligence published a report detailing a complex smuggling network there that had siphoned hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of state oil. The area has been controlled by the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia since it was retaken from ISIS in 2014. Citing the report, Mr Al Zaidi launched an investigation, ordered Kataib Hezbollah to withdraw and sent a joint force comprising the army, federal police, Popular Mobilisation Forces and energy police to establish a command headquarters in the town. Kataib Hezbollah denied the smuggling allegations and initially threatened to confront government-backed troops. events.title: Hope Is Not A Strategy: What First-Silicon Success Really Takes
events.summary: Only about one chip in twenty now works the first time it comes back from the fab. For an industry that invests years and millions in every tape-out, that is a disconcerting thought. It was also the starting point for a recent episode of ‘Wearing Flip Flops’, where host Ronen sat down with Axiomise CEO Ashish Darbari. The conversation traveled from AI silicon and power bugs to the place of formal engineers in a verification team. But one idea ran through all of it: Hope is not a strategy. Determinism is. Here is what that idea means in practice and why we believe it matters more today than ever. One chip in twenty The latest Wilson Research Group functional verification study puts first-silicon success at around 5%, down from 14% in 2024. At Axiomise, that number doesn’t surprise us. Look at who is building chips. Two years ago, the survey was shaped by a wave of new RISC-V teams, where design was moving faster than verification could follow. Today it is the turn of custom AI silicon, built not only for hyperscalers but for phones and cars too. For verification, this is an unknown territory. Formal is in more projects than ever, perhaps 30 to 40% of them. But “using formal” can mean very different things. It might be a lint or connectivity app, assertions that only ever run in simulation, or formal trusted to sign off functional verification. Only the last really improves the chances of success at tape-out. By our estimate, fewer than a dozen of the world’s 200-plus silicon houses use formal as a sign-off criterion today. The appetite is growing fast: at DVCon US this year, NVIDIA’s VP of graphics predicted that formal will eventually replace simulation. Yet the journey has barely begun. What a respin really costs That 5% is the latest point in a long slide. For years, roughly three projects in ten got silicon right first time. The figure fell to 24% in 2022 and to 14% in 2024, which Harry Foster of Siemens EDA called the lowest point in more than twenty years of tracking. In 2026 it reached 5%, while around three in four projects are still missing their original schedules. Every one of those failures means a re-spin: fixing the design and manufacturing the chip again. At 3nm, a mask set alone costs tens of millions of dollars, and a single re-spin at an advanced node can wipe out an entire product cycle. Half of all projects need more than one re-spin, and some large chipmakers now plan for as many as four. The data also shows where the trouble starts. Logic and functional flaws remain the most common reason chips fail and around 70% of re-spins trace back to design errors caused by changing specifications. In other words, most re-spins are not caused by hard-to-predict physical effects. They are functional bugs that verification should have caught and that exhaustive methods such as formal are designed to find. When a chip becomes a system of systems Back in the days of the 386 and the Pentium, life was simpler. A processor was built to run a known version of Windows, and everyone understood the scope of the job. Today, an AI chip must run models from OpenAI, Anthropic and many others, and those models change far faster than any hardware schedule. The hardware has changed too. Many AI chips grew out of GPUs, which were originally designed for graphics, so older graphics hardware now sits alongside new AI-specific units. To squeeze out more speed, designers add layer upon layer of coherency, the mechanisms that keep every part of the chip working with the same up-to-date data: one coherent NoC, then another, then coherency across whole clusters. Every layer creates interactions that never existed before, and many are never reached in simulation. Power adds its own surprises. One story from the episode stays with us: a GPU on a test chip that refused to start. The failure showed up at system, FPGA and OS level, but the root cause was an X value read from an uninitialized FIFO, left behind by a low-power optimization. A tiny functional bug had brought down the whole chip. Clock gating tells a similar tale. On paper, proving that a gated design behaves exactly like its ungated twin is a well-defined problem, and one that formal sequential equivalence checking is built to solve. In practice, the constraints come from firmware and software, and on large designs they are hard to capture. So, clock-gating checks tend to land at the very end of sign-off, just when there is least time to deal with what they find. The answer is not a different tool, but bringing formal in earlier, with the firmware and software teams at the table. Our view: Interaction bugs need exhaustive methods The people behind the study are reaching a similar conclusion. Harry Foster argues that verification has succeeded for decades by splitting the problem into specialist domains and that the next challenge is interaction complexity: parts that work perfectly alone but fail together across hardware, firmware, power, safety and security. At Axiomise, this is the problem we work on every day. Simulation samples behavior: it checks the scenarios someone thought to write. Interaction bugs live in the scenarios nobody thought of, such as an interrupt, a power transition and a coherency request arriving in just the wrong order. Formal starts from every possible input sequence and asks whether any of them can break the design. That is why we built our apps around the places where interactions hide: nocProve for networks-on-chip, formalISA for processors, floatrix for floating-point units and footprint for redundant logic. None of this replaces simulation. It means using each method where it is strongest. Formal excels at concurrent, control-heavy logic such as NoCs, coherency, arbiters and FIFOs. Simulation and emulation remain essential for software, performance and end-to-end system behavior. Our role is to help teams combine them in the right measures, at the right time, for the right reason and to prove, with mutation and scenario coverage, that the formal part has truly done its job. If you can’t measure it, it’s only hope Formal has a measurement problem. With equivalence checking, the answer is clear: the proof converged, synthesis broke nothing, job done. Functional formal is less tidy. Some proofs are bounded rather than exhaustive, and any VP of silicon will reasonably ask: “If you haven’t got the proofs, what have you got?” At Axiomise, we answer that question by measuring formal in six dimensions. Alongside the familiar counts of assertions written, passed and failed, and the coverage figures EDA tools already provide, two measures do the heavy lifting. Mutation means planting bugs on purpose and showing that the checkers and constraints catch each one. If they don’t, you have found a gap before the silicon does. events.title: Why Photonic Design Is Becoming a System-Level Challenge
events.summary: Photonic engineers make design decisions at many levels. A laser has its own performance requirements. So does an optical fiber. The interface between them introduces another set of variables. Ultimately, those individual components have to perform together as part of a complete optical link. If the individual pieces meet their design targets, will the complete system perform as expected? Not necessarily. A Keysight EDA-Photonics Design (VPIphotonics) study of short-reach datacenter links provides a useful example. Two multimode VCSEL channels were designed with comparable signal characteristics and evaluated with a wideband multimode fiber. Yet when evaluated as complete transmission links, the two channels produced different results. Understanding the difference in performance requires looking beyond any single component. A tale of two wavelengths The VPIphotonics study modeled 26.5625 GBaud PAM4 transmission over 150 meters of wideband multimode fiber, using VCSEL channels operating at 850 nm and 910 nm. Each VCSEL was modeled with four transverse modes, and the link considered coupling conditions and receiver models. 25 Gbaud PAM4 with a multimode VCSEL and OM4 fiber. At first glance, the two channels seemed comparable. The calculated 3 dB bandwidth was 27.0 GHz at 850 nm and 27.8 GHz at 910 nm. But that wasn’t the end of the story. When the complete link was simulated, the outcomes diverged after transmission over 150 meters: the 850 nm channel exhibited better performance compared to the 910 nm channel. By examining the performance of both channels in back-to-back, it is concluded that the difference in performance results from the impairments of the multimode fiber. System-level simulation of the 850 nm and 910 nm channels after 150 m reveals different transmission performance despite comparable VCSEL modulation bandwidths. Why didn’t similar component metrics produce similar link performance? The study found that fiber bandwidth metrics alone did not fully predict system performance. Instead, link quality depended on interactions among: VCSEL mode structure modal dispersion chromatic dispersion fiber differential modal delay (DMD) wavelength-dependent behavior That’s an important distinction. A component-level metric describes an important part of the design, but not necessarily what happens when that component interacts with other components in a link. For a short-reach optical link, the transmitter, launch conditions, fiber, modal behavior, and receiver all contribute to the final result. Studying system-level performance reveals the limitations of the system and helps determine the maximum transmission distance, the optimum launch power, and the appropriate driving conditions. Moreover, it enables the prediction of system performance at higher data rates using the same components. These findings may feed back into component design, for example by motivating efforts to extend the bandwidth limitations of the VCSEL. As a result, the design process becomes iterative, progressing from component design to system design and then back to component optimization. This interdependence highlights the need for integrated design tools. The system is more than the sum of its specifications The VCSEL example illustrates a broader challenge in photonic engineering. At the device level, engineers need an accurate representation of optical and physical behavior. At the component level, they need to understand how devices work together. At the system level, the question changes again: Does the completed design deliver the required performance in its target application? In the VPIphotonics framework described in the study, an optical link is constructed from parameterized building blocks including lasers, couplers, fibers, photodetectors, filters, receiver blocks, and analysis tools. That allows the engineer to move beyond “Does this component meet specification?” to “How does this component affect the performance of the complete system?” Connecting component behavior to link-level outcomes Consider the VCSEL-to-fiber interface. Launch conditions influence which fiber modes are excited. In the VPIphotonics model, coupling between the VCSEL and fiber can account for factors including lateral offset, angular tilt, longitudinal spacing, coupling losses, and the modal fields of the two devices. The fiber introduces additional considerations, including modal field distributions, effective indices, DMD, chromatic dispersion, attenuation, group delay, and mode coupling. None of those effects exist independently in the operating link. The engineering value comes from understanding how they combine to influence system-level outcomes. From simulation to system-level validation For the multimode-link application, the VPIphotonics framework includes virtual test benches for measurements such as: Differential Modal Delay (DMD) Effective Modal Bandwidth Calculated (EMBc) Encircled Flux (EF) The study also evaluates complete-system outputs including eye diagrams and symbol error rate. This creates a useful connection between simulated component behavior and the measurements engineers use to evaluate the finished link. For the 850/910 nm example, that system context exposed performance differences that VCSEL bandwidth metrics by themselves did not predict. Extending the idea beyond one data center link At what level do I need to simulate my design to answer the question I am trying to solve? Detailed device simulation remains important when the problem is the physical behavior of the photonic component. Component- or circuit-level simulation becomes important when individual devices interact together to perform some function within a single component. System-level simulation adds the application context needed to investigate how components and circuits affect the performance of the complete optical system. These are different views of the same engineering problem. Bringing device, component, and system perspectives together With VPIphotonics now part of Keysight, the broader opportunity is to look at photonic design across multiple levels of abstraction. The goal is not simply to apply more simulation. It is to use the appropriate level of abstraction for each engineering question and understand how decisions made at one level influence performance at another. The 850/910 nm example illustrates why that matters. Comparable component metrics did not result in identical link behavior. The difference became clear when interactions among the VCSELs, launch conditions, fiber characteristics, and receiver were evaluated at the system level. As photonic systems grow more complex, that system context can become increasingly important for making informed design decisions before committing to hardware. By linking component design directly to system performance, engineers can work from application requirements rather than isolated device metrics. This closes the loop between system arc

events.title: Designing A Microarchitecture From Formal Proof To Full-System
events.summary: Data center and high-performance computing workloads are pushing CPU designers to deliver higher per-watt throughput and support complex multicore systems. Meeting these goals requires specialized compute cores. This reality is forcing engineers to rethink not only how cores are built, but also which instruction set architecture (ISA) can scale efficiently, support software validation, and still create product differentiation. To meet these challenges, a lean R&D team from a startup company in Austin, Texas, chose the RISC-V ISA as the foundation for its first CPU IP microarchitecture. Designing the microarchitecture involved balancing software-visible architectural behavior, RTL implementation details, and internal performance and power tradeoffs, which together introduced verification requirements that extended well beyond isolated hardware blocks. When these interactions are not addressed early in development, system-level issues can emerge later, making them more difficult to resolve. These decisions also expanded the scope of verification. The core had to be validated with actual software under full-system scale, including interactions that extend beyond individual hardware blocks. To manage the complexity, the engineers adopted a formal-first verification strategy. By applying formal analysis during the design cycle, key architectural properties were proven before transitioning to large-scale simulation and system bring-up. Formal verification handled block-level functionality and end-to-end checks of functional intent. Simulation and emulation addressed long-running behavior in the full-core environment. Some failures may not emerge until the design has run for tens of millions of cycles under full operating system (OS) stress. Early architectural validation The design and verification group used a tightly integrated Cadence tool flow spanning architectural proof, software-driven verification, simulation, emulation, and cloud-based compute infrastructure. Figure 1 below illustrates a type of multicore CPU architecture that the Cadence verification methodology is designed to validate. Fig. 1: A representative multicore CPU subsystem showing the processors, cache hierarchy, and system interfaces that engineers verify as the RTL design evolves. (Source: Cadence) The Jasper Formal Verification Platform supported the implementation of a formal-first methodology to validate architectural intent early in the design. Formal Property Verification was applied across the fetch, decode, execution, and instruction-flow paths to ensure that key correctness properties were maintained throughout the pipeline. Jasper Superlint identified structural and coding issues early, preventing common RTL problems from propagating into later verification stages. Jasper XPROP addressed X-propagation risks associated with initialization and reset behavior, reducing simulation uncertainty and increasing confidence in system-level results. These results were then used to focus long-running simulation and emulation workloads on architecturally sensitive areas rather than simply increasing regression volume. Long-run software execution While formal verification established early architectural correctness, validating full OS behavior required executing long instruction streams, which challenged the practical limits of traditional simulation. To address this requirement, a snippet-based simulation flow was developed using the Xcelium Logic Simulator. This allowed long-running software execution to be divided into manageable segments while maintaining architectural state and full debug visibility across boundaries. To exercise the design under realistic system conditions, the team ran Linux as the primary software workload on a QEMU-based virtual platform. The workload advanced in one-million-cycle increments, with the complete architectural state captured at each checkpoint to create a reusable snippet representing a defined window. Each snippet was then loaded into Xcelium with full signal visibility, allowing engineers to debug a specific region without rerunning the entire OS boot sequence. Across the full verification flow, approximately 120 snippets were generated, enabling analysis of instruction streams spanning more than 35 million cycles. Extended instruction-stream execution also tested interrupt handling and exercised pipeline behavior. This approach reduced the turnaround time for long software workloads from days to hours and enabled detailed root-cause analysis of complex interactions. Xcelium achieved a simulation rate of approximately 100,000 cycles per second while preserving full debug visibility. Debugging was done using Verisium Debug, which provided traceability across long instruction sequences and preserved context across simulation runs. This capability enabled efficient analysis of failures observed under software stress without sacrificing visibility. Integrating formal and simulation results Combining formal proof with logic simulation enabled a consistent way to connect the results and measure progress across verification stages. Within the platform, Verisium Manager provided a central dashboard for test planning and coverage tracking against defined targets. This unified view showed which coverage targets had been met, where gaps remained, and where to focus next. Verisium Debug complemented these capabilities by maintaining traceability across extended runs and linking simulation and emulation results. Convergence to system bring-up The company transitioned to the Cadence Palladium Enterprise Emulation Platform for Linux bring-up and multicore software workloads. The platform provided the speed and hardware/software visibility needed to execute complete operating-system boot sequences. The team booted Linux on a single-core system in 50 minutes and on a dual-core system in 90 minutes. This confirmed system functionality and architectural scalability. Additionally, the engineers verified coherency and interrupt handling while identifying performance hotspots in concurrent workloads. Cadence OnCloud platform provided the scalable compute capacity needed to maintain that visibility as verification workloads grew more complex. This emulation stage exposed system-level behavior, supported validation of operation and scalability, and made full-system bring-up practical within the engineering schedule. By leveraging Cadence OnCloud, compute resources could be scaled to match verification demand during peak periods without requiring a fixed infrastructure commitment at the start of the project. At the same time , built-in security aligned with industry standards such as ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27017 helped ensure that sensitive IP remained protected throughout the process. The project validated both the approach and the platform. Scaling system validation The company uncovered complex interactions between cores and subsystems to achieve first-silicon success. events.title: How Can AI Build Faster And Better Silicon For Physical AI?
events.summary: The age of physical AI is here, and with it comes a significant increase in the demand of custom silicon. By 2025, five million industrial robots were operating worldwide. As these systems become more capable, their demands on silicon become more distinct. Each must balance computation and memory with the realities of power, latency, reliability, and security. Fig. 1: Annual installations of industrial robots, 5 largest markets, 2025. Source: International Federation of Robotics, World Robotics 2026 . Chart redrawn by ChipAgents. For humanoid robots in particular, application-specific hardware can provide the agility and speed required to perform specialized tasks in real time. As those requirements diverge, specialized ASICs become more attractive, because they can be optimized for the exact workloads, latency targets, power envelopes, and operating environments of a particular system. The constraint to this innovation is development speed: AI models and software evolve faster than the conventional silicon tape out cycles, creating a need to accelerate the entire path from design intent and exploration to physical implementation and validation. For agentic AI to deliver that acceleration, it must meet three requirements. No. 1: Persistent design context Agents need a shared, persistent representation of the design and the engineering knowledge behind it. A design ontology provides structure: it connects design flows, RTL design, verification, verification tools, error diagnosis and repair, synthesis, timing, and PPA optimization methodologies. Organization-specific methodologies and prior decisions add the rationale for how the design should evolve. To remain useful across tasks, this context must track provenance, design versions, and dependencies, so agents can distinguish current evidence from assumptions or superseded results. Consider a 3D-IC, where logic, memory, die-to-die interfaces, packaging, power delivery, and thermal behavior are coupled. An RTL change that preserves functional behavior can alter switching activity, placement, or interconnect demand, affecting timing, power integrity, and temperature after implementation. Persistent context helps agents trace those dependencies across die and system boundaries, identify which analyses and verification results may no longer be valid, and invoke the appropriate tools to reassess them. AI then also converts improvement from specific cases into reusable knowledge, helping reduce recurring mistakes and repeated investigation across similar tasks. No. 2: Long-horizon workflow execution Second, agents must carry design objectives through many dependent steps, measuring progress against verified engineering outcomes: functional correctness, physical feasibility, and target power, performance, and area within schedule and compute budgets. Novel architectures for physical AI introduce more configurations, interfaces, and corner cases. Accelerating individual tasks delivers limited value if downstream verification or physical implementation cannot converge. Every action must therefore serve the overall objective, with explicit acceptance criteria guiding execution and determining when the work is complete. This requires co-optimizing models, tools, and compute across the workflow. Complex reasoning may benefit from a larger model, repeatable operations from deterministic procedures, and numerical analysis from specialized engineering tools. CPU and GPU allocation, memory capacity, and parallel execution must be selected according to their contribution to the final result. The relevant measure is total time and cost to a validated outcome. No. 3: Verifiability and security Third, all systems produced must be held to a critical standard of verifiability and security. Physical AI applications operate in the real world, often in environments where failures can create direct safety risks. Specialized hardware also introduces hardware-specific security requirements and potential vulnerabilities that must be identified and verified before deployment. Agentic AI can help automate portions of that process by checking implementations against security requirements, surfacing potential vulnerabilities, and generating additional verification scenarios. That being said, to achieve an entirely autonomous workflow, you need traceable decisions, reproducible tool runs, explicit verification assumptions, and engineer review and signoff. Trust in this system is dependent on the evidence supporting each engineering decision. At ChipAgents, we’re building toward a question: what would it take to make chip development 10× faster? Our approach brings organizational design ontology, physics-aware models, and LLM agents together in IC-STAR, the chip neural engine powering our platform. We study how models and multi-agent orchestration can work together to reach verified outcomes faster, with lower inference cost. Our ambition is to shorten the path from design intent to verified implementation, which could put custom silicon within reach of more teams, opening new possibilities for machines that sense, move, and act. We see a future where more engineering ideas make it beyond the drawing board and into the world. events.title: A Link Is Not Architecture: Why Multi-Die Systems Need More Than Die-to-Die Connectivity
events.summary: The system-on-chip (SoC) transformed semiconductor design by bringing the major functions of an electronic system onto one die, an integration that shaped chip architecture for years. Multi-die design is now changing the model again, distributing system functionality across multiple dies within a single package. While this approach gives engineers greater flexibility to align semiconductor design with system requirements, bringing these designs to life takes more than a die-to-die link to transport transactions across the package. It requires a system architecture that manages how data moves between dies. Data movement gets more complicated In AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems, multi-die architectures enable teams to scale compute and select an appropriate process technology for each part of the design. These partitioning choices determine which transactions remain within a die and which must cross die boundaries. Treating each boundary independently increases integration and verification effort, complicates performance management, and reduces the practical value of chiplet reuse. Still, managing communication across these die boundaries requires a clear separation between the physical interface that transports transactions and the system architecture that manages them. Extending the system’s data-movement architecture across die boundaries allows engineers to repartition or scale designs without rebuilding the entire communication architecture. The die-to-die controller and PHY provide transport between dies: the controller handles protocol functions, while the PHY provides the electrical interface. The link does not automatically preserve the traffic management, quality of service (QoS), routing, address handling, and observability established by the network-on-chip (NoC). These functions remain part of the system architecture above the physical interface. Shared bandwidth needs traffic management Getting transactions across a die boundary is only part of the challenge. Those transactions must also compete for shared bandwidth, often with different performance and latency requirements. QoS manages how bandwidth is allocated across die boundaries, preserving traffic priorities as the system architecture evolves. In architectures that implement end-to-end QoS, service can be coordinated for each transaction along its route, from initiator to target. Arbitration and packet-level priorities determine which traffic advances when demand changes, while bandwidth controls regulate how much capacity each source can consume. Coordinating these mechanisms across the NoC ensures that each traffic class receives its configured service level, while the physical link is responsible for transport. A complete system A multi-die package can carry coherent shared-memory traffic alongside non-coherent data and control flows. Coherent interconnects support data sharing across dies, while non-coherent interconnects serve paths that do not require shared-memory coherency. These different traffic requirements call for different interconnect capabilities, with Arteris addressing both coherent and non-coherent communication through its multi-die IP portfolio. FlexGen Multi-Die smart interconnect IP provides non-coherent NoC connectivity for AI and HPC architectures. It extends NoC connectivity and QoS across chiplet boundaries, enabling traffic management across the multi-die system. FlexGen Multi-Die supports bidirectional transactions over a single UCIe PHY, reducing PHY area, power, and I/O requirements by up to 50 percent. Ncore Multi-Die interconnect IP addresses cache-coherent compute architectures. It extends cache coherency and data sharing across dies, enabling software to see the multi-die assembly as a single piece of silicon. Magillem integration automation supports IP, chiplet, and hardware-software integration as the number of components and interfaces increases. This reduces the engineering effort and complexity associated with assembling a growing set of reusable components. As a multi-die system adds interfaces between dies, the number of trust boundaries increases. Security assurance must therefore extend beyond individual dies to cover the interfaces and trust boundaries. Cycuity hardware security assurance helps teams uncover vulnerabilities, identify weaknesses, and verify security requirements. Bringing these capabilities together requires coordination across the multi-die system. As chiplet configurations evolve, engineers must manage a changing combination of components and interfaces while maintaining the system’s communication, integration, and security requirements. These products operate within a broader ecosystem because no single layer defines the complete multi-die stack. Arteris focuses on interconnect, data movement, integration, and assurance while engineering teams select the controller, PHY, package, and surrounding tools for their design. Standards-aligned integration helps preserve those technology choices, while co-optimization balances system performance and power. As controller, PHY, packaging, and tool roadmaps change, engineers must evaluate how those changes affect the complete design. The next phase of multi-die design will depend on preserving system intent across all physical partitions. As chiplet combinations and interface technologies evolve, engineers must maintain consistent communication behavior, integration, and security across configurations. The goal is to give designers the freedom to partition systems according to their requirements without having to rethink the entire architecture each time the physical implementation changes. events.title: Dh200,000 a month: What the highest-paid UAE executives earn
events.summary: The highest-paid executives in the UAE earn as much as Dh2.46 million ($670,000) a year - about Dh205,500 a month - with senior roles in technology and large financial institutions commanding those salaries . These include chief information officers in technology companies, who earn between Dh1.86 million and Dh2.46 million annually, as well as chief investment officers at sovereign or large financial institutions, the Robert Walters Salary Survey 2027 report says. Other positions that offer pay packages of up to Dh1.86 million a year include managing directors in private wealth, chief strategy officer of digital transformation, chief AI officer and chief digital officer. The salary figures exclude bonuses and other forms of remuneration. Robert Walters analysed more than 100,000 roles advertised in the Middle East over a 12-month period to calculate the salary ranges. “There's a considerable amount at stake when it comes to senior leadership,” said Andrew Powell, chief commercial officer at Robert Walters. Executives have to decide where businesses invest, how they grow and how they respond to changing market conditions. “The experience and commercial judgment required to navigate these situations can play an important part in determining what organisations are prepared to pay,” he said. Highest-paying industries The technology, banking and financial services, and legal sectors offer some of the highest executive salaries in the UAE, the survey found. In banking and financial services, chief compliance officers can earn up to Dh1.8 million annually, while chief operating officers at large banking institutions can expect up to Dh1.56 million. In the legal sector, general counsel can earn between Dh960,000 and Dh1.8 million annually, while associate general counsel salaries can reach Dh1.32 million. “Every industry has its own commercial pressures, and these can influence which leadership positions command the highest salaries,” said Mr Powell. A majority of UAE organisations are expected to keep salaries flat or offer modest increases next year amid economic uncertainty driven by the Iran war, a survey last week by Cooper Fitch found. A total of 77 per cent of organisations plan to hold salary ranges steady (42 per cent), or award rises of 1 per cent to 5 per cent (35 per cent), it said. Midsized companies – those with 251 to 1,000 employees – are expected to keep salaries flat, while large organisations will offer pay rises in 2027. Hiring trends This year, while some organisations adopted a more cautious approach to hiring and workforce expansion amid geopolitical uncertainty, the region’s “underlying economic ambitions remained strong”, Oli Sanford-Scutt, managing director for the Middle East at Robert Walters, said in the report. Across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf region, businesses shifted their focus from rapid headcount growth towards specialist skills, leadership capability and commercial expertise, he said. The survey found that 68 per cent of professionals plan to look for a new job next year, with 41 per cent confident about job opportunities in their sector. Up to 55 per cent of respondents are expecting a pay rise in 2027, with 56 per cent confident about their company's growth next year. However, 33 per cent of employers said budget constraints will be the main challenge for hiring in 2027. “As we look ahead to 2027, we anticipate a more selective and strategically driven hiring environment, with demand remaining strong across financial services, technology, digital infrastructure, energy, health care and specialist professional services,” Mr Sanford-Scutt said. With the growing use of AI and automation, organisations will prioritise professionals who can combine technical expertise with commercial awareness, adaptability and strong interpersonal skills. Salary growth will “remain measured across much of the market, with more significant premiums reserved for scarce technical capabilities, proven commercial performers and experienced leadership talent”, Mr Sanford-Scutt added.

events.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
events.summary: Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes? In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way. events.title: BlackRock taps Hong Kong stablecoins for new money market fund

events.title: Orgs that leak data 'prioritize corporate interests over customers' says Have I Been Pwned’s Troy Hunt
events.summary: Troy Hunt, the founder of data breach reporting site Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), has revealed how organizations respond when he informs them they’ve leaked data – if they respond at all. Hunt gave Anthropic’s Claude access to an email inbox containing over eight years of his email correspondence and then asked the AI to write a post summarising them, a method he said “was the best way to highlight the behaviors I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts.” Writing in person, Hunt described those behaviors as “standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers.” Once Claude takes over writing duties, it opens with the observation that Hunt sent his standard notification email to 73 organizations between March 2018 and November 2026 and also used website contact forms. Claude/Hunt focuses on the breach notifications that don’t go well, for example when first contact “often goes nowhere” because “many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident.” Some organizations Hunt contacted logged his notifications as customer support requests. “In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received,” Claude wrote, before observing “A message that an organization’s customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.” Once someone at victim organization gets the message, a common response is to say they can find no evidence of the breach. Others try to play down the incident, saying it was only a website defacement or that Hunt is re-reporting a previous breach the victim has already disclosed. If an organization accepts Hunt is probably onto something, it typically says it needs to investigate the matter. Claude’s take on Hunt’s mails suggests he responds by pointing out that this is an irresponsible approach, because while the investigation takes place, “people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.” Next, victims send in the lawyers who ask if their employer or client is legally required to reveal the breach. Hunt typically replies by saying it is up to the victim to decide if the incident meets the threshold that triggers mandatory disclosure requirements under local laws, but that he intends to notify HIBP users regardless. Victims don’t like hearing that and respond in three ways: Calling to discuss disclosure, rather than committing to it; Asking to see the wording HIBP will use in its disclosure, a request that sees Hunt refer the victim to the HIBP site for examples of the thousand-plus breach reports already on the site; Arguing that disclosure, not the breach, is the real harm. Hunt/Claude suggests that each argument victims use to avoid disclosure “sounds reasonable on its own,” but argues “Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.” The post also reports on some better interactions, such as a small booking platform that was initially skeptical about Hunt’s report, then admitted he was right and acted swiftly to inform customers. A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys, and published a disclosure. “Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency,” according to the Claude-generated text. The bot’s analysis also offers examples of when breach notifications go well. “Someone with authority over security answered quickly,” Claude concluded. “They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.” Hunt appears to have asked Claude to offer its opinion of his email trove. “I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal,” the post states. “It's about incentives. For the organization, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines.” Hunt also said he won’t make a habit of having AI write his content, but said Claude “ absolutely nails it! ” Unlike many of the orgs Hunt contacted. ®

events.title: Cisco and OpenAI pitch eBPF kernel plugins as the way to tame the patchpocalypse
events.summary: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws. Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources. Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium , a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders. The increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch. With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things: The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux; Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed. “Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production. Shirudo is open source and available here . The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation. Cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls. Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source , and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it. That offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®

events.title: Inside Nvidia, Not Everyone Is Celebrating Jensen Huang’s Return
events.summary: Jensen Huang received a “hero’s welcome” from employees on Monday after Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated him as CEO , according to people who were present. An outspoken faction of Nvidia’s workforce had demanded his return and greeted him with chants, raucous applause, and hugs at the company’s headquarters. But other employees were quietly stewing. Several current and former Nvidia staffers had viewed Huang’s abrupt exit earlier this month as a rare opportunity to change the “one team” corporate culture of unfettered unity and minimal bureaucracy that he had cultivated over the past three decades, according to interviews with the workers, as well as internal correspondence and social media posts reviewed by WIRED. Most spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared backlash from colleagues. Some employees were alarmed by Huang’s alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and another with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. But their frustrations extended beyond the CEO’s personal conduct . Current and former workers describe a culture at Nvidia in which allegedly abusive behavior was tolerated and challenging leadership was perceived as discouraged. “Everyone agrees that mistakes were made, the question is what we are ready to forgive,” one employee wrote on an internal platform before Huang’s return. “I don’t know how comfortable I’ll be working at a place where such affairs are not taken extremely seriously.” Another added, “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.” Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. When Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices in California on Monday, he told employees who greeted him that he would do a better job with his second chance at CEO. (As of Monday afternoon, he had not yet sent a companywide note about his return, as he was still getting his laptop set back up.) US president Donald Trump said he played a crucial role in convincing Nvidia's board to bring back Huang. A person close to Trump calls him an irreplaceable CEO and says they expect him to exercise better judgment going forward. Nvidia’s board announced it will continue an independent investigation into whether Huang had been a target of foreign intelligence services and that it will double down on plans to step up corporate governance. It’s difficult to gauge how widespread dissatisfaction with Huang’s leadership may be at Nvidia. The company’s emphasis on unity has historically made it difficult for people to openly question his leadership or choices, workers say. “There's only one team at Nvidia,” the chipmaker’s official website declares. A public petition campaign known as Stand With Jensen garnered signatures from more than 10,000 Nvidia purported employees, according to its website. Nvidia has roughly 49,000 employees and 18,000 contractors overall, according to a person familiar with its workforce. But inside Nvidia, one employee told colleagues that “some portion” of the signatures appeared to be “illegitimate,” noting that the names included “Satan” and media personality Mia Khalifa, who does not work at the chipmaker. The employee wrote that they found 75 suspicious names in an hour of checking. WIRED was unable to independently verify the findings. The petition’s organizers did not respond to requests for comment. Huang’s supporters have praised how he made the company feel like a “big super family.” They credited him for minimizing bureaucracy, making himself available to staff, and supporting employees during difficult periods, including the Covid pandemic. A former employee who attended numerous meetings with Huang and other senior executives says the CEO was particularly adept at preventing bureaucratic infighting. He could detect corporate “politics and nonsense before it was even born,” says the worker. There are also powerful financial reasons for Nvidia employees to feel loyal to Huang. His bets on chips and software for artificial intelligence have transformed Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies and made many longtime employees wealthy in the process. But for some employees, the revelations about Huang’s behavior have forced them to question that loyalty. Jason Sequeira, a longtime engineering leader at Nvidia, wrote on LinkedIn last week that he ultimately couldn’t decide whether he wanted Huang back as he weighed arguments from both sides. “Some believe his contributions to Nvidia and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” Sequeira wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. … I don’t have a clear answer.” Several current and former workers say that Huang’s management style could come off as overly harsh at times, including, for example, toward longtime colleagues he viewed as having grown complacent as Nvidia’s market value surged.

events.title: Scoop: Thanksgiving air travel expected to hit 16-year high
events.summary: Data: FAA; Note: The numbers cover the Monday before Thanksgiving through the Tuesday after. The data includes flights tracked by air traffic control under instrument flight rules.; Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios Thanksgiving week air travel is expected to reach a 16-year high, with 417,775 flights forecast over the nine-day holiday period from Nov. 23 through Dec. 1, according to FAA figures obtained by Axios. Why it matters: The surge comes on the heels of a historic ground stop that disrupted flights nationwide this month and put a spotlight on potential outages in the nation's aging air traffic control system, which the the FAA is working to modernize. The Thanksgiving rush will be a major test of the Trump administration's push to improve the system's reliability and minimize flight delays and cancellations. By the numbers: The FAA is projecting a 2.2% increase in flights over Thanksgiving week last year and a 7.5% increase over pre-pandemic levels in 2019. Tuesday is expected to be the busiest day, with more than 52,000 flights. Behind the scenes: A newly assembled team tasked with improving the air traffic control system's reliability has been meeting daily for the past week, a White House official said. The FAA is exploring ways to remove vulnerable components from the system and bolster its monitoring capability to detect and quickly address any technical problems before they cause widespread disruptions. The agency also is monitoring potential stormy weather that could disrupt holiday travel, particularly in the East and Midwest. What they're saying: "From standing up a 'Tiger Team' to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we've taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told Axios. "The American people can rest assured we will continue to work around the clock 24/7 to get families where they need to go." White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said the administration is "working around the clock to ensure they reach their destinations safely."

events.title: Commerce adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist
events.summary: The Trump administration on Monday added the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors. The Singapore-based company was added to the Commerce Department’s entity list on Monday afternoon, plans that were first reported by Semafor. The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a license from the US government. The news comes the same day the Nvidia board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, after President Donald Trump implored them to do so. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scrutiny over his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. According to a filing from Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security posted to the Federal Register Monday afternoon, seven total entities were added to the list from Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including various affiliates of Megaspeed, MSFusion, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, and Swiftdata. “These additions are being made because of the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users,” the filing reads. “These entities will be added with a license requirement for all items subject to the [Export Administration Regulations] and licenses will be reviewed under a presumption of denial.” Technology exports already en route to the targeted companies will be allowed to go through, the filing suggests. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under pressure to place Megaspeed on the department’s entity list from others inside the administration, tensions that became public after news broke of Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who was an executive at Megaspeed. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China. Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his agency along with the Pentagon, the State Department, and the US Trade Representative had backed putting Megaspeed on the entity list “for months” but that “Commerce holds the pen.” Bipartisan lawmakers have pressed Lutnick to put Megaspeed on the entity list and explain his decisions around Nvidia, Megaspeed, and chip export controls. “The Commerce Department placed Megaspeed on the Entity List. This makes it unlawful to export any US-origin goods, software, or technology to Megaspeed,” BIS spokesman Thomas Wackman told Semafor. “It is also now unlawful to export advanced SI chips to Megaspeed, even if the chips are produced outside the United States. Commerce will continue to vigorously enforce export controls, including these new Entity Listings.”

events.title: Anthropic says Claude solved an age-old math problem, but the written proof is 250,000 pages of slop
events.summary: The leaders of the great model houses, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, desperately want the world to believe AI is the skeleton key which will unlock the secrets of the universe. But if the AI can’t explain what it’s “proven,” are we actually any closer to understanding anything, or have we simply built another black box? That question is top of mind among mathematicians and computer scientists this week after Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge claimed to have solved a mathematical conjecture so elusive it's gone unproven for more than 150 years. The fact that this note came out one day after Anthropic's record-setting IPO is a coincidence, we're sure. In a four-page post to his website, the researcher described how with the help of Claude, he believes he has proven the Riemann Hypothesis, one of seven Millennium problems so complex and so important that the Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize to anyone who is successful in solving them. The Riemann Hypothesis, conjectured by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, contends that all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function – those with a real part between zero and one – have a real part equal to 1/2. Confused? Don’t worry. We’ve linked to an explainer that goes into more detail here . What's important is that, if the Riemann Hypothesis is right, mathematicians can place tighter bounds on the difference between the actual distribution of prime numbers and mathematical estimates of that distribution. Researchers have previously attempted to disprove the conjecture through computational brute force, and therein have shown the hypothesis holds to at least 10 trillion zeros . There’s reason to believe that the Riemann Hypothesis is accurate, but the possibility remains that over a sufficiently long series the pattern might diverge. And so, more than 150 years after Riemann published his hypothesis, it has remained just that. Alpöge’s proof, if it can even be called that, is now the subject of great debate. The four pages in which Alpöge remarks on the discoveries he and Claude made aren’t exactly a proof, but rather 14 tarballs worth of Lean code totaling roughly 240 MB. Lean is an open source programming language commonly used to help validate mathematical proofs. The Clay Mathematics Institute, which oversees the seven Millennium Problems, has promoted the Riemann Hypothesis from “unsolved” to “active” status, but it is not yet considered solved. For Clay to consider the problem solved and award the prize, the proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, remain available for scrutiny for at least two years, and receive broad acceptance from the mathematics community. As it stands, Alpöge describes the 250,000 pages of text generated by the model for its written proof as a “massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop.’” Not long after Alpöge's remarks and Lean code were published, Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil released a nearly 1,000-page draft proof by Alessandro Maria Masullo, who earned his PhD at Stanford in 2020. Masullo has reportedly spent more than a decade pursuing the problem. Frameworks like Lean make mathematics a prime candidate for AI-assisted discovery for many of the same reasons that the technology has proven so successful in software development: code either compiles and runs or it doesn’t. Code can also be audited and could, with great effort, be deciphered. But a proof written in Lean isn't a mathematical proof in the traditional, human-readable sense. Although its logical validity can be checked by a computer, understanding the reasoning behind it can be another matter. Traditional proofs ideally explain their arguments in a way that other mathematicians can follow. Cantor's Diagonal Argument offers a comparatively accessible example. While the clock hasn’t even started for the Clay Math Institute, the Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative have already declared the Riemann Hypothesis solved. “We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the orgs wrote in a joint statement. “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct.” Even if the code ends up being right, if we still don’t know why it’s true, have we really learned anything meaningful? "At the minute, we don't even know why the theorem is true," Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said in a recent Al Jazeera interview. Alpöge’s proof may simply be the product of a black box. To quote the late Arthur C Clarke, “any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.” The implications of such a technology aren’t lost on researchers. Months ago, several prominent researchers called for greater scrutiny and oversight regarding the application of AI in mathematics. “Mathematics produces not only a body of results, but also understanding, clarity, and judgment among the communities of mathematicians who have shaped them, often in the context of their own autonomously guided research,” the Leiden Declaration reads. “This expert knowledge is essential, both to effectively use mathematics, and to continue to articulate new and significant research questions.” ®

Experts have ascribed the disruptions mostly to groups using AI to patch numerous preexisting software vulnerabilities, which one expert likened to dead timber: “All that tech that’s on fire [is] going to burn down,” a former National Security Agency official said, clearing the way for new growth. “ But we’ve got to live through this era where stuff’s on fire .” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Inception - possibly a ShinyHunters reboot - claims seven victims in a week
events.summary: Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group. ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI , resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark. “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday. Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group. While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters. The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media. On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims. None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register ’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information. Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions. In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.” The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added. The Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting , digital extortion, real-life shootings , and other physical violence . Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com , along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure. “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.” Regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. Consider yourself warned - and turn on phishing-resistant MFA.®
