events.title: How to Win Big Betting on Jensen Huang? Listen to Trump
events.summary: Just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from the AI hardware giant following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence services. As more reports emerged about Huang’s alleged bad behavior , Nvidia’s board insisted it had no plans to reinstate him. By early Sunday morning on the East Coast, traders on Polymarket’s US platform put his chances of returning at just 10 percent. But by Monday, Huang was back in charge. The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming. The New York Times reported that President Trump played a crucial role in convincing the board to bring Huang back. Traders who paid attention to what Trump and his allies wanted appear to have fared much better than those who did not. On Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped 6 percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement. The president said he wanted to help revive the stock market, which had plunged following Huang’s scandal, a sign of Nvidia’s enormous influence over the AI industry and broader US economy. According to the prediction market intelligence firm Betting Intelligence, the odds on both Kalshi and Polymarket largely tracked with public signals about the likelihood of Huang’s return. They rose when Huang said he was open to coming back, fell when the board dismissed the possibility, and climbed again when Trump threw his support behind the former CEO. But Betting Intelligence and the prediction market forensics firm MSR Decode also identified clusters of trades that did not appear to be driven by news or public commentary. Kalshi and Polymarket declined to comment on whether they are currently investigating potential insider trading in markets related to Huang’s return. Despite these anomalies, Betting Intelligence CEO Dan Zimmermann says the Huang-related markets showed fewer signs of potentially suspicious activity than usual. “The group that could have known the board’s decision in advance was small. So the market was mostly headline chasers and long-shot buyers,” he says. For traders who profited from Huang’s comeback, the lesson is clear: Don’t discount Trump. Isaac Rose-Berman, a research and policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys & Men and a professional sports bettor, says he made approximately $10,000 wagering on Huang’s return on Kalshi. He placed his trade after the Nvidia chief said on X that he was open to reclaiming his old job. Rose-Berman says he figured that people like Trump, who had an interest in boosting Nvidia’s stock price, would successfully pressure the board to reinstate Huang. (Never mind the concerns about national security or Huang allegedly threatening employees that he would “ pee in your brain .”) “It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” Rose-Berman says. “Should’ve bet more.” A pseudonymous prediction market trader known as Domer tells WIRED he cleared approximately $600,000 by placing an early wager last week on Huang’s return. He wasn’t focused explicitly on Trump’s desires, but he says his understanding of power dynamics ultimately guided his approach. “Boards can be very malleable,” he tells WIRED. Other prediction market “sharps” say that commentary from Trumpworld was the strongest signal available about Huang’s return. As some bettors noted, there was a notable opportunity for profit after Trump suggested to a PBS NewsHour reporter that Huang would be back in power soon, but before Nvidia officially announced his reinstatement. “The key was looking at Trump’s support and the recent performance of the stock market,” says Kalshi trader Caleb Davies. Aaron Courtney, a data analyst and cofounder of a prediction market analytics firm, says he took a loss on his Huang position. Looking back, he says his mistake was not paying attention to what Trump and other administration officials said over the weekend. “Trump saying he hoped Nvidia would bring Jensen back would be the clearest signal,” he says. Update 11/23/26 9:05 pm ET: This story has been updated to clarify Isaac Rose-Berman’s reasoning for wagering on Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO. events.title: Amazon scoops up AI accelerator tech to keep chips busy at all times
events.summary: Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations. The house of Bezos on Monday announced a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount. Amazon also plans to bring Decart’s three founders and their engineering team into the fold. Decart’s DOS is designed to push AI hardware closer to its maximum performance across different AI models and hardware platforms. The company claims that most AI chips live their lives without reaching their full potential – practically a sin in this age of increased hardware costs and limited availability – and DOS aims to fix that by operating between the model and the chip, optimizing kernels, compilers, and runtimes for the underlying hardware “so every core stays busy.” DOS is hardware-agnostic, with Decart saying it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, and, most critically for our purposes here, AWS Trainium chips. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost,” Peter DeSantis, Amazon SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing, said in the announcement. “That's the pillar Trainium and our AI efforts are built on, and from our earliest work with Decart, we knew they … would help us push it even further.” Decart doesn’t offer much in the way of details about its proprietary AI-maxxing tech, but claims it can reduce latency, improve throughput, and reduce the costs associated with training and inference runs. An Amazon spokesperson clarified to The Register that the deal is an asset purchase and not a full company acquisition, with Amazon only acquiring DOS and the tech behind it as well as personnel. As for what may become of Decart after the deal, that’s unclear. Amazon told us to reach out to Decart to learn what may happen to any remaining employees and the company’s other technology, but we didn’t hear back. Along with offering its optimization stack, Decart has a couple of different AI models: Lucy, a live video model marketed toward advertisers, live streamers, and the like; and Oasis, a world model AI marketed toward companies working on embodied AI applications. Decart’s non-DOS assets weren’t mentioned in the press release, and per the Amazon spokesperson we talked to, that means they weren’t part of the deal. We can’t imagine that the Decart team is too upset about the potential abandonment of those models, though: While neither company has disclosed a price, Bloomberg claims its sources value the deal at around $7.5 billion. If Bloomberg's figure is accurate, that would make this deal one of the most expensive in Amazon’s history, right between its $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and its $8.5 billion purchase of film studio MGM . ®

events.title: Mississippi's election fights didn't end with Scott Colom's historic Senate win
events.summary: Mississippi is facing two fights over its election rules after Democrat Scott Colom 's historic Senate victory: one over voters marked inactive and another over deadlines for receiving mail-in ballots . Why it matters: The disputes could affect how easily eligible voters cast ballots and which mail ballots count when Mississippi elects a new governor and other statewide leaders next year. Driving the news: The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus demanded an investigation Thursday into whether the state's use of credit-reporting data to verify voters' addresses led election officials to incorrectly mark voters as inactive. Lawmakers want to examine the credit-reporting data contracts, instructions sent to county officials and how many eligible voters were incorrectly marked inactive. In one case, a Hinds County voter learned she'd been marked inactive when she arrived at her usual polling place, according to Angela Grayson, director of civic engagement and voting rights at the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable. Her vote ultimately counted, Grayson said. The caucus acknowledged it doesn't know how many voters were flagged in error. Advocacy groups are seeking records to find out. What they're saying: "Nothing has changed fundamentally here in Mississippi," Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi, tells Axios. "The laws are still the laws. The governor is still the governor. The state legislature is still overwhelmingly Republican," he said. "It's also plainly obvious that the playbook of reducing turnout, culling the active voter rolls, that's not going to stop." By the numbers: More than 230,000 voters were listed as inactive before the 2026 midterms, up from roughly 171,000 in 2024, according to the Associated Press . Mississippi recorded 21,484 affidavit ballots, the state's version of provisional ballots, this year. That's nearly identical to the 21,321 cast in 2024's presidential election, when overall turnout was higher, per a statement from Secretary of State Michael Watson. About 75% of affidavit ballots were accepted statewide. But in majority-Black Hinds County, which includes Jackson, just 34% of 2,426 were accepted, down from 60% in 2024. It's unclear whether credit-reporting data contributed to the decline. "Those are huge alarms and red flags for us," Grayson told Axios, calling for more information about why ballots were rejected. Yes, but: Watson defended the state's voter-roll practices as legal and effective. He said election officials review flagged voter registrations and that voters still had an opportunity to cast affidavit ballots. "Our team welcomes an investigation because we have continuously followed the law," his office told Axios, adding that local election officials maintain voter rolls. Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves and Secretary of State Michael Watson support eliminating the state's five-business-day grace period for receiving mail-in ballots, with Reeves pitching that ballots should instead arrive by 5 p.m. on Election Day. Watson successfully defended Mississippi's authority to maintain the grace period before the Supreme Court months earlier, despite personally opposing the practice. Reeves had called for its repeal months before Colom's victory. "We see that as just a further suppression of voter rights here in the state," Grayson said of Reeves' proposal. Zoom out: Reeves said last week he intends to call a special legislative session to redistrict before Mississippi's 2027 elections, amid President Trump's push to redraw political maps to benefit Republicans. King imagined Republicans responding to Colom's win: "Holy crap, we've got to figure out how to build a moat around our majority in the state legislature." What we're watching: It's unclear whether lawmakers will launch an investigation, proposed voter-roll reforms will attract GOP support or Reeves' mail-ballot proposal will become a bill. King is skeptical: "The Mississippi legislature is not known for oversight." Go deeper: Scott Colom's win in Mississippi puts political change to the test

events.title: Huang's return stokes bipartisan worry over national security
events.summary: The News The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as president and CEO of Nvidia is turbocharging congressional oversight plans and training lawmakers’ bipartisan focus on a central question: how the Trump administration came to the conclusion that Huang’s return posed no national security risk. The move — and President Donald Trump’s involvement in it — is inflaming tensions between the president and his own party. Several Republicans had joined Democrats in planning to scrutinize Huang and chip export controls on China in the wake of the scandal. After being ousted as Nvidia’s CEO earlier this month, Huang had agreed to testify privately before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, House Intelligence Committee, and House China Select Committee next month as well as publicly before the Senate Banking Committee. Trump has said that Attorney General Todd Blanche had affirmed no national security risk from Huang’s rehiring, but the Justice Department is currently conducting ongoing investigations that could affect that question. Huang’s closed-door appearance before the House panels is currently expected to move forward as planned, people familiar with the plans said, but spokespeople for the panels did not respond to requests for comment. Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who leads the Senate Banking Committee, announced later Monday that Huang would appear at a public hearing on Dec. 3. “I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement,” Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., said of Huang, adding that the company needs to be “answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips.” Huang’s return to the company is also likely to affect his legal representation before Congress. In its statement Monday, Nvidia’s board cited “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left them “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Trump dialed into a board meeting to push for Huang’s return, Semafor first reported. ‘Based on what?’ The Hill’s plans to bring Huang to testify set up a potential collision course with the Trump administration in the final weeks of the lame-duck session, just as the GOP must reckon with its last opportunity to push through its party-line agenda. Congressional Republicans have taken a more hawkish approach to restrictions on chip exports to China in the last month, with leadership in both parties leaning towards using upcoming defense legislation to close gaps in US-China chip-export policy at the center of the Nvidia fallout. “No national security risk?” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, wrote on X . “Based on what?” A White House official told Semafor that Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Huang “will preserve America’s technological edge over China, strengthen our national security, and ensure the future of SI continues to be built in America,” using a moniker for super intelligence, Trump’s preferred term for AI. Democrats lie in wait Even if Republicans adjust their plans to grill Huang, he’s sure to face considerable scrutiny when Democrats take over control of Congress next year. So, too, will the Trump administration face Democrats’ questions about its interactions with and investigations related to Nvidia as well as its export control policy. “We still don’t know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia’s own board has completed its investigation,” the top Democrat on the House China Select Committee, Rep. Ro Khanna of California, wrote on X . “Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him.” Democrats also want to hear more about “what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials,” as Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., put it. Warren, who’s poised to chair the Senate Banking Committee next Congress, said the move “only increases the urgency” of passing more stringent restrictions on chip exports. Trump’s direct involvement is further fueling Democrats’ outrage. “The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some f*cking donation to his ballroom,” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., wrote on X . Notable Nvidia will also be holding its annual DC conference next week.

events.title: "Troubling and problematic": Gov. Moore rips Trump's Nvidia actions on "The Axios Show"
events.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore criticized President Trump's involvement in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang , calling it "troubling and problematic" in an interview for "The Axios Show." Why it matters: Moore, chair of the National Governors Association and often seen as a 2028 presidential contender, is one of the most outspoken state leaders pushing for stronger federal oversight of AI companies — but not like this. Driving the news: Trump told CNBC Monday that he spoke directly to Nvidia's board about Huang's return. Trump had previously pushed for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to become Nvidia's leader, but changed tune over the last few days to favor Huang. What they're saying: "The president is not a board member of Nvidia. So, why he is involved in board dealings, I have no idea. ... It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee," Moore told Axios' Mike Allen in an interview just minutes after the news broke. "You have the wealthy and the powerful and the well-connected that are now making decisions to reinstate, where, frankly, if that was any of us, we would be held to a different type of standard." Zoom in: Moore said the "market is being inflated essentially by seven companies," including Nvidia. Huang's return — which led to a stock surge — "highlights how problematic this entire thing is," Moore said. "We are talking about not just millionaires, but billionaires, who are sitting in a quiet room by themselves, making this decision because they know this company is that important." Subscribe to "The Axios Show" on YouTube to watch the full interview with Moore when it's available.

events.title: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia sparks bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill
events.summary: Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is drawing criticism and scrutiny — including about national security risks — from members of Congress in both parties. Why it matters: President Trump's push to reinstate Huang creates a headache for Republicans and new fodder for Democrats eager to deploy their investigative powers when they take control in January. "No national security risk? Based on what," Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked in a social media post following the news. "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed," Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said in a statement to Axios. "The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who's been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang. The worst part of this is what we may never know," Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) posted on X . Driving the news: The House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China committees have announced that Huang would testify next week. His reinstatement "changes nothing," an Intelligence Committee spokesperson told Axios on Monday. "When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursing the facts." The spokesperson added: "There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee's commitment to oversight." Huang is scheduled to appear before the Senate banking panel on Dec. 3. What we're watching: Top Democrats say they will open their own investigations into Huang's reinstatement when they take power next year. "Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said. "We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions," said Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the House Oversight committee. "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,"Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a post on X . Said Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Finance Committee: "In January, Democrats will hold this corrupt administration accountable." Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told Axios: "We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO and why his administration failed to restrict the PRC's access to our most sensitive technology." What Democrats are saying: "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security," Schumer said. Jeffries called for the annual defense authorization bill to include "ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries." "The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some fucking donation to his ballroom," Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said . "Jensen Huang's reinstatement shows that under Trump, Vance, and Rubio, our national security is for sale," Wyden said . Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the top Banking committee Democrat, called the decision "reckless" and said the board still owes Congress "answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," adding that the Trump administration "needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement." "Yet another example where, in Trump's America, the wealthy and well connected are held to a different standard," Meeks told Axios. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), the top Democrat on the China Select Committee, called the decision "outrageous." Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), a member of House Democratic leadership, blasted it as "irresponsible." What Republicans are saying: " Nvidia's board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions," Curtis said in his statement to Axios. "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?" "Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. His own board described his behavior as lacking 'candor.' ... His behavior does not support reinstatement," said Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), adding that he looked forward to Huang's testimony next week. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Monday morning that it would reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, president a board member after ousting him earlier this month. The board voted unanimously for Huang's return. The reinstatement comes after Trump repeatedly urged the board to bring Huang back. Stocks saw an early, massive rally following the news. Huang's departure had sent the stock market into correction territory. The bottom line: Both sides have a lot of questions. Democrats will soon have the power to get answers. Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from Sen. Kevin Cramer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Rep. Robert Garcia.

events.title: "Too big to fail": The economic fear behind Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback
events.summary: President Trump pushed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO after allies argued he was " too big to fail " for the U.S. economy and a victim of "deep state" maneuvering, sources familiar with the discussions told Axios. Why it matters: Trump put the weight of the presidency behind a private company's decision about who should run it, an intervention that strengthened Huang's allies inside the administration and put officials critical of the company in an increasingly uncomfortable position. Driving the news: "Jensen is too big to fail," one source familiar with the discussions told Axios. Huang resigned amid allegations he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and subordinates. The stock market's slump prompted President Trump and allies within the administration to push for his reinstatement. "The President was pushing harder than Jensen," one source said. Trump called into Nvidia's board meeting Sunday night to argue for Huang's reinstatement, he told CNBC. Behind the scenes: Huang's allies appealed to Trump's longstanding distrust of the intelligence community, portraying the Nvidia founder as a victim of persecution by unnamed government insiders. A Trump adviser said allies sought to convince Trump that "deep staters" were working against Huang. The intelligence included findings about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated to senior officials in a memo earlier this year. A Rubio ally said the secretary of state was "mortified" when the memo leaked with his name attached. Zoom in: The memo came as Nvidia lobbied the Trump administration to open up China's access to its chips. Despite the intelligence, Huang remained close to the president while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's inaction fueled tensions between him, Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and others. A senior administration official argued the intelligence never established Huang was compromised, knowingly violated U.S. law or had sex with a spy. "People are weaponizing some true information and spinning it to reflect as negatively as possible against Huang. That's the president's concern," the official said. Vance's role Trump and Vice President JD Vance viewed Huang as an important champion of open models offering Americans more control and lower costs than closed models like OpenAI's and Anthropic's. The two were briefed on the national security concerns involving Huang and concluded they had not seen evidence of personal wrongdoing, the source said. Anthropic has been warning the Trump administration that Nvidia's advanced chips power Chinese open source models closing in on the AI race. Yes, but: These conclusions come as more and more connections between Alice Huang — the alleged Chinese spy Huang had an affair with — and the Chinese government and military come to light. "He let the U.S. stock market and economy demand his return — along with the pressure from the president — and the outcry was deafening," the source said. Huang's reinstatement is a "big win" for Vance, a source close to Rubio said. Vance's Silicon Valley relationships helped the administration navigate the board's concerns, according to a source familiar with the discussions. Keeping Huang as CEO was seen as the best option for national security, a source close to Vance said. What we're watching: Huang's opponents in the administration now risk backlash from the president. Bessent has been the loudest, criticizing Lutnick's inaction on TV and calling for the Nvidia board to find a new outside CEO and a "dramatic shakeup," but on Sunday softened his stance. What's next: Trump's intervention settled the immediate fight over Nvidia's leadership but raised questions about the U.S. government's role in the board's decision. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wants to know which officials provided the national security input that Nvidia cited in reinstating Huang. Three Republican-led House committees have scheduled interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2. Nvidia says its independent investigations and cooperation with government inquiries will continue.

events.title: 3 questions that can help universities turn AI experiments into results
events.summary: How higher education leaders can turn institutional intelligence into impact Higher education institutions don’t need another conversation about whether AI matters. The more important question now is how to turn growing experimentation into meaningful, measurable progress across the academic mission. In our recent Microsoft Education Blog post, “ Higher education’s AI advantage is the intelligence institutions already hold ,” we introduced a simple idea: a university’s greatest AI advantage may not be access to another model or tool. It may be the unique intelligence already held across its people, data, research, systems, policies, and everyday work. Now comes the harder question: how do institutions put that intelligence to work? Our new guide, How to Unlock Intelligence in Higher Education , is designed to help leadership teams move from AI experimentation toward impact at scale. It provides a practical framework, built around priority AI use cases, for bringing leaders together around three critical conversations: where AI can advance university priorities, what information needs to be connected, and how to build the trust needed to innovate responsibly. Start with university priorities, then scale the AI use cases that advance them Across higher education, faculty, staff, researchers, and students are already exploring AI. Connecting those experiments to shared priorities is what turns them into university-wide transformation. A more useful starting point is the mission. Which outcomes is the university trying to improve? Where are people spending time on work that creates friction rather than value? Where might better access to university knowledge improve a decision, experience, or workflow? This frames the conversation around “What are we trying to achieve, and which AI use cases can help us get there?” Use cases give universities a repeatable pattern to adapt and scale. Take academic advising: AI can help advisors see where each student stands in their degree progress and reach out sooner, while advisors remain responsible for the conversation. A university can prove that pattern in one college, then scale it across campus. For more examples across teaching, research, student experience, operations, and cybersecurity, explore the white paper: Empowering Every Leader and Learner: AI Use Cases in Higher Education. Answering that question requires more than IT leadership. The guide encourages institutions to bring together executive and academic leaders, faculty, research, student services, legal and compliance, IT and cybersecurity, finance, operations, and administration. That multidisciplinary conversation matters because university intelligence doesn’t sit neatly inside one system or organizational function. It exists across the university. The guide organizes that work into three conversations. Each one builds on the last: where AI can make the greatest difference, what intelligence needs to be connected, and what will let people innovate with confidence. Conversation 1: Where could AI make the greatest difference? The first conversation is about focus. Many institutions have already accumulated promising pilots. The next opportunity is to connect those experiments to university strategy and identify where AI can make a meaningful contribution to priorities like student success, academic work, research, operations, and university effectiveness. Start with outcomes rather than capabilities. Where could reducing administrative burden give faculty and staff more capacity? Where could faster access to trusted information improve a student’s experience? Where could AI augment a research or institutional workflow while keeping people responsible for judgment and decisions? Research is a good place to see this in practice. Microsoft worked with the Research Data Alliance and researchers worldwide to identify Global Community Priorities for Agentic AI in Research and outline a Data Director Agentic AI Tool Blueprint that shows how agents can support research workflows. This is also an opportunity to look across existing AI activities. Universities can ask what their teams are learning from experimentation, which approaches could be reused, and where separate initiatives might become more valuable if connected. The objective is to apply AI where it can contribute most meaningfully to the university’s mission. The University of South Carolina shows what AI can deliver when aimed at increasing capacity for high-value work. Following the deployment of Microsoft Copilot and AI agents in the tools people use every day, 84% of pilot users reported saving one to five hours per week, and eight in 10 reported satisfaction. That reclaimed time is capacity the university can direct toward teaching, research, and student success. Realizing that value at scale depends on giving AI access to the right university knowledge and context, which leads to the second conversation. Conversation 2: What intelligence needs to be connected? Once priorities are clearer, a second question quickly emerges: What does AI need to know to be genuinely useful in the context of our institution? Every university possesses a distinctive body of intelligence: academic programs and curriculum history, student records and outcome patterns, research data and intellectual property, faculty and staff expertise, policies and governance, operational processes, and information contained in documents, meetings, messages, and decisions. Too often, that intelligence is fragmented across systems and organizational boundaries. Connecting fragmented information can help AI deliver more relevant, consistent results across workflows rather than requiring each agent to reconstruct context independently. This is where Microsoft IQ becomes important. Microsoft IQ is designed to provide a shared intelligence layer that helps Copilot and agents use context about how people work, how the university operates, and what it knows. Fabric IQ establishes consistent definitions, relationships, metrics, and rules so AI can reason with university context across its data. Work IQ brings real-time context from everyday activities, collaboration, relationships, and workflows across Microsoft 365 , including what needs attention. Foundry IQ makes knowledge from connected sources accessible through governed, reusable knowledge bases for AI applications and agents. And Web IQ adds timely, relevant context from the web, such as news, images, and videos. Together, these capabilities help AI deliver more relevant, consistent results across university workflows while working with existing security, identity, and governance controls. Making the right knowledge available in the right context, with appropriate permissions and governance, helps people make better-informed decisions and lets AI support more useful workflows. Conversation 3: What will allow people to innovate with confidence?

events.title: How Microsoft Discovery helps scientists learn from failure and find new possibilities
events.summary: Three Things You Should Know About Microsoft Discovery Some of the most meaningful scientific breakthroughs start with a hunch: connecting seemingly unrelated ideas, exploring what hasn’t been tried, and following the evidence wherever it leads. And when the failure modes stack up, it takes the determination to keep going and figure it out. This sort of work takes a different kind of AI. One where every capability, every tool, every interaction is designed around how science actually gets done. One that can connect decades of research, reason through complex problems, explore leads, run simulations, and help researchers decide where to go next. That is Microsoft Discovery . The purpose-built AI platform for science and engineering. Here are three things you should know about it: 1. Hypothesis is just the beginning A hypothesis is a starting point. It’s not a scientific result. Ask an AI model to suggest a new cooling fluid, and it can generate compelling candidates. But which ones actually meet the constraints? Which survive simulation? Which deserve further testing? That's where the real work begins. Discovery Engine moves beyond one-shot answers to advance scientific investigations over time, building on evidence as new questions and directions emerge. It brings together AI reasoning, specialized tools, and high-performance computing, while keeping experts in control of where the investigation goes next. And we're already seeing what this can unlock. Microsoft researchers used Discovery to identify a novel datacenter immersion-cooling prototype with promising properties in approximately 200 hours , combining AI models with HPC simulations. It was not a production-validated coolant, but a promising candidate backed by computational evidence and ready for further investigation. The value isn't generating more possibilities; it's finding out which ones are worth pursuing. Most AI remembers the answer. Great science remembers how you got there. Ask any scientist, and they'll tell you: some of the most valuable lessons come from experiments that didn't work. But those lessons often disappear into notebooks, abandoned hypotheses, and research that never gets published. Microsoft Discovery is designed to preserve that. In our joint organic redox flow battery research with Yale Engineering , Canam Bioresearch , and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory , Discovery explored multiple molecular designs across several rounds. In one round, none of the parallel explorations produced a viable candidate, but those failures were not wasted. In another, four of six explorations produced candidates worth pursuing. Discovery preserved what it learned, recognized limitations in its predictive tools, and adapted its approach. In the next round, four of six explorations succeeded. That's where capabilities like Discovery Bookshelf become powerful: preserving not just results, but the reasoning, evidence, and lessons behind them so future investigations can build on what came before. For Discovery, failures matter. They’re the one thing that make every experiment count. 3. Staying at the frontier of what scientists expect For Discovery, the bar isn’t simply generating or explaining scientific outputs. It’s enabling researchers to work directly with them. Molecular exploration is a good example. For many of our users, the ability to inspect and manipulate molecular structures isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s table stakes. With our app users can already visualize molecular structures, inspect them, make changes, and carry those changes forward into an investigation. A molecule isn’t just an output Discovery can show you. It becomes something you can actively work with, explore, and use to decide where the investigation goes next. That’s the bar we’re holding: moving beyond consuming scientific outputs to working directly with them. The future of science deserves a different kind of AI Science has never been a straight line from question to answer. It's a process of exploring, experimenting, learning, and sometimes starting over. And that's why science deserves more than AI that simply knows the answers. It deserves AI built for the way discoveries actually happen. And that is the purpose behind Microsoft Discovery.

events.title: Trump presses pause on Army's Iowa lead detonation
events.summary: President Trump ordered the Army to pause plans to detonate unstable explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant, saying the blast cannot proceed without approval from an appeals court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand . The big picture: State officials said last week they only recently learned of the plan to detonate tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, sparking frustration about a perceived lack of transparency from federal officials. The Army, which had delayed the detonation until Wednesday, advised people who live or work nearby to avoid the area, stay indoors and clean surfaces once the branch declares the airborne exposure risk over. But the threat also sparked warnings in neighboring Illinois, with the American Lung Association saying that residents of eastern Iowa and western Illinois could be exposed to lead. Driving the news: Trump warned Monday that he would hold Sand responsible for "any and all death or destruction" if the governor-elect refuses to approve the detonation. " If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," he wrote in a pointed Monday Truth Social post . Sand said in a statement that the administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks." He added, "Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward." State of play: The Middletown, Iowa, blast was initially set for Friday, then delayed to Monday and then to Wednesday. In a Friday letter to Gov. Kim Reynolds, regional EPA administrator Jim Macy said the Army had documented recrystallization of the lead azide, raising the risk of an accidental explosion. The lead azide "is now so sensitive to temperature, friction and shock that it cannot be safely moved, opened, or treated without a significant risk of explosion," per an administration court filing . Friction point: Earthjustice sued last week to halt the detonation on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter. A federal appeals court subsequently paused an EPA emergency permit allowing the blast. But even with the permit stayed, the administration argued in a Sunday filing to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that the Army could still move forward with a controlled detonation. Catch up quick: The Army announced Sunday night that the controlled detonation plan would be pushed to Wednesday "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced." "The health and safety of all Americans has and always will be our first priority," the Army added. But on Monday, Trump halted those plans. What they're saying: Incoming Hawkeye State leaders Josh Turek, who will join the Senate in January, and Sand , the incoming Democratic governor, have condemned the Army's communications. "The public also deserves answers as to why the U.S. Army's communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning," Turek said in a Sunday statement . Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) slammed the saga as "an extreme failure of communication, planning and leadership," adding the Army "must be held accountable for the harm done." events.title: Huang reinstatement came at Trump’s behest
events.summary: Hours before Nvidia reinstated ousted CEO Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday board meeting to argue for his return. The remarkable direct engagement by Trump, first reported by Semafor and confirmed by multiple sources, underscores how fully he has redefined the role of the US government in private enterprise. Trump wasn’t alone. Vice President JD Vance and other members of the administration have also gotten actively involved in the inner workings of one of the US’ most valuable companies, even as members of Trump’s own party raise questions about his statement that reinstating Huang poses no national security risk. By Monday morning, the company had announced Huang’s return and made no secret the decision was made based on “input” from the White House, which told the company the administration felt comfortable despite Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The pitch that resonated with Vance and Trump, who had been close to Huang, centered around the Nvidia CEO’s role as a protector of open-source models, and a check on the increasing power of closed frontier model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI, a person familiar with the matter told Semafor. The pressure was also heightened by the tech rout in the markets, which sent the S&P 500 into correction territory over worries of AI risks. On Monday, Nvidia’s stock jumped 30%, the biggest increase in more than two decades, lifting the entire market with it. Despite multiple active legal and regulatory probes that touch on the company — and potentially Huang personally — the president and vice president pushed back privately and publicly on allegations that he posed a threat to national security. Both were personally engaged over the weekend to bring Huang back, the person added. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor. Unanimous vote Two weeks after the board voted unanimously to accept Huang’s resignation, which came after allegations of affairs with two subordinates , Nvidia’s board met late Sunday night and voted unanimously to bring him back, according to a person familiar with the matter. Huang, who co-founded the chipmaker in 1993 and built it into an AI giant, benefited from a mounting defense campaign by some Silicon Valley figures who called for his return. Semafor had previously reported that despite a unanimous vote to oust him a couple weeks ago, a faction of directors had continued to push for him to come back. The anti-Huang camp was dealt a blow when they learned a leading replacement candidate, Arm CEO Rene Haas, wouldn’t be available since he had signed a new contract with Arm extending his employment until 2033, according to another person familiar with directors’ thinking. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey Jones, who was elevated to board chairman at the time of Huang’s Nov. 12 ouster, said in its statement. Nvidia’s senior leadership was not aware of the decision to restore Huang until shortly before the general public knew, according to a person familiar with the matter. Washington probes Huang’s return is guaranteed to amplify the already vocal bipartisan calls for Congress to investigate his behavior and the company’s lobbying against export controls that would curtail Nvidia’s overseas chips business. He is already slated to appear in private before House members and in public before senators next week. Several Republicans greeted his reinstatement with open skepticism of the Justice Department’s claim that there was no evidence Huang’s affair presented a national security risk. Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, questioned the “basis” for that judgment. Huang “was right to step down when the affair came to light,” he posted on social media. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the ranking member of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, called the decision to reinstate Huang “reckless.” Huang’s return “only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk,” she wrote. DOJ continues to probe two key Nvidia customers, Alice Huang’s Megaspeed and Supermicro, over export control violations, and Nvidia itself over antitrust concerns, Semafor previously reported and confirmed with a Justice Department official.

events.summary: Qatar’s state visit to Germany has brought another Gulf pledge to invest billions in Europe’s largest economy. events.title: The irony in Anthropic's huge payday to Gulf backers
events.summary: Some of the Gulf’s largest investors stand to make billions from Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO, a little over a year after CEO Dario Amodei expressed misgivings as he prepared to take the region’s money. In the July 2025 memo, first reported by Wired, Amodei said it would be “ substantially harder ” to stay at the frontier without Gulf capital as the Claude developer fundraised in Abu Dhabi and Doha. Combined stakes owned by Gulf investors are worth an estimated $100 billion after shares priced at $83, according to sovereign wealth fund tracker Global SWF. Abu Dhabi’s MGX has an unrealized gain of about $20 billion , Bloomberg reported. Alpha Dhabi, a unit of Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed’s International Holding Co., also has indirect exposure through Alpha Wave. Qatar Investment Authority, which bought in at a $183 billion valuation in 2025, was seeking more shares right up until the IPO, Semafor reported. Dubai property mogul and global data center builder Hussain Sajwani told CNBC his personal stake is worth about $3 billion . — Kelsey Warner

events.title: The Gulf prepares to face a tougher Democrat-controlled Congress
events.summary: The Democrat-controlled Congress taking power in January could reshape US relations with Gulf partners, bringing greater scrutiny over arms sales, military basing, and technology transfers. Democrats have historically been more critical of Gulf states than Republicans: An analysis by Mahdi Ghuloom of ORF Middle East found that Democrats sponsored 103 of 131 “ negative or critical measures ” targeting the six Gulf states between 2009 and 2026. That scrutiny could intensify, with Democrats using oversight powers to probe the Trump administration’s Gulf ties, particularly over AI exports and technology transfers. Arms sales could face renewed pressure, while Gulf reconstruction after the Iran war may raise questions over funding needed to repair and restart operations on US bases. But translating scrutiny into constraints on the Iran war itself will be harder, given the executive branch’s sweeping foreign policy powers. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Iran signals plans to challenge the US naval blockade
events.summary: Iranian and Houthi attacks over the weekend , along with a possible effort by Tehran to test the US blockade of its oil exports, are raising the prospect of escalation as diplomats race to find a resolution to the nine-month conflict. Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile and drone, Bahrain said an Iranian strike on an industrial facility injured two people, and two oil tankers were hit near Oman. Violence in the Strait of Hormuz could intensify if Iran follows through with plans to move 14 vessels recently loaded at Kharg Island in an attempt to break the US naval blockade . Meanwhile, diplomatic efforts continue, even as the gap between the two sides shows no sign of narrowing. Iran’s foreign minister said the June agreement — the memorandum of understanding signed by US President Donald Trump in Versailles and remotely by Iran’s president — is no longer valid, but could provide a basis for a future deal . events.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is getting his CEO job back, but history shows companies perform better when corporate boards take executive misbehavior seriously
events.summary: President Donald Trump is among those who pushed to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis. This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the Nov. 12, 2026, ouster of its CEO , Jensen Huang, who remarkably returned to his job just 11 days later. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd. Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – albeit in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit. Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s original decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan – not to mention President Donald Trump , who reportedly directed the effort to get Huang reinstated. As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board had made the right call to force him out. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something. CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. This is likely why the board chose to reinstate Jensen Huang. And why his return sets a terrible precedent. The costs of misconduct One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows. One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it. Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first. Chip Somodevilla/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well. In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks . Another issue is moral hazard : when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation. My research has found that risk to be high. When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first. Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991. Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship. In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future? In reinstating him, the board said it “was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” Nvidia’s board has come under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted, then reinstated, its CEO, Jensen Huang. Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images A question of culture Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive. Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees. It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. events.title: Schumer puts Nvidia, Trump on notice after Huang reinstatement
events.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that Congress is coming for answers — whether he's back at the top of the company or not. Why it matters: The embattled CEO's return to the board came as a shock to investors but sent Nvidia's stock through the roof . Now, some lawmakers are warning that his return raises national security concerns. What they're saying: "The Trump Administration's rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act," Schumer wrote Monday on X. "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he's learned nothing from his resounding election defeat. Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain." "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries." Nvidia did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment. The other side: White House spokesman Davis Ingle slammed what he described as "Trump Deranged Dumocrats and the Fake News' continued attempts to fabricate conflicts of interest" in a statement provided to Axios. "President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses," Ingle added. In an interview on CBNC, Trump said his "intervention was very important" in Huang's reinstatement. Asked what comes next for the company given the hit to Huang's credibility after his reported affairs, Trump predicted he'd "start off at an almost higher level," adding, "sex sells, fellas." Driving the news: Nvidia announced Huang's reinstatement as CEO, president and a member of the board Monday morning, less than two weeks after his resignation. Despite saying last week that it did not intend to bring him back, the board did so anyway, amid urging from the White House. Shortly after the announcement, Trump praised the board's decision, calling it "correct and proper," and saying "[t]he Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." Catch up quick: The whirlwind saga around the chipmaking behemoth was sparked by Huang's admitted relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang , was a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer that the Wall Street Journal reported arranged to send nearly $12 billion in top chips to Chinese companies. Zoom in: "This underscores that enough people believe that our economy and national security are not just dependent on one company, but on one man," Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser at the State Department, emailed Axios. "I suspect this is being driven by last week's stock market drop and now it's clear that Nvidia sits at the center of an enormous web of deals and investments that appear increasingly dependent on one individual." "From the standpoint of both democracy and healthy financial markets, no one person should wield that kind of influence. It is fundamentally corrupt." Between the lines: Huang's resurrection also exposes the company to heightened liability and political turmoil. He'll have to lead the company as it faces congressional and federal investigations. But after his exit contributed to a sharp drop in tech stocks over the last two weeks, his return sent Nvidia shares skyrocketing. What we're watching: How much appetite Congress has to expand its investigations into Huang and Nvidia after the stock market rallied significantly following his return. events.title: Jensen Huang Is Back, and So Is Nvidia’s Stock
events.summary: Jensen Huang is back, baby , and Wall Street is thrilled. The chipmaker’s shares have surged more than 30 percent following the board’s announcement that it was reinstating Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The company’s valuation has soared by more than $1 trillion, which puts it on track to break Microsoft’s record for the greatest single-day gain in market value by hundreds of billions of dollars. Huang departed the company he helped found on November 12 amid suspected asset-kissing and allegations of extramarital affairs with employees . Each report chipped away at the company’s value until nearly $2.2 trillion was erased over the past month . Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said during the company’s earnings call that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” WIRED also reported that Nvidia’s board had been alarmed by Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying.” And yet, despite all this, the board announced on Monday that it had brought Huang back— with some help from the US government . Semafor reported that, hours before Huang was reinstated, President Donald Trump dialed into the publicly traded company’s board meeting to argue for the ousted CEO’s return. Many questions remain unanswered . What happens at the conclusion of the board-led investigation into Huang’s behavior? Multiple government agencies and lawmakers are reportedly investigating Huang; given the Trump administration’s aggressive support of the executive, what sort of accountability can anyone reasonably expect? The turmoil has also raised red flags about what happens when so much of the market revolves around one person at one company. Nvidia has massive sway over the wider artificial intelligence ecosystem, due to its deals with and investments in other companies . Last week, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 10 percent, in part due to Nvidia’s struggles —the index’s biggest decline since March 2020 . On Monday morning, CNBC asked Trump if Nvidia’s influence on the stock market influenced his decision to push for Huang’s return. “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump responded . Trump, who has worked closely with Huang during his second administration, established himself as a vocal supporter of the CEO amid the recent chaos. Trump told The New York Times that he believed the board responded positively to his argument for Huang’s return because of the stock market dip, with the president suggesting that investors didn’t have much confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress. “I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” Trump told The New York Times. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it, actually. The stock is up.” According to Trump, however, his decision wasn’t guided solely by the market. “The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,” the president told CNBC. events.title: A red bra, an Nvidia flag and Trump's iconic rally pose: "Sex sells"
events.summary: President Trump posted a doctored image of newly reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holding a red bra in front of a Nvidia flag, posing as Trump after his viral assassination attempt at a rally in Pennsylvania in 2024. The post came shortly after the embattled Huang was reinstated Monday. Why it matters: The post highlights just how much the White House views Huang as an ally and how the president appears to see Huang's fall from grace and comeback as similar to his own history-making return, despite warnings about national security risks. Driving the news: Nvidia's board reinstated Huang early Monday, declaring him the right person to lead the company. After the announcement, Nvidia shares surged more than 30% by midday, lifting the broader stock market. The reinstatement followed reported pressure from the Trump administration and prompted accountability experts to question the board's judgment . What Nvidia's saying: "The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Trump wrote in a separate Truth Social post Monday. "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." "On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security," Trump wrote. Catch up quick: Huang was ousted after he admitted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, who allegedly used her relationship with Huang to help funnel Nvidia chips to China. Reports also alleged he had affairs with at least two subordinates. What Trump's saying: Trump suggested in a CNBC interview Monday that Huang's sex scandal could ultimately boost his reputation. "Sex sells, fellas," Trump said, predicting that the controversy could be a "net positive" for the Nvidia CEO. Trump said he didn't think Huang would be diminished by the scandal and argued that people respected what he had gone through. Zoom out: Lawmakers on the Hill were immediately taken aback by the decision, as Nvidia's board had previously said it would not bring Huang back. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned that Democrats would investigate Huang and characterized his reinstatement as the president "putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security." Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) who will likely soon chair the House Oversight committee, questioned why Trump was congratulating Huang after the affairs, and asked why the White House was allegedly "putting China's interests first." "Is it just the tens and hundreds of millions of dollars they're making out in the open or does Huang have even more damning information on them? A real Congress will find out," he wrote. Nvidia did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. The White House referred Axios to the president's comments on Truth Social and CNBC . events.title: Jensen Huang’s return raises troubling questions for corporate America
events.summary: Andrew’s view Nvidia’s board added $1 trillion to the chipmaker’s market capitalization after reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday. The longer-term impact on corporate America may be far more profound. The decision to grant Huang a second act will only strengthen the unchecked powers of the “imperial CEO,” and confirms the Trump administration’s readiness to treat corporate America as an instrument of presidential power. The most important line in the company’s 465-word announcement was the one saying that “input from senior levels of the United States government” had reassured the board that Huang’s return would pose no national security risk. Even before Semafor reported that US President Donald Trump had dialed into Nvidia’s board meeting , the statement left little doubt as to where that input had come from. On Sunday, Trump posted on social media that rehiring Huang would be “the best thing for the Company, and also, for the USA.” Nvidia’s uncommonly long-serving board was facing enough pressure even before this intervention: The company’s stock had fallen 40% in a month, erasing $2 trillion of market value and unleashing a chorus of calls from investors, employees, and customers for Huang’s return. The chip giant’s directors found themselves in this position because they failed in their duty to develop a credible replacement for a co-founder who became Nvidia’s indispensable chief salesman, chief technologist, and chief diplomat. Its belated steps — investigations, committees, executive searches — do little to suggest that the events of the past two weeks have taught Nvidia’s directors much about the importance of succession planning or corporate governance checks and balances. US business leaders and investors have traditionally railed against government meddling. This time, they cheered one of the most extraordinary White House interventions that corporate America has ever seen. Future governments may not have the same taste for “state capitalism” that the Trump administration has shown, but this is a new era, where the largest corporations have such enormous market influence that the question of who should lead them becomes a matter of national strategic significance. And one of the world’s most critical companies has just sent a clear signal to the rest of the business community: that the last word on a CEO appointment or a founder’s survival may rest not with shareholders or their representatives, but with the president of the United States. Notable Trump’s involvement in reinstating Huang has attracted scrutiny from both sides of the aisle , with one Republican senator asking on X: “Who in the government weighed in?”

events.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.  Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.  This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).  But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place. Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer. You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.  The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences . But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet. Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?” It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.  Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines . If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place. Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement. But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process. Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

events.title: McConnell may block his conservative critic's year-end ambassadorial confirmation
events.summary: The Scoop Mitch McConnell may knock former Kentucky Senate candidate Nate Morris’ nomination as ambassador to Colombia out of the Senate’s year-end nominations package, a move that could imperil the McConnell critic’s bid to join the Trump administration. The Kentucky senator has not signed off on Morris’ addition to a large group of executive branch nominees, according to two people familiar with the discussions. His office said that he hasn’t made a final decision. “Senator McConnell will evaluate the en bloc package when it is presented to the conference,” said David Popp, a spokesperson for McConnell, who’s retiring at the end of the year. Morris ran for Senate this cycle before endorsing Andy Barr, who won the seat in November; the ally of Donald Trump Jr. was then tapped as ambassador to Colombia by President Donald Trump. His nomination advanced to the Senate floor earlier this month, but he may not get a standalone vote given the limited floor time remaining for the last days of the Republican majority. A single GOP senator can object to including any single nominee in an en bloc package, giving McConnell significant sway over his confirmation in the waning days of GOP Senate control. Morris repeatedly criticized McConnell during his Senate campaign, running an ad showing a cutout of him and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the back of a garbage truck and vowing to “trash” McConnell’s legacy. Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, asked Morris during his confirmation hearing if he wanted to say anything to “rectify” his relationship with McConnell; Morris said he was “proud of the campaign we ran.” Though McConnell has not consented yet to adding Morris to the package, a third person familiar with the confirmation discussions expressed confidence that any issues “will ultimately be worked out and he will be confirmed as part of the bloc” at the end of the year. Morris “respects Senator McConnell for his longtime service to Kentucky, particularly his work getting judges confirmed,” the person added. Notable Morris jumped into the race to succeed McConnell early last year, as Semafor reported .
